We found everything in good condition; but as we knew that most such items were already gathered in the museum at Paris, we took only those that seemed to us the most curious, leaving the rest to whoever might want them. At seven in the evening I withdrew aboard as usual, and I learned that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in my absence.

1800-11-09.journal_baudin: On the eighteenth [Brumaire, 9 November 1800], as soon as it was light we began work aboard to stow in the hold the wine and beer we had shipped the day before, so as to be able afterwards to put back in their places all the articles we had been obliged to shift. This work occupied us almost the whole day, and we could not even finish it entirely. That part of the crew not employed on this task was set to taking in hand our lower shrouds, fore and aft. As our cordage was new, the standing rigging had stretched a great deal, and it suited us better to do this work in the roads than to wait until our deadeyes were altogether close together, which would not have failed to happen after a month at sea. In the course of the morning the governor, informed that I counted on sailing very shortly, sent back aboard by the harbour master the voyages of Lapérouse and of Vancouver, which he had asked me to lend him the day after my arrival. It appears, from the report made to me, that he was not pleased with what Lapérouse says in speaking of the difficulties he met with on his journey to the Peak. In the afternoon we saw two launches arrive from Gran Canaria loaded with people, and we were then told that this was part of the crew of the truce vessel that had sailed two days before. The English prisoners had seized the ship, not wishing to go to Gibraltar. According to the report of those who returned, it appears that this vessel is to make for New England, where she will perhaps have great difficulty arriving, having few provisions and making a great deal of water. All the people of the two corvettes whom I was sending back to France are among those who have come in the launches. Towards six in the evening I went ashore to announce my approaching departure to the consul and to let him know that I was waiting only for the refreshments I had asked him for and which he had promised to have delivered aboard that day. His answer was that he was expecting them from Gran Canaria and that they would surely arrive during the night, since they had not come during the day. After speaking with him I went straight back aboard, where I found the crew still at work shipping the water taken in to replace what had been consumed since our departure from France, the quantity of which was considerable enough despite the short time we had been at sea. That day another rather disagreeable little scene occurred aboard. One of my officers, much too young to be one, had since our arrival in port made the acquaintance of a Frenchman known only for his bad conduct and for various most dishonest actions. I am glad to think that Citizen Freycinet, of whom I mean to speak, had no information on the subject, although the consul had told us publicly how matters stood. At all events he invited the man to dinner, and this fellow took the liberty of bringing four other companions, so that we were at table when this new and numerous company, which I certainly was not expecting, arrived. Mr Freycinet's eagerness to receive them and to seat them at table made it plain enough to me that it was only on his invitation that they presented themselves; and I showed not the slightest displeasure, only I withdrew from the table shortly after they had taken their places. Towards evening I sent for Mr Freycinet and represented to him that he had been wrong not only in failing to warn me of the invitation he had given, but far more in having placed me at table with a man of such ill repute. I asked him at the same time that, should the like occur in future, he warn me in advance so that I might be excused from sitting at table if the company does not suit me. I hope that hereafter he will have regard to my request and that the like will not happen again.

1800-11-10.journal_baudin: On the nineteenth [Brumaire, 10 November 1800], having finished filling our casks with the water shipped the day before, I signalled the Naturaliste to take in her launch and large boat, and I did the same on my side. The rest of the day was spent restowing the ship and preparing for our approaching departure, which I hope will take place tomorrow, as we are to receive during the day the various refreshments the consul has sent to Gran Canaria for. In the afternoon, seeing no sign of the boat we had been expecting for two days, I went ashore about six in the evening to learn from the consul whether he knew anything of the cause of the delay. His answer was that he was as astonished as I that it had not yet come, but that it would certainly not be long in appearing. I resolved therefore to be patient; and as I was not entirely ready aboard, we suffered no delay on account of shipping these provisions, which were too necessary to us to be given up even had we been ready. At half past seven I returned aboard, giving orders to the astronomer, who had set himself up ashore, to bring off the next morning all the instruments I had had carried to the observatory.

1800-11-11.journal_baudin: On the twentieth [Brumaire, 11 November 1800], from early morning we went on preparing aboard for our departure, and we could have made sail at noon had our supplies from Gran Canaria arrived. At ten o'clock the harbour master came to visit us on the governor's behalf to invite us to dine with him the next day, the anniversary of His Majesty the King of Spain, if we were still in the roads. I replied to this officer that we would accept his invitation if we had not sailed, but that there was every appearance we would make sail during the night, the more so as at that very time we had sighted two boats coming from Gran Canaria, one of which was probably for me. For the rest, I proposed to go and take leave of the governor myself in the course of the day. After this first conversation the harbour master informed me that he was charged with a second commission, more disagreeable than the first, since its object was to bring me a complaint about the desertion of four grenadiers of the Altona regiment, said to have taken refuge aboard one of the two vessels. To give the governor entire satisfaction I made a most exact search aboard on the spot and in his presence, and at the same time I invited the captain of the Naturaliste to join me. Neither soldiers nor even any sign that might give grounds to suspect they had meant to come aboard was found in the Géographe. Captain Hamelin having arrived meanwhile, I made known to him the governor's complaint and the report given him that these four men were certainly aboard one of the two vessels. Captain Hamelin assured me he had no stranger aboard, and he offered, as I had done, to have the harbour master accompany him to his ship and to have the most rigorous search made in his presence. Neither of us could have gone about it better to put an end to the suspicions conceived against us, and we were ourselves too much concerned not to have four useless men aboard not to employ every possible means to verify the fact and give up these deserters if we found them. While we were engaged in this search, Consul Broussonet, his wife and his daughter came aboard, and we received them as best we could. After the first compliments the consul showed me a letter from the governor concerning the four deserters I have just spoken of. I informed him of the search I had had made aboard, as well as the one being made at that very moment in the Naturaliste. I hope, should they not be found aboard that vessel, that the governor will be quite convinced we do not have them and that the reports made to him are without foundation. At one in the afternoon I accompanied the consul and his ladies ashore, and Captain Hamelin having joined us, we dined at his house. The soldiers in question were not found aboard the Naturaliste. While we were at table, one of the gardener's boys shipped in the Géographe arrived at the consul's, covered in wounds and his face full of blood, scarcely able to stand. At first I thought he had quarrelled with someone and that the state I saw him in was the result. But as soon as he had explained himself, we had the grief of learning that, having gone ashore in the morning with the head gardener Riedlé to botanise, both had fallen from a very high rock they had climbed to get at a very rare plant or flower called Eranthemum salsoloides, which grows only on the edge of rocks and almost always in inaccessible places. The rock they had managed to climb having given way, they fell nearly thirty feet. The boy's fall was more fortunate than the other's, for he had kept strength enough to come more than a league to tell us that his companion had been left on the spot, all broken and unable to move. This accident made us all shudder at the state in which we should find Riedlé on our arrival. We left our dinner at once to go to meet him, and we took care on setting out to bring a stretcher from the hospital to have him carried to the port. The consul and Citizen Le Gros accompanied me on this occasion. Having got to about half a league from the town, we met Riedlé making his way in, supported under the arms by two men of the country who were with him. This meeting was very welcome to us in showing that he had nothing broken. When we had come up with him we had him rest and examined him. We found first a severe contusion between the nape and the occiput, a second and more considerable contusion in the lumbar region, and several wounds more or less considerable, but happily no fracture. His complexion, pale as death, showed us how much he was suffering and must have suffered from his fall. He would not, however, have the stretcher used to carry him to the port, and he made his way there with the help of the men accompanying him. When we had reached the landing place I had him taken aboard at once and put into the hands of the surgeons, who bled him a little and gave him vulnerary water. He was then without fever, his pulse only somewhat raised. This accident, befalling so essential a man, grieved me greatly; but I retain the hope that his recovery will not be long — at least that is the surgeons' opinion in the report they have made me on his present state. Before withdrawing aboard I went to take leave of the governor, who as usual received me with much politeness. He spoke to me of his deserters, and I believe I persuaded him that they are not aboard. Before letting us go he renewed the invitation he had sent me in the morning by the harbour master, in case our business from Gran Canaria not having arrived we should not sail. The light wind all day having prevented the boats we had sighted from arriving, we could not learn whether what we were waiting for was aboard them.
1800-11-11.journal_breton_geographe: The watches and the astronomical instruments were brought back on board. The French consul Broussonnet and his family came aboard.

1800-11-12.journal_baudin:
On the twenty-first [Brumaire, 12 November 1800] our head gardener was somewhat better than the day before, having passed a fair enough night and without fever; the surgeons dressed his various wounds, and we all hope that the restoring of his health will not be very long. Two boats from Tenerife having arrived during the night, we were informed by the consul that they had nothing for us, but that the one bringing our things would without fail arrive the next day. In consequence of this declaration I decided to wait; and as that day was a great feast for the Spaniards, I gave orders to dress both vessels, which was done at eight o'clock, the hour at which the Spaniards hoisted the colours of the fortresses. In the course of the morning there came into the anchorage a prize of the privateer La Mouche, from America, laden with grain, flour and timber for London. As this vessel entered the anchorage with English colours at her main masthead, I do not think her American, although her build might give grounds to suspect it. The pilot who brought her in piloted her very badly and moored her directly over our north-west cable. I sent him a boat at once with orders to weigh that anchor immediately, failing which I would have the cable cut. A launch was at once sent for from shore to carry out this manoeuvre; nonetheless I fear that before that anchor is weighed our cable may have been damaged. At one o'clock I went to the governor's invitation, and while waiting for the dinner hour I called on the consul. On arriving I found there seven mules loaded with bananas, fruit and various other refreshments which the Marquis de Nava, founder of the botanical garden of this island, had the kindness to send me. Having thanked Citizen Le Gros, charged with offering them on his behalf, I ordered them shared equally between the two vessels and asked Citizen Le Gros to be so good as to present to the Marquis de Nava, as the only thanks I could offer him, one of the medals the government had struck for our expedition. The dinner the governor gave us was very cheerful and even agreeable. We drank to the success of the voyage and all passed off as well as possible. At the end of the meal there came up, as I expected, the question of the deserters said to be hidden aboard. I did my best to persuade the governor and the colonel of the Altona regiment, who claimed them, that we did not have them. But I had the more difficulty convincing them as a soldier in disguise, having been aboard the Naturaliste and then come ashore, declared he had seen them. As two of the Naturaliste's officers were present and affirmed that no stranger had appeared aboard, I asked that the soldier in question be sent for, to see whether he would make the same deposition in our presence. The governor would not allow it, and nothing more was said. As the boat we were expecting from Gran Canaria had not appeared, and as the threatening look of the weather made me fear being too much exposed in the roads, I went to the consul to tell him that I absolutely would not wait any longer and that I had irrevocably fixed my departure for the next morning. I asked him accordingly to send aboard as soon as possible his account of expenses during our call, and our crew lists with a note of the changes that had taken place. He promised me that all would be ready by nine the next morning and that we would suffer no delay on that score. Before leaving him I gave him, for the Minister of Marine, a duplicate of the letter I had entrusted to the truce vessel, to which I added the following.

"The Commander-in-Chief of the Expedition of Discovery to the Minister of Marine and the Colonies. By my letter of the 14th of this month I informed you of my arrival at Santa Cruz de Tenerife. The vessel carrying my packets had seemed to me a favourable enough opportunity to entrust them to; but two days after sailing, the English being carried to Gibraltar seized the ship, put the crew and passengers ashore at Gran Canaria and made sail — according to the depositions of those they landed — for the Cape Verde Islands or the coast of Africa. I leave with the consul the duplicate of the letter I had addressed to you, and I announce by this one my departure, fixed for tomorrow after nine days in these roads. The scarcity of wine and the exorbitant price to which the English have driven what remains have not allowed me to take the quantity we needed, and I judged it better to keep part of the funds you procured me in order to supply ourselves at Mauritius, where the price, whatever the scarcity, cannot but be well below this one, wine being sold here at a hundred and twenty piastres the pipe, and crowns of six livres having only the value of the piastre. Greetings and respect. N.B."

Before returning aboard I called on the harbour master to ask him not to fail to send me launches at daybreak to unmoor us, which he promised to do. Leaving him, I went to Mr Carta's to thank him for having lent us his house for our observatory, and I offered him, as a mark of our gratitude, one of our medals, which he received with great pleasure. About seven in the evening I went aboard, leaving many people still ashore, for never were the officers and others punctual in answering the gun as had been ordered. On arriving I had the satisfaction of learning that our gardener Riedlé had passed the day without fever, having suffered only the contusions that followed his fall. On the other hand the surgeons are persuaded that no serious illness will result, though they think complete recovery will be slow. During the night the breeze, which had been very strong all day, fell somewhat, but the sea remained very swelly and the ship laboured a good deal at her anchors.
1800-11-12.journal_breton_geographe: We dressed ship in honour of the King of Spain's name day; the shore batteries fired all day. At noon an English brig, taken by the privateer La Mouche, having anchored on our cable, we hailed her to shift her berth. In the evening the topgallant sails were bent and the masts rigged. During our stay at Santa Cruz the weather was fine, except on the 21st [Brumaire, 12 November 1800], when it rained in the night. The wind was from NNE to SE, light and a fresh breeze. The variation, the mean of a great number of observations, was 20° 0' 30" NW on board. The roads of Santa Cruz are the best in the island. The holding ground is good; the cables must be buoyed up on casks, without which one would risk losing them. The landing place is on the mole. When it blows from seaward the sea breaks there with force and it is then dangerous to land. Water is very easily got there, at a fountain on the mole. The water comes to the town by a wooden aqueduct nearly two leagues long.

1800-11-13.journal_baudin: On the twenty-second [Brumaire, 13 November 1800], in the morning, not receiving as promptly as I could have wished the launches I had asked the harbour master for the day before, I sent my boat ashore with a midshipman to fetch them. At the moment the boat left the ship, three or four of the naturalists came to ask my leave to go ashore on various matters they said they had to settle there. I refused them all this leave, the more so as, having warned them three days earlier that I meant to sail at the first opportunity, they had surely had more time than was needed to be entirely ready. At eight o'clock the launches promised to be alongside by six at last arrived, and I at once signalled the Naturaliste to unmoor. In weighing our north-west anchor we noticed that our cable had one strand cut about thirty fathoms from the clinch. This damage was caused by the vessel that came into the anchorage the day before, as I had foreseen, the pilot's bad manoeuvring having fouled her anchor in our cable. As the harbour master was aboard at that moment I had the damage attested in his presence, and I wrote at once to Consul Broussonet so that he might have the damage paid for by the owners of that prize, as they had agreed with me the day before should the cable have suffered. At half past nine the consul's clerk having come aboard to settle our accounts of expenditure, we were informed that one of the two boats in sight from Gran Canaria carried our things and our supplies, and that waiting for them would mean only a delay of a few hours. I therefore decided once again to wait, in the hope that this launch, intended for us alone, would come alongside and that we would lose far less time. To make sure of it I sent my boat off to her, but this step was useless, the master in charge of her refusing to consent. For greater vexation she went and moored half a league from us. I sent my launch to her at once so that the transfer might be made from ship to ship, and still he would do nothing, because an order was needed from the customs house, which did not come until two in the afternoon. At last, after a long wait and much ill temper, my launch came back aboard and delivered to us about half the provisions we should have had, the agent charged with procuring them at Canaria not having been able to obtain what was asked of him. At two o'clock there came aboard three seamen of La Mouche who were prisoners at Tenerife for having missed that privateer's sailing, and who asked to ship with me. I took them in place of those I had left ashore either through sickness or through incapacity. At three in the afternoon, all our business being shipped, I signalled the Naturaliste, which had likewise received hers, to get under way without further signal; and as soon as she was under sail I did the same. The winds were then north-east and the weather fine enough, the breeze coming in gusts that were often strong. Our getting under way was not done without trouble, for each of the scientists, wanting to see what was going on aboard or on the mole, got everywhere among the working parties and hampered us extremely. To restore order and avoid confusion I was obliged to ask them to keep below until we were under sail.
1800-11-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE, E and ENE. At 7.30 signalled the Naturaliste to unmoor. A Spanish longboat weighed our mooring anchor and then went aboard a boat arriving from Grand Canary to fetch us two bullocks, poultry and vegetables. At 2.15 p.m. made the signal to get under way, and at 3 got under way. At 3.30 shaped our course S 33° 45' W after making the signal to close. At 4 signalled and shaped the course S 45° W. At 4.45 Captain Hamelin informed the commander that he had found 4 foreign seamen aboard his ship. At 5 took the bearing of Punta de Candelaria N 36° W, the Peak N 75° W and Punta Roja S 56° W. From this bearing I took my point of departure in 28° 19' of latitude and 18° 48' of longitude. During the night a little rain fell.
1800-11-13.journal_geographe: The commander having taken leave of the consul, we weighed anchor with the help of the port's boats and made sail for Mauritius. During our stay we dressed ship on account of the King of Spain's name day. All the forts of the town fired several salvoes. The consul also came aboard with his wife and his daughter, who was very pretty.

1800-11-14.journal_anonyme: We made sail, the winds being in the ENE quarter. We had manoeuvred so as to cast to starboard, but the anchor, having first broken out, then took hold again and forced us to cast to port, heading for the land. Citizen Milius, the officer of the watch, wore ship. After standing on for some time we closed the commander and headed SW. At 5 p.m. we took the bearing of the Peak of Tenerife W 29° N, distant 2 leagues and a half from the land.
1800-11-14.journal_baudin: On the twenty-third of Brumaire [14 November 1800], about three in the afternoon, I made sail from the roads of Santa Cruz de Tenerife to reach Mauritius as soon as possible, much regretting the eleven days I had lost in these roads, since the reasons that had brought me there had no good effect for us; and on the contrary I have every reason to fear that most of the crew will find themselves much the worse for the conduct they kept with the women of the country, most of them infected with the itch and with other diseases more disagreeable still. In vain did I represent to most of my officers and to the scientists aboard the drawbacks that could not fail to result from their asking to be taken ashore two and more often three times a day; far from paying any heed to what I told them, they seemed on the contrary to wish to go more often, and under pretext of instructing themselves in a country too well known for there to be anything new to learn there, they came and went as one comes and goes at a fair. When I was under sail I hove to about a league from the mole to take in my boat and dismiss the Spanish launch I had kept aboard since morning. This launch was very useful to me in getting under way; otherwise I might, like the Naturaliste, have paid off the wrong way and done damage to some of the vessels lying very close to me — a risk the Naturaliste did not run, being further out and clear of them all. At five o'clock I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south-west and shaped the same course myself, carrying no sail but the topsails and foresail, while the Naturaliste had already set all her studdingsails and other light canvas. At five o'clock, the two corvettes being close to one another, Captain Hamelin let me know that he had aboard four persons not belonging to his crew. It was not difficult for me to see that the governor of Tenerife had been well informed and that those who maintained these four deserters were aboard had been quite right. I was truly vexed to learn this news; and as Mr Hamelin surely has no need of men, he might well have refrained from taking these four deserters, who, although they call themselves seamen, can be of no great use to him. I confess that had I been nearer Santa Cruz I would have had them put ashore on the spot. The governor's conduct towards us did not deserve that men should be taken from him, especially as we had no need of them. During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth [14-15 November 1800] the sky was very hazy and we had a little rain from time to time. The winds varied from north-east to east and even from east to east-south-east; it blew a fresh breeze and we made good way, continuing to steer south-west by compass. Bearings of the point of departure at five in the evening: Punta de Candelaria north 36° west; the summit of the Peak west 15° north, by compass. Further bearings at six: the westernmost point of Tenerife west 26° south; the summit of the Peak west 30° north, by compass. The fog covering Gran Canaria prevented us from sighting it.
1800-11-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE. In the forenoon the cables were unbent and the anchors stowed; one of the cables — the one on which the brig had anchored on the 21st — was chafed. At noon in 26° 3' 30" of latitude observed and in 18° 59' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 32' NW.

1800-11-15.journal_anonyme: The winds ENE, a fresh breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth; we kept a short distance from the commander, heading SW. Obs. lat. 26° 4', long. 18° 58'. Var. 17° 32' NW.
1800-11-15.journal_baudin: On the twenty-fourth [Brumaire, 15 November 1800] it continued to blow a fresh breeze from east to east by north. The weather was fine, but the horizon was so thick and hazy that we could not see the sun until about eight o'clock. We went on steering south-west until noon, when, reckoning myself far enough west to weather Cape Blanco at a good distance even supposing an error in the reckoning and in the longitude given by the watches, I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south-west by south, the course I shaped myself. During the morning the cables were unbent to be struck below. Ours had suffered so much during our stay at Tenerife that we shall be obliged to serve them before using them on our arrival at Mauritius. That same day I gave orders to the purser's steward to issue the crew coffee twice a decade and three meals with beer, so as to husband our wine. According to the note the surgeon has given me, there were already seven of the crew afflicted with venereal disease. Among the seven, two might well have spared themselves catching it. Our gardener Riedlé is going on better and better, and at the moment I am writing of him he is being carried on deck to take the air. It is a great consolation to me to see that he will soon be recovered. His loss would have been the more unfortunate for me as I believe I can say in advance that he will serve as an example to the others in his assiduity at work — it remains to be seen whether they will care to imitate him. In the afternoon the weather held fine without the horizon opening any further. At sunset 18° of north variation was observed, but this figure is not certain, the sun being covered with haze and visible only at a fair height above the horizon. At half past six we were obliged to clew up the weather clew of the foresail and to back the mizzen topsail to wait for the Naturaliste, which had dropped far astern and could not rejoin us until the middle of the night, which was fine enough. The winds having drawn to the east, the breeze was strong, and yet the horizon remained always very short. The sea became swelly and the ship laboured a little, not having sail enough. During the day I had clothing and linen issued to the four men taken aboard in place of those I had left behind, seeing that they had shipped with nothing but what they stood up in.
1800-11-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE. At 10.45 a.m. crossed the Tropic of Cancer in 21° 23' of longitude. At noon the course was shaped S 33° 45' W. At noon in 23° 20' 0" of latitude observed and in 21° 31' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 0' 0" NW.

1800-11-16.journal_anonyme: The wind ENE, a fresh breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth. We crossed the Tropic of Cancer on the 24th at 2 p.m. in 21° 50' of west longitude. Saw some flying fish. Lat. 23° 16', long. 21° 31'.
1800-11-16.journal_baudin: On the twenty-fifth [Brumaire, 16 November 1800] the sky remained dark and hazy most of the day. As the breeze was strong the sea became swelly and even a little heavy. At six in the morning I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south-south-west, and at noon we laid the ship's head south by west so as to make no more westing, finding ourselves midway between the Cape Verde Islands and the coast of Africa. From the latitude observed at noon we found a difference of eight minutes thirty-five seconds, the reckoning of our course placing us further south. The agreement, however, between the longitude given by the watches and that by working up the courses showed that the distance run was being estimated tolerably well by the log. During the morning I received from the steward a complaint against Mr Freycinet, who had taken the liberty not only of speaking to him improperly but even of threatening to kick him in the belly whenever he did not do as he was ordered. To prevent the like from happening again, I sent for Mr Freycinet and asked him very civilly to inform me if the steward should fail in his duty to him; but I added that I would not have him take the liberty of striking anyone. I greatly fear that this officer, of whom I had formed a tolerable opinion at Le Havre, may hereafter oblige me to deal severely with him in a way that will be agreeable to neither of us. Before leaving Le Havre, being little pleased with his conduct, I had wished to place him aboard the Naturaliste and take his brother, whose character seems less turbulent; and it was only at the request of the other officers that I consented to keep him, for I had put little faith in the personal promises he had made me at the time to behave better. All afternoon the sky remained dark and overcast, even more than it had been in the morning. It continued to blow a fresh breeze and we made a good run south by west. At six o'clock one of the bullocks we had shipped was killed to be issued as rations to the crew. After sunset the weather became much hazier and damper than we had had it until then. Our horizon scarcely extended half a league. During the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth [Brumaire, 16-17 November 1800] it blew a good breeze from east-north-east; we did not profit by it as much as we might have, being often obliged to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste, which sailed no better than usual, although Captain Hamelin, during our stay at Santa Cruz de Tenerife, had made several changes in her stowage in the hope of giving her more speed.
1800-11-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE. At 6 a.m. the course was given and signalled S 22° 30' W; at noon it was given S 11° 15' W. At noon in 20° 4' 0" of latitude observed and in 22° 33' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 14° 54' 0" NW. During the night dark weather, with lightning. At 11 the Naturaliste sent up a rocket.

1800-11-17.journal_anonyme: The wind east, variable to ENE. Hot, the air thick and the sea rather high. Saw many birds known as terns. Lat. 16° 42', long. 22° 24'.
1800-11-17.journal_baudin: On the twenty-sixth, about two in the morning, the weather being extremely overcast and dark, the Naturaliste sent up a rocket, no doubt to show us her position, which we did not know, having lost sight of her for nearly an hour. We answered with a stern light, on which she shaped her course; and as we had shortened sail considerably she was abreast of us by four o'clock. At daybreak the sky was darker and thicker still than it had been the day before, and I feared a change of wind, the clouds driving fast enough to the north-east. But in the morning the sun, when it appeared, having dispersed them, the winds held in the same quarter and the breeze was fairly strong. We had before noon two moments of amusement very different from one another. The first was occasioned by the sight of some flying fish. The scientists, who were no doubt seeing them for the first time, were so marvelled at them that each time the ship's wake brought one out of the water, whichever of the company had first caught sight of it became an object of consideration to the others; and the direction or the length of the leap it made gave rise to a scientific discussion which ended without settling anything, but through the attention given to another that showed itself. The second, disagreeable as it was for Citizen Péron, did not fail to delight all his fellow men of science and most of the officers who witnessed it. Towards noon Citizen Péron, being in the port quarter gallery making some observations with the thermometer, was flooded by a sea that covered him from head to foot, so that his notebook of observations and his thermometer were both carried away. This accident, caused by the sea, which was running very high, did him no apparent harm; but he thought himself drowned beyond recovery, and when the water that had come into the gallery had drained away he found it most extraordinary not only to find himself alive but even not to have shifted place, for it had seemed to him that he had been carried out into the middle of the sea. During the morning, despite the dampness of the weather, I thought it right to order a general fumigation in every part of the ship; accordingly there was a complete clearing of decks aboard and all the quarters were smoked with powder and vinegar. At noon, the sky being overcast and the horizon very short, the observed latitude was doubtful; we have reason to believe, however, that it is not more than five minutes out. All evening the sky was extremely overcast and hazy, the horizon did not extend beyond a league and a half, and the wind continuing to fall I began to fear a change in the weather. The clouds then driving fairly briskly from the south-west made me fear to see the winds draw into that quarter. During the night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh [Brumaire, 17-18 November 1800] the sky was so overcast and dark that we could scarcely make one another out on the quarterdeck, and it would no doubt have been impossible to recognise anyone in the gangways. I do not believe that in Europe in the depth of winter it is possible to have a darker night. The wind fell a great deal, however, but did not change, and we were troubled only by the heat, which was extremely oppressive. So that the Naturaliste might be sure of our position we kept our stern lantern burning all night, during which we often shortened sail so as not to draw too far ahead of her.
1800-11-17.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and warm weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE, NE and E. At noon in 16° 48' 0" of latitude observed and in 22° 9' of longitude by account.

1800-11-18.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from east to ENE. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 7 a.m. we were steering south, and at 4.45 p.m. we observed a tide rip setting NE. Lat. 14° 14' 17", long. 22° 10' 0".
1800-11-18.journal_baudin: On the twenty-seventh [Brumaire, 18 November 1800] the weather was as on the day before, that is, still laden with vapour and very damp. During the morning the winds were less variable than they had been in the night and seemed inclined to settle in the east, drawing a little northerly. During the morning the surgeon informed me, by a written report, that a kind of intestinal flux of no settled character was beginning to show itself aboard; but to prevent the consequences he feared might bring on a true dysentery, he asked that a few pints of vinegar be put into the water issued in rations to the crew. I ordered what he asked to be carried out at once, and I invited him to give me a list by name of those feeling any indisposition, so as to satisfy myself of their true condition. About ten o'clock, the sea being very smooth and the breeze slight, we began exercising the helmsmen aboard in heaving the hand lead, so as to accustom them early to a way of sounding in which they have no practice and which is too much neglected in the naval service. It is certain that there ought to be in the ports of the Republic a particular instruction relating to this single matter, which is of greater consequence than one imagines. At noon we had no observation of latitude; but our reckoning placing us in fourteen degrees forty-six minutes six seconds, we found we had passed Cape Verde at a distance of forty-six leagues, the longitude by reckoning being twenty-two degrees ten minutes west of Paris. In the afternoon the sky grew somewhat finer, though still overcast. The horizon was more extended than on the preceding days and we could see four or five leagues off. We spent almost the whole day under topsails waiting for the Naturaliste, which seemed to us to sail worse than usual that day, though she was covered with canvas. During the night of the twenty-seventh to the twenty-eighth the weather was fine enough; we saw a few stars, which had not happened to us for three days. The sky was not clear enough, however, to excuse us from keeping a light in our stern lantern to show our position to the Naturaliste. About nine o'clock we had the sight of part of a rainbow by night. Its colour was yellowish, in the north-east, and it presented to us the form of a band longer than it was wide, parallel to the horizon. This phenomenon lasted four or five minutes. Its length seemed to us to be twelve to fifteen degrees and its elevation above the horizon thirty. The rest of the night held nothing out of the ordinary; the weather was fine enough and the winds light at ENE. During the day, as during the night, we often crossed tide rips which the agitation of the sea made very perceptible to the eye. Their direction seemed to us to be east-south-east and west-north-west.
1800-11-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE and ENE. At 6 a.m. the course was signalled and shaped south. At noon we passed through several tide rips setting ESE and WNW. At noon in 14° 24' 9" of latitude observed and in 21° 55' 30" of longitude by account. Saw many tuna and porpoises. At 9 a yellowish glow was seen, in the form of a band parallel to the horizon, which lasted 4 or 5 seconds; its length may have been 12 to 15° and its height above the horizon 30°.

1800-11-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea and a thick horizon. The winds variable from east to ENE; by the commander's order we steered S by E. Lat. 12° 11', long. 21° 46'. Var. 16° 45' NW.
1800-11-19.journal_baudin: On the twenty-eighth [Brumaire, 19 November 1800] we had finer weather than usual; the sky, although of a dull whiteness, was less laden with vapour and damp than it had been since our departure from Tenerife. I do not know whether it is to the neighbourhood of the African coast and the Cape Verde Islands that one must attribute the frequent fogs ordinarily found in these waters; but what is certain is that every time I have passed this way, though always at different seasons, I have constantly found the sky the same, without nevertheless having had the breeze so fresh. At eight o'clock, the sun being already hot, decks were cleared generally and all the hammocks and blankets were hung up and exposed all day to the open air, to take out whatever dampness they might have gathered over the past days. In the morning coffee was issued to the crew for breakfast, and I renewed the order that it be given twice each decade. This consumption used eighteen pints of water more than usual; but as I find myself well provided, no inconvenience can follow for the rest of the voyage. At noon the observed north latitude was twelve degrees eleven minutes, and we found, by working up the courses since the last observation, that the currents had set us some three leagues to the west. The longitude given by the marine watches placing us in twenty-one thirty, from a mean between the two watches, it follows that our reckoning by the log differed by very little, allowing for the corrections made to the distance run by the ship. In the evening the weather seemed inclined to turn fine and we had the appearance of a fine night, which had not yet happened to us since leaving Tenerife. After sunset the whole crew had orders to come aft to make merry and dance. The ball began at once and lasted until eight o'clock with great gaiety. During the night of the twenty-eighth to the twenty-ninth [Brumaire, 19-20 November 1800] the weather was very fine and even cool, although the thermometer stood at twenty degrees and the winds from east-north-east were very moderate. The Naturaliste kept close enough to us to be held in sight, and with our topsails and foresail we kept pace with her while she had all the sail she could carry.
1800-11-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE and ENE. At 6 a.m. the course was signalled and shaped S 11° 15' E. Saw many porpoises. At noon in 12° 10' 10" of latitude observed and in 21° 47' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 49' 0" NW. We were in tide rips throughout.

1800-11-20.journal_anonyme: Winds light, the sea smooth and the course S by E. Lat. 10° 10', long. 20° 43'. Var. 16° 59' NW.
1800-11-20.journal_baudin: On the twenty-ninth [Brumaire, 20 November 1800] the breeze was a little stronger than it had been the day before, and at six o'clock I made the signal to steer south-south-east so as to gain easting and be able to cross the line between the twelfth and thirteenth degrees of west longitude if the winds would allow it. During the morning the sky became less clear than the day before and the horizon was little extended, being closed by a fog to which the sun gave a dull white colour. At sunrise, however, we were able to observe its amplitude, which gave us twelve degrees forty-nine minutes of north-west variation. At nine o'clock this observation was confirmed by an azimuth, and the mean of the two gave 13° 49′ 10″ for the true variation of the place we were in. At noon the observed latitude was ten degrees twelve minutes twenty-four seconds north and the longitude by reckoning twenty degrees nineteen minutes. That of watch no. 31 placed us in 20° 43′ 4″ and no. 38 in 20° 47′ 27″. During the evening the sky was dark enough and there was much moisture in the air. We had the sight of a land bird which came to settle in our rigging. A musket was fired at it which happily for the bird missed. It was of the sparrowhawk kind. At sunset 15° 57′ of north-west variation was observed; but as the sun was not clear nor the horizon distinct, no great account should be made of this observation. From six to eight o'clock there was a grand ball aboard, and the crew amused themselves greatly, some dancing and others at various games. During the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth the weather was very soft and the breeze light. To wait for the Naturaliste we were obliged to carry very little sail and very often to back the mizzen topsail. The state of the sea, which was perfectly calm, made us fear a calm for the next day; but as towards the middle of the night many clouds formed in every quarter of the horizon, we hoped that if the wind did change we should at least have some, from whatever side, and would thus be able to hold on our course. Two porpoises were harpooned by the crew during the day, but at the moment they were being hoisted aboard they came off the hooks, to everyone's great regret and above all to that of the scientists, for whom this fish was a new object.
1800-11-20.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE and NE. At 6 a.m. the course was signalled and shaped S 22° 30' E. At noon in 10° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 20° 43' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 59' 0" NW. A sparrowhawk came and perched on our yards.

1800-11-21.journal_anonyme: Wind ENE, heading SSE, the sea smooth. At 7.15 a.m. the commander ordered us to crowd sail; the wind almost calm from the ENE. Lat. 8° 50', long. 19° 14'. Var. 16° NW.
1800-11-21.journal_baudin: On the thirtieth [Brumaire, 21 November 1800] the breeze was very light from early morning. The wind did not change as we had feared, but it kept falling, and by noon we were almost becalmed. The sky became very dark during the morning and we could get only a very doubtful observed latitude. As it was the day of the decade the crew was excused work; but a general inspection of linen was made, and I saw with satisfaction that, with two or three exceptions, all were fairly well provided with clothing and changes, though they were generally short of shoes and hats. I had some issued to those who needed them and replaced the hats with leather caps. I also gave notice to the midshipmen of the first and second class that they were to present me their journals at the end of each month for me to endorse. By this means I meant to satisfy myself of the particular work of each of them. When they learned of this decision some of them grumbled secretly and even took the liberty of saying that it was not the custom, and that none of the captains they had sailed with before had subjected them to this formality. I pretended to know nothing of their conversation, but I required the journals to be presented none the less. At noon, the weather not being too fine, we had only a very doubtful observation of latitude. The longitude by reckoning at that time was nineteen degrees fourteen minutes west of the meridian of Paris. During the evening we had everything ready to take a lunar distance from the sun, but the sky was so hazy that we could not manage it. Among the midshipmen's journals presented to me, one alone was in order, and it belonged to Citizen Breton. Most of the others were not up to date and several looked like nothing but rough drafts. I expressed to those at fault the displeasure their carelessness and idleness deserved, and I warned them all that if by the end of the month we were about to enter they were not up to date and in order, I would take a course that would in all likelihood not be agreeable to them. During the night the weather was fine enough though dark and damp, but the breeze was so light that we made very little way, especially being obliged to wait for the Naturaliste under our topsails. About ten in the evening there was taken aboard a kind of land swallow which came to settle in our chains. The zoologist Maugé, having examined it, found it very pretty and put off skinning it until the next day. The rest of the night held nothing out of the ordinary.
1800-11-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE and NE. At noon in 8° 50' 37" of latitude observed and in 19° 44' 0" of longitude by account. Variation 16° 2' 0" NW.

1800-11-22.journal_anonyme: The wind extremely light, the weather fine, the sea with a little swell from the ENE.
1800-11-22.journal_baudin: On the first of Frimaire [22 November 1800] the weather was fine, but we had very little wind and the state of the sky promised us no more. The breeze freshened a little in the morning, however, and we made a fair run compared with that of the night. At sunrise we observed a variation of 18 degrees north-west. It seemed to us that this figure was rather large, especially according to our reckoning; but as we obtained confirmation of the amount by an azimuth at nine o'clock, it follows that our reckoning was too small. All morning, or rather all day, we sailed through very considerable tide rips which came constantly from the south-east to east quarter. We concluded from this that a strong current must be setting us to the west and south-west, which was confirmed by the longitude given at noon by watches nos. 31 and 38. In fact our longitude by reckoning, which until then had differed little from that of the watches, was within two days 48 minutes further east than our true position. At noon the observed latitude was 8° 5′ 37″ north and the longitude by reckoning 18° 39′ 36″, while that of the watches reduced to noon was for no. 31 only 19° 27′ 51″ and for no. 38, 19° 32′ 17″. After noon, the winds being almost calm and the sky hazy, I hove to in order to carry out an experiment.
1800-11-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE and NE. Saw a shark and tropic birds. At noon in 8° 5' 3" of latitude observed and in 19° 26' 48" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 33' 0" NW. At 1.30 p.m. we hove to for a moment to draw water from 100 fathoms' depth. At 3.30 we spoke the Naturaliste. The commander informed Captain Hamelin that he would send him half a bullock the following morning. During the night there was much thunder, with lightning in the south.

1800-11-23.journal_anonyme: The wind ENE, heading SE by S, the weather fine, the sea smooth. Lightning played from every point of the horizon, followed by thunder whose dull sound showed it to be far off. At 6.30 a.m. we hove to to wait for the commander's boat, which was bringing us fresh meat. At 7.30 the commander signalled us to send a boat aboard him to fetch our officers who had stayed there. Lat. 8° 5', long. 19° 27'. Var. 16° 33'.
1800-11-23.journal_baudin: On the second of Frimaire [23 November 1800] we spent most of the morning becalmed, the ship scarcely answering her helm. At half past six, the Naturaliste being to leeward of us abeam and at a short distance, I had a boat put in the water and sent aboard that vessel a hundred-odd pounds of fresh meat from a bullock I had had killed the day before. I wrote by the same occasion to Captain Hamelin to let him know our longitude by reckoning and that indicated by the watches, asking him to let me know the results of his in return. As soon as my boat had reached her I saw it come back with two people from the Naturaliste. As I was busy working in my cabin I did not see them come aboard. The officer then of the watch having come to ask me whether the boat should be sent back to return to the Naturaliste the persons who had come in her, I asked their names; and when I learned that one was an officer, I was not a little astonished not to have had the pleasure of seeing him. This conduct on his part seemed to me so inconceivable that, to show him my displeasure, I ordered the boat hoisted aboard and at the same time signalled Mr Hamelin to send me his. When it arrived the two persons who had come embarked in it. Then someone from the ship having observed to Mr Freycinet — that is the name of the Naturaliste's officer — that it was in the last degree improper for him to have come aboard without speaking to me, he came back and presented himself in my cabin; but the better to make him feel his rudeness I would not receive him and forbade any notice to be taken of his departure. I then wrote Mr Hamelin the following letter: "I beg you, Citizen, when you allow one of your officers to come aboard, to be so good as to choose them better mannered than the one who has come to us; for at the moment I write to you, and as he is going back, I have not had the pleasure of seeing him. You will have the kindness, the moment you note his arrival aboard your ship, to have him placed under arrest for two days in his cabin, to teach him that when he goes aboard any vessel whatsoever he ought on entering to go and salute her commander. N.B." Having given this letter to the coxswain of the boat, we trimmed our sails and stood close-hauled, the winds — or rather the air — being from the eastward. At noon we observed the latitude 7° 39′ 43″ north and the longitude by reckoning was 18° 9′ west; by no. 31 we had 19° 2′ 40″ and by no. 38, 19° 7′ 52″. In the afternoon we took two sea nettles different from those Mr Fleurieu speaks of in Marchand's voyage, but which seem to me well described in Bomare. As they were uncommonly beautiful I have had a drawing made of them from nature. The night of the second to the third [Frimaire, 23-24 November 1800] passed in calm, the ship scarcely answering her helm. The part of the horizon between south-west and north-west was extremely laden with cloud and gave a great deal of lightning and sometimes even thunder. We hoped, but in vain, that the winds would come to us from that quarter.
1800-11-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine, warm weather, the wind light from NE and ENE, with light airs from south and SE. At 6.30 a.m. we put a boat in the water and it carried aboard the Naturaliste the half bullock that had been promised. It came back with Citizen Freycinet the younger, who was taken on board, and we signalled the Naturaliste to send hers; she came and left again at once. Here is a note in the ship's log, in the commander's hand: "Captain Hamelin having sent my boat back on board at the request of Citizen Freycinet, ensign. This officer, no doubt quite new to the service, had no sooner come aboard than he disappeared as far as I was concerned, and I should not have had the pleasure of seeing him had it not been pointed out to him that it was in the last degree improper to come aboard a ship at sea without going to salute her commander. So that such thoughtlessness, or such incivility, should not happen to him again, I wrote to M. Hamelin to put him under arrest in his cabin for two days. The letter setting out the fact and this officer's conduct is in my journal. Signed N. Baudin." At noon in 7° 36' 40" of latitude observed and in 19° 3' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 9' 20" NW.

1800-11-24.journal_anonyme: The same weather and the same winds, the ship not answering her helm. At 5, the wind having blown a little from the south, we went onto the starboard tack. Lat. 7° 43', long. 18° 43'.
1800-11-24.journal_baudin: The day of the third [Frimaire, 24 November 1800] was entirely lost to us. Except for a few cat's-paws felt from time to time we lay in a flat calm, the ship not answering her helm. We took advantage of this weather, disagreeable as it was, to set up our shrouds and topmast backstays fore and aft. In the course of the day we were not troubled by the heat as sharply as I should have thought. About ten in the morning we repeated the experiment we had already made two days earlier to get the temperature of the sea water at a certain depth; and to obtain a better result than the first time we rigged our apparatus differently, and after veering it to a hundred fathoms we left it under water for a space of time, after which we hauled it up. The notes of Citizens Péron and Depuch will make known the results we obtained. At noon the observed latitude was, within a few seconds, the same as the day before, and the small difference there was proved to be northerly, contrary to our expectation; for from the courses the ship appeared to have made we had expected some minutes to the south. From the longitude of the watches it did not appear to us that the currents had set us either east or west, since there was only one minute's difference from the previous day's longitude. During the night of the third to the fourth [Frimaire, 24-25 November 1800] we felt a fairly sharp heat, but one to be attributed rather to the exhalations of the bodies aboard than to that of the atmosphere, although there was almost no wind.
1800-11-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine, warm weather, calm with light airs from SSW, S, SSE, SW, WSW and NW. In the forenoon water was drawn from 100 fathoms' depth to learn its weight and its temperature. At noon in 7° 43' 1" of latitude observed and in 19° 2' 0" of longitude by No. 38; by 18° 43' 17" of longitude. Variation 15° 7' 0" NW.

1800-11-25.journal_anonyme: Calm, the weather overcast, the ship not answering her helm. At 3 a light air sprang up from NNW, with a great deal of lightning and at intervals in the west. Lat. 7° 30', long. 19° 1'.
1800-11-25.journal_baudin: On the fourth, in the morning [Frimaire, 25 November 1800], we were scarcely more fortunate than the day before. About two o'clock, however, we felt a light breeze from north-north-east varying to north-east which allowed us to give the ship steerage way. As the sky was hazy enough at that time we flattered ourselves it would strengthen after sunrise, but our hope was not confirmed. On the contrary it fell away as the sun rose above the horizon, and by noon we were becalmed again. The observed latitude was 7° 30′ 24″, that is 0° 13′ 19″ further south over two days. The longitude given by watch no. 31, reduced to noon, was 18° 49′ 21″ and no. 38, 18° 54′ 43″. Thus these two watches still kept the same relation to one another. During the evening we lay entirely becalmed, and we were no more fortunate during the night. We spent the afternoon setting up our topmast shrouds and mending some of our sails which the calm had chafed through.
1800-11-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine and very warm weather, a light breeze from NNE, NE and ENE, steering on our course S 22° 30' E. In the forenoon the topmast shrouds were set up. Saw many dolphinfish, bonito and porpoises. At noon in 7° 30' 0" of latitude observed and in 18° 49' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 37' 0" NW.

1800-11-26.journal_anonyme: A light air from ENE, the weather stormy and squally. On the 5th at 10 a.m. we had five squalls which forced us to reef the topsails and take in the mizzen topsail. They were attended with thunder, and it struck a league and a half from us in the SE. We had just gone onto the starboard tack. Lat. 7° 0', long. 18° 27'.
1800-11-26.journal_baudin: On the fifth, in the morning [Frimaire, 26 November 1800], we had a light air from north-east to east with the help of which we made a little way; but the sky looked so threatening in almost every point of the horizon that we could not tell from which side the storm that menaced us on all sides would come. About six o'clock thunder began to be heard from south round by west to north-west, and another thunder from north-east to south-east answered the first, so that we could not fail to have one or the other. The Naturaliste at that time was much too close to us, and I greatly regretted having no signal to tell her to draw off to a good distance. At ten o'clock the two storms threatening us began to rise above the horizon, and both were driven with some speed by different winds. The north-easter, however, seemed to have the greater force; for at the moment when the two edges of cloud met, the north-east storm drove off that from the south-west, and we received only the one that favoured our course. During its duration, which was about two hours, the thunder rolled long over our heads in frightening fashion, but no ill effect followed for us. The rain during the storm was very heavy and we caught a fair quantity of it. The sailors took the opportunity to wash their linen, and everyone was the better for it. The wind this storm brought us was not very violent, and had we been able to foresee its force we would not have lowered our topsails to the caps by way of precaution. In the afternoon it went on blowing a little; but as a calm was announcing itself in proportion as the sky cleared, we truly regretted seeing the storm pass over so quickly. At six o'clock the ship no longer answered her helm, and by then the weather was fine. The night of the fifth to the sixth [Frimaire, 26-27 November 1800] passed entirely in calm and most of the time without steerage way. Fresh storms formed in various parts of the horizon but none had force enough to reach us.
1800-11-26.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and warm weather, calm and the wind a light and then a strong breeze from ENE and E. Rain at 8 a.m. At noon in 6° 56' 36" of latitude by account and in 18° 28' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 17' 0" NW.

1800-11-27.journal_anonyme: Wind ENE, the weather stormy and rainy; at 2 it cleared and we made all sail. Went about at 6.30 and headed SSE. Lat. 6° 48', long. 17° 56'.
1800-11-27.journal_baudin: The sixth [Frimaire, 27 November 1800] was another day lost, having been spent in calm. People aboard were already beginning to weary of this weather; and although I did not show it, I was certainly more vexed by it than anyone — but one had to bear the misfortune patiently. About eleven o'clock we took a shark of fair size, and it was a great object of diversion, above all for the scientists, who were seeing a live one for the first time. Little used to such a spectacle, all wanted to be close by; but when it had given two or three lashes of its tail right and left, they were the less eager to approach as some of them nearly fell victim to it, although care had been taken to warn them beforehand what would happen if they did not go about it prudently. Citizen Péron and the surgeon Lharidon, however, were more persistent than the others; and when the sailors had it well secured, they both set to work on it. I was far from foreseeing that this poor shark was to become the cause of a very serious quarrel between the two anatomists, each of whom wished to have the glory of dissecting it. But at length, as I was walking on the quarterdeck, I saw Citizen Péron coming, dripping with blood, to complain that Mr Lharidon had taken the shark's heart from him, and that after a seizure of that nature he would not work on it. I did my best not to laugh at the subject of the complaint, which Doctor Péron made out to be very grave; but to console him I promised that the first one we took would be for him alone, and that he might count on no one touching it without his leave. Doctor Péron was consoled by this promise, and the surgeon Lharidon remained peaceable possessor of the shark's heart. At noon we observed the latitude six degrees forty-eight minutes north and the longitude by reckoning was seventeen forty-three. For several days we had noticed that the currents were setting us well to the north, and the watches confirmed that they had little tendency east or west. Having been unable to get an hour angle, we had no longitude from the watches for that day. In the evening the weather remained calm, as did most of the night, during which we made no way at all. The sky was fine enough and we saw no storms come our way, though there was no lack of them in various points of the horizon.
1800-11-27.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and warm weather, calm with variable light airs. A shark of seven feet was taken. The shrouds were set up and the topsails and topgallant sails repaired. At noon in 6° 48' 57" of latitude observed and in 18° 31' 0" of longitude by No. 38. At 1 we had a squall with rain.

1800-11-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the horizon loaded all round with lightning in the SW. At 6.30, the breeze having settled in the south, we went onto the starboard tack. At 7 went about onto the port tack to close the commander. Lat. 6° 36', long. 17° 56'.
1800-11-28.journal_baudin: On the seventh [Frimaire, 28 November 1800], calms continuing, with no prospect of when it would end. In the course of the day we took several small fish, extremely pretty, as may be seen in the drawing I have had made of them. I do not think they ever grow larger than they are in the form they have on this paper. I only recall having seen them on various voyages playing about the rudder, where they seem to come and take refuge to be sheltered from the pursuit of dorados or bonitos. To keep the crew occupied during the day I had the after lower shrouds set up, keeping those forward for the next day if, as everything foretold, we had a continuation of calm. At noon we observed the latitude of six degrees thirty minutes fifty-three seconds north, and the longitude given by the watches was for no. 31, 18° 31′ 48″ and for no. 38, 18° 38′ 22″. It was observed that since the third [Frimaire, 24 November 1800] they had an acceleration of nearly two seconds in twenty-four hours, no doubt to be attributed to the constant heat we have had since that time. The fresh difference to the north between the latitude by reckoning and that observed confirmed that the currents were setting fairly briskly in that direction, since in forty-eight hours they had given us a difference of fifteen minutes thirty-three seconds. In the afternoon we met with no more wind than in the morning. The sky, however, did not foretell a calm, and the clouds were driven fairly briskly through the air by a north-east wind which could not reach us. About four o'clock the Naturaliste, which was about a league from us to leeward, made us a signal which she kept flying until sunset without our being able to make it out. During the night of the seventh to the eighth [Frimaire, 28-29 November 1800] the ship was for the most part without steerage way, and we expected to have another difference to the north the next day, although we had for the most part laid the ship's head to the southward.
1800-11-28.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, a flat calm. At noon in 6° 36' 10" of latitude observed and in 18° 33' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 15° 30' 0" NW.

1800-11-29.journal_anonyme: Wind SE and rain. At 6 a.m. we sighted a three-master in the SW by S. We signalled her to the commander. At 10 a.m. we went about onto the starboard tack. We showed our colours and the jack at the foremast head; we could not make out hers. Lat. 6° 43', long. 17° 54'.
1800-11-29.journal_baudin: On the eighth [Frimaire, 29 November 1800] at daybreak, having passed most of the night in calm or without steerage way, we sighted a vessel ahead of us, likewise becalmed. In the morning there was a light air from various points of the horizon, which gave us the means of closing with the ship in sight. At eight o'clock she made us a signal at the foremast which we could not answer, not knowing what it meant. About three quarters of an hour later this vessel hoisted a large English ensign at her stern. We answered with our national colours, and as soon as she made them out she crowded sail on a course opposite to the one she had been steering when we first sighted her. We judged her to be an English Company ship, no doubt much vexed at having made herself known and at having let us come so close. Although we paid no attention to her manoeuvre, we saw plainly that fear prevented her from noticing that we were quietly holding our course without seeking to give her chase. At noon the observed latitude was six degrees forty-three minutes, which gave us a considerable difference from our reckoning, which had led us to hope for some minutes to the south. Watch no. 31 gave for longitude reduced to noon 18° 32′ 58″ and no. 38, 18° 38′ 30″ — much the same longitude as the day before, so that the currents had set us entirely to the north. At sunset the English vessel could be seen only from the mastheads, and tomorrow she will no doubt be well pleased to see us no more. During the night of the eighth to the ninth [Frimaire, 29-30 November 1800], entirely calm.
1800-11-29.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, calm with very variable light airs. At 6 a.m. a ship was sighted in the S 45° W; at 9 she hoisted English colours. Saw many bonito, dolphinfish and flying fish. A shark of 4 feet was taken. At noon in 6° 43' 0" of latitude observed and in 18° 33' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 11' NW. The shrouds were set up. At 6 the English three-master bore from us S 29° E. At 6.30 fired a gun for our consort.

1800-11-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, little wind, sailing a short distance from the commander. Squally weather, the sea smooth and heading SSW.
1800-11-30.journal_baudin: On the ninth [Frimaire, 30 November 1800] the sky was so laden in every point of the horizon that we hoped that after sunrise we would surely have one of the storms forming there, and wind with it. The crew were already beginning to find the time long, and although care had been taken to keep them occupied, they were weary of seeing the ship always in the same place. About eight o'clock we began to feel a breeze from the south-west which lasted until eleven, when we took a heavy squall from east-south-east. As we were not too well prepared to meet this blast — which in truth did not promise as much wind as it gave, and above all not so suddenly — there was at first some disorder in the working of the ship, which was nevertheless done with enough smartness. During the height of the squall we were obliged to furl most of our sails and to lower our topsails to the caps. Neither rain nor wind held the crew back, and everyone did his duty well, but with too much noise. When our sails were laid aback the ship behaved very well and seemed stiff. At noon we did not see the sun, and we had a light soft rain until about four in the afternoon, after the worst of the squall had passed. Most of the evening was spent with the topsails on the caps waiting for the Naturaliste, which bore north-north-west of us at about a league and a half. About three in the afternoon the men of the hold, having had occasion to go below, presumed from the smell they found there that a cask of wine must have leaked, and came to report it. It was inspected at once, and it was seen that one was indeed almost empty. This accident had been caused by the iron hoop at one end having given way. We were the more vexed at this loss as our wine was of excellent quality and we had but a small quantity of it. During the night of the ninth to the tenth [Frimaire, 30 November – 1 December 1800] it blew a light breeze. The sky was very hazy and we had a few light squalls from time to time, but of little consequence.
1800-11-30.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, calm, light airs, and a fresh breeze from ESE, E and SE, which began at 11 a.m. with a fairly heavy squall and pouring rain. At noon in 6° 26' of latitude by account and in 18° 26' of longitude by account. Variation 14° 54' NW.

1800-12-01.journal_anonyme: The same course and the same wind. We had several squalls from the SSE. A high sea, the weather very thick.
1800-12-01.journal_baudin: On the tenth, in the morning [1 December 1800], the winds were very variable from east to south-east, and we took advantage of them to make southing as much as we could; but the Naturaliste's poor sailing prevented us from making as much way as we might, not wishing to leave her too far astern. At nine o'clock we took a squall like the previous day's; but as we were well prepared the sailors only laughed at it and busied themselves catching a good quantity of rainwater to wash their linen. This squall was strong enough to oblige us to lower our topsails right down. At its height, being two points free, we ran eight knots with the topsails down. I found the rain very cold, whereas the day before I had found it quite warm. This difference no doubt comes from the greater moisture in the air. After the squall had passed the winds settled from south-east to east-south-east, varying, and it went on blowing a light breeze. At noon we had no observation of latitude, and we did not even see the sun for the whole rest of the day, which was rainy until moonrise, when the sky grew clearer. About three o'clock, the weather looking threatening enough, I had a reef taken in the topsails. This manoeuvre gave the Naturaliste time to close with us, and by the end of the day she was a league astern in our wake. About half past seven, while part of the crew were dancing on the quarterdeck, a porpoise was taken forward. One may well judge that the country dance was promptly ended and that everyone crowded to the forepart of the ship. When this fish was aboard, all the naturalists and other scientists surrounded it, and each wanted to make use of it that instant. Some called for lanterns, others for paper, several for instruments, so that to bring everyone to agreement I took possession of the fish, which I had hung by the tail from the mainstay, asking these gentlemen to moderate their eagerness for the moment and assuring them they would have time enough the next day. This fish weighed about two hundred pounds. Scarcely had it been made fast to the stay as I had ordered than we took a squall of rain and wind which made all the scientists vanish, and we could quietly attend to the working of our sails, which did not take long, having only the topsails and foresail. During the squall, which was stronger in rain than in wind, we lowered our topsails halfway down. About ten o'clock the weather became hazy and fine enough. We had no further squalls during the night; but the winds drew more to the south and made the course we had steered until then less good. During the evening so foul a smell came from the hold that everyone below was almost overcome by it. I had about ten hogsheads of sea water let in by means of our head pump, which was pumped out an hour later. The water that came out was black as ink. I mean to do the same tomorrow and until it comes out quite clear.
1800-12-01.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to SE; rain and violent squalls, with lightning. At noon in 5° 14' 0" of latitude by account and in 18° 34' 0" of longitude by account. A porpoise was harpooned.

1800-12-02.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from ESE. The sky cloudy, the sea smooth. Saw a ship in the NW. Took some porpoises and bonito.
1800-12-02.journal_baudin: On the eleventh [Frimaire, 2 December 1800], in the morning, the breeze having fallen a great deal, we feared falling calm again; but as the horizon was very hazy we hoped the wind would hold, which indeed it did, though it drew rather more southerly and made our course less good. At sunrise the painters, the naturalists and the anatomists did not fail to come and visit the porpoise taken the day before; and the difficulty that resulted was that all wished to work on it at the same moment, so that the draughtsmen, who wanted it laid on its belly and in a position fit for taking its shape, could not agree with the anatomists, who wanted it on its back to open it. From this want of agreement there resulted complaints of one against the other, and I found myself much embarrassed to decide who was right; but the anatomists settled the dispute, for while the draughtsmen were making their complaint to me they opened the poor fish, and when the painters returned to the work they meant to do, they no longer found in the animal any of the forms they needed. I had no other means of satisfying the latter than to promise them, as I had done for the shark, that the first one taken would be entirely at their disposal. In the course of the morning I again had a dozen hogsheads of sea water let into the hold by means of the head pump; and after leaving it there two hours it was thrown out. The smell it gave off, though less strong than the day before, was still considerable. At noon we observed the latitude of four degrees twenty-eight minutes north. The longitude given by the watches, reduced to noon, was for no. 31, 18° 49′ 47″ and for no. 38, 18° 54′ 3″. The acceleration observed these four days past continued to be noticed; but as it was common to them both, it changed nothing in their usual relation. During the evening the breeze went on light, and at sunset we were obliged to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste, which was rather too far astern. The night of the eleventh to the twelfth [2-3 December 1800] held nothing out of the ordinary. The wind was soft and the weather fine enough. About eleven o'clock the Naturaliste closed with us.
1800-12-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to ESE. At noon in 4° 28' 0" of latitude observed and in 18° 48' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 13° 36' 0" NW.

1800-12-03.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from SSE, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth. At 6 a.m. the commander signalled us damage to his fore topmast. Lat. 3° 37', long. 19° 11'. Var. 18° 48' NW.
1800-12-03.journal_baudin: On the twelfth, in the morning [3 December 1800], the winds held at south-south-east and the breeze was rather fresher. At the morning inspection the carpenter of the watch came to warn me that the fore topmast was sprung. I at once had the fore topgallant sail furled and signalled this damage to the Naturaliste, which was close enough to us. I then sent for the master carpenter so that he might make a more exact examination himself. His report was that the mast was not broken as had been announced, but only split along more than half its length. He judged that this had been caused by the setting up of the backstays and by the fid, whose breadth was not sufficient, so that it had entered more than three inches into the mast and caused the split that followed. However, as he judged the mast quite fit for service, we did not change it. We were content merely to pass a woolding over it to support it better. During the morning the weather was very hazy, and at noon we could get only a very doubtful observation of latitude. The longitude by reckoning, reduced to that moment, was 18° 48′ 44″. In the afternoon we found the sea swellier than usual from the south. We also saw several fairly considerable flights of birds which, coming to us from the south-east, were making for the east-north-east. They were no doubt following some fish; at least that was our conjecture, for we know of no land in that direction where they might withdraw. Besides, these were the first we had met since leaving Tenerife. At five o'clock we took a rain squall from east-south-east which from the outset obliged us to reef our topsails. This squall did not last long, but we had a fair amount of rain long after it had passed. During the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth [Frimaire, 3-4 December 1800] we had very little wind, and the heavy swell from the south prevented us from profiting by the little there was, the ship having great difficulty answering her helm. The sky, stormy in various points of the horizon, did not however foretell a calm, and the thunder heard now and then had given us hope of making a little southing, for it was the northern quarter that was the most laden.
1800-12-03.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ENE. At 5.30 a.m. the carpenter on his rounds found that the fore topmast was split from the fid to the end of the hounds. At noon in 3° 41' 32" of latitude observed and in 19° 12' of longitude by No. 35.
