Variation 14° 39' NW. Saw several shoals of pilot fish. Squalls and rain; sent up rockets to give the Naturaliste our position.

1800-12-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running, and calm; in the afternoon we had several squalls. Lat. 3° 11', long. 19° 13'.
1800-12-04.journal_baudin: On the thirteenth [Frimaire, 4 December 1800], in the morning, the calm continued until about eight o'clock, when we had a light air from south-south-west which made us haul close on the starboard tack. The weather was fine enough in the morning, but the horizon was so laden in the east that there was every appearance we would have the winds from that quarter during the day. During the morning decks were cleared and all the sailors were obliged to change their clothes so as to dry those of the day before, which had been fairly well soaked. At noon we observed the latitude of 3° 11′ north. The longitude of the watches was for no. 31, 19° 58′ 54″ and for no. 38, 20° 2′ 32″. The mean of these two longitudes placed us in 20° 0′ 43″, while our longitude by reckoning was 18° 50′ 44″, giving 1° 9′ 59″ difference, the watches being further west. In the afternoon we likewise had very little wind until about half past five in the evening, when we took a considerable storm, at first from the south-east and then from the north-east. This storm gave us very little wind but a continual rain, almost without interruption, for four hours together. The sky was so dark while it lasted that we could scarcely see from one end of the ship to the other. While this squall lasted we took several zoophytes which made the sea extremely brilliant by the vividness of their colour. This gave us a moment's pleasure which kept us from noticing the foul weather. I shall try to give a description of this zoophyte, which seems not to have been described, at least by the authors we have. The night of the thirteenth to the fourteenth [4-5 December 1800] was extremely rainy and we caught several hogsheads of water. As we had not the Naturaliste in sight I had a few rockets sent up and kept the stern lantern burning so that she might show us her position, which she did by likewise sending up a few rockets between the squalls. When the moon had risen a little above the horizon we saw somewhat more clearly; but our sight could not reach beyond a quarter of a league, so dark was the sky and so low the clouds.
1800-12-04.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE, WSW, SW, SSW, NE, NNE and N. At noon in 3° 10' 50" of latitude observed and in 19° 59' 0" of longitude by No. 38 and 19° 14' by No. 35. Stormy weather, rain and squalls, with lightning. At nightfall we had an incredible quantity of marine phosphorescence in our wake, which made us seem ringed with fire.

1800-12-05.journal_anonyme: The winds SSW and S by W, a fresh breeze. At 6 p.m. the winds shifted to WNW. Lat. 2° 39', long. 18° 41'. Var. 18° 20' NW.
1800-12-05.journal_baudin: On the fourteenth [Frimaire, 5 December 1800], after sunrise the weather seemed inclined to turn fine, and the horizon from south-east round by east to north became very clear. The winds then drew to the south-east. We were almost becalmed. During the morning all the clothes soaked during the night were dried, as were our sails, and decks were cleared everywhere for fumigating, so as to draw from the ship as much moisture as possible. A simple fumigation was used for this, but a very thick one. About ten o'clock the sky, though fine enough, became very hazy, and at noon we could not get the sun's altitude. About three o'clock the winds drew to the south, and at sunset we had them at south-south-west and almost calm, which made us go about onto the other tack. At the evening inspection the master carpenter came to warn me that the fore topmast could no longer be relied on, the split it had having opened more than four inches since we passed a woolding over it, which ought nevertheless to have supported it. I gave orders for the fore topgallant mast to be struck at once, and by seven in the evening it was down. During the night we had a few squalls, little wind and a fair amount of rain. In the midnight watch, when the sky was fine enough, we made ready as far as possible to begin at daybreak to change our topmast if the weather allowed. We did not see during the night the same phenomenon we had met with the night before, although it was often as dark — which gives grounds for thinking that these molluscs are not to be found indifferently in all places.
1800-12-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE round to SW by way of south. At noon in 2° 44' 30" of latitude observed and in 18° 42' 0" of longitude by No. 35. At 4 the Naturaliste asked for the course should the winds draw aft; we signalled her S 22° 30' E. The fore topgallant mast was struck to make ready to shift the fore topmast, whose damage had grown worse. Rain during the night.

1800-12-06.journal_anonyme: Winds south, the sky overcast, the sea choppy. We spoke the commander, who gave us the course SSE in case the winds should draw aft. At 5 a.m. wore ship. At 9 we passed under the commander's stern. Lat. 2° 20' 30", long. 18° 41'. Var. 18° 28'. He was then shifting his fore topmast; the captain asked his leave to send an officer aboard him on the service. We hove to and at once put out the small boat. On its return at noon the commander's fore topmast was swayed up. During the night we showed a light at the gaff to give the commander our position.
1800-12-06.journal_baudin: On the fifteenth [Frimaire, 6 December 1800], in the morning, what little wind there was came from south-south-east, and the sky promised us a fine enough morning, the horizon showing no squall anywhere round. At six o'clock everyone had orders to set to work, and we began to fit the mast that was to serve us. This job was bound to take some time, seeing that we were much encumbered by our spare spars and that the mast we needed lay right at the bottom. Yet the work was not long, for by nine o'clock it was swayed up and the other struck down. As I was pleased with the crew's work I had a double ration issued at breakfast. As we carried little sail the Naturaliste soon came up with us. When that vessel passed under our stern, Mr Hamelin asked me to send him by his boat a paper I had asked him to keep ready for the first opportunity. The weather being fine and the wind light, I consented the more gladly as I had something to say to him, and something of interest at that. Accordingly I wrote him the following letter. "The Commander to Citizen Hamelin, captain of the Naturaliste. I beg you, Mr Hamelin, to be so good as to let me know as often as possible your position relative to mine, when through the darkness of the night or any other cause we cannot make each other out. These past days when the weather was not fine I have been in continual anxiety for fear of being either too far from you or too close; which would not have happened had you, by lights or a rocket, put me in a position to judge our distance from one another. I therefore beg you in future to let me know when you think me too far off, so that I may shorten sail to the purpose and not at hazard, as I have done until now when it has not been possible to make you out. For the rest, I wish you good health, as I do all your gentlemen and crew." The boat Mr Hamelin sent me delivered a letter letting me know that all were well aboard, and he asked me to send him a magnetised bar to touch up his compasses. At one in the afternoon we had finished all our work and our fore topgallant mast was crossed. I was very satisfied with the way the crew behaved. It is true the weather and the sea were very favourable to us; but there was no less work for that, and no one idled. At noon the observed latitude was two degrees thirty minutes forty seconds north. The longitude given by the watches was for no. 31, 20° 12′ 52″ and for no. 38, 20° 15′ 57″. That of no. 37 aboard the Naturaliste showed at the same hour 20° 24′ 0″. In the course of the afternoon we set our fore topsail and then had a fresh breeze from south-south-east. The stowage of the upper deck, which the morning's work had thrown into disorder, was completed.
1800-12-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. The fore topmast was shifted. We communicated with the Naturaliste. At noon in 2° 28' 52" of latitude observed and in 20° 6' of longitude by No. 38 and 18° 42' by No. 35. In the afternoon a little rain, with squalls.

1800-12-07.journal_anonyme: The wind south, a fresh breeze, the sea rather high, lying close-hauled on the port tack. Not seeing the commander, we sent up a rocket to which he answered, and we took his bearing S by W.
1800-12-07.journal_baudin: On the sixteenth [Frimaire, 7 December 1800], in the morning, the winds held in the south, almost calm; but the sky looked so threatening in every point of the horizon that we had to expect bad weather during the morning. We were not disappointed in our expectation, for at half past six we took a squall from north to north-north-east which was heavy enough. We were not obliged, however, to lower our topsails. The Naturaliste, which was far to leeward of us, took advantage of it to close with us; and as she got it first she came up with us almost as soon as it did. This squall lasted about an hour, after which the winds were very variable and light; but the weather turned to rain and we had it in abundance until after noon. At one o'clock we fell calm again and the ship lay without steerage way until nine, when the sky cleared. The winds were then from the south-east, varying to south, a light breeze. We stood all night on the west-south-west to south-west board as being the one that gave us most southing. During the night of the sixteenth to the seventeenth [Frimaire, 7-8 December 1800] the weather was fine enough, and the sky, though hazy, gave us no rain and very little wind. After six o'clock, as it was some time since the crew had danced, the weather not having allowed it, everyone was sent aft and the ball lasted until eight with much gaiety and contentment.
1800-12-07.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SE, and from NW to E, and calm. At a quarter to one in the morning the Naturaliste sent up a rocket, to which we answered. Saw a frigate bird. At noon in 2° 1' 33" of latitude by account and in 20° 42' 42" of longitude by account. Variation 14° 20' 0" NW. The 17th [Frimaire, 8 December 1800]. Overcast and rainy weather, with squalls, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 2° 12' 9" of latitude observed and in 22° 20' 18" of longitude by No. 38. A shark of 5 feet was taken.

1800-12-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather; the shifting winds forced us to change tacks three times. At 6.30 it freshened from the SE and we lay close-hauled on the port tack. The commander in the WSW at a middling distance.
1800-12-08.journal_baudin: On the seventeenth [Frimaire, 8 December 1800] the wind fell a great deal from what it had been during the night. The sky grew laden with storm clouds in several quarters of the horizon and we expected wind and rain. We had neither, however, and the weather turned fine until about two in the afternoon, when the horizon became very heavy from south to south-east with a very threatening look. During the morning, the weather being fine, I had all our studdingsails and other sails dried on the yards, and for the same reason the reef I was carrying in the topsails was shaken out. As there was little wind all morning we took a shark of fair size, which made the time seem less long and gave the scientists and the crew a moment's diversion. At noon we observed two degrees twelve minutes nineteen seconds north, which greatly surprised us, for from the reckoning of our course we counted on having gained something to the south. We had certainly noticed for several days that a current was setting us north and west, but we had not found it so strong as at this time; and even when we were surrounded by very violent tide rips we had not met with such great differences, since in two days — that is, since the last observation — we found we had lost thirty minutes seventeen seconds to the north and almost as much to the west. In the afternoon the winds were south-south-east and very light until about seven o'clock, when we had a flat calm. The horizon was so laden in every quarter that we had the appearance of a bad night, and I made my dispositions accordingly. About eight o'clock, the winds having come to us from south to south-south-west, we took the board to the south by east, which we held all night; and it was not a fine one, for we often had squalls very heavy in rain but generally with little wind.

1800-12-09.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast and rainy, a high sea. At 4.30 the course was signalled south in case the winds should draw aft. At 6 went onto the starboard tack. The commander a short distance off.
1800-12-09.journal_baudin: On the eighteenth [Frimaire, 9 December 1800], in the morning, the weather turned very foul and the winds seemed inclined to settle in the south. We had constant rain and squalls often strong enough but of short duration. At eight o'clock I had a reef taken in, and we held on the eastern board under our courses. About ten o'clock we saw the sun for an instant and took advantage of it to get an hour angle so as to know the longitude given by our watches. At eleven we had rain and squalls again, which continued until evening. At noon, the winds being variable from south round by east, we went about in the hope of making a little southing. To carry out this manoeuvre we had to try three times, for we missed stays on the first two. From the longitude given by our watches I signalled the Naturaliste to let me know hers, since for two days the difference from the reckoning had been so considerable that I feared they might have gone out of order. But she signalled me 21° 54′ for the previous day's longitude. I concluded from this that the current which had set us so far north and west had had the same effect on her as on us. In the evening the weather continued squally and rainy, and the winds went sometimes as far as south-east by south, but not for long. After sunset we took a fairly vigorous squall which happily came to us from the north and made us gain a little southing. We were nevertheless obliged to reef our topsails to let it pass. Independently of the wind this squall brought us, I do not recall ever having seen rain fall in such abundance. At eight o'clock the wind ceased, but there was a continuation of rain which lasted all night, so that it was the more wearing for the crew as the variety and inconstancy of the winds often obliged us to different manoeuvres. Although the observation of latitude at noon was very doubtful, the sun having been obscured three or four minutes before its passage of the meridian, it is no less true that we found we had a difference of twenty-eight minutes fifty-six seconds from our own to the south; for by our reckoning of the distance run we counted on having made fourteen minutes to the south, whereas by observation there were thirteen minutes fourteen seconds to the north. It appears, from what has been happening to us these several days, that the nearer we approach the equator the more the currents act to the north and west. As on my other voyages I have met with no such difference, perhaps the present season is to be held responsible for the one we meet with every day.
1800-12-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW, SSW, S, SSE, SE, NE and N, with rain. At noon in 2° 24' 22" of latitude observed and in 22° 6' 6" of longitude by No. 38. At 6, the wind having drawn round to NE, the course was given south. Saw a manta ray.

1800-12-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze. At half past noon went about and headed WSW. In the afternoon, the winds having drawn aft, we steered SSE. At 7 p.m. we headed on our course. At 3 a.m. a waterspout passed alongside. At the same instant the wind shifted violently to ENE.
1800-12-10.journal_baudin: On the nineteenth [Frimaire, 10 December 1800], in the morning, the weather seemed inclined to turn fine and the rain ceased, but the wind fell a great deal. At eight o'clock the calm took us again and the ship lay without steerage way until after noon. We counted on being able to observe the sun at that time, and altitudes had already begun to be taken when it was obscured by a cloud which did not let us see it again until it was too late. During the morning I had all the crew's clothing, continually wet these several days, put out to air. Air was likewise given to various parts of the ship which the foul weather and the continual rain had obliged us to keep closed. We were already beginning to notice a bad smell aboard, the inevitable consequence of too long a damp. So we were well pleased to see that the weather allowed us to let in a change of air. All hands were nonetheless well, and apart from the men who caught venereal diseases at Tenerife, all are in good health. In the afternoon the winds drew to the west, and with the help of the light breeze we had from that quarter we were able to lay the ship's head south and give her steerage way. The heat was so sharp in the evening that we do not doubt it will bring us fresh storms in the night. At sunset the weather was very dark and the sky extremely overcast in the north; we hoped to have some squalls from that quarter, but all dispersed and we had only a few light showers without wind. Most of the night passed in calm without steerage way, which was the more disagreeable as the Naturaliste was very close to us. After midnight the winds drew to the south-east. We took advantage of them to draw away from the Naturaliste and stood close-hauled on the port tack, having for a moment all sail set.
1800-12-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, calm and a light breeze from NE, ENE, WSW and NW. At 4 we had a heavy squall from ENE. At noon in 1° 46' 0" of latitude observed and in 22° 6' 12" of longitude by account. Variation 11° 33' NW.

1800-12-11.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, the weather fine, the sea smooth, the ship not answering her helm.
1800-12-11.journal_baudin: On the twentieth [Frimaire, 11 December 1800], in the morning, the weather was fine enough, or at least without appearance of rain. We counted on being able to take some lunar distances from the sun; but about nine o'clock the sky having become very hazy, we could do nothing of the kind. During the morning it blew a light breeze from south-east varying towards south, and we held on our course close-hauled on the port tack. About eight o'clock all the clothing was put out to dry, and a great part of our sails with it. At noon the observed latitude was 1° 18′ 45″ north, which gave us a difference of 0° 18′ 18″ 35‴ further north than we made ourselves. The longitude given by the watches, reduced to the same hour, was for no. 31, 23° 26′ 0″ and for no. 38, 23° 28′ 3″. That of our reckoning was then only 19° 1′, making a difference of four degrees twenty minutes of west longitude. The various tide rips that had surrounded us for several days had told us plainly enough that we must be losing a great deal to the west. I should never have imagined, however, that the resulting difference would be so considerable. I await the time when they change direction, to see what the daily rate of this current must have been — one which will no doubt soon take a different course. About three in the afternoon I let the Naturaliste know our observed longitude so that she might tell me hers. Her answer was that she made herself in 23° 42′, a difference of fifteen minutes between her watches and ours. The evening of the twentieth was fine enough and we had a fresh breeze more from the south-east, varying at times towards the south, so that we flattered ourselves the trade winds would not be long in reaching us, to make up for the length of the calms and the foul weather we had met with these several days. The night of the twentieth to the twenty-first [Frimaire, 11-12 December 1800] was very fine and the winds settled at south-east, a fresh breeze. As the Naturaliste had fallen much to leeward we were obliged to bear away to close with her and to shorten sail considerably once she was in our wake.
1800-12-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and SSE. At noon in 1° 18' 14" of latitude observed and in 23° 26' 30" of longitude by No. 38, and 21° 47' by No. 35. Variation 11° 32' 0" NW. At 8.45 sent up a rocket; the Naturaliste answered.

1800-12-12.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth and the sky cloudy. At 10 p.m. the commander sent up a rocket and we answered him. In the forenoon we shifted three tons and a half of weight aft. We noticed that the ship steered, but that the Géographe held her course better than we did.
1800-12-12.journal_baudin: On the twenty-first [Frimaire, 12 December 1800] the weather held fine and the winds were somewhat variable from south-east to south-east by east and south-east by south, which made us think we had reached the south-east trades. During the morning all the crew's clothing was again put out to air, so as to take from it whatever dampness it must have contracted during the heavy rains we had had. At noon we observed the latitude of 0° 18′ 56″ north; and to our great astonishment the longitude given by our watches was for no. 31, 24° 47′ 33″ and for no. 38, 24° 49′ 1″, which gave us in twenty-four hours a run to the west of 1° 21′ 33″, whereas by our reckoning we counted on having made only 0° 34′ 12″ — so that in these twenty-four hours the current had set us 0° 47′ 21″ to the west and 4 minutes 58 seconds to the south. The Naturaliste's longitude at the same time was 25° 0′ 6″, differing from the mean of ours by 0° 11′ 49″. In the afternoon the weather held fine and the breeze was fairly steady from the south-east. From the result of four different azimuth observations the variation was found to be ten degrees fifty-five minutes fifty seconds north-west; and as all the observations were made with great care by Citizen Gicquel, there is reason to believe they come very close to the true figure. While we were at table a courier came to announce the approach of the crossing of the line and to ask leave to perform the ceremony customary on such an occasion. I consented willingly, so as to give our gentlemen an idea of it, and on condition, however, that all should pass off with the greatest decency. During the night of the twenty-first to the twenty-second [Frimaire, 12-13 December 1800] the weather was very hazy and the air damp. We had no rain, however, and the winds held in the southern quarter; we held on our course close-hauled, always conforming to the Naturaliste's rate of sailing, which made us lose a great deal of ground.
1800-12-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE and SE. Saw gulls and flying fish. At noon in 0° 18' 54" of latitude observed and in 24° 51' of longitude by No. 38 and 21° 21' by No. 35. The lunar distances gave 25° 3' 30" for mean. The variation observed 11° 6' 20" NW. At 6 we crossed the Line in 25° 6' of west longitude. The rigging was set up. From the 21st at 6 o'clock, latitudes given without a name are to be understood as south.

1800-12-13.journal_anonyme: The wind SE, a strong breeze. At 7.15 we sent the whole crew aft to see whether we should sail equally with the Géographe, whose canvas was the four courses and topsails. Within three quarters of an hour we had gained 3° on her; she bore from us S by E.
1800-12-13.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 22nd [Frimaire, 13 December 1800], reckoning ourselves south of the Line and the winds holding south-east with a fresh breeze, we had no doubt we had picked up the trades, so that everyone reckoned himself halfway on the passage to Mauritius. I am nevertheless far from believing that we shall not take longer to reach it than the number of days at sea it has taken us to come this far. Be that as it may, at seven o'clock the drum announced the moment of the baptism, and everyone made ready to receive it. The ceremony was performed with all the customary apparatus and no one had cause to be dissatisfied, which is rare enough on such occasions. It must have been very agreeable to the petty officers, whom it brought some fifty Spanish piastres from what each gave freely. As the corvette herself came under the baptism, it cost the Republic a double ration and myself eight piastres. At noon the observed latitude was 1° 9' 48" South, giving us 13 minutes of difference from the reckoned latitude. The longitude of the watches reduced to noon was, for No. 31, 25° 38' 59", and for No. 38, 25° 39' 37", whereas that of the dead reckoning at the same hour was only 20° 2' 56", so that this gave a difference from the watches of 5° 37' 41". By a lunar distance observed on the 20th there was a difference of only 0° 9' 47" 15‴. I would not correct my reckoned position on this last observation, in order to see whether in the sequel there may be found a current setting south and east to make up for the one that has carried us west and north — which will very likely happen, since we are already beginning to notice that for two days its set has been south and west. In the evening the sky turned very hazy and after sunset we had some squalls with rain, but they did not last long. In the night of the 22nd to the 23rd [Frimaire, 13-14 December 1800] it blew a fresh breeze but in squalls. At midnight we got one that brought us a great deal of rain and wind enough to oblige us to clew up the mainsail, which had been set I know not why, for we had no need of it to keep way with the Naturaliste, who was as usual astern. The manoeuvre made during the squall was slow and the officer of the watch did not acquit himself too well. The rest of the night had nothing remarkable; the sky stayed very hazy throughout and the sea became rather high, with a swell running.
1800-12-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and ESE. In the forenoon those who had not yet crossed the Line were baptised; a short moment of pleasure made us forget for an instant all the unpleasantness and mortification we are made to suffer by the unworthy man to whom the government has entrusted our lives. At noon in 1° 9' 42" of latitude observed and in 25° 42' 24" of longitude by No. 38 and 22° 55' by No. 35. Variation 10° 58' 0" NW. Squalls and pouring rain during the night.

1800-12-14.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a high sea, the wind SE, a fresh breeze; a great deal of rain fell.
1800-12-14.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 23rd [Frimaire, 14 December 1800] the weather was finer than it had been in the night, and although the sky was loaded with cloud we had neither squalls nor rain. At seven o'clock we cleared decks generally and put the hammocks and blankets out to air. In the forenoon the breeze was fresh enough, but as the sea was rather hollow the Naturaliste could not carry much sail and fell so far to leeward that in the afternoon we were obliged to bear away to west-south-west to close her. About eight o'clock we saw a tropic bird, the kind the men call a boatswain bird. It was the first of that species we had met with up to this moment, which is not usual on the track we have followed. At noon the longitude shown by the watches was, for No. 31, 26° 29' 48", and for No. 38, 26° 29' 55". The observed latitude was 2° 13' 12" South, so that this time there was little difference from the reckoning; the current had nevertheless set us west again, by very little in truth, but it was proof to us that it had not yet entirely changed its set. The Naturaliste having signalled us the mean longitude given by her watches as 26° 31', we found a difference of 0° 22', which we were not accustomed to have. In the afternoon we broke out part of the after hold to shift wine, beer and biscuit forward into the steward's room. We needed to do this, for it seemed to us the ship was too much by the stern and that on this account she answered her helm badly in coming to the wind. During the night of the 23rd to the 24th [14-15 December 1800] the sky was very hazy and we had squalls from time to time, one only of which brought a little rain and wind. We were obliged to bear down on the Naturaliste to close her, as she had fallen a long way to leeward.
1800-12-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE. Saw tropic birds and flying fish. At noon in 2° 13' 12" of latitude observed and in 26° 33' 12" of longitude by No. 38 and 23° 25' by No. 35.

1800-12-15.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SE by S, fine weather, the sea rather high. Between eight o'clock and noon, the commander having gained on us considerably, we struck our starboard anchor into the hold.
1800-12-15.journal_baudin: On the 24th [Frimaire, 15 December 1800] the winds were south-east, varying a point to the south, and the breeze, which had looked well at sunrise, fell away a great deal in the course of the day, so that we made little way by the reckoning. Yet by the sun's observation at noon we had a difference of 0° 11' 43" to the north, and by the result of our watches a second of 0° 34' 19" to the west, so that the current seemed to have taken up its former set again, whereas the day before it had been barely perceptible. At noon the observed latitude was 3° 2' 29" South; the longitude given by No. 31 was then 27° 39' 56", and by No. 38, 27° 39' 13". That announced by the Naturaliste differed by only 0° 2' 35", which led us to suppose there had been an error in the one she signalled the day before, which differed by 22 minutes. As the weather was very fine all day, we aired every part of the ship, which still felt the damp the rains before crossing the Line had brought into her. In the afternoon the breeze was light and the wind dropped as the sun went down towards the horizon. On inspecting the masts it was found that the fid of the mizzen topmast was broken. Another was at once made from a piece of oak that seemed sound, but scarcely was it in place and the shrouds set up than it broke too. To prevent the same happening to a third, I had an iron fid fitted that we had in reserve for our topmasts, and it was placed in position. The night of the 24th to the 25th [Frimaire, 15-16 December 1800] was very fine and clear, but there was little wind, and now and then the winds varied from south-east to south-east by east. As the Naturaliste was carrying a point or two freer than we were, we often had to bear away to close her.
1800-12-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and SSE. At noon in 3° 0' 16" of latitude observed and in 27° 31' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 9° 3' NW. The rigging was set up.

1800-12-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea quiet enough, the winds a light breeze from the SE. At 4 the commander signalled us his position; we shifted one of the bower anchors forward of the mainmast as a kedge.
1800-12-16.journal_baudin: On the 25th [Frimaire, 16 December 1800] the weather was fine but the breeze still light. On board we set about airing part of our spare sails, and in the course of the day the ship was fumigated throughout by burning juniper. As the hold was again giving off a bad smell, its water was renewed by letting sea water into the ship by means of our head pump. At noon the observed latitude was 3° 52' 18" South, and we found a difference of 9' 23" to the north on the reckoning of the distance run by the log, and 34' 23" to the west. The longitude given by the marine watches was, for No. 31, 28° 41' 10", and for No. 38, 28° 39' 18". On board the Naturaliste they signalled us 28° 51', giving a difference of 20' 63" from ours. It is hard enough to account for this difference, the more so as the day before the observations agreed perfectly with one another. In the afternoon it continued to blow a light breeze, but the winds veered towards the east and we had them from east-south-east. I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south-south-east if the winds allowed us to lie that way. By our position at noon we were east and west of the island of Fernando de Noronha at a distance of eighty leagues. Various observations of the variation of the needle gave for mean term, reduced to noon of the day, 8° 36' NW. At sunset the sky turned very hazy, with the look of a good breeze for the night. We also saw some tunny about the ship, but they did not come near enough to give us any hope of taking one. The night of the 25th to the 26th [Frimaire, 16-17 December 1800] was fine but there was little wind. The breeze came to us at times from the east [word struck out, illegible]; it seemed inclined to settle at east-south-east, which allowed us to head south.
1800-12-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and ESE. At noon in 3° 54' 17" of latitude observed and in 28° 39' 24" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 8° 29' NW. We signalled the Naturaliste that if the winds drew aft we should steer S 22° 30' E.

1800-12-17.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from SE to ESE, the weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind pleasant enough.
1800-12-17.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 26th [Frimaire, 17 December 1800] we had the winds east-south-east and the breeze freshened a little after sunrise. As the weather was fine all day, the decks and between-decks were fumigated with powder and vinegar to drive out the damp and the bad smell the hold water may have brought in. As it had been supposed that the ventilators set up by Citizen Garos by means of his new galley would suffice, no others were shipped to replace them. Obliged to break up those galleys, which could be of no use to us, we had no other resource to make up for what we lacked than the windsails ordinarily used. At noon the observed latitude was 5° 0' 39" South, and we found ourselves five minutes further south than the reckoning gave. The longitude of the marine watches put us at noon in 29° 28' 18" for No. 31, and 29° 18' 31" for No. 38. The reckoned longitude was then 21° 52' 32". In the twenty-four hours there was a difference of 0° 31' 44" to the west. The Naturaliste, being rather too far from us, did not signal these observations. In the evening the weather continued fine but the breeze fell away as the sun went down towards the horizon. From a series of azimuths observed morning and evening with great care, the variation was 7° 21' NW in the evening and 7° 16' in the morning. The night of the 25th to the 26th [17-18 December 1800] was very fine and the sky almost without cloud. We lost sight of the Naturaliste, who answered none of our signals although all night we had our stern light shown from time to time.
1800-12-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE and E. At noon in 5° 0' 30" of latitude observed and in 29° 12' 6" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 7° 19' NW.

1800-12-18.journal_anonyme: The wind ESE, a light breeze. The ship slack. During the night sent up rockets to let the commander see us. At daybreak we sighted him in the ENE.
1800-12-18.journal_baudin: On the 27th [Frimaire, 18 December 1800] at daybreak we sighted the Naturaliste, who was nearly two [leagues] from us to leeward. As that ship had made us no signal during the night, we had been unable to judge her distance from us. We bore away to close her, and at eight o'clock she was at her usual distance. After sunrise the breeze was rather stronger than it had been during the night, but the winds drew round more to the south-east. In the forenoon the crew were employed serving the cable that had been damaged at the anchorage of Santa Cruz de Tenerife. At noon the observed latitude was 6° 30' 33", and we saw with pleasure that the current might perhaps be beginning to change its set, since for two days we had been finding differences to the south, whereas before they were almost always to the north. That of this day was 17' 33" further south than the reckoning. The longitude given by the watches, reduced to noon, was for No. 31, 29° 46' 3", and for No. 38, 29° 41' 57". The reckoning put us in 21° 55' 2". The Naturaliste signalled us her longitude as usual, but we could never make out her signal; although I let her know it could not be distinguished, she kept it always in the same place. During the evening the sky turned very hazy, and some clouds even gave us a little rain. We were still too far from the coast of America to believe that its nearness caused this change in the atmosphere. At eight in the evening, while we were at the dance, one of those birds the seamen have named the booby came wheeling about the ship and upset the whole order of the dancing. We reckoned it had come to be caught, but after showing itself well it disappeared. The night of the 27th to the 28th [Frimaire, 18-19 December 1800] had nothing remarkable. It blew a light breeze, but the sky was still loaded with cloud and damp.
1800-12-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to SE. At noon in 6° 30' 33" of latitude observed and in 29° 45' 30" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 7° 16' NW.

1800-12-19.journal_anonyme: The wind ESE, a fresh breeze. The weather fine, the sea rather high and the sky clear.
1800-12-19.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 28th [Frimaire, 19 December 1800], the Naturaliste being about two leagues to leeward of us, we bore away again to close her. It appears that during the night that ship steers freer than we do, and that this is why for two days she has been found so far to leeward every morning. At eight o'clock we had closed her and I made her the signal to steer close-hauled, which she did. In the forenoon the breeze was steady enough, at east-south-east. The sky, which had been much loaded with cloud, became fine, and we found the sea less rough than the day before. At noon the observed latitude was 8° South, whereas our reckoning put us only in 7° 40' 18", so that we no longer had any doubt that the set of the currents had changed, given the large differences to the south we were beginning to find. That of the twenty-four hours was 19' 18", and only 15' 34" to the west. Watch No. 31 gave us for longitude 30° 7' 34", and No. 38, 30° 2' 21". The reckoning by the log was 22° 1' 14". The results of our watches compared with those of the Naturaliste differed by [blank]. In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the breeze fell away as it had been in the habit of doing since we came into the trades. After sunset, however, it freshened a little and was steady enough all through the night, which was very fine and clear. From various azimuths taken morning and evening the mean variation was found to be 6° 38' north-west.
1800-12-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE and E. Saw flying fish. At noon in 8° 0' 18" of latitude observed and in 30° 3' 12" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 24' NW.

1800-12-20.journal_anonyme: Wind ESE, a fresh breeze, the sea smooth and the sky cloudy. The log line being too long, we shortened it to 43½ feet.
1800-12-20.journal_baudin: On the 29th [20 December 1800] the weather continued fine and the winds were variable from east-south-east towards east, a fresh breeze. We were often obliged to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste, who for two or three days has seemed to sail even worse than usual. In the forenoon we shifted the collar of the stay of our mizzen mast — that is, the stay to the mainmast that holds it — finding it placed far too high. At noon the observed latitude was 9° 36' 2" South, whereas that of the reckoning was only 9° 15' 19", giving a difference of 0° 21'. So there was no longer any doubt that the set of the currents had changed. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 30° 21' 59", and for No. 38, 30° 15' 29", which gave only 19' of westing more than the reckoning, which then put us in 28° 4' 38". The Naturaliste not being within reach to let us know her observations, I made her no signal for them. In the evening the weather continued fine and the sea was rather less hollow than it had been in the morning. From several azimuth observations taken morning and evening, the variation of the magnetic needle was found to be [blank]. After sunset the officer of the watch came to tell me that the jib boom had just carried away. It must have been very rotten indeed, since the wind was very moderate and the breeze light with a smooth sea. It was at once rigged in to be repaired next day. The night of the 29th to the 30th [Frimaire, 20-21 December 1800] had nothing remarkable; the sky was very clear and the winds variable from east to east-south-east. The Naturaliste was kept in sight until midnight, after which she disappeared without making us any signal to show her distance from us. We continued to keep close to the wind under our usual sail. From the 29th to the 30th Frimaire, Year 9, etc. [20-21 December 1800]. On the 30th [Frimaire, 21 December 1800] we had for the greater part of the day the winds east, variable towards east-south-east, a fresh breeze, but the weather was extremely hazy and we got several squalls with rain. In the forenoon, when the crew least expected it, they were all sent aft under the quarterdeck and a general search was then made of the bags and chests in the hope of finding a watch that had been stolen, belonging to Citizen Le Brun. A midshipman was also missing a silver spoon. The search was thorough and even scrupulous; nevertheless nothing was found. These articles being of too small a bulk, whoever took them will have taken care to put them in a safe place. At noon we observed the latitude 11° 11' 10" South, which gave us a difference from the reckoned latitude of 0° 8' 54". The longitude given by watch No. 31 put us in 30° 27' 32", and that of No. 38 in 30° 19' 32". That by the reckoning was 21° 53' 38". In the afternoon the winds stayed east, towards east-south-east, very variable and at times light. The sky turned hazier still than it had been in the morning, and about half past four we had a fairly heavy squall, of rain only. All day the sea had been much agitated with a hollow sea, but towards evening we found it far calmer. During the night of the 30th [Frimaire, 21 December 1800] to the 1st Nivôse [22 December 1800] the sky was now dark and damp and overcast, now very clear. The winds varied as far as east-north-east, but for a short time only. The stern lantern was lit almost all night to show the Naturaliste our position, and I cannot conceive why for three days she has never shown us hers, although she was at a considerable distance.
1800-12-20.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ESE. At noon in 9° 35' 20" of latitude observed and in 30° 22' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 14' NW.

1800-12-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea and a fresh breeze from ESE. During the night hoisted a light at the gaff to let the commander see us. From the 30th [Frimaire] to the 1st [Nivôse, Year 9, 21-22 December 1800]. The wind ESE, a fresh breeze, a high sea; we shifted our jib boom, which was broken.
1800-12-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to ESE. A jib boom was rigged in place of the one that had carried away the day before; a little rain. At noon in 11° 10' 33" of latitude observed and in 30° 27' 24" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 31' NW.

1800-12-22.journal_baudin: On the 1st Nivôse we had very fine weather all day and the winds held in the quarter variable towards the north. The breeze was even fresh enough, but we found the sea rather rough with a somewhat hollow swell. The Naturaliste being to windward of us, I hauled close to the wind to weather her, but as she did the same we could not get the wind of her until the evening. At noon the observed latitude was 12° 45' South, which gave us a very large difference to the south in the twenty-four hours, since it was 24 minutes. The observed longitude reduced to noon was for No. 31, 30° 14' 9", and for No. 38, 30° 5' 11". The reckoning put us in 21° 50' 38", and we found a difference of 8 minutes to the west. The watches on board the Naturaliste were 3 minutes further east than ours. In the evening we were obliged to change one of our topsail ties, which had already carried away twice. Yet the rope seemed to us sound. From a result of the morning and evening amplitudes compared with the azimuths, the variation of the needle was observed to be 5° 30' NW. During the night of the 1st to the 2nd [Nivôse, 22-23 December 1800] the weather was very fine and the breeze fresh enough, but the Naturaliste's poor sailing prevented us from profiting by it. We often showed our stern lantern to give her our position and learn hers, and as she did not answer us we had to shorten sail to wait until she was in sight.
1800-12-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE and E. At noon in 12° 44' 3" of latitude observed and in 30° 14' 12" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 29' NW. The lunar distances gave 30° 29' 30" of longitude. Saw tropic birds and flying fish.

1800-12-23.journal_anonyme: The wind ENE, a fresh breeze, the weather fine, the sea with a little swell; the commander bearing from us SSE 5° S.
1800-12-23.journal_baudin: On the 2nd [Nivôse, 23 December 1800] the weather continued fine and the breeze was east, varying to east by north, and rather light. The sea, which the past days had been hollow and rough, became smoother. We held on south-south-east so as to make more way, and to see whether, with the sheets a little eased, the Naturaliste would go better. By the end of the day little difference could be seen. She was, however, less bad than usual and did not fall so far to leeward. In the forenoon we took advantage of the fine weather to set up our fore shrouds, whose deadeyes were nearly together. At noon the observed latitude was 14° 19' 39" South, and we had a difference of 19 minutes 14 seconds to the south. The longitude given by the watches was, by No. 31, 30° 2' 38", and by No. 38, 29° 52' 24". The reckoning put us in 21° 30' 38"; in the twenty-four hours the currents had carried us 13' 29" to the west and 19' 14" to the south. From the mean result of several longitude observations by lunar distances of the sun from the moon, reduced to noon of the 1st Nivôse, we had for west longitude 30° 25' 49", which put us 0° 11' 40" further west than No. 31 gave, which was the one we had been using. In the afternoon, and especially after sunset, the sky turned very hazy and there was even the look of some squalls for the night; the wind, however, did not change, and we did not get the squalls that had made up on the horizon from south-east to north-east.
1800-12-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ENE. At noon in 14° 17' 40" of latitude observed and in 30° 8' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 41' NW. The lunar distances gave 30° 3' of longitude. The rigging was set up.

1800-12-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the commander in the SSE, the winds variable from SE by E to east.
1800-12-24.journal_baudin: On the 3rd [Nivôse, 24 December 1800] we had the winds east, variable towards the north, and very fine weather all day. In the forenoon we went on setting up the fore shrouds, this work begun the day before not having been finished before the end of the day. In the forenoon a very disagreeable scene occurred on board, which obliged me to send for Citizen Le Brun in my cabin — a man whose sour and unsociable character displeases everyone. After breakfast he had had a quarrel with Citizen Milbert over some pleasantries the latter had made at his expense, at the end of which he threw a glass of water in his face. Citizen Milbert, who was with reason very much offended by so unhandsome a way of answering a joke, would have given him a sound correction had not some of the ship's officers been there to prevent blows. On the report made to me of what had just happened, and having satisfied myself from the depositions of those who had witnessed the affair that Citizen Le Brun was entirely in the wrong, I had him asked to come to my cabin; and as this was not the first complaint laid against him, I told him very seriously that if he went on behaving badly I would put him under arrest in the gunroom and that he would only come out of it to be landed at Mauritius. At noon the observed latitude was 15° 42' South and that of the reckoning 15° 28', so that we again had a difference of 14' to the south. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 29° 44' 45", and for No. 38, 29° 33' 20". By the reckoning it was 21° 8' 38", and by the observation the current had again carried us 10 minutes 48 seconds to the west. On board the Naturaliste the longitude was signalled as 30° 6' 0", which gave a difference, taking a mean of our two watches, of 0° 26' 8". In the evening we took several distances of the sun from the moon, the result of which gave us for mean longitude, over fifteen observations, 30° 6' 15"; so these observations again put us 0° 27' 15" further west than the watches. In the night of the 3rd to the 4th [Nivôse, 24-25 December 1800], the winds having come to us from the north-east, I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south and myself steered that way at eight o'clock.
1800-12-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE, NE and NNE. At noon in 15° 41' 58" of latitude observed and in 30° 6' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 46' NW. The lunar distances gave 29° 50' of longitude. At 8 the course was given S 45° E. A little rain during the night.

1800-12-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the sky cloudy, a strong breeze from NE. The commander signalled us his position and we signalled him ours.
1800-12-25.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 4th [Nivôse, 25 December 1800] I was informed that during the night the greater part of the men of the port watch had got drunk and that it had not been possible to discover how this debauch had come about; but that among them some were so drunk that two came onto the quarterdeck, where, in the presence of the officer of the watch and all the quartermasters' mates, they set about breaking open the midshipmen's daily provision chest. When Citizen Le Bas was up I had a general search made, and after much looking it was found that they had drunk part of a small cask of Tenerife wine belonging to Citizen Le Brun, which they had discovered in the between-decks although it was well stowed among other goods. When I was satisfied that this was how they had got drunk, the whole watch was condemned to drink water until the cask was full again, and then to eight days on water for having been drunk. This last penalty applied only to the men who were drunk. In the forenoon we had very fine weather and the winds east-north-east, variable to north-east, which allowed us to steer full and by to the south-east. At noon the observed latitude was 17° 26' 54", which gave us a difference of 29' to the south beyond the reckoning. The longitude given by the marine watches was, for No. 31, 28° 47' 25", and for No. 38, 28° 34' 46". The reckoned longitude put us in 20° 14' 38", and there had been in the twenty-four hours a difference of 12' 34" to the west. In the evening the weather continued fine and it blew a fresh breeze. At sunset the sky turned extremely hazy, and although the night was clear enough we got about midnight a heavy shower of rain without any increase of wind, which lasted more than half an hour, after which the sky became fine again.
1800-12-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE. At noon in 17° 26' 33" of latitude observed and in 28° 57' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 50' NW. Heavy rain during the night.

1800-12-26.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind NE, a strong breeze. The commander signalled us the course SE.
1800-12-26.journal_baudin: On the 5th [Nivôse, 26 December 1800] we had the winds north-east and north-east by east, a fresh breeze. The sky was somewhat hazy and we had now and then a few small showers of rain, but of little consequence. In the forenoon part of the after hold was broken out to get at some casks of vegetables stowed there which we needed. During this work the ship lost much of her way and the Naturaliste, for the first time since the beginning of the voyage, gained on us, although we made more sail as she came up. The officer of the watch, Citizen Baudin, whose carelessness of his duties as a seaman is beyond anything one can imagine, put me so much out of humour that I was obliged to take part of his watch. I had already warned this officer that it was my intention that those on watch should, during that time, keep the conduct and bearing proper to such a duty. This one, however, almost always taken up while he is on deck with idle or at best useless things, and having no longer the means of amusing himself with the midshipmen of his watch, with whom he kept up a conversation always harmful to the good of the service, was this time busy drawing, leaning carelessly on the capstan. I found him so on coming out of my cabin, having watched him for some minutes. When he caught sight of me he put away his work and I went back in. Half an hour later I came out again and found him still busy with his drawing. Then, without saying anything to him, I took the watch and had the sails trimmed to the wind, which he ought to have done two hours before. I reserve for my arrival at Mauritius to let this officer know how dissatisfied I am with his conduct on watch. Although he knows where he stands on that head from all I have already said to him, there is every reason to believe we shall be obliged to part company if he does not change over the passage that remains to us. At noon the observed latitude was 18° 59' 9" South, which gave us 12' 15" of difference to the south. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, [blank], and for No. 38, 27° 0' 9". That of the reckoning put us in 18° 59' 9". The currents [blank]. In the afternoon the after part of the ship was restowed where it had been disturbed in the morning, and at once the Naturaliste returned to her station, that is, astern and to leeward. At sunset we had a slight shower of rain and some mist with a little wind, but both were of short duration and the sky became clear. The night of the 5th to the 6th [Nivôse, 26-27 December 1800] was fine enough despite a very hazy sky and clouds that did not look well. There was little wind.
1800-12-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to E. At 6.30 a.m. signalled the course S 45° E. At noon in 18° 56' 15" of latitude observed and in 27° 49' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 56' NW. Light rain during the night.

1800-12-27.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from NE, the sea with a little swell, the sky cloudy, the commander in the SSE at a great distance.
1800-12-27.journal_baudin: On the 6th [Nivôse, 27 December 1800] the winds were east-north-east in puffs, the sky much overcast and at times rainy, or rather misty. In the forenoon the ship was cleaned and fumigated from forward aft, and water was let into the hold to renew what was there, as it was beginning to smell bad. At noon the observed latitude was 20° 7' 33" South and this time we found no difference at all from the reckoning. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 26° 24' 21", and for No. 38, 26° 8' 53". The reckoning put us in 17° 49' 38", and, as with the latitude, we found no difference. Our position at noon laid down on the chart put us within sight of the Martin Vaz islets, and we should surely have sighted them had the longitude assigned to them been right. But we were the less surprised not to meet with them since, by Lapérouse's observations, they lie in 20° 30' 35" of latitude and 30° 30' of longitude, which put them about sixty leagues from us to the west by south-west. In the afternoon the breeze was very light and the wind unsteady. The sky, though fine, turned very hazy, and we had at times some misty clouds that gave us a little rain. The result of two amplitudes, morning and evening, gave for the mean variation of the two observations 5° 34' 12" NW. After sunset we had a few small squalls with rain and wind, which were of short duration. During the night of the 6th to the 7th [Nivôse, 27-28 December 1800] the wind was very uneven and often attended by misty clouds that brought some fairly strong gusts, but which were followed by a calm as soon as they had passed us. We carried very little sail all night to wait for the Naturaliste, who was at a considerable distance, though we had her in sight by the moonlight when the sky was clear.
1800-12-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE, NE and ESE. At noon in 20° 5' 43" of latitude observed and in 26° 59' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 34' NW. At 3 squally weather, with continual rain.

1800-12-28.journal_anonyme: The wind NE, a light breeze, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, a swell running. At 9 the winds drew round to ESE and we went onto the port tack. At daybreak sighted a ship in the WSW, which we signalled to the commander.
1800-12-28.journal_baudin: On the 7th [Nivôse, 28 December 1800], as soon as it was light we sighted a large ship to leeward of us, about two leagues off. The Naturaliste, who was far to leeward, seeing that we made her no signal about it, reported her to us, no doubt believing we had not seen her. As that ship appeared to be running north-north-west, we judged she might be an American bound for the continent. In the forenoon the winds were north-east but very unsteady. We were now becalmed, now making five and six miles under squalls that did no more than pass over and followed one another quickly. The sky would then be darkened by a kind of very damp mist, and a quarter of an hour later it could not be finer. At noon, as we were taking the altitude, one such cloud took the sun's light from us and we could get no observation of latitude. In the evening the same squalls came on again, but they were less frequent. At sunset we closed the Naturaliste, who was far to leeward. It seemed to me that although the winds allowed us to lie full and by to the south-east, that ship was steering some other course. The night of the 7th to the 8th [Nivôse, 28-29 December 1800] had nothing remarkable. The winds were light and very unsteady. At times we had a fine sky, but more often it was covered with misty clouds that gave us a soft, light rain which did our plants a great deal of good.
1800-12-28.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to ENE. At daybreak sighted a ship in the S 45° W, 9 miles off, standing on the opposite tack. The Naturaliste signalled her to us. At noon in 21° 5' 15" of latitude observed and in 26° 26' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 5° 50' NW.

1800-12-29.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from ESE, the sea smooth enough and the weather very unsettled. The commander bearing from us in the ESE.
1800-12-29.journal_baudin: On the 8th [Nivôse, 29 December 1800] the greater part of the day passed in calm, or at least with so little wind that we made very little way. What breeze there was proved extremely variable from east to south-east and even to south-south-east, which made the Naturaliste fall much further to leeward than usual. All through the forenoon the sky was very fine, though hazy, but about eleven o'clock a cloud came up which, obscuring the sun for more than three quarters of an hour, prevented us from observing its altitude, while the whole horizon all round was of a remarkable beauty. In the evening we met with a heavy swell from the south, which made us fear we should have the winds from that quarter. At sunset the sky turned very hazy and we were almost becalmed. During the night of the 8th to the 9th [28-29 December 1800] the breeze was rather steadier and the winds held in the quarter from east-north-east to east, a light breeze. We had at times some small misty clouds, but they soon cleared away and gave little wind. We were often obliged to make various changes in our sails to wait for the Naturaliste, who was rather too far astern. The southerly swell that had begun to be felt in the evening grew heavier, and everything led us to believe we should have the winds from that quarter next day.
1800-12-29.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SE. At noon in 21° 59' 43" of latitude by account and in 26° 3' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 5° 45' NW. Squalls and light rain at intervals.

1800-12-30.journal_anonyme: Wind east, a strong breeze in squalls, the weather very unsettled, a heavy swell running. At 10.30 we signalled the commander that our topsails were damaged; we at once unbent and repaired them. From the 9th to the 10th [Nivôse, Year 9, 30-31 December 1800]. Fine weather, almost calm. We crossed the Tropic of Capricorn on the 10th about 6 a.m. in 22° 2' 18" of latitude.
1800-12-30.journal_baudin: On the 9th [Nivôse, 30 December 1800] the breeze was very light and the winds extremely variable from east towards north and from east towards south. The sea, though smooth, was disturbed by a fairly heavy swell from the south which foretold winds from that quarter, or showed that they must have been blowing pretty hard there. About nine o'clock the Naturaliste signalled us several splits in her sails which she was going to repair at once, and as soon as we had answered her she took in her topgallant sails and main topsail, which obliged us in turn to shorten sail. At two in the afternoon she was in a state to go on under all plain sail, and we did the same. At noon the observed latitude was 23° 13' 42", so that we had the sun almost in the zenith. A singular enough remark is that since crossing the Line we had not had a single hot day, even at the times when there was least wind. The hygrometer, which had always stood above 90°, showed clearly that there was a great deal of moisture in the air, but we should never have imagined the quantity could be large enough to absorb so great a part of the sun's rays, towards which we were advancing each day; and yet when we were nearest to it the thermometer stood steadily at 17 and 18°. For two days we had been unable to observe the sun's meridian altitude, which, although the horizon was fine, was wrapped in cloud at that hour. That of this day was 23° 13' 42", which gave us in 72 hours a difference of 10 minutes 15 seconds to the south. The observed longitude was for No. 31, 26° 15' 42", and for No. 38, 25° 56' 17". The difference which the longitude of the watches gave us over these three days against the reckoning was far more considerable than the one we had to the south, since it was found to be 1° 0' 45" to the west — proof that the currents had not yet left us, as we had hoped from the small difference given by the last two observations. In the evening as in the night there was little wind, and the sea continued swelly from the south. The sky was fairly hazy and the very variable winds came at times as far round as south-south-east, almost calm.
1800-12-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E and ESE. At noon in 23° 13' 42" of latitude observed and in 26° 9' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 59' NW. At 9.15 crossed the Tropic of Capricorn.

1800-12-31.journal_baudin: On the 10th [Nivôse, 31 December 1800] the winds continued extremely variable and we had a very light breeze. In the morning we found that the southerly swell had increased considerably during the night, and all day we had a heavy sea, long and hollow, which did not promise fine weather and which would have tried the ship greatly had it blown a strong breeze. But as we were making little way we were not incommoded by it. About nine o'clock we had a light rain that lasted more than an hour and which, without being very heavy, still wetted through all the men of the watch. There was very little wind while it lasted, and less still when it had passed. At noon the observed latitude was 24° 2' 12" South, and we found no difference at all to the south from the reckoned latitude. The difference to the west by the result of the watches was almost as nil, for it was only 29 seconds. The longitude given by No. 31 was 26° 5' 29", and by No. 38, 25° 41' 41". That of the reckoning was then [blank]. At two in the afternoon we had a second squall which gave us more rain than the first and lasted longer too, without wind. For the rest of the day the weather was very unsettled and the winds extremely variable. We observed that since we had passed the sun the squalls always brought us calm, whereas those we had before reaching it gave us puffs that made us go a little way. In the night of the 10th to the 11th [Nivôse, 31 December 1800 - 1 January 1801] the sky became very fine and clear after moonrise, but what little breeze there was meant we made little southing. The heavy sea we had found that morning had become much less long and hollow, and the sea became smooth.
1800-12-31.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE and E. Saw a shearwater and flying fish. At noon in 24° 5' 1" of latitude observed and in 26° 14' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 3' NW.

1801-01-01.journal_anonyme: The weather hazy, the wind very light. Rain and fog in the afternoon; a swell running. The commander very close.
1801-01-01.journal_baudin: On the 11th [Nivôse, 1 January 1801], from the morning the little wind we had from the eastward fell away as the sun rose above the horizon, and everything foretold that the greater part of the day would pass in calm, as indeed it did, for at noon the ship would hardly steer, and after noon we were in a flat calm, obliged to clew up our courses. In the forenoon we took advantage of the fine weather to have the crew's clothes and hammocks put out to air, for they had taken the damp the day before, and I was obliged, with the officers, to see it done; for the surgeon-major whom we have in charge on board occupies himself with anything but his trade. As he is a maker of phrases and pamphlets, he is no doubt preparing some new production which he will not fail to send to the press by the first opportunity. I had put off until this day entering his daily conduct in my journal, being persuaded that the various warnings I have given him would bring about some change; but as he goes on as he began, and as his self-esteem suffers at being shipped as a surgeon, regarding that station as beneath him, I shall have patience until Mauritius, where I shall explain to him so plainly the conduct he is to keep on board that, if it does not suit him to conform to my intentions as to his duties, he shall be free to land — or, to put it better, I shall land him, even against his will. At noon the observed latitude was 24° 54' 18", which gave us a difference of 8 minutes to the south from the reckoning. The longitude by watch No. 31 was [blank], and by No. 38, 25° 31' 53". The reckoned longitude was then 16° 43'. The whole afternoon passed in calm, as did the greater part of the night, during which the sky was very fine.
1801-01-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from E and ESE. Saw several sharks. At noon in 24° 55' 30" of latitude observed and in 26° 12' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 23' NW.

1801-01-02.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the sea smooth, almost calm. We were busy setting up our main and fore shrouds.
1801-01-02.journal_baudin: On the 12th [Nivôse, 2 January 1801] we were no better off for wind than the day before, and it continued calm or nearly so until sunset. We employed our time on various jobs, and above all in cleaning the ship's outside, which already had much weed and barnacles fast to her wales. The small boat was put in the water for this. If the day was a blank for our progress, it was not so for natural history, for we took several very curious objects — among others a small marine animal in the shape of a lizard which seemed to us quite new, but which to our great regret we found described by M. de la Martinière in Lapérouse's voyage. As the description that naturalist gave of it is very exact, we could not be mistaken; but it is not the same with the engraving, which departs from it greatly. The drawing I give of it is much more exact, and it would be a pity that so pretty an animal should be known only by its description. Among the most curious objects we took, after the little animal I have just spoken of, is the Nautilus spirula, of which Linnaeus's description gives an idea, but which, though agreeing in several characters, differs in many others. I shall make particular mention of it in the journal of the voyage. We also took various species of Physsophora hydrostatica, which have been drawn in their natural colours and as true to life as it was possible to make them; for it is no easy thing to paint marine animals with all their detail and their brilliance. At noon the observed latitude was 24° 55' 35" South. The longitude given by No. 31 was at that noon 25° 31' 15", and that of No. 38, 25° 7' 45". The reckoning put us in 16° 22' 30" at the same hour. Neither the observation nor the watches gave any difference from the reckoning, so the current we had met with so constantly appeared to have ceased. In the evening the calm continued until sunset, when a light air came to us from south to south-south-east. During the night the weather was very fine, and the winds having drawn round to the south-east we went onto the port tack, signalling the Naturaliste to do the same; she was then half a league from us to leeward.
1801-01-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SW, S, SSE and SE. At noon in 24° 50' 34" of latitude observed and in 25° 52' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 17' NW. At 2 p.m. a boat was put in the water to clean the ship's outside. At the same time the draught was taken: 14 feet 4 inches aft and 12 feet 9 inches forward, which gives 1 foot 7 inches of difference.

1801-01-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind east, a light breeze. At 10 went about to close the commander.
1801-01-03.journal_baudin: On the 13th [Nivôse, 3 January 1801] the winds were nearly as calm as the day before and we made little way. This day, on which we had founded great hopes for natural history, was not a fortunate one, for everything we took in molluscs or other objects was like what we had already gathered. We met with no more of those little lizard-like creatures that were so pretty and singular, as may be seen from the very exact drawings I have given of them in the abridged journal. All we met with that was new was a kind of jellyfish, extremely pretty but which it is not possible to draw from what remains of it. At noon the observed latitude was 25° 22' South, and the longitude by the watches put us, for No. 31, in 25° 17' 15", and for No. 38, in 24° 52' 9". That of the reckoning gave 16° 30'. The small difference we had from the reckoning confirmed that the strength of the current was much diminished, or rather nil. The Naturaliste being rather too far off, we could not compare the results of our timekeepers. About eight in the morning the winds had drawn round to east-south-east, variable to east, and the breeze had freshened a little; but in the afternoon it fell calm again and we made very little way. Some moments after sunset the Naturaliste, for whom we were waiting and who had closed us considerably, put a boat in the water; and as it drew well away from the ship we thought it was coming aboard, which made me heave to. But seeing it turn back after going a good quarter of a league from its ship, it appears something had been seen on the water and they had gone to find out what it might be. As that ship made us no signal, it can have been nothing much. The night of the 13th to the 14th [Nivôse, 3-4 January 1801] was fine and the wind still calm, or at least so light that it came to much the same thing. The sky was often hazy and seemed to promise wind, but it all cleared away without giving any.
1801-01-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to NE. At noon in 25° 24' 12" of latitude observed and in 25° 34' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 20' NW.

1801-01-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At 7 p.m. we hove to and put a boat in the water to save a bag that had fallen overboard; a moment later we filled and stood on.
1801-01-04.journal_baudin: On the 14th [Nivôse, 4 January 1801] the breeze was still very light and we made little way. The winds varied from east to north-east in the forenoon, and in the evening they came round as far as north-north-east; but they had no strength in them and we went very little ahead. We flattered ourselves, however, that we had reached the region of the variable winds, in which we hope to find winds that will make up for the little we have met with until now. All day the sky was very fine. For all our watchfulness to see whether some mollusc of a new species might pass along the ship, we saw none that could hold our attention, and even the species we had met with on the preceding days had disappeared. At noon the observed longitude was [blank] for watch No. 31 and 24° 12' 48" for No. 38. The observed latitude had been found at noon to be 26° 5', which gave us a difference of one minute from the reckoning, so that the current we reckoned ourselves rid of still existed, only with less force. In the afternoon we made various shiftings in the hold to get at several articles of consumption we needed. They told considerably on the ship's sailing, since, under almost equal canvas, the Naturaliste passed ahead of us. It was, I think, the second time that had happened to her since our departure from France, and it will perhaps be the last once we have restowed what we have broken out. During the night of the 14th to the 15th [Nivôse, 4-5 January 1801] there was little wind. The sky was very hazy and nevertheless fine. The winds went round to the south-west, which persuaded us that we had the general winds from south-east and east behind us.
1801-01-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to N and WNW. At noon in 26° 5' 30" of latitude observed and in 25° 2' 0" of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 16' NW. At 10.15 there was a lunar rainbow in the west which lasted five minutes.

1801-01-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze from the south. The commander a long way off.
1801-01-05.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 15th [Nivôse, 5 January 1801] the Naturaliste was more than two leagues ahead of us and to windward. I do not know why, during a night that was often fine despite various squalls that made up on the horizon, she was allowed to draw so far off. Be that as it may, after sunrise she clewed up her courses to wait for us, which she might well have spared herself, for we should not have been long in joining her. At nine o'clock she made us a signal which, for all our attention, could not be made out, and which she hauled down half an hour later. At eleven o'clock, the wind having freshened a little, we had soon weathered her, and she had no other advantage left than being about a league to windward. In the forenoon several squalls made up on the horizon, which did not last long. We got some of them, which gave a little rain without much wind. At noon the observed latitude was 26° 33' 9". The longitude by watch No. 31 was 24° 23' 42", and by No. 38, 25° 56' 22". The reckoning put us in 14° 47' 30". On board the Naturaliste they signalled us 24° 31'. In the afternoon I signalled the Naturaliste that I had been unable to make out the signal she had made me in the morning; and as she mistook my question, or made out the flag wrongly, she took it for an order to close, so that she very quickly lost the small advantage she had gained in passing ahead of us. As the sky did not look well and there was the appearance of squalls and wind for the night, we furled the topgallant sails and took a reef in each topsail. I let the Naturaliste know before sunset that the course would be south-east if the winds, then south with a good breeze, drew aft during the night. As that ship did not hold her wind, we were obliged to bear away two points and a half to close her. In the night of the 15th to the 16th [Nivôse, 5-6 January 1801] it blew a fresh breeze from south to south-east and we went on running east, keeping close to the wind. There were now and then a few small squalls, but of little consequence. By the result of the watches reduced to noon, we found the currents had carried us 14 minutes to the west.
1801-01-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW, WSW, SW, SSW, S and SSE. At noon in 26° 34' 35" of latitude observed and in 24° 20' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 17' NW. In the afternoon overcast weather, with a little rain.

1801-01-06.journal_anonyme: The wind south, a fresh breeze, the weather squally, the sky cloudy. The commander ordered us to close him; when we were abeam of him he ordered us to steer SE as soon as we could.
1801-01-06.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 16th [Nivôse, 6 January 1801] the breeze was rather stronger and the sea somewhat rough, with a disposition to get up. After sunrise, the Naturaliste being far to leeward, we bore down on her to close her. In the forenoon the breeze increased, but it began to fall away as soon as the sun had passed the meridian. At noon the observed latitude was 26° 6' 5". The longitude given by No. 31 was 22° 48' 4", and by No. 38, 22° 19' 18". That of the reckoning put us in 12° 44' 0". From a series of twelve observations by lunar distances of the sun from the moon, the mean longitude was found to be 28° 38' 55" reduced to noon, which gave a difference from No. 31, the one we ordinarily used, of only 9' 9" further east than that watch. In the evening the winds were east-south-east, not strong, though the sky was loaded with cloud and there were several squalls on the horizon. We went on lying close-hauled on the east tack to reduce our longitude a little. At sunset we took a reef in each topsail and in the mizzen topsail, and closed the Naturaliste again, who was carrying much freer than we were. In the night of the 16th to the 17th [Nivôse, 6-7 January 1801] a few squalls passed over which brought a great deal of damp that made the air cold, but there was little wind. The sea was nevertheless beginning to get up, and there was no appearance of fine weather for the morrow.
1801-01-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. At noon in 26° 7' 30" of latitude observed and in 22° 28' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 6° 42' NW. The lunar distances gave 22° 40' of longitude.
