1801-01-07.journal_anonyme: The winds from SSW to SSE, the weather fine, the sea choppy. At 6 the commander signalled us to wear ship. We at once went onto the port tack.
1801-01-07.journal_baudin: On the 17th [Nivôse, 7 January 1801], at six in the morning, the winds seeming settled in the south-east, I signalled the Naturaliste to alter course and lie close-hauled on the port tack. I did the same myself and we both wore ship. In the forenoon the weather turned very bad and squally. As the sea, which we took head on, came very high, I had a second reef taken in the mizzen topsail and the topgallant masts struck. In the course of the forenoon, however, the sky became fine, but it blew hard until noon. The winds had drawn round to east-south-east. The observed latitude at noon was 25° 46' 2". Preparations had been made to take several lunar distances of the sun from the moon, which we could not observe, any more than an hour angle to learn the way we had made in longitude. The difference in the twenty-four hours was, by the log, [blank]. In the afternoon the sky was very fine and the breeze fell away a great deal. The sea too became smoother, and the look of bad weather we had had in the morning disappeared entirely. At sunset the variation of the needle was observed to be [blank] by an amplitude at setting. At seven o'clock we bore down on the Naturaliste, who was far to leeward, to close her and keep her in sight during the night. That ship, to make more way, always carried a point or two freer than we did. In the night of the 17th to the 18th [Nivôse, 7-8 January 1801] the winds varied from east-south-east to east and the breeze was steady enough. The sky cleared quite fine and the sea was smooth enough.
1801-01-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to E. At noon in 25° 46' 36" of latitude observed and in 21° 29' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 8° 40' NW. The lunar distances gave 21° 32' of longitude.

1801-01-08.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from SSE to ESE, the sky cloudy, a high sea.
1801-01-08.journal_baudin: On the 18th [Nivôse, 8 January 1801] we had a very fine breeze from the east and a clear sky all day, which gave us the opportunity of checking our longitude observations by taking fresh distances, which, reduced to noon of the day, gave 21° 35' 45". The longitude of No. 31 reduced to the same moment was 22° 4' 37", and that of No. 38, 21° 33' 27". The observed latitude was 26° 58' 26", which gave us little or no difference from that of the reckoning; but by the result of No. 31 we found the currents had carried us 31' 3" to the west in forty-eight hours, having had no observation of latitude the day before. In the forenoon decks were cleared generally and the ship was fumigated throughout. All the hammocks were also washed and spare ones issued until those just washed were dry. In the course of the evening the weather was fine, the winds east with a light breeze and a smooth sea. In the night of the 18th to the 19th [Nivôse, 8-9 January 1801] the sky for some hours did not look well, but after moonrise it all cleared away and turned fine again. The Naturaliste being rather far off, a light was shown for her to which she did not answer. At midnight, however, that ship was seen a little ahead of us. We then went on watching her and saw that she was keeping much too close to the wind, and that this was the chief reason why she made so little way and made us lose still more.
1801-01-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to E. At noon in 26° 58' 26" of latitude observed and in 21° 13' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 8° 48' NW. The whole hold was broken out to look, in vain, for a cask of rice; no one knows where it is, or whether it is aboard at all.

1801-01-09.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from ESE to east. The sky clear and a high sea. During the night we showed a lantern at the foremast head every half hour to give the commander our position and ask for his; it was not until 3 a.m. that we made out his stern light S ½ E.
1801-01-09.journal_baudin: On the 19th [Nivôse, 9 January 1801] the weather continued fine and the winds in the course of the day drew a little from east towards north. We should have made a fair run in these twenty-four hours had they steered on board the Naturaliste on the course indicated, and had that ship, instead of keeping her sails always shaking in order to work to windward, borne away a point to go faster. In order to show Captain Hamelin the bad seamanship practised on board his ship, especially at night, I had every sail set, which obliged him to bear away and consequently to make some way. In the forenoon we took fresh distances, the result of which will be found on the log table when they have been worked out. At noon the observed latitude was 28° 30' 27", which gave little difference from the reckoning. By the result of watch No. 31 we were at noon in 21° 30' 23", and by No. 38 in 20° 57' 44". The longitude by the observation of the sun's distance from the moon was 21° 16' 15", which gave 0° 14' 8" of difference to the east from No. 31. That of the reckoning was 11° 5', and we no longer had any hope that a current contrary to the one we had experienced would win back for us the way it had made us lose. In the afternoon we went on crowding sail to force the Naturaliste to keep her sails full and not amuse herself hugging the wind. The weather was very fine and the sea foretold calm. The breeze was even beginning to fall away. During the night we had to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste. The weather stayed fine but there was little wind.
1801-01-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ENE. At noon in 28° 32' 24" of latitude observed and in 20° 36' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 9° 2' NW. The lunar distances gave 21° 4' 24" of longitude.

1801-01-10.journal_anonyme: The wind east, blowing hard, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth. The commander a league ahead of us; we hoisted a light at the gaff to mark our position for him.
1801-01-10.journal_baudin: On the 20th [Nivôse, 10 January 1801], during the day the winds varied from east to north-east and the breeze was fine. Had the Naturaliste been able to keep up with us we should have made a good run in these twenty-four hours; but though she was covered with sail and we had only the foresail and topsails, how could she follow us? In the forenoon all the crew's spare clothing was put out to air, so that the ship looked like a clothing manufactory in which one might have found every shape and every colour. At noon the observed latitude was 29° 43' 9". The longitude by watch No. 31 was 20° 55' 36", and by No. 38, 20° 1' 24". Citizen Bissy, our astronomer, gave me for the first time since our departure the result of a longitude observation by a lunar distance of the moon from the sun, which, reduced to noon of this day, gave 19° 48' 0"; referred to the rate of No. 38, which he ordinarily uses, it differed by 0° 13' 24" to the east. In the afternoon the weather continued fine and the winds drew round to the north-east. From various azimuths taken morning and evening, the variation of the needle was found to be 8° 50' NW. The night of the 20th to the 21st [10-11 January 1801] had nothing remarkable. The winds drew round to the north, very light, and we went on steering south-east, keeping in sight of the Naturaliste, who was a little astern.
1801-01-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE and NE. At noon in 29° 42' 33" of latitude observed and in 20° 16' by No. 38. Variation 8° 50' NW.

1801-01-11.journal_anonyme: The winds from ESE to ENE, a light breeze, the sea smooth and the sky serene. At eight o'clock we could not see the commander; we made him signals to which he did not answer.
1801-01-11.journal_baudin: On the 21st [Nivôse, 11 January 1801], at daylight the Naturaliste was very far astern of us, although we had carried no sail during the night. As that ship was well to windward, it seemed to us she had not steered south-east. It had been noticed that for two days that ship did not follow the course indicated during the night. This was losing ground to no purpose, especially when the wind was not free. I do not know whether it is for the small pleasure of being to windward of us in the morning that such a manoeuvre is made. In the forenoon it blew a fresh breeze, and as usual we could not profit by it, having to wait for the Naturaliste. At noon the observed latitude was 31° 3' 0" South and the longitude of the watches reduced to noon was, for No. 31, 19° 10' 45", and for No. 38, 18° 35' 53". By the reckoning we ought to have been in 8° 32'. The difference given by the observation was 9' to the south and 0° 4' 21" to the west. After the sun's observation at noon I steered SE by E and made the signal to the Naturaliste, who probably will not have seen it given the distance she was at; but as she fell into our wake she must have seen that we had changed course from south-east to south-east by east. In the evening the breeze fell away a great deal and the stillness of the sea made us fear a calm. The course of the day was a fortunate one for natural history. We took several species of mollusc, one among others bearing a great resemblance to a set of organ pipes, and we gave it that name. We have found it described in Linnaeus under the name Salpa maxima. The fish were of the kind called Diodon holocanthus. But the most interesting thing we took was the Nautilus spirula wrapped in the mollusc in which it is found, and which I have had drawn from life. In the night of the 21st to the 22nd [Nivôse, 11-12 January 1801] the winds were the same and the breeze light. We held on south-east by east under little sail to give the Naturaliste time to join us.
1801-01-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to N. At noon in 31° 4' 40" of latitude observed and in 18° 43' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 8° 23' NW. At noon the course was given S 56° 15' E. All night the Naturaliste was not seen.

1801-01-12.journal_anonyme: The winds NE and ENE, a light breeze. The sky serene, the sea smooth, the commander ahead at a great distance. At 8 p.m. we lost sight of him, and it was not until 1.45 the next morning that we sighted him to windward of us. Crowded sail to close him.
1801-01-12.journal_baudin: On the 22nd [Nivôse, 12 January 1801] the winds varied from north by east to north-east by north and the breeze was very light all the forenoon. At daylight the Naturaliste was far to leeward of us, which led us to suppose she had not seen the signal announcing the course south-east by east, which is very likely. But as she had come into our wake the day before and had steered the same course as ourselves, I did not think she could have imagined we should steer south-east during the night. In the forenoon we took a dozen fish of the kind we had chased the day before, and almost all proved to be of the same size. Although the drawing I give of them is in their natural colours and perfectly well executed, several were stuffed and others put into spirits. At noon the observed latitude was 31° 45' 20" South and the reckoned longitude 7° 8' 9". That of No. 31 was 17° 48' 25", and No. 38 gave 17° 11' 22". During the evening the breeze was a little fresher than in the morning, but it fell away as the sun went down towards the horizon. The mean of two amplitudes and two azimuths gave for the variation of the magnetic needle 8° 24' north-west. The night of the 22nd to the 23rd [Nivôse, 12-13 January 1801] had nothing remarkable. There was little wind, and the Naturaliste having closed us within sight, we held the same course. In the middle of the night a very heavy swell from south to south-south-east began to be felt; and as this sea took us abeam, both the ship and ourselves were somewhat incommoded by it.
1801-01-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N and NNE. At daybreak the Naturaliste was sighted to leeward at a great distance; she had run during the night on the last course signalled (S 45° E). At 6 we signalled her the course S 56° 15' E. At noon in 31° 44' 40" of latitude observed and in 17° 8' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 8° 35' NW.

1801-01-13.journal_anonyme: The winds ENE and NE, a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth. At noon the winds freshened a little. At 7 a.m. we sighted a brig standing on the opposite tack and bearing from us NE by E. We signalled her to the commander.
1801-01-13.journal_baudin: On the 23rd [Nivôse, 13 January 1801] the winds were the same as the day before and the breeze fresh enough. After sunrise we sighted a sail to windward of us, bearing north-east. The distance we were at did not allow us to make out what ship she might be nor what course she was steering. In the forenoon I was informed by the chief medical officer on board that Citizen Millebert had passed an extremely troubled night, and that several times it had been necessary to wake him to calm the agitation caused him by his regret at being parted from his wife, his children and indeed all his family. For a long time it had been noticed that he had grown extremely melancholy, and the doctor, fearing this might tell on his health, begged me to speak to him in a way that would set his mind at rest. It is no doubt hard at sea to make cheerful a man who takes pleasure in being melancholy, and often all one can say to him only makes him feel more keenly the privations he is forced to bear. Nevertheless I asked Citizen Milbert to come to my cabin, and I used every means to let him know how sorry I was to see him in a state that could not but become fatal to him. After we had parted, I was told of one of the causes contributing to increase his anxieties. Someone — who no doubt had reproaches to make himself over his own conduct — had put it into his head that at the time of our departure from Tenerife I had written to the Minister of Marine about him in unflattering terms. I was at first astonished that he could have believed it, and I reproached him in a friendly way for not having told me of it sooner. It seemed to me the most straightforward course was to show him my letter, and I read it to him in full. I hope this condescension on my part will restore his cheerfulness, and I shall count myself very fortunate if it helps to do so. About eleven o'clock we saw an albatross, or more commonly a Cape sheep. This meeting was a subject of amusement, but it lasted little, for the bird, after going once or twice round the ship, disappeared. At noon the observed latitude was 32° 26' South and the reckoned longitude 6° 50' west. That given by watch No. 31 was 16° 9' 55", and that of No. 38, 15° 32' 47". During the evening there was little wind, and the swell we had met with in the night had increased greatly and caused us considerable rolling, as it took us abeam. At four in the afternoon I signalled the Naturaliste to steer east-south-east and headed that way myself. During the night the weather was fine and the breeze rather light. The heavy swell we had had for twenty-four hours began to go down.
1801-01-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NNW. A heavy swell from the SW. At 6.45 a.m. a ship was sighted in the N 45° E, standing west and 15 miles off. Saw an albatross. At noon in 32° 28' 37" of latitude observed and in 15° 26' of longitude by No. 38. The variation is 9° 52' NW. At 4 the course was given S 67° 30' E.

1801-01-14.journal_anonyme: The same winds, the weather fine, the sea smooth but with a swell from the SW. Saw several albatrosses.
1801-01-14.journal_baudin: On the 24th [Nivôse, 14 January 1801] we had a fine breeze from north-north-east to north-north-west and fine weather. Alone we should have made a great deal of way, but as we had to wait for the Naturaliste the run of the twenty-four hours was small for the wind there was. In the forenoon an albatross that was sitting on the water passed near the ship and was fired at from on board. I sent the boat for it, and it was handed to Citizen Maugé to skin. Its flesh, which I had dressed as a salmi, was generally found good, and although the table was well served nothing was left of the dish. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 1' South and the reckoned longitude 5° west. The longitude given by No. 31 was [blank] and that of No. 38, 13° 32' 52". In the afternoon the winds drew round to north-north-west and the breeze freshened a little until sunset. The sea was driven by a heavy swell from west-north-west which led us to judge that it had blown hard from that quarter in these parts. The variation of the needle, from the result of an amplitude at sunset and an azimuth after sunrise, gave 9° 6' north-west. During the night of the 24th to the 25th [Nivôse, 14-15 January 1801] the weather was very hazy with much damp in the air; nevertheless it was fine, and the Naturaliste, who was near enough to us, could carry all sail.
1801-01-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW and NNE. At noon in 33° 0' 54" of latitude observed and in 13° 38' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 9° 2' NW. At 1 p.m. hove to and put a boat in the water to fetch an albatross that had just been shot; it had 9 feet 8 inches of wingspan and 4 feet from head to tail. At 1.15 stood on again. At 3 the course was signalled and given S 78° 45' E.

1801-01-15.journal_anonyme: The winds drew round successively to N, NNE and NNW, the sky fine, the sea choppy. At half past noon we passed under the commander's stern; he ordered us to steer ESE.
1801-01-15.journal_baudin: On the 25th [Nivôse, 15 January 1801] the weather continued fine and the breeze, which was north-north-west and fresh enough, carried us a little to the east. In the forenoon the ship was cleaned and fumigated throughout, and a general inspection was made of the state of the crew's clothing. That of several needing repair was handed to the tailor with pieces of cloth to put it in a serviceable state. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 5' South and the reckoned longitude 2° 25' west. That of watch No. 31 put us in 11° 31' 55", and No. 38 in 10° 52' 37". As the observations of the 24th were doubtful, having been set about too late to be had with accuracy, we found that in the forty-eight hours the currents had carried us 0° 5' 51" to the south and 6° 15' 42" to the east. In the afternoon it continued to blow a fresh breeze, but the sky turned hazy and extremely charged with vapour. The horizon in various quarters was ringed with great dark black clouds that did not look well. The night, however, was fine, and the Naturaliste, so as not to lose ground, furled only her royals. By an amplitude at sunset the variation of the needle was found to be 9° 53' north-west. This observation does not deserve much confidence. The heavy swell from west-north-west that we had had for two days began to go down and the sea gave no sign of bad weather. During the day we saw several albatrosses and two or three storm petrels.
1801-01-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW and NW. At noon in 33° 5' 20" of latitude observed and in 11° 1' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 9° 45' NW.

1801-01-16.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, a light breeze, the sea smooth and the weather squally. The commander bearing from us ESE at a short distance. At noon the weather turned clear.
1801-01-16.journal_baudin: On the 26th [Nivôse, 16 January 1801] the weather was bad all day, although the wind stayed south-south-west and moderate. At sunrise the whole horizon was extremely dark and loaded with great black clouds, so that we hardly knew from where the wind would come. The barometer, which had fallen three lines, gave us clear enough warning of the change that was preparing, and we were in a state to bear it should it turn bad in the course of the day. At seven o'clock, as the worst appearance was in the south, I had a reef taken in the mizzen topsail and the mizzen topgallant mast struck, being useless to us. The halliards of the lower yards were also rove. Shortly afterwards it came on to rain. The winds during the squall came to west and south-west, where they stayed for the rest of the day. Although we often had light puffs with mist, the Naturaliste, in order to close us, took in none of her sails. At noon there was a clear interval that allowed us to observe the latitude. It was found to be 32° 59' South. The reckoned longitude at noon was [blank]. As there was no hour angle this day, we could not learn by our timekeepers how far we had advanced to the east. After the sun's observation I signalled the Naturaliste the course east-south-east and steered that way myself. During the evening the weather was no finer than in the morning. We had alternately a misty rain and fine weather. The slight motion of the sea, however, did not positively foretell bad weather, and the clouds, though fairly low, did not drive with any great speed, from which we concluded that the middle region of the atmosphere was calm enough. Before sunset, our horizon being far from fine, I had a reef taken in each topsail, and everything was made ready so as not to be embarrassed in the night should it turn bad. In the night of the 26th to the 27th [Nivôse, 16-17 January 1801] the weather was better than the look of it promised. It blew a fresh breeze from south-south-west, and alone we should have made a great deal of way.
1801-01-16.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW, W, SSW and south. The mizzen topgallant mast was struck. At noon in 32° 59' 30" of latitude observed and in 8° 21' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 14° 52' NW. At noon the course was given S 67° 30' E.

1801-01-17.journal_anonyme: The winds drew round from N to NNW, a strong breeze. The weather overcast, the sea smooth; the commander signalled the course ESE.
1801-01-17.journal_baudin: On the 27th [Nivôse, 17 January 1801] the winds were south-south-west with a fresh breeze, but the sky was not fine and the barometer promised no fine weather. In the forenoon I had our lower-mast preventer backstays got up and fitted, so as to have only to put them in place should circumstances require it. The sea, which had smoothed in the night of the 25th to the 26th [Nivôse, 15-16 January 1801], became swelly again and the ship was tried by a heavy sea which we judged must give us a fairly large difference to the north, and perhaps to the east as well. Our conjectures were true up to a point, for at noon the observed latitude was 32° 55' 56" South, whereas by the course we had run it should have been much greater; so we found a difference to the north of 0° 16' 0". The longitude given by watch No. 31 was 6° 6' 4", and that of No. 38, 5° 25' 23". By the reckoning we were 2° 49' 24" east of the meridian of Paris. During the day we saw neither albatrosses nor petrels such as we had met with on the preceding days. But several people were positive they had seen two or three different species of fucus pass along the ship. As I did not see them, I do not know what species they may be, supposing there was no mistake; for from the way they have been described, I know of no species of fucus to which they can be referred. In the evening it continued to blow a fresh breeze from south-south-west. In a squall that did not last long the winds drew round to the east, but they came back at once to south-west by south. I signalled the Naturaliste the course south-east by east and headed that way myself. After sunset the sky stayed dark and several very black squalls made up in various parts of the horizon. The night, however, was not bad, and although the sky was very dark and the weather squally, we were obliged to shorten sail only to wait for the Naturaliste.
1801-01-17.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to south. At noon in 32° 58' 42" of latitude observed and in 5° 57' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 22' NW. At 1.30 signalled the course S 67° 30' E. At 2 it was signalled and given S 56° 15' E. During the night, squalls and rain.

1801-01-18.journal_anonyme: The wind SSW, a fresh breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth. The commander signalled us his position, after which he signalled us the course SE by E.
1801-01-18.journal_baudin: On the 28th [Nivôse, 18 January 1801] the weather continued to look bad until about three in the afternoon, when it cleared fine enough in the quarter of [blank], foretelling the winds from that point of the horizon, from which they did indeed come to us after sunset. During the day the ship was cleaned and fumigated throughout. We also set up our topmast shrouds and backstays, which needed it. At noon we had no observation of latitude. That by the reckoning of the run from the log was 52° 49' 31" South and the reckoned longitude 5° 18' 4" east. In the afternoon, although the weather had mended a little, we bent our storm sails in case we should need them during the night. A short time after sunset the sky turned dark again, very hazy and overcast. During the night the winds were variable from south to south-east, and I went on holding the east tack towards the north in the hope that the winds would come back to the south. During the night we had regulated our canvas so as to keep the Naturaliste at the same distance she was at the end of the day. Nevertheless at midnight, not seeing her, we clewed up our mainsail and made her various signals to get her to let us know her position, to which she did not answer, which obliged us to keep a light burning at the stern until daybreak. It appears that ship did not see our signals, for I must believe she would have answered had she known of them.
1801-01-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. Saw petrels and albatrosses. At noon in 32° 52' of latitude by account and in 3° 47' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 16° 14' NW. At 5 signalled the Naturaliste to haul close to the wind. We passed through a tide rip.

1801-01-19.journal_anonyme: The winds from SSW to south, a strong breeze, the sea smooth, the weather overcast. At 5 p.m. the commander made us the signal to haul close to the wind. At 8 a.m. the crossjack yard lift parted with a heavy pitch; it was repaired at once. At noon wore ship.
1801-01-19.journal_baudin: On the 29th [Nivôse, 19 January 1801] the weather was no finer than the day before. The sky in the forenoon was even more overcast and darker. The wind, however, was moderate and the heavy puffs that passed did not last long. At daylight we saw the Naturaliste very far to leeward of us; it seemed to us that ship, having been afraid of bad weather, had greatly shortened sail. To give her the means of closing us more quickly we bore down on her and at the same time took a second reef in the topsails. At noon the sun showed itself between the clouds and we observed its altitude which, though doubtful within a few minutes, was still better than our reckoning. The latitude was thus found to be 31° 46' 30", which gave us about one degree twelve minutes of northing in two days. Our longitude by the reckoning was then 7° 32' 24" east. As soon as the latitude was observed I made the signal to go about, and we took the south tack on the port tack. The winds came shortly afterwards from south-east to east-south-east. The sky was fine enough until three o'clock. At that hour the clouds had broken up in various parts of the horizon and we even reckoned on being able to observe a distance of the moon from the sun. Our hopes did not last long, for by four o'clock the weather was as dark and overcast as it had been for two days. The barometer, however, had risen a great deal, and the sea, though swelly, gave no sign of bad weather. At six o'clock I signalled the Naturaliste that if the winds came fair during the night we should steer south-east. The night of the 29th to the 30th [Nivôse, 19-20 January 1801] had nothing remarkable; we passed it under the foresail and close-reefed topsails to keep in sight of the Naturaliste, who was to leeward within gunshot. The sky was very overcast, we saw neither the moon nor the stars, and the gusts were less frequent than the night before.
1801-01-19.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 31° 48' 10" of latitude observed and in 2° 20' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 18° 13' NW. At 5 signalled the course S 45° E should the winds draw aft. During the night rain and the wind in gusts.

1801-01-20.journal_anonyme: The wind SSE, a fresh breeze in squalls, the weather overcast, the sea rather high. At 7.45 the course was signalled us ESE. Took in the reef of the mizzen topsail.
1801-01-20.journal_baudin: On the 30th [Nivôse, 20 January 1801] the winds held steadily between east and south and were very variable. The sky seemed disposed to clear fine, and the clouds breaking up let us catch sight of the sun from time to time. The barometer, which had risen a great deal, also seemed to promise fine weather, and we hoped by that means to see the winds change. The sea too had gone down a great deal and we had almost lost that heavy south-west swell which had troubled us on the preceding days. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 10' 24" and the longitude by the reckoning 7° 3' 24" east. As no hour angle could be had that morning, we had no longitude from the watches. In the evening the sky, which had seemed inclined to clear, turned dark and overcast again, and we had now and then some gusts, but of little consequence and short duration. We went on holding the south tack, regulating ourselves by the Naturaliste's sailing, keeping her to leeward of us within gunshot. At six o'clock I signalled her that if the winds drew aft during the night we should steer south by east. This day we took a small marine animal which, without having the elegant shape or the brilliant colours of the lizard described by M. de la Martinière in Lapérouse's voyage, seemed to us far more interesting for its structure and the liveliness of its movements. The drawing I give of it is not perfect, because this animal changes shape so suddenly that it is impossible to seize one; but we recognised it plainly for a kind of mollusc which there is every reason to believe has not been observed up to this moment. I have put several specimens in spirits which seem likely to keep well, and perhaps on our return the naturalists will be able to make an exact description of them. We also took a kind of fucus which we did not know to what genus to refer. It was found to have various points of resemblance with the longissimus and the giganteus, but those two plants have not, in their description, all the particulars offered by the one of which I give the drawing. In the night of the 29th [Nivôse] to the 1st Pluviôse [20-21 January 1801] the sky stayed dark, overcast and damp. The cold was even rather sharp. The winds held, as during the day, between east and south and were very variable.
1801-01-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At noon in 33° 11' 50" of latitude observed and in 1° 57' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 52' NW. At 5 signalled the course S 56° 15' E should the winds draw aft.

1801-01-21.journal_anonyme: The winds SE and SE by E, a strong breeze, the weather overcast, a swell running.
1801-01-21.journal_baudin: On the 1st Pluviôse [21 January 1801] the weather was the same as the day before; the sky, however, seemed at various times inclined to throw off the gloom that had hidden it from us for several days. In the forenoon we saw several albatrosses and some petrels of a species we had not yet noticed. There was some amusement on board in firing at several of them, but none was hit, although they were well within range. At noon we observed the latitude 34° 31' South, and the reckoned longitude was 6° 34' 24" east by the run measured with the log. That given by watch No. 31 was 3° 46' 56", and that deduced from No. 38, 3° 4' 56". In the afternoon, the weather having allowed us to take several distances of the moon from the sun, we found the longitude 3° 49' 30", which gave a difference from No. 31 of 2' 34" further west than that watch. During the evening the winds were as they had been in the morning, that is, very variable between east and south. The breeze we had during the day, though moderate, was not without unsteadiness, and we had several times some strong gusts, but of short duration. During the night the sky was dark and damp. The cold was even found rather sharp, although the thermometer had not fallen below thirteen degrees. The barometer, on the contrary, was beginning to rise and promised fine weather, as did the sea, whose swell and motion had much diminished. We went on holding the south tack under the courses and close-reefed topsails, this canvas being enough to keep way with the Naturaliste, who had all sail set.
1801-01-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to E. At noon in 34° 30' 0" of latitude observed and in 2° 20' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 15° 50' NW. The lunar distances gave 2° 9' of longitude.

1801-01-22.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from SE to SSE. A light breeze, the sky cloudy, a swell running, the commander to leeward at a middling distance.
1801-01-22.journal_baudin: On the 2nd [Pluviôse, 22 January 1801] in the morning the winds were less variable than on the preceding days and drew more to the east. The sky too was less overcast and we had the look of a fine day, but also of very little wind, and the sea foretold calm. About eight o'clock we spoke the Naturaliste and asked whether she could spare us a little rice, ours being so stowed that it has not been possible up to this moment to come at it. Captain Hamelin answered that he would send us some. His longitude, observed the day before by distances of the moon from the sun, was 2° 25' west of Paris, and that by his watches 2° 57', so that there was a considerable difference between the rate of his watches and his observations and ours, since it was, for the watches, 14' 44" taking a mean with ours, and by his observations 53' 45", taking likewise the mean of M. Gicquel's and my own. In the forenoon we had no hour angle to determine the rate of our watches since the last observation, but the latitude was found to be 35° 49' South. Our reckoning put us in 6° 38' 24" of east longitude. About three o'clock Captain Hamelin signalled to ask leave to send a boat on board, which was granted. By the letter he wrote me he let me know that all his crew and the naturalists were in good health and that good harmony and understanding reigned among them all. He added, however, that he had been obliged to have one of his seamen punished. He did not tell me for what cause. He also sent us a portion of the rice he had left. In the evening the weather was almost calm and the winds very variable. We took a great number of distances to check those of the day before, the mean result of which put us in 3° 5' 57". This day was very profitable for natural history: we took several new species of mollusc, a small fish of the greatest beauty, and a kind of shell that seemed to us entirely new. The animal it lodges is also very singular; it has the faculty of swimming, and even very fast, carrying its house with it. We took a great number of them. It appears this animal serves as food for various fish, for we recognised the same fragments of shell in the stomachs of those we had taken some days before. The coloured drawing I give of all these objects will make them far better known than any description I could make. Besides, I think the anatomists would have taken up that work, which properly belongs to them. Nevertheless I have preserved some in spirits for the Museum. After sunset the winds drew round to the north-east, and in the night they veered as far as west-south-west, where they stayed a short time before returning to the north. The breeze was light and the sky extremely damp, the horizon loaded with squalls that at times gave rain, but in small quantity. We shook out a reef from the topsails and went on steering south-east by east with the Naturaliste in our wake at a short distance.
1801-01-22.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to N. At 9 we spoke the Naturaliste. The commander asked Captain Hamelin to give him a little rice. He answered that he would share with him the little he had. At noon in 35° 50' 26" of latitude observed and in 2° 15' of longitude by No. 38. The lunar distances gave 2° 30' of longitude. At 2.30 the Naturaliste having asked to communicate, we granted it and hove to. Her boat brought rice for the commander. At 3.30 we filled and stood on. At 6, the breeze having drawn aft, shaped the course S 56° 15' E.

1801-01-23.journal_anonyme: The winds from east to ENE. The weather fine, the sea with a little swell. At 3 p.m. we sent a boat aboard the Géographe. At 4 the weather squally and the horizon much loaded in the east, spreading towards the west. At 8 a.m. the commander signalled us the course ESE.
1801-01-23.journal_baudin: On the 3rd [Pluviôse, 23 January 1801] in the forenoon the winds, which during the night had been from east round to north-west with a light breeze, drew successively from north-west to south-west. The sky, loaded with clouds that drove with great speed from that quarter, promised no fine weather, and the barometer had indeed fallen a great deal. About ten o'clock, the winds having drawn round to the south-west, it began to blow a fresh breeze, and it went on increasing until about four in the afternoon, when I had a second reef taken in the topsails to wait for the Naturaliste and to keep her from carrying too much sail to follow us, for at that hour she still had her topgallant sails set. At noon we observed the latitude 36° 13' South, and as no hour angle had been observed in the morning we had no longitude from the watches. That of the reckoning, without correction since our departure from Tenerife, was 7° 44' 44" east. In the afternoon it blew a strong breeze from south-south-west and the sea got up. At six o'clock I had the topgallant masts struck, and at seven a third reef was taken in the fore topsail. At that hour the Naturaliste was about half a league astern of us and in our wake. During the night of the 3rd to the 4th [Pluviôse, 23-24 January 1801] it continued to blow a strong breeze until about eleven o'clock, when the winds, having drawn round to the south, began to fall away. We kept our stern lantern lit all night, thinking the Naturaliste would do the same, or that at least she would show us a light from time to time to give us her position; but for all our care in watching for her we saw nothing. At midnight, although the wind had fallen a great deal, I had the mainsail furled, being persuaded that ship was astern. We lay thus waiting for her, the ship labouring a great deal for want of sail; and at four o'clock we were greatly astonished to see her half a league ahead of us and to windward. It appears she had concealed her sailing from us for the sorry pleasure of finding herself next morning ahead of us and to windward, while we had let ourselves be much knocked about by the sea in waiting for her.
1801-01-23.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW, NW, WSW, SW, SSW and S, with squalls and rain. At 8 the course was signalled and given S 67° 30' E. At noon in 36° 13' of latitude observed and in 1° 38' of west longitude by No. 38.

1801-01-24.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from ESE to east and to NE. A high sea. At 9 p.m. the main jib stay parted; it was repaired at once. Lightning from every point of the horizon.
1801-01-24.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 4th [Pluviôse, 24 January 1801] the winds were south, varying to south by west and at times south-south-west. The breeze was moderate and there was even the look of its falling further, but the sea was much agitated from the wind of the night and of the day before. We also had a heavy swell from the south-west that tried us a great deal. In the forenoon, however, we shook out a reef from the topsails and set the mizzen topsail, which had been furled the day before, as well as our staysails, in order to come up quickly with the Naturaliste, who was ahead of us. By noon we had closed her and passed her to leeward, to do her the honours of our sailing. At noon the observed latitude was 35° 49' South. Neither was there any longitude this day for the rate of the watches, no hour angle having been had. That of our reckoning put us in 10° 40' 36". In the afternoon until sunset the wind was slack and in the same quarter; the sea, still high and swelly, tried us a great deal and we felt at times some considerable rolling. During the night of the 4th to the 5th [Pluviôse, 24-25 January 1801] the winds were very variable from SSW to south-south-east; and as we carried little sail so as not to draw too far from the Naturaliste, the ship laboured a little in the heavy swell that was still running, though it had gone down a great deal from what it had been on the preceding days. During the day we had seen many albatrosses, petrels, and a kind of black gull with an entirely white belly whose flight came singularly close to that of the snipe. It was the first time we had seen this species of bird.
1801-01-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S and SSE. At noon in 35° 39' of latitude observed and in 1° 5' of east longitude by No. 38. From today, longitudes given without a name are to be understood as east. The topmast studdingsail booms were rigged in.

1801-01-25.journal_anonyme: The wind SW, a fresh breeze, the sky overcast, a swell running.
1801-01-25.journal_baudin: On the 5th [Pluviôse, 25 January 1801] the sky, though hazy and overcast, was less dark than it had been for several days, and we had hopes of being able to take an hour angle to get the longitude from our watches, of which we had been deprived for several days. In the forenoon the sky was fine enough and the winds south, variable to south-south-east. The weather was cold and everyone had got out his winter clothes. We were astonished to find the winds in this latitude so constant in the quarter from south towards east as they were; and as the moon's first quarter was past, we had no further hope of seeing them change before she came to the full. Well for us if our hopes are not disappointed. At noon, the sun being clear, we observed the latitude 35° 10' South, which gave us a difference of a few minutes from our reckoning. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 2° 11' 20" east, and for No. 38, 2° 55' 52" east. On board the Naturaliste they signalled us 2° 45', so that for a fortnight past their watches, which had always been nearly a degree ahead of ours, seemed to have lost considerably, which we put down to the change of temperature. By our reckoning from the log we were in 12° 30' 54" east, and consequently very near the Cape of Good Hope. In the evening the breeze fell away a great deal and there was even the look of calm for the night. At seven o'clock we bore down on the Naturaliste to close her, as she lay nearly a league to leeward. At eight, having got her into our wake, we resumed our course east-north-east, regulating our canvas by her sailing. In the night of the 5th to the 6th [Pluviôse, 25-26 January 1801] the winds were extremely variable, always from [blank] to SSE and yet at times south-south-west. We made little way, but on the other hand we were not a little tossed about by the sea, which had become swelly again. During the day several albatrosses and petrels had been seen, as well as gulls like those of the day before. Some claimed to have seen a pintado petrel, but I did not see it myself.
1801-01-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 35° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 2° 33' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 20° 13' NW.

1801-01-26.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from south to S by W, the sky cloudy, the sea rather high, the commander a short distance off.
1801-01-26.journal_baudin: On the 6th [Pluviôse, 26 January 1801] in the forenoon the sky, though still half overcast, was fine enough. We could not, however, see the sun to observe an hour angle. The winds continued very variable, but at least they were from south to south-south-west; and though they were fair, the breeze was very light, and indeed we could not profit by it, being obliged to take in all our staysails to wait for the Naturaliste, who was far astern. During the forenoon we were obliged to break out part of our after hold to get at wine and other provisions we needed. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 45' South, which gave a single minute of difference from the reckoning. About ten o'clock we began to feel a very heavy swell from the south-west which, coming on us all at once, made us think that the wind sending it might not be far off and that we might soon see it arrive. The reckoned longitude at noon put us in 13° 54' 54". About three o'clock, the sun having shown itself, Citizen Bissy observed an hour angle which, referred to No. 38, the watch he uses, gave 4° 4' 54" of east longitude. In the evening we restowed our hold, and in doing that work we had the pleasure of coming upon one of our casks of rice which we had looked for in vain several times over. At sunset it continued to blow a light breeze from south-south-west, but in the night the winds veered to the south and it fell a good deal calmer. We steered close-hauled, taking care to keep a reasonable distance from the Naturaliste.
1801-01-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon in 34° 44' 30" of latitude observed and in 3° 57' of longitude by No. 38. At noon the course was given S 56° 15' E, and it was signalled to that point of the compass at 5.15.

1801-01-27.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from SSE, the weather fine, the sea with a little swell. At 8.30 a.m. the commander signalled us the order to bear down on him; at 9 we repaired a split in the main topsail and signalled him at once.
1801-01-27.journal_baudin: On the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1801] in the forenoon the winds were from south-east to south and nearly calm, and we made very little way. In the evening they drew round to the south-west and even west-south-west, but there was very little wind; we swayed up our topgallant masts to close the Naturaliste, who had gained a great deal on us by means of all her light sails. At eight o'clock we had her abeam, about half a league to leeward. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 36' 50" and the longitude by the reckoning 15° 9' 32" east, so that by our position from the log we were very near the Agulhas Bank; but as nothing gave us any sign of its nearness, we were not surprised to find ourselves still very far from it. By watch No. 31 the longitude was 4° 22' 15" east, and by No. 38, 5° 11' 2". The mean of these two watches, putting us in 4° 46' 38" 30‴, was much more likely than our reckoning, of which we had long made very little account. In the evening the weather turned fine, and the sky, which had long been covered with cloud and very dark to us, became clearer, and we had a fine sunset, which had not happened to us for many days. The air too had grown less cold. During the night of the 7th to the 8th [Pluviôse, 27-28 January 1801] the winds were variable from south-west to west-north-west, but there was so little wind that we did not go far. During the day of the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1801] we took various objects of natural history, the most interesting above all in the mollusc kind; the coloured drawings I give of them are made with the greatest exactness, and no doubt when they are seen it will be hard to believe that such things can exist. For what we took has far more likeness to a beautiful flower than to a living animal. After drawing these objects we put the marine animals into spirits; their shape has changed a great deal, but at least the gelatinous matter of which they are composed seems to have taken consistency enough to give hope of preserving them. It is particularly to Citizen Maugé that we shall owe the knowledge these captures may bring, for they were no doubt unknown until this moment.
1801-01-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE, south, SW and NW. At 8, she being abeam to leeward at a short distance, we signalled her to open the distance between the columns. At noon in 34° 37' 5" of latitude observed and in 5° 12' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 21° 44' NW.

1801-01-28.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from east to ENE, the weather fine, the sea smooth; the commander far off in the WNW. We found our main topgallant mast was rotten and shifted it at once.
1801-01-28.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 8th [Pluviôse, 28 January 1801], the Naturaliste being about three leagues ahead of us, I had the reefs shaken out of the main and fore topsails and we rigged out our studdingsail booms to starboard to join her. I still do not know for what reason she was allowed to draw so far off. In the forenoon the breeze was very light and we made little way. We were in no way compensated for the loss of this time by meeting with any new objects on the water, for we took only a single Portuguese man-of-war, though of a new species, whose filaments were ten or twelve feet long. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 21' 29" South, which gave us a considerable difference from our reckoning, since we found we had been set to the north 26' 9" more than we reckoned. The longitude given by No. 31, reduced to noon, was 4° 46' 43", and that of No. 38, 5° 31' 23", which gave a difference of rate between these watches of 0° 44' 40". In the afternoon, going through the log book kept by the officers, I noticed a remark I was far from expecting to find there. As Citizen Baudin had the watch from noon to four, I asked him, talking with him, by what singularity the Naturaliste had gained so much on us during the night. His answer was that we had carried little sail. I made him no other objection than this: who prevented you from making more? — and we changed the subject. I was far from having shown him any displeasure, the more so as the officer who had had the middle watch was perhaps as much in the wrong as he. Yet when I had gone back to my cabin he sent for the log book and entered a remark in it which I have struck out only in such a way that it can still be read. I asked him to explain his remark and what it was meant to say. His answer was that it was for the officer to whom he had handed over the watch, so that his answer, like his remark, was as meaningless as the other. In the afternoon the breeze continued very light. I gave the course south-east so as to make up for the effect of the currents and to keep to the south of the Cape, since we shall surely still have winds from that quarter before we have doubled it. At sunset we found, by the mean result of two amplitudes with different compasses, that the variation of the needle for the place we were in was 22° 30' NW. In the night of the 8th to the 9th [Pluviôse, 28-29 January 1801] there was very little wind but the sky was fine. Citizen Bissy was to take a longitude by an observation of Jupiter from the moon.
1801-01-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from W to SW. At noon in 34° 21' 31" of latitude observed and in 5° 45' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 23° 2' NW. At noon the course was given S 45° E and was not signalled until 6 o'clock. We spoke the Naturaliste. Captain Hamelin informed the commander that he had shifted his main topgallant mast, which was rotten.

1801-01-29.journal_anonyme: The winds from south to SW. At 6 p.m. the captain asked the commander's leave to put a boat in the water on the first calm day, to clean the ship's outside, which was granted him. The weather very light, the sea smooth and the sky serene.
1801-01-29.journal_baudin: On the 9th [Pluviôse, 29 January 1801] the weather continued fine, but there was so little wind in the forenoon that we scarcely went ahead. We took advantage of this calm to repair our main topsail, which was split, and to give ourselves to fishing, which was fortunate and abundant this day in objects new to natural history. We took above all a small fish of the trunkfish kind, of the greatest beauty and of the most extraordinary shape. The various species of mollusc are no less interesting and extraordinary in their shape and the brilliance of their colour. I even think that if most of the originals we have put into spirits to preserve should decompose, it will be hard to believe that living animals can exist of a shape like those we met with, and of which the coloured drawings have been taken with the greatest exactness. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 13' 50", to our great astonishment; for after steering south-east with the sea smooth enough though swelly, we did not expect to find a difference of 19' 57" to the north and one of 24' 13" to the west by the rate of our watches. No. 31 put us in 5° 20' 16" and No. 38 in 6° 5' 13" of east longitude. That of the reckoning at noon was 17° 9' 38". In the afternoon the breeze was much the same and the winds variable from SSW to SW, very light. We spoke the Naturaliste, who let us know that the day before, while she was far ahead of us, she had shifted her main topgallant mast, which had been found rotten. Everyone on board that ship was very well, but they had taken little in the way of natural history. We had, however, shown them how to set about it. From a series of observations made the day before, the variation of the needle was found to be 22° 25' 30" for the place the ship was in. In the night of the 9th to the 10th [Pluviôse, 29-30 January 1801] there was little wind; the sea, or rather the heavy south-west swell we had had the day before, went down a great deal and the sea became smooth enough. When the moon was on the meridian the sky clouded over without the wind increasing, and there was no appearance of a fine day for the morrow.
1801-01-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SW. At noon in 34° 14' 6" of latitude observed and in 6° 25' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 22° 5' NW. Saw a shark.

1801-01-30.journal_anonyme: The wind SW, very light. At noon the commander laid his mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for us. The weather fine, the sea smooth.
1801-01-30.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 10th [Pluviôse, 30 January 1801] the winds varied from south-south-west to south-west by west, and it blew a fresh breeze in the forenoon. We went on steering south-east by compass to balance the effects of the currents, which for several days had been setting us singularly to the north and west. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 29' 49", which gave us little difference to the north from our reckoning; but it was not the same with our observed longitude. That of No. 31 put us, reduced to noon, in 6° 17' 37", and that of No. 38 in 7° 3' 44". The run we had made by the reckoning gave 30' 33" of difference in twenty-four hours, and it was not the first time it had happened to us to be so far set off the course we had run. During the evening the winds came round as far as west-north-west with a fresh breeze; and as the sky was fine we were already persuading ourselves that they would hold at least some days in that point of the horizon, from which they had blown so little since we came into the variables, and that they would carry us round the Cape of Good Hope. After sunset and at moonrise they were the same, but at midnight they shifted suddenly to south-south-west, from which they blew so hard that we had to bear away several points to furl our sails conveniently. For a moment the ship ran ten knots, and it was the second time that had happened to us. But this time we had at most two points of free wind in the sails. The Naturaliste, who was near us, was soon out of sight, although the sky was still clear and the horizon wide enough. After midnight it continued to blow a strong breeze from the same quarter, and the sky covered with clouds which, flying past with great swiftness, promised us wind for the rest of the night. I then had a reef taken in the topsails, and shortly afterwards, the winds continuing to increase, a second had to be taken and all our staysails furled. As the sea was still smooth the ship made good way. At two o'clock we saw the Naturaliste to leeward at a considerable distance; but as we had greatly shortened sail she was not long in closing us. For the rest of the night it went on blowing hard and the sea began to get up.
1801-01-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSW to WSW. At noon in 34° 30' 54" of latitude observed and in 7° 50' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 23° 40' NW.

1801-01-31.journal_anonyme: Wind SW, very light, the sea smooth. The commander in the ESE.
1801-01-31.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 11th [Pluviôse, 31 January 1801] the winds drew round more to the south and blew with some force during the forenoon. As we were steering close-hauled and the sea was beginning to get up, we made a great deal of leeway, although we were under our courses with only two reefs in the topsails. The Naturaliste, who was carrying all the sail the weather could allow and even her topgallant sails, went worse still, and we were often obliged to lay the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for her, and to bear down on her to close her when she was abeam of us. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 56' South and the longitude by the reckoning 21° 21' east. That given by No. 31 was 8° 48' 18", and No. 38 put us in 9° 32' 45". The Naturaliste, to whom we made the signal, proved to have a difference of 7 minutes from the mean of our two watches. In the afternoon the winds were the same, with little appearance of change. As they were not so cold as usual, however, we hoped they would not stay long in the southern quarter from which they had blown constantly for nearly twenty days, causing us much vexation and delay in passing the Cape of Good Hope. I had fully expected to find southerly winds, and it was for that reason that I had worked up to the thirty-sixth degree of latitude; but I did not think that, in steering south-east and south-east by east from the moment the variation was small, we should from then on find a strong current setting west and north with as much speed as if we had been close in with the coast — for we began to feel them more than two hundred leagues off, as may be seen from the tables I have drawn up. In the night of the 11th to the 12th [Pluviôse, 31 January - 1 February 1801] the sky was very damp. A light mist made the moon's light very pale. The sea was beginning to get up although the wind was moderate. It varied as far as south-south-east but was more commonly south. We kept the same canvas during the night, taking care not to draw away from the Naturaliste.
1801-01-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. At noon in 34° 55' 29" of latitude observed and in 10° 32' of longitude by No. 38.

1801-02-01.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from WSW to SW. The commander in the SE. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-02-01.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 12th [Pluviôse, 1 February 1801] the sky was very dark until about ten o'clock, when it began to grow clearer and hazy. The winds were south with a fresh breeze and the sea rather rough, with the look of getting up further if the wind held. In the forenoon an inspection was made of part of the crew's linen, to see whether they took care to keep clean what they were not wearing; for I had laid it down as a general rule that shirts should be washed every time they were changed, and this had been regularly practised since our departure from France. About ten o'clock the Naturaliste signalled us a mishap to a sail, and we saw that it was the weather sheet of the fore topsail that had parted. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 2' South, which gave us a considerable difference from that of the reckoning. It appeared to us, from the longitude observed by the watches, that the currents had set us north-easterly by some minutes, which would begin to indicate a set contrary to the one we have found in them up to this moment. By No. 31 the longitude at noon was 10° 55' 38", and by No. 38, 12° 11' 17" east. In the evening the winds drew round to south-south-west with a strong breeze and the sky became clear. We steered south-east by compass to win back to the south, if possible, what we had lost over several days; but as we took the sea head on and the sea was hollow, the ship pitched very heavily. The Naturaliste, however, carried her topgallant sails and even her mizzen topgallant, whereas I would not have shaken out a reef from the topsails. It is true I had no need of it to keep way with her, since I was often obliged to shorten sail to let her come up. At sunset the sky darkened a great deal and the winds were very variable from south to south by west, which made the sea somewhat rough. During the night of the 12th to the 13th [Pluviôse, 1-2 February 1801] the sea got up and the winds varied as far as south-south-east in fairly strong gusts. The sky was hazy and very damp. As the barometer had been falling a great deal for some days, we feared some squalls.
1801-02-01.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 33° 58' 44" of latitude observed and in 12° 25' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 25° 55' NW.

1801-02-02.journal_anonyme: The winds a fresh breeze, varying from south to SSE. We struck our topgallant masts, the main one being split by the violence of the wind. At 5.30 the course was signalled SE by E. The sky cloudy, a swell running.
1801-02-02.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 13th [Pluviôse, 2 February 1801] the winds came to us from the south-west, and in the forenoon they even drew round to the west, from which they blew moderately. The sea, which the day before had been rough and high, was becoming smoother, and the sun, rising above the horizon, made the weather clear enough to give us hopes of a fine day. At noon we observed the south latitude 34° 6' 58", and after working up our courses by the wind we had steered we found a difference of 16' 4" to the north. The longitude given by No. 31 was 12° 37' 12", that of No. 38 gave 13° 23' 10", and on board the Naturaliste they signalled us 13° 15', so that the mean of our watches put us then in 13° 15' 7" east of Paris, that is, 3° 4' 53" from the Cape of Good Hope, which we fully expected to see in the course of the following day if the breeze, which had freshened a great deal after the sun's observation, held until then. At one o'clock the Naturaliste, who was in our wake a league off, signalled a sail in the NW. We saw her too; she seemed to us to be shaping a course further east than ours, from which we concluded she meant to go into Table Bay. About three o'clock we found the sea all at once extremely changed, and had one been able to judge its depth by the colour it showed us, one would not have thought there could be more than fifty fathoms. As we had to wait for the Naturaliste we sounded, but a line of a hundred and twenty fathoms run out up and down brought no bottom. A very strong smell of the tide was to be felt, and the kelp, like the seals we saw in the evening, left us in no doubt that we were not far from seeing land. At six o'clock the Naturaliste, who had rejoined us, asked by signal to pass under our stern. Her request was granted and we shortened sail. After we had spoken, we were told that everyone without exception was well on board that ship. Captain Hamelin made his remarks to me on the change in the colour of the water, adding that he believed us to be on soundings. I answered that I was of the same opinion, but that not having found bottom at a hundred and twenty-five fathoms it must be far deeper than appearances indicated. Before parting we agreed that at eight in the evening we should steer south-south-east until four the next morning, so as to make up for the effect of the current, which set so markedly to the north, and that we should then haul south-east to come and make the land. In the evening the winds had been west-south-west to west with a fine breeze, but at sunset they fell away and there was little wind until midnight. At that hour we were preparing to sound, but the winds having shifted suddenly to south-west and blowing hard, the lead had to be abandoned to attend to our sails. The winds, in coming to the south-west, gave us rain for half an hour and in fairly large quantity; and when the squall was past they came back to west-south-west blowing hard, and the sky had so bad a look that at two o'clock we struck our topgallant masts, furled the mainsail and took a third reef in our fore topsail. For the rest of the night the sky was continually squally with strong gusts, and overcast and loaded all round. The barometer had fallen to 28.
1801-02-02.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to NNW. At 4 the course was given S 33° 45' E. At noon in 34° 4' 35" of latitude observed and in 13° 48' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 25° 13' NW. At noon the colour of the sea changed completely, which announced the approach of land. The rigging was set up. At 1 the Naturaliste signalled us a ship in the N 45° W; she was standing for the Cape of Good Hope. Saw a seal and kelp. At 3.30 we ran out 100 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 4.30 signalled the Naturaliste that at 8 o'clock we should steer S 22° 30' E. At 5.15 she asked to pass under our stern and we spoke. At 8 shaped the course S 22° 30' E.

1801-02-03.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SW. At 3 p.m. sighted a sail in the NW, distant 5 leagues. We noticed that the sea had changed: it had turned a dirty blue and showed reddish streaks at intervals, which we put down to the currents and to the nearness of the Agulhas Bank. At 3.30 the commander hove to to sound and found no bottom.
1801-02-03.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 14th [Pluviôse, 3 February 1801] the weather was very bad, and from four o'clock until eight the rain did not stop falling. It was then blowing hard from the west and we were running under the foresail and close-reefed topsails, the topmasts still up, so as not to draw away from the Naturaliste. The sea was getting very high and the rolls we felt from time to time were very heavy. We had many that ran to twenty-five degrees of heel, measured with our oscillometer; the ship's pitching also rose at times to 13 degrees by the same instrument. Our scientists, who until then had always had very fine weather, were shaken rather roughly and were somewhat disconcerted by the ship's motion. As I had had all the shrouds set up forward and aft the day before, our masts behaved very well. At four o'clock, as I had agreed the day before with M. Hamelin, we headed south-east. But at five I signalled him to resume the course south-south-east, the weather looking too bad to try to make the land, which I reckoned only fifteen or twenty leagues off at that time. At eight o'clock the weather seemed inclined to clear and the horizon from west to north-west became fine. Little by little the clouds lifted in the north and north-east, and at nine o'clock we made the land plainly. The Naturaliste, always more diligent than we, made us the signal for it, although I had seen it before her; but as everyone was busy looking, too long was spent before carrying out the order I had given to announce it to her. From eight o'clock till noon we did not lose sight of it, and precisely at noon we took the bearings of False Cape, whose bay we made out perfectly, N 41° E, and the furthest land seen to the eastward, E 24° N. The observed latitude at the moment of taking the bearings was 35° 8' 41", so that the bearing laid down on the large chart of the Neptune Oriental put us in 16° 15' of longitude east of Paris. That given by watch No. 31, reduced to noon, gave 15° 0' 17", and No. 38 gave 15° 47' 1". It follows that No. 31 was 1° 14' 43" slow and No. 38 0° 27' 59", according to the rates found for these watches since our departure from Tenerife; but by the rates found at Paris, No. 31 differed by 1° 3' 3" and No. 38 by only 0° 0' 12", both to the west. On board the Naturaliste they signalled us for observed longitude at noon 15° 57'. In the afternoon it continued to blow a good breeze from west to west-south-west and the sky became fine enough. But the sea was still very high and swelly. We went on steering south-south-east, both to get away from the land and to double Cape Agulhas easily, and in order to make the southerly winds favourable to us should they settle again in that point of the horizon where we had had them so long before doubling the Cape. In the night of the 14th to the 15th [Pluviôse, 3-4 February 1801] the winds were at times south-west and very unsteady. The sky, however, was fine enough and we made tolerable way although it did not blow as hard as during the day.
1801-02-03.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to W. A high sea and rain. At 6.30 the course was signalled and given S 33° 45' E. At 9 the land was sighted in the N 45° E, 30 miles off. At 9.30 the course was signalled and given S 22° 30' E. At noon took the bearing of False Cape N 41° E and the southernmost land N 66° E. The latitude observed 35° 8' 33" and the longitude 16° 22', from the observed latitude and the bearing of False Cape. The variation 27° 56' NW at 30 miles from the land.

1801-02-04.journal_anonyme: The wind a strong breeze from WSW but variable. At 7 we sighted the land to the north. The commander in the NNW, with a great deal of lightning in the SSE. At noon the course was signalled SE. The weather fine, the sea rather high.
1801-02-04.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 15th [Pluviôse, 4 February 1801] the winds drew round to the NW, where they stayed, and they seemed inclined to settle in the western quarter, working round to the south. As we were on the edge of the Agulhas Bank the sea was very high and swelly; nevertheless, as the winds were fair and we had to push east as quickly as possible, I had a reef shaken out of the topsails and the topgallant masts swayed up. At four in the morning I had signalled the Naturaliste the course south-east, and from that moment we both steered that way. In the forenoon it blew a fresh breeze and we made good enough way, having for our amusement the sight of much kelp and many albatrosses, as well as various species of petrel we had not yet seen. Several were fired at from on board but none was killed, although every marksman claimed his shot had gone home entire on the bird he had aimed at. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 12' 8" South and the longitude given by the watches was worked out for No. 31 as 18° 53' 42" and for No. 38 as 18° 54' 5". We found we had had in the twenty-four hours a difference of 17' 54" to the north and a second of 10 seconds to the east. The reckoned longitude, corrected on the sight of the land, was [blank]. In the afternoon it continued to blow a fresh breeze, but the sky had a very bad look. After sunset many squalls made up on the horizon in the south and south-south-west which threatened us for a long time, but which, having passed ahead of us, incommoded us little. They did, however, once take us aback and obliged us to go onto the port tack. But it was only for a moment, for they came back at once to the south-west when the tail of the squalls we had had was past. Shortly before sunset we took two fine shells of the turban kind, on a very pleasing blue ground. This meeting was the more fortunate in that one of them is perfectly entire and preserved in spirits with the animal that lodges in it, whose extraordinary shape is surely not known, although the shell is well enough. Its most remarkable feature is its operculum, of which one is far from having any idea, and which the drawing will convey better than all the discourses of the learned. The drawing is exact and made from nature. We also took a new species of mollusc which I have named the mushroom from its perfect resemblance to that plant. In the night of the 15th to the 16th [Pluviôse, 4-5 February 1801] the winds were very variable; they even came round as far as the south, but stayed there a short time and returned to the south-west with a fresh breeze. The ship was extremely tossed about by the sea when there was little wind, and laboured a great deal. For the rest, the night was finer than we had expected. The squalls partly cleared away, and though we had lightning very often, no thunder was heard. I held on south-east for fear of the southerly winds coming on.
1801-02-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to NW. At 4.30 the course was signalled and given S 45° E. At noon in 36° 12' 0" of latitude observed and in 18° 38' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 27° 1' NW. During the night overcast weather, rain at intervals, lightning in the S 22° 30' E.

1801-02-05.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from WSW. Squally weather, a high sea; the commander at a middling distance in the ESE.
1801-02-05.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 16th [Pluviôse, 5 February 1801] the weather was fine and the winds went on giving us a fresh breeze from the south-west, variable to west-south-west. We went on steering south-east, keeping the canvas suited to the Naturaliste. Although the sea was high and swelly, the ship laboured little; we had, however, some pitching during which she rose and fell 12 degrees by our instrument, of which I hope it will be possible to make a useful application to the naval service when, after several trials, its usefulness has been recognised. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 50' 8" South, which gave us only four minutes of difference to the north. I had expected, on the contrary, to find a more considerable difference to the south; but it appears we were too far from the coast to feel the set of the currents in that quarter, which are known to run north-south-west with very great speed. The longitude by the reckoning of our course, corrected on the sight of the Cape of Good Hope, was 20° 51', and that given by the watches was, for No. 31, 20° 59' 54", and for No. 38, 21° 0' 36". In the evening the winds were the same and everyone rejoiced at having such favourable weather. The day of our arrival at Mauritius was already fixed and no one doubted any longer that we should have the wind fair all the way. In the afternoon, however, the sky covered with cloud, and I feared that during the night the winds might come to the south and perhaps even to the south-east, which would have much disappointed these hopes and upset the calculations. During the night of the 16th to the 17th [Pluviôse, 5-6 February 1801] the weather was very fine until midnight; the clouds that had formed during the evening had disappeared, and at that hour the sky was superb. But in an instant it turned very hazy and dark; nevertheless the winds stayed north-west by west and it blew a fresh breeze. We were even obliged to shake all the reefs out of our main topsail and to set our lower studdingsails forward to join the Naturaliste, who had been allowed to draw off to a considerable distance.
1801-02-05.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW. At noon in 36° 47' 46" of latitude observed and in 20° 47' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 27° 2' NW. At noon the course was signalled and given S 56° 15' E.

1801-02-06.journal_anonyme: WSW, a strong breeze. The weather fine, a swell running. At noon the course was signalled E by S. On the 17th our mainsail split and we repaired it at once. Saw many albatrosses.
1801-02-06.journal_baudin: On the 17th [Pluviôse, 6 February 1801] the weather was extremely dark in the morning, and the winds, which had drawn round to the south-west, were not long in coming to south-south-west. The sea was very high, agitated by several crossing seas that made it bad and uncomfortable. As we had come up with and passed the Naturaliste, the studdingsails were taken in and shortly afterwards the topgallant sails. At eight o'clock we took in again the reef of the main topsail that had been shaken out the day before, and there was every appearance that the day would not pass without our being obliged to take other reefs in our sails. At noon we could not observe the latitude, the sky being too overcast; the sun could be seen at intervals, but the clouds covering it were driven with such speed and followed one another so quickly that we could not bring it down to the horizon. The longitude by the reckoning was 23° 27' east. The albatrosses and petrels that had accompanied us since the sight of the Cape began to grow scarce, and we saw only two or three of the first kind during the day and none at all of the others. In the evening the sky stayed dark and hazy; the sun, nevertheless, showed itself clear enough. But as the winds were drawing much closer to the south, those who had reckoned on continual fine weather began to think they might be mistaken and that it was possible to have contrary winds more than once again before reaching Mauritius. The sea, however, gave no sign of bad weather, and though high it was smoother than we had found it in the morning. We were then steering east-south-east to make more way. During the night of the 17th to the 18th [Pluviôse, 6-7 February 1801] the sky was very dark, the winds came to us in gusts with strong puffs, and they were in the southern quarter, variable to south-south-east, which obliged us to lie close-hauled and consequently made the Naturaliste drive far to leeward; for all the sail she carried she could not keep to windward, so that, from the information she gave us of her position, we often bore down on her to close her.
1801-02-06.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW, SW, SSW, S and SSE; a high sea. At 9 the course was signalled and given S 67° 30' E. At noon in 36° 52' 46" of latitude by account and in 24° 14' of longitude by account. Variation 27° 30' NW. At half past noon the course was signalled S 78° 45' E.

1801-02-07.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from W to NW and SSW. The course E by S. A high sea, the sky cloudy.
1801-02-07.journal_baudin: On the 18th [Pluviôse, 7 February 1801] the winds, which had drawn round to the south, were not long in hauling more and more towards the east, and by the forenoon they were already south-east and even south-east by east, which much disconcerted those who had judged they must always be favourable to us. In the forenoon the breeze was very strong and I had a second reef taken in each topsail, and I went on holding the east tack towards the north. Although the sky was not very fine there was no appearance of bad weather, the barometer standing steadily enough between 28.4 and 28.3.
