At noon the observed latitude was 35° 10' 22" South, which gave us a difference to the north in forty-eight hours of 32' 24" from the reckoning by the courses run. By an hour angle taken in the morning, No. 31 gave for longitude reduced to noon 26° 48' 43" and No. 38, 26° 34' 3", whence followed a second difference to the east from the reckoning of 37' 27". During the evening the sky was very dark and the winds extremely variable; we had them now south-south-east, now south-east and sometimes east-south-east. This inconstancy kept me from changing course. At six in the evening, however, I had the Naturaliste signalled that if during the night the winds came to the south-east I should go about, and that if they drew aft I should steer east by south. After she had answered me, she let me know by signal that she had a considerable split in her main topsail and that it was such as to oblige her to shift it. We then shortened sail and closed her the better to watch her. At ten in the evening, the winds seeming settled enough in the south-east, I made the signal to go about, and we at once put the helm down. Although under double-reefed topsails, the ship stayed very well, but the manoeuvre was slow and even fumbled. The Naturaliste having done the same, we lay close-hauled on the port tack. The winds during the night varied from east-south-east to east and we often had strong puffs.
1801-02-07.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind unsteady from SSE to SE. At noon in 35° 9' 10" of latitude observed and in 26° 4' of longitude by No. 38. At 5.15 signalled the Naturaliste that if the wind came to the ESE we should go onto the port tack, and that if it drew aft we should steer S 78° 45' E.

1801-02-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea and the winds varying from south to SSE. At 6 we shifted our main topsail, the old one being split; we repeated the signal of our damage.
1801-02-08.journal_baudin: On the 19th [Pluviôse, 8 February 1801] the winds stayed east, and in the forenoon they came round as far as east-north-east, very irregular and in strong gusts; the sea was getting up and the weather did not look well. About eleven o'clock we shifted our main topmast staysail, which needed a considerable repair. At noon, although the sky was dark and misty enough, we nevertheless had sight of the sun and observed its meridian altitude, which was found to be 35° 25' 29". It gave a difference to the south from our reckoning of 13' 1". By an hour angle taken in the evening and reduced to noon, the longitude given was, for No. 31, 27° 22' 54", and for No. 38, 27° 24' 34". We found that in these twenty-four hours the current had set us 9' 10" to the west. During the evening the sky became clear and the weather seemed inclined to turn fine; but as the sea was getting up and the ship and her masts were labouring, I had the topgallant masts struck, being for the most part useless to us. At sunset, the wind still increasing, I had the mizzen topsail furled and even the mainsail; we closed the Naturaliste, who was crowding sail to follow us; but when she saw that I did not mean to carry much during the night, so as not to inconvenience her too greatly, she had a second reef taken in her topsails and then lay under her courses, carrying all she could bear. During the night of the 19th to the 20th [8-9 February 1801] it blew a strong breeze from east by north to north-east by east; but as the sea was much agitated and there was a great deal of leeway, the course was of little advantage to us. The sky stayed dark throughout and very damp. We often had a light rain in the form of mist which very quickly soaked through the clothes of those on watch. Care was taken during the night to show a light every hour to the Naturaliste, who answered us in the same way.
1801-02-08.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from E and ENE. At noon in 35° 25' 21" of latitude observed and in 26° 59' of longitude by No. 38. Light rain during the night.

1801-02-09.journal_anonyme: The winds SE and east. A strong breeze, the weather fine, a swell running.
1801-02-09.journal_baudin: On the 20th [Pluviôse, 9 February 1801] the sky stayed very dark in the forenoon and the breeze was less strong than the day before. The winds held in the quarter from north-east to north-east by east, moderate, and allowed us to set our mizzen topsail, which had been furled the evening before. Despite our care not to draw too far from the Naturaliste, that ship was found at daylight to have fallen far to leeward. In the forenoon, the sky having become clearer, we hoped that the winds in the quarter they were in would bring us a clear sky and that we should at last be free of that disagreeable damp which had incommoded us especially since doubling the Cape of Good Hope. At noon the latitude was observed as 36° 7' 40" South, which gave us a difference to the north in the twenty-four hours of 12' 45". By the rate of our watches the longitude reduced to noon was, for No. 31, 28° 40' 11", and for No. 38, 28° 42' 16", with four minutes of difference to the east from the reckoning. During the evening the winds settled at north-east and moderate, but the sea was still high and swelly. We closed the Naturaliste, who was falling more and more to leeward, and I signalled her that we should steer east by south if the winds came fair, and that I should go onto the other tack if they drew round to the south-east. After sunset the sky covered again with cloud and a thick mist that was still more troublesome to us than that of the past days. As I was much dissatisfied with the way Citizen Baudin — who is no relation of mine, but only one of my lieutenants — conducted himself, I spent on deck the four hours of his watch, of which I took the command, having no confidence in him because of his slight attention to watching the weather, which I thought was likely to turn bad from the look of it and from the movements of the barometer, which was falling a great deal. The weather, however, was mild enough; and the Naturaliste, who was within musket shot to leeward, gaining on us, I had the third reef shaken out of the topsails and the mainsail set, to keep as usual to windward and ahead of her.
1801-02-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE and NNE. At noon in 36° 8' 11" of latitude observed and in 28° 1' 0" of longitude by No. 38. At 6.30 signalled the Naturaliste that if the wind came to the SE we should go onto the starboard tack, and that if it drew aft we should steer S 78° 45' E.

1801-02-10.journal_anonyme: Winds SE and east. A fresh breeze. The sky cloudy. At 6.30 the commander signalled the course E by S if they drew aft, and that otherwise he would go about. The commander in the NNE at a middling distance.
1801-02-10.journal_baudin: On the 21st [Pluviôse, 10 February 1801] the weather was very disagreeable during the forenoon; we often had rain and fairly strong puffs. The sea, however, had become calmer, and although the barometer had fallen to 28 inches two lines there was no appearance of bad weather. The winds, which were north-east, varied a little towards the north and allowed us to lie east by south. This course would have served us well had the leeway caused by the east-north-east swell not been so considerable. The damp that reigned on board was so great and so continual that I began to fear it might bring on some sickness among the crew; so I had care and attention redoubled to prevent that inconvenience, having as yet no sick man on board. At noon, the sun having shown itself, we observed the latitude 36° 41' 41" South. But as we could get no hour angle either morning or evening, there was no observation for the longitude of our watches. That of the reckoning put us in 28° 42' 18" east. In the afternoon, having noticed the observation Citizen Baudin had entered in the log book because I had had various manoeuvres carried out that I judged proper during his watch, I had made up my mind to write him a letter telling him that, however much I should have wished to keep him until our arrival at Mauritius, I found myself under the necessity of having him replaced, because the safety of the men entrusted to me, like that of the ship, required that precaution of me. But Citizen Sainte-Croix Le Bas, my second, having learnt of my intentions, came to me and pressed me so earnestly not to take that step, which seemed to me absolutely necessary, that I could not refuse him. But I asked Citizen Baudin to come to my cabin, and in M. Le Bas's presence I read him the letter I had firmly resolved to send him, and let him know that it was solely to Citizen Le Bas's entreaties that he owed the delay I was willing to allow before withdrawing from him the command which his want of care obliged me to take from him. In short, I remonstrated with him most strongly on his conduct and his want of care when on duty. The promise he has made me to be more attentive will perhaps be kept, but I shall be no less uneasy when he is on deck at night. In the evening the weather was finer than we had had it in the morning; the winds drew round to north-north-east, from which they shifted little during the night, which was fine enough although extremely damp. In the evening I had signalled the Naturaliste the course east if the winds allowed, and we hauled up as close to that course as was possible.
1801-02-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE to NNE. At 1 a.m. Commander Baudin came onto the quarterdeck and, taking no notice of Citizen Baudin, lieutenant and officer of the watch, had the mainsail set and a reef shaken out of the topsails, after which he went quietly off to bed. Citizen Baudin, justly indignant at his conduct, entered the following note at the end of his watch: "The commander had various changes made in the canvas, which he ordered directly of the master; which is, I believe, contrary to the service regulations, which prescribe the hierarchy of authority in command." The commander wrote at the foot of Citizen Baudin's note: "The answer to the remark made by Citizen Baudin is in the letter I address to him under today's date. N. Baudin." At noon in 36° 42' 30" of latitude observed and in 29° 13' of longitude by account. The course was signalled east.

1801-02-11.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from NE to NNE, blowing hard. At 4 the course was signalled east. At 6 p.m. the main topsail sheet parted and we repaired it at once. The weather misty, a high sea.
1801-02-11.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 22nd [Pluviôse, 11 February 1801] the winds went on blowing a fresh breeze from north-north-east, variable to north-east by north. At daylight we found on the forecastle a kind of cuttlefish that had jumped on board during the night. As this creature had no bone like those of the kind I know, it may well be a variety of the species. I have accordingly had it drawn in its natural colours, which are very brilliant while it is in the water. All the past days were lost for natural history, for Citizen Maugé, for all his vigilance and assiduity in watching, could take nothing and indeed saw very little. It is no doubt to the agitation of the sea that we must ascribe this dearth of the marine animals one sees at its surface when it is calm. During the forenoon the weather was fine enough and we often had sight of the sun. At noon the latitude was observed as 36° 47' 34", which gave us, to our great astonishment, a difference of 11' 29" to the south; for from the course we had run in these twenty-four hours we had expected to have made some way to the north. By an hour angle taken at three in the afternoon, the longitude given by the watches, reduced to noon, was for No. 31, 32° 54' 44", and for No. 38, 32° 58' 7", so that we found we had met with a current which in forty-eight hours — the interval since the last observation — had set us 1° 15' 4" to the east; and we were far from expecting it, having seen nothing at the surface of the water that could make us suspect it. In the afternoon the weather was fine enough and the winds in the same quarter. At sunset we observed two amplitudes with two different compasses, the result of which gave 28° 38' 40" for the variation NW. It was the first time since passing the Cape of Good Hope that we had had occasion to see the sun set. During the night of the 22nd to the 23rd [Pluviôse, 11-12 February 1801] the winds went on north-north-east with a fresh breeze, varying a little towards the east; we lay as close to the east as possible, the sea having become smooth, and wishing to work a little to the north so as not to come too near the bank M. d'Après speaks of, which is thought to lie in 37° of south latitude.
1801-02-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to N. At noon in 36° 45' 14" of latitude observed and in 31° 11' of longitude by account. Variation 28° 12' NW.

1801-02-12.journal_anonyme: The same winds, the weather rainy, a high sea. Heading east.
1801-02-12.journal_baudin: On the 23rd [Pluviôse, 12 February 1801] the winds in the forenoon were in the northern quarter, variable north by east, and the breeze was fine enough until after the sun's passage of the meridian, when it fell away a little. But as the sea had become very smooth we made good enough way, with the Naturaliste astern of us within gunshot. As she had out all she could carry and was gaining on us, I had a reef shaken out of the topsails, by which means she kept her usual station, that is, astern. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 15' 2", which gave us a little northing and put us in a position to have nothing to fear from the bank the Dutch say they discovered and which they place in 37° 20', under the parallel of 36°, east of the meridian of Paris. By our observed longitude at noon we reckoned ourselves a degree and sixteen minutes east of it, and nothing gave us any sign of the approach of this rocky bank on which a great number of birds must take refuge. We had indeed lost sight of them for some days. By watch No. 31 the longitude at noon was 34° 40' 44", and by No. 38, 34° 44' 34", and we had a difference of 13' 3" to the west, whereas on the preceding days we had had it very large to the east. In the evening the winds were the same as in the morning but lighter, and the sea still smooth; towards evening, however, the sky turned dark and the horizon misty. From various observations of amplitudes and azimuths, the variation of the needle was found, in the part we were in, to be 28° 17' 24" NW. During the night the weather was very fine and clear. We were not troubled by that thick, damp mist that had incommoded us for two days, but the winds fell away a great deal and held at north by east.
1801-02-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to N. At noon in 36° 14' 20" of latitude observed and in 33° 30' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 28° 40' NW.

1801-02-13.journal_anonyme: NE and NNE, blowing hard, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth. Saw a small whale estimated at 20 to 25 feet in length.
1801-02-13.journal_baudin: The 24th [Pluviôse, 13 February 1801] was for us one of the finest days of our voyage for the beauty of the sky, but there was little wind. We made up for it by taking for natural history various new objects in fish and molluscs. Both were of rare beauty, and the fish above all. Of that kind we took only two different species. One offered us, in the singularity of its shape and the brilliance of its colours, all that can be seen of the most extraordinary and rare; and the other gave rise on board to a scientific dispute whose conclusion has not yet settled the question at issue. Here is the case. We have often seen jellyfish of the kind commonly known as the Portuguese man-of-war holding among their filaments small fish so entangled that it was no longer possible for them to free themselves. Several have claimed that these fish serve as food for the man-of-war, and others said on the contrary that it was the fish that ate the man-of-war. Which is right I do not know; but from the examination I have made of three fish taken in the long filaments of the man-of-war, I remain persuaded that the fish, wanting to eat the creature and not knowing its means of defence, is seized when it comes too near, and ends by being so entangled that it can no longer get free and finally dies a victim to its own greed. If this is not the true cause, it is at least the most likely, and until the contrary is clearly proved to me it will be my opinion. Among the molluscs we took, and to which I have given names according to the resemblances I found in them to various objects, there are some very extraordinary ones which will no doubt have deserved brilliant descriptions; but I doubt whether it is possible to make them as well known as the coloured drawing I give of them. At noon the observed latitude was 35° 48' 48", which gave us only two minutes of difference from that of our reckoning. The longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 36° 7' 53", and for No. 38, 36° 12' 5", with only 1' 37" of difference to the west. The great rocky bank said to have been discovered by the Dutch, from the way it is placed on the charts of the Southern Ocean, then bore from us south at about thirty leagues' distance; but we had no sign of it, either from the sight of birds, which had entirely deserted us, or from any other appearance. In the evening the weather continued fine and we were almost becalmed. The winds varied a great deal and came at times as far as east-north-east. During the night of the 24th to the 25th [Pluviôse, 13-14 February 1801] the sky was extremely clear and serene and the wind calm; a fairly heavy swell from the south was beginning to be felt and there was the appearance that we should have the winds from that quarter; nevertheless they stayed north-east, variable towards east, and it was almost calm — which is hardly usual in the parts we were in, of which seamen have often had cause to complain.
1801-02-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to E. At noon in 35° 48' 45" of latitude observed and in 34° 57' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 28° 28' NW.

1801-02-14.journal_anonyme: Winds NE, a fresh breeze. In the evening the commander could hardly be made out from the forecastle. At 10 a.m. a flat calm.
1801-02-14.journal_baudin: On the 25th [Pluviôse, 14 February 1801] we were nearly becalmed all day, and this day would have been entirely lost for the voyage as for natural history had we not given the greatest attention to watching along the ship's side to take something that might make up for the loss of our time. But besides three or four new species of mollusc, we took an albatross of grey plumage which I believe to be the female of the white one. We saw this bird sitting on the water and at once I had a boat put out to see whether we could come within musket shot. This means succeeded, for it was killed; but four shots had to be fired at it. The first two had put it out of a state to escape us, but when we tried to take it, it defended itself so vigorously that we were forced to fire a third, which apparently had little effect, since it went on defending itself and even attacking the men who tried to seize it, so that a fourth was sent which killed it outright. This bird had ten feet of wingspan, four feet seven inches in length, and weighed only eleven pounds, although larger and bigger than the first we had taken, which weighed thirteen. It was handed at once to Citizen Maugé to preserve the skin, and he has put off skinning it until tomorrow. I await that moment impatiently, to learn whether it is a female and confirm me in my opinion. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 23' 50" South and the longitude given by the watches put us, by No. 31, in 36° 55' 22", and by No. 38, in 36° 59' 34", which gave us a difference to the south in twenty-four hours of 13' 34" and one to the east of 4' 29" on the reckoned course run by the ship. In the evening, although the weather was fine and the sky clear of cloud, various squalls formed in the quarter from south-west to west which made us hope we might have the winds from that point of our horizon; but at sunset our hope had not yet been realised and it went on blowing a light breeze from the east, variable to east-south-east. Nevertheless, as I reckoned myself near the Dutch bank, I signalled the Naturaliste that I should go about at eight o'clock; and as we could not make out whether she had understood our signal, being far to leeward of us, I bore away to repeat it when we were nearer. At seven o'clock the signal to go about was hoisted again, and the Naturaliste having answered us, we went on lying close-hauled, the winds being east-south-east and almost calm. At eight we went onto the starboard tack, and during the night we held the north tack. The winds were very variable from south-east towards east and the sky was dark and damp. The breeze having been very light, we made little way.
1801-02-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from NE to SE. At noon in 36° 22' 17" of latitude observed and in 35° 52' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 28° 32' NW. At 2.15 an albatross was seen sitting on the water a short distance off; a boat was at once put out and two marksmen embarked in her and went and shot it; it had 10 feet of wingspan. The boat had just been hooked on to her tackles when a seaman's hammock, with a mattress, a blanket and other effects in it, unluckily for the poor man fell overboard; as the hammock was of no use to natural history, it was left. At 5 a paper nautilus was seen swimming at the surface; we hove to at once and the boat was going into the water when, unluckily for natural history, the nautilus dived.

1801-02-15.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from NE to east. A light breeze, the weather stormy and a swell running from the east. At 8 p.m. went about. At 10 a.m. the mizzen topsail tie parted and the damage was repaired at once.
1801-02-15.journal_baudin: On the 26th [Pluviôse, 15 February 1801] the winds, still in the quarter from east to south-east, were very variable. We went on lying close-hauled on the north tack. The sky during the forenoon was misty and the horizon narrow. In the forenoon we closed the Naturaliste, who was ahead and far to leeward. Citizen Maugé spent part of the day preparing the albatross we had killed the day before, and we judged it to be a female, which confirmed me in the opinion I had adopted that the males are white-plumaged and the females grey. But as a single fact is not enough to adopt this idea generally, I leave the decision of the question to those we may meet with hereafter — a decision that would run counter to the system established by M. de Lacépède, who makes of it a separate genus. At noon the observed latitude was 36° 2' 42" South and the longitude given by the timekeepers 36° 58' 21" for No. 38 and 37° 8' 2" for No. 31. That of the reckoning had for several days been falling behind the rate of the watches. It was then only 35° 30' 18", so that we were being set to the east by the current, which had not however a constant set, as may be seen in the table I give of it for each day. In the afternoon the winds were the same and the sky had a very bad look. The horizon in the quarter from south towards south-west was much loaded with cloud and we expected to have the winds from that direction during the night. But we were mistaken again this time, for they were the same as during the day. The night of the 26th to the 27th [Pluviôse, 15-16 February 1801] was very damp and the sky overcast. There was little wind. We held the same course. A fairly heavy swell from the south-east made us fear the winds would stay in that quarter, which was positively the most disagreeable thing that could happen to us, since neither of the two tacks we could lie on was of any advantage. In the course of the day we saw very few birds and took nothing new for natural history either. We ate as a salmi our albatross of the day before, which was found better and more tender than the first we had got.
1801-02-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE. At noon in 36° 3' 41" of latitude observed and in 36° 12' of longitude by account. During the night the weather was overcast and it rained.

1801-02-16.journal_anonyme: The wind in the east, a light breeze, the weather very damp and the sky cloudy and misty. The commander asked us by signal how many days' water we had left on board. We answered him that we had fifty days'.
1801-02-16.journal_baudin: On the 27th [Pluviôse, 16 February 1801] the winds were east-south-east with a light breeze. We had a little rain at sunrise, but it did not last long. The sky was nevertheless very damp and misty during the forenoon and there was the appearance of wind, the sea being driven by a south-east swell that was no good omen for us. Between eleven and noon we met with two albatrosses on the water, one white in colour and the other dark grey. I had no doubt it was a male and a female, and I was delighted to have an opportunity that might show me whether my opinion, which led me to believe the grey ones are the females of the white, was well founded. Accordingly I had a boat put out and two of our gentlemen embarked in it to go and shoot these birds, which I suspected could not fly off, given how little wind there was. I was not mistaken in this conjecture; for when the boat had come within range to shoot them entirely at leisure, they were pleased to take wing, but both were killed. One of them, which was not killed outright although two shots had been fired at it, stayed some time on the water struggling, so that its movements drew other albatrosses which we did not suspect were in the neighbourhood, and in a moment there were six wheeling about the boat. One was killed on the wing, and the boat came back on board with three of these birds, two with white belly and back and the other grey. They were handed as usual to Citizen Maugé to be skinned, and one was also given to Citizen Péron to make the anatomy and a skeleton. All this work was put off to the following day, as they were too fresh to be skinned. Citizen Péron set about working on his at once. We found in the bodies of these birds the remains of a cuttlefish of enormous size; they had no doubt been busy eating it, for the parts taken out, which the seamen ate with pleasure, were very little spoiled. At noon the observed latitude was 34° 51' 48" South and the longitude given by the watches was, for No. 31, 37° 6' 13", and for No. 38, 37° 6' 39". That of the reckoning put us in 35° 58'. We had in the twenty-four hours a difference of 10' 10" to the south and one of 4' 10" to the west. In the evening the winds continued variable from east-south-east to SE by E and very light. I signalled the Naturaliste that if the winds drew aft during the night we should steer east-south-east, and that if they headed us we should lie on whichever tack came nearest to that course. During the night of the 27th to the 28th [Pluviôse, 16-17 February 1801] the sky was overcast, dark and very damp with a kind of mist that incommoded us greatly. We held on upon the east tack towards the north, the winds having been steadily enough east-south-east and very light.
1801-02-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SE. At 11.45 we hove to and put a boat in the water to shoot albatrosses. At noon in 34° 52' of latitude observed and in 36° 12' of longitude by No. 38. At 12.15 the marksmen came back with three albatrosses and we filled and stood on. At 6.30 signalled the course S 67° 30' E should the wind draw aft. During the night the weather was overcast, damp and squally, with mist.

1801-02-17.journal_anonyme: The wind ESE, a fresh breeze. At 10.30 we spoke the commander and asked him what the land was that he reckoned to have seen near the Cape of Good Hope. He answered that it was False Cape.
1801-02-17.journal_baudin: On the 28th [Pluviôse, 17 February 1801] the weather turned fine in the forenoon and we had the winds south-east with a fresh breeze. The heavy swell we had met with in the night had gone down a great deal, but the winds were very little favourable to us. In the forenoon Citizen Maugé worked on the two albatrosses I had had handed to him the day before; and to my great astonishment the one I had thought must be a male proved to be a female, and the one I believed of that sex a fine male. So my opinion was nothing but an error. For the rest, the characters peculiar to the white as to the grey are so perfectly alike that it seems to me beyond doubt that it is the same species, offering no variety but in the plumage. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 34' South and the longitude of No. 31, 36° 58' 16". By No. 38 it was 37° 2' 54". We found we had only 4' 37" of difference to the south, but that to the west was for the twenty-four hours 34' 39", which, with a contrary wind, was not very agreeable to us. In the evening the winds were south-east, variable to south-south-east, with a light breeze, and the sea had become so smooth that there was the appearance of calm. The sky, which had been fine enough until sunset, covered with mist, and we even had a little rain without wind, which did not last long. During the night of the 28th to the 29th [Pluviôse, 17-18 February 1801] there was little wind and the breeze was always in the eastern quarter, with a misty, damp sky. We found the sea that night very phosphorescent, but for all our attention we could not succeed in getting any of the marine animals that made it so. As the Naturaliste was rather far off and to leeward, we carried little sail, taking care to show her a light from time to time. The night was very dark, and in a clear interval we saw she was much nearer us than we thought.
1801-02-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. Saw whales and spoke the Naturaliste. At noon in 33° 31' 13" of latitude observed and in 37° 4' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 28° 3' NW. During the night the weather overcast and misty, with rain.

1801-02-18.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from east to ESE. The sky overcast and the weather misty; we lost sight of the commander at 8 a.m. [two words illegible], and he having gone about we did the same.
1801-02-18.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 29th [Pluviôse, 18 February 1801] the weather was very fine and clear. The winds having drawn round to the east, we went about and signalled the Naturaliste to do the same. The breeze was very light all the forenoon and the state of the sea foretold nothing but calm. Reflecting on the vexations we had so long been suffering from the winds, we could not but be much astonished to see them settled so long in the quarter we had them in, the more so as in a latitude like ours it is very rare to see them several days running in the same points of the horizon. All this did not fail to sour tempers, and for some days past people had been taking offence at one another over the least thing. I have spoken privately to those who were the least tolerant, and I hope the friendly representations I made them will not be useless hereafter. In the forenoon we took a new mollusc of great beauty; its perfect resemblance to a Polish cap led me to give it that name. The drawing I give of it is of the greatest regularity and exactness. At noon the observed latitude was 32° 53' 3" and the longitude by No. 31, 37° 15' 7". That of No. 38 was 37° 16' 34". There was in the twenty-four hours 8' 17" of difference to the south and 5' 7" to the west. In the afternoon the weather continued calm. We met with, floating on the water, two different species of mollusc of enormous size and of the greatest beauty. As they passed too far from the ship to be taken with our net, I had a boat put out. The man who took them looked after them so ill that he brought them on board all broken, so that nothing could be made out in them; I was very vexed not to have given that commission to someone more skilful. In the evening Citizen Maugé took a new fish of great beauty which is now in the collection of those already gathered. During the night of the 29th to the 30th [Pluviôse, 18-19 February 1801] the weather was calm, the sky still misty and damp, the winds variable from east-south-east to SSE.
1801-02-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from ESE and E. At noon in 32° 51' 40" of latitude observed and in 37° 32' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 28° 14' NW. At 2 a boat was put in the water to take an enormous mollusc; she was hoisted in again at 5.15.

1801-02-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds ESE. Almost calm. At 6.30 p.m. wore ship.
1801-02-19.journal_baudin: On the morning of the 30th [Pluviôse, 19 February 1801] the winds were the same as the day before and the breeze very light. In the course of the forenoon we took some molluscs and several small fish; but as these objects were not new, having met with the same elsewhere, we made little of them, so that the day was lost for our progress as for natural history. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 16' 53" and the longitude by the reckoning 36° 31' 30". That given by our timekeepers put us, by the rate of No. 38, in 37° 18' 25", and by No. 31 in 37° 29' 59" east of Paris. In the afternoon we took various distances of the moon from the sun, the result of which was not very satisfactory: a sextuple observation taken with my sextant gave 36° 45' 30", and three series of observations with the circle put us in 39° 8' 54", so that the mean of all these observations gave a difference of 23' to the east of the watches. During the evening the winds were east-south-east and the breeze freshened a little. The sky had become extremely fine and the sea foretold calm. Although we were in the finest season of this part of the southern hemisphere, we were none the less astonished to see the winds hold with such constancy in the quarter from north-east to east-south-east and south-east, and blow with such moderation. To all appearances our passage of the Mozambique Channel will give our young seamen no idea of the squalls usually met with there, and they will form a charming notion of the navigation from Europe to Mauritius from the weather we have experienced. In the night of the 30th [Pluviôse] to the 1st [Ventôse, 19-20 February 1801] the winds drew round to east-north-east and east, which made us take the south-south-east tack. I signalled the Naturaliste to go about, and we lay close-hauled on the port tack under our usual canvas. The night was very fine and clear; there was, however, a great deal of damp.
1801-02-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from E to SE; we passed through several tide rips. At noon in 33° 18' 20" of latitude observed and in 38° 4' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 28° 5' NW.

1801-02-20.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from east to ENE, a light breeze. At 2 a.m. wore ship.
1801-02-20.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to NE. At noon in 33° 8' 45" of latitude observed and in 38° 29' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 28° 2' NW. The lunar distances gave 39° 26' of longitude.

1801-02-21.journal_anonyme: The sky cloudy, the sea smooth and the wind a fresh breeze, variable from ENE, NE and NNE; the commander in the NNE.
1801-02-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NNW. At noon in 33° 34' 35" of latitude observed and in 38° 19' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 27° 48' NW. The lunar distances gave 40° 54' of longitude.

1801-02-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze and very variable from NNE, N, NNW, west, SW, south and SSE. At midnight the breeze got up from the SW, the sea rather high, the sky overcast and heavy and the wind a strong breeze.
1801-02-22.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW, S to SE. A high sea, with rain and squalls. At noon in 33° 18' 17" of latitude by account and in 42° 23' of longitude by account.

1801-02-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind very fresh from SE to SSE. The commander bearing from us NE at a short distance.
1801-02-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 31° 50' 12" of latitude observed and in 42° 23' of longitude by No. 38.

1801-02-24.journal_anonyme: A high sea, the sky overcast and the wind blowing hard from SSE to SE. The commander in the SSE a long way off. At 9 a.m. we signalled him damage to the mizzen topsail; by ten everything was ready again.
1801-02-24.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 30° 24' 27" of latitude observed and in 43° 36' of longitude by account. During the night, rain and squally weather.

1801-02-25.journal_anonyme: The weather grey and hazy, a high sea, the winds fresh and variable from SSE to SE. Saw a stem of kelp pass alongside. At noon the sea smooth enough and the wind blowing pleasantly.
1801-02-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to SSE. At noon in 28° 51' 37" of latitude observed and in 45° 6' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 23° 36' NW. During the night, squalls and rain.

1801-02-26.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from SSE, SE, east and ESE. At 2 a.m. the commander made the signal to wear ship. The main topsail bowline cringle having carried away, we lowered and clewed up the sail to replace it.
1801-02-26.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to ESE, with rain. At noon in 28° 34' 2" of latitude observed and in 45° 30' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 22° 5' NW. For several days the Naturaliste has sailed worse than ever; not a watch passes without our being obliged to bear away and lay the mizzen topsail to the mast.

1801-02-27.journal_anonyme: A very high sea, and squally weather with heavy rain, the wind a light breeze and variable from ESE to east and ENE. At 10 the weather cleared and the ship was extremely slack.
1801-02-27.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast, squally and rainy weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to ENE. At noon in 29° 28' 29" of latitude observed and in 45° 44' of longitude by No. 38. At 5.15 the course was signalled S 56° 15' E, but the Naturaliste could not make out the signal, being far astern. During the night we kept a light at the gaff and sent up rockets, without her answering.

1801-02-28.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the wind varying from ENE to SE and NE; a great deal of rain fell. At 10.55 p.m., the commander being out of sight, we kept a light constantly at the gaff, and after sending up some rockets we sighted him in the N by NW. At 8 a.m. the course was signalled SE by E.
1801-02-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NE. At 5.30 the Naturaliste was sighted ahead at a great distance. At 8 we signalled her the course S 56° E. At noon in 30° 11' 33" of latitude observed and in 46° 36' of longitude by No. 38.

1801-03-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At 7 p.m. took the reef in all three topsails; the weather very damp and the wind a strong breeze from NE to NNE.
1801-03-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE and NNE. At noon in 30° 46' 48" of latitude observed and in 48° 21' of longitude by No. 38. The variation 24° 9' NW.

1801-03-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from NE.
1801-03-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE and ENE. At noon in 31° 27' 22" of latitude observed and in 50° 7' of longitude by No. 38. At 1.30 signalled the course N 78° 45' E.

1801-03-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from NE to ENE. At 1 the commander signalled the course E by N. The weather very damp, the clouds driving from the NW.
1801-03-03.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to ENE. At noon in 31° 56' 38" of latitude observed and in 51° 5' of longitude by No. 38. At 3.45, being in a flat calm, the wind blew all at once from the SSW with force, and then from S and SSE. Signalled the course S 78° 45' E, with orders to follow our movements; took the lower reef in the topsails. During the night the wind a strong breeze, a high sea and pouring rain. At 9 sent up a rocket.

1801-03-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the wind light and variable from ENE, SSW, south, SSE, SE, ENE, NE. At 3 p.m. went about. The course signalled E by S. At 4 took the reefs in the topsails. The main topsail clewline having parted, it was spliced at once; but it tore because it took too long to repair. At 8.30 a.m. wore ship. Shortly afterwards the main topsail strop, the fore staysail halliard and the futtock shrouds carried away, and we were left under the foresail and fore topsail. We had one of our bobstays broken by the force of the sea, which was continually breaking aboard.
1801-03-04.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and misty weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts from SE to NE and north; a very high sea. At 8.15 lay to under the foresail, the storm staysail and the mizzen staysail. At 5 p.m. the Naturaliste was sighted in the S 45° W at a great distance. At nightfall the weather cleared and the wind and sea went down. Sent up a rocket every hour.

1801-03-05.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea; the winds drew round successively from NE to north, variable to NNW, NW and WNW, blowing hard and in gusts. At 10.30 p.m. the sea was extraordinarily high and still breaking aboard. We set the mizzen staysail; but wanting to set the foresail, the tack block broke and we clewed it up at once. We set the storm staysail, but not having succeeded at this first attempt owing to the parting of the stay, we hauled it down with great difficulty; and after repairing the strop we hoisted it again and lay to under that canvas, heading E by S. At 10.30 a.m. the weather having turned fine, we set the foresail and the topsails close-reefed. The commander out of sight. On the morning of the 14th we sighted a sail in the ESE which we believed to be the commander.
1801-03-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to WSW. At 5 filled the topsails. At 6 the Naturaliste was sighted from aloft in our wake. At 9 lay close-hauled on the port tack to wait for her. At noon in 31° 13' 22" of latitude observed and in 53° 49' of longitude by No. 38. The Naturaliste made the private signals, to which we answered. At 1, having closed, we signalled the course N 67° 30' E and stood on. At 4 we spoke; Captain Hamelin informed the commander that during the bad weather he had had his courses blown away and his bobstay carried away, which had forced him to lie to.

1801-03-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea with a little swell and the wind light. At 2.30 the commander answered the private signals and signalled us the course ENE. At 4 we spoke him and gave him an account of the damage we had suffered during the gale. The wind varying from W to WSW, SSW and SSE, a light breeze.
1801-03-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SW to SE. At daybreak the cheeks of the main topgallant crosstrees were found broken; the crosstrees were at once lashed under the cap with a stout seizing. The rigging was set up. At noon in 30° 31' 47" of latitude observed and in 54° 44' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 19° 47' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 21' 30" of longitude. At noon the course was signalled and given N 56° 15' E.

1801-03-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light variable air from SE. At 4.30 made all sail and trimmed close-hauled.
1801-03-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE and SSE. At noon in 29° 43' 12" of latitude observed and in 55° 24' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 19° 27' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 10' of longitude. At noon the course was signalled and given N 45° E. At 6 the Naturaliste asked to pass under our stern, which we granted. At 7 we spoke, and Captain Hamelin gave us the result of his lunar observations.

1801-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, the wind SE to SSE, a light breeze.
1801-03-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from SE to SW. At noon in 28° 40' 40" of latitude observed and in 55° 52' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 17° 58' NW. The lunar distances gave 55° 38' of longitude. Light rain during the night.

1801-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind light and variable from SSE, SW, WSW, NW and SW. The sea smooth. At 10 we had a squall which brought the winds round to SSW.
1801-03-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to south. At noon in 28° 3' 32" of latitude observed and in 56° 49' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 18° 8' NW. The lunar distances gave 56° 2' of longitude.

1801-03-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy and the winds a strong breeze from SSW to south. The mizzen topsail sheet having parted, we clewed the sail up to leeward to repair it.
1801-03-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 25° 2' 50" of latitude observed and in 57° 29' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 14° 17' NW. At noon the course was signalled and given N 33° 45' E. At 4 signalled the course N 22° 30' E for midnight.

1801-03-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea and the wind light from south, SE and SSE. At noon the course was signalled us NE by N until midnight, when we were to steer NNE.
1801-03-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At 2 a.m. we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the second time, in 58° 6' of longitude. The rigging was set up. At noon in 22° 48' 50" of latitude observed and in 58° 9' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 55' NW. At 5.30 we spoke the Naturaliste; the commander told Captain Hamelin to bend his sheet cables without waiting for the signal.

1801-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind light from SE, south, SSW and south. We asked the commander whether we should bend the cables without waiting for a signal; he answered no.
1801-03-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SSE. We bent our cables and got the anchors ready to let go. At noon in 21° 29' 40" of latitude observed and in 58° 14' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 49' NW. At 1.30 the course was signalled and given N 11° 15' E.

1801-03-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a light breeze from south, SSE and SSW. At 3 the winds shifted all at once to WSW. At sunrise land was thought to be seen in the WNW; the wind fell light. Saw a great number of tropic birds.
1801-03-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to ESE. At 6 a.m. the course was signalled and given N 45° W. Saw a great deal of weed. At noon in 20° 19' 50" of latitude observed and in 58° 1' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 35' NW. At 3 the weather turned overcast, with light rain. At 4.45 signalled the Naturaliste to pass under our stern; at 6, being within hail, the commander informed Captain Hamelin that he meant to steer N 67° 30' W, that at 8 he would regulate his canvas so as to run only 3.5 knots, and that if the weather turned bad he would heave to on the starboard tack, of which he would warn him by two lights. After speaking the Naturaliste we bore up N 67° 30' W. At 11 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack under close-reefed topsails; the breeze light, with lightning in the ESE.

1801-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind light and variable from SSE, SE, N, NE, east and SE. At 5 passed under the commander's stern; he gave us verbal orders to run no more than three and a half knots to the WNW, and that if the weather turned bad we should heave to. At a quarter past eleven the commander hove to on the starboard tack. We did the same. At 4 a.m., the wind having shifted to the north, we went onto the port tack.
1801-03-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to SE. At 5 a.m. shaped our course west, crowding sail. At noon in 19° 54' 0" of latitude observed and in 56° 34' of longitude by No. 38. Variation 11° 53' NW. At 5 p.m. the land was sighted in the S 75° W. At 6 took the bearing of Round Island N 68° W, the southernmost point of Mauritius in sight S 70° W, and the most conspicuous peak S 88° W. At 8.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 9.30 the Naturaliste passed under our stern; Captain Hamelin asked the commander his intentions for the night, and he told him he would stand off and on until daybreak. During the night overcast and squally weather, with rain and lightning in the ESE.

1801-03-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At 5.30 we made the land, and a moment later the commander signalled us the course WSW. At 1 a.m. went about, the weather stormy and squally. At daybreak we sighted the land WNW, distant about 6 leagues. The commander hailed us to steer for Round Island and to keep in his wake as close as possible. He asked whether we had anyone on board who knew the passage; we answered that we had Citizen Piquet, ensign.
1801-03-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. At 5.15 a.m. shaped our course for the North West Port. At 7 the commander gave verbal orders to Captain Hamelin to keep in our wake at a cable's length. At 8 took the bearing of Serpent Island N 24° W, Mauritius from N 75° W to S 50° W; signalled the Naturaliste to make ready to let go a bower anchor. At noon Round Island N 45° E, Flat Island N 34° W, Pointe aux Canonniers S 79° W. At 1.30 we hoisted our colours and confirmed them with a gun. The fort of Pointe aux Canonniers hoisted the national flag and confirmed it. At 2, being abreast of it, it saluted us with the flag; we returned the salute. At 3 the breeze drew round to SSW, variable to W. We stood on whichever tack served us best, firing guns to call the pilot. At 4 took the bearing of Pointe aux Canonniers N 75° E and Pointe aux Tonneliers S 24° W. At 8, being almost becalmed, we anchored under the coast in 20 fathoms, coral bottom, the light of Île aux Tonneliers bearing south and that of Fort Diane S 22° 30' W. The shore under which we lay anchored sent up two rockets every two hours.

1801-03-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth and a fresh breeze from ESE. After doubling Coin de Mire the commander signalled us to follow his movements; he was lying close-hauled on the port tack. At 3, the commander having fallen calm under the land, he went onto the starboard tack. A moment later the winds shifted to SSW; we stood on on our tack and went about a moment afterwards to run in for the land. We struggled all along against the fickleness of the winds to reach the anchorage under Île aux Tonneliers, but their weakness did not let us come near enough to the land to let go the anchor. At nightfall we fired a gun and hoisted our ensign at half mast to call a pilot. At 8.30 p.m. we stood off to seaward, the currents setting us WSW. At 10.30 p.m. we went onto the starboard tack. The winds having shifted, we ran in for the land and sounded without finding bottom; it was not until 10.35 that we found 26 and 17 fathoms. We let go the anchor in 14 fathoms, coral bottom, and veered 36 fathoms of cable. We sent a boat to sound all round the ship, Port Louis bearing from us S by E at a short distance, the commander in the NE by E at a great distance; the weather fine, a flat calm. At daybreak we showed our colours and our ensign at the stern half mast. At 6.45 we sighted a boat coming off from the shore towards us, approaching only with caution; when within hail she called to us, and on our answer she came aboard. The captain of the port, who was in her, left us a pilot and gave us a signal to identify ourselves from the shore. We were visited by the health officers and by the colonial assembly; the said captain of the port went aboard the Géographe. At 7.30 hove up, broke the anchor out and catted it. We got under way, casting to port. Favoured by a breeze off the sea, we shaped our course for Port Louis, doubled the Deux Frères at 9, leaving them to port, and doubled Île aux Tonneliers. At 10 we anchored in five fathoms and a half; shortly afterwards the Géographe came and anchored ahead of us.
1801-03-16.journal_breton_geographe: The wind a light breeze from SE. At 5 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course for the North West Port. At 7.30 an officer of the port and a pilot came out to us; they did not come aboard until they had asked whether there was any contagious sickness. At 10 we anchored in the North West Port in 4 fathoms, black mud mixed with grey sand, the flagstaff of Île aux Tonneliers bearing N 18° W, that of the Discovery Hill S 30° W, Le Pouce S 15° E and Pieter Both S 40° E. Several members of the colonial assembly and of the municipality came aboard. Orders were given to hand over all letters for the colony. The commander and Captain Hamelin went ashore shortly afterwards; leave to communicate with the shore was brought out to us, and many boats loaded with people, who had been waiting only for that leave, came alongside. The port's longboats helped us to moor; the boats were put in the water. Continuation. At 9 p.m., being charged with the duty of the roads as commanding ship, Citizen Ronsard, officer of the guard, went the rounds; Citizen Le Bas, frigate captain, went with him, knowing the usage of the service at Mauritius. He hailed a Danish ship that had a fire burning; a man who was on deck answered him rudely, and, having said he was a petty officer, Citizen Le Bas had him put into his boat. On reaching the ship he wanted to make him go first. The stranger then told him he was an officer like himself; in spite of which he pushed him by the shoulder. The gunner's mate tried to do the same; the unfortunate man's feet caught in the lashings that were on the gangway and he fell into the hold and was badly bruised on the shoulder. He was dressed and sent back to his ship. The 26th [Ventôse, 17 March 1801]. The brig L'Utile got under way for Réunion. An officer from La Cayenne came to tell us that we should no longer be charged with the duty of the roads. A water lighter came out to us. The topgallant masts were got down.

1801-03-17.journal_anonyme: During the day, the pilot being on board, we weighed to warp further in; by nightfall we were moored in six fathoms with 70 fathoms of cable out to starboard and the port cable made fast to a mooring buoy. On the morning of the 26th we laid a third anchor astern. Stay at Mauritius, Germinal to the 5th Floréal [Year 9, 25 April 1801]. During our stay at Mauritius we were busy overhauling the rigging and caulking the ship, and fresh provisions were embarked. The nights were cool enough and the days calm. By day the winds were fairly regularly from SE to SSE, and by night from NW to WNW. We had many deserters, and several officers and scientists of the two corvettes stayed behind at Mauritius. To prevent desertion the commander made us get under way to lie at the outer anchorage. On the morning of the 28th [Germinal, Year 9, 18 April 1801] the officers of the Naturaliste were assembled aboard the Géographe by the commander's order. They all went with the captain to the appointed place. The commander said he had held a council to determine what measures it would be best to take to bring back our deserters; and at the same time he read out the petition addressed to the constituted authorities of the colony to reclaim them. The commander having asked each man's opinion, all were of the view not to sign this petition; and by unanimous agreement among the officers of both ships the following declarations were entered in the Géographe's log: The officers forming the wardrooms of the two corvettes Géographe and Naturaliste, convened in council by the commander-in-chief of the expedition of discovery to deliberate on the most effective means of bringing back the deserting seamen of both ships, have declared that the commander alone had the right to take whatever measures should appear most fitting. All the officers signed this declaration, but Citizen Hamelin stated that he would not sign it, and the commander said he ought not to do so. Captain Baudin having announced that the purpose of the meeting was fulfilled, we took leave of him and all our officers returned on board; we hoisted in our longboat and our large boat. At 6 a.m. on the 2nd Floréal [Year 9, 22 April 1801] a naval gendarme brought us ten men by order of the fitting-out office. On the 3rd Floréal [Year 9, 23 April 1801] a boat sent by the fitting-out office brought clothing and money for various seamen shipped the day before. At 3.30 p.m. on the 5th [Year 9, 25 April 1801] the commander gave the order to unmoor; we at once sent a longboat to weigh our kedge anchor. At 5 a.m. on the 5th the winds ESE, a light breeze; at a quarter to seven the commander made us the signal to get under way. We at once hove short and hoisted our topsails to the mastheads, and as soon as the anchor was aweigh we filled and stood on. Bearings at eight in the morning: Coin de Mire NE by E; Île aux Tonneliers E by S 5° S. The winds variable from east to ESE and to west. Noon bearings: Coin de Mire N 60° E; the discovery hill of the port E by S; Morne Brabant SSW 5° S.

1801-04-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SE. At 6 a.m. made the signal to get under way. At 7 got under way and shaped our course west. At noon Coin de Mire bore from us N 55° E and Le Pouce S 70° E; shaped the course S 45° W, running along the land at 4 miles' distance. At 4, Le Pouce N 67° 30' E, the Piton of Rivière Noire N 80° E and Morne Brabant S 10° E. At midnight, Morne Brabant N 85° E, 12 miles off. The 6th [Floréal, 26 April 1801]. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ESE. At 8 took the bearing of Morne Brabant N 5° E, 24 miles off, from which I took my point of departure in 21° 8' of latitude and 55° 7' of longitude. The anchors were secured in their stowage and the mizzen topgallant mast struck. At noon in 21° 19' 0" of latitude observed and in 55° 12' of longitude by account. Variation 13° 26' NW. At 2.30 took the bearing of Réunion S 67° 30' W, at the limit of sight.

1801-04-26.journal_anonyme: The winds from the WNW, light. Bearings taken at 5.30 p.m.: Morne Brabant south 5° E, estimated distance 3 leagues and a half; the signal hill of the NW port NE by E. Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze.

1801-04-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high and the wind a strong breeze from east to ESE, the sea running from the south.
1801-04-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E. At noon in 22° 40' 30" of latitude observed and in 55° 24' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 29' NW.

1801-04-28.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from ESE. The sea smooth enough. The weather fine and the sky serene. At 10 a.m. we found the third forward shroud of the mainmast had parted above the futtock shrouds; the damage was repaired at once.
1801-04-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E and ENE. At noon in 23° 58' 0" of latitude observed and in 55° 31' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 53' NW. At 2 the course was signalled S 45° E should the wind draw aft. At 3.45 the Naturaliste signalled us damage to her main shrouds; we bore down on her and spoke.

1801-04-29.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 4 the course was signalled SE, and we signalled the commander the damage to our lower shrouds.
1801-04-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE to SE. At 6 a.m. a young Black man was found in the hold, where he had hidden himself at Mauritius. Want of food had left him so weak that he could not stand; he said he belonged to M. Gluaux, an inhabitant of Mauritius. At 9.45 the Naturaliste made us a signal that could not be understood. At noon in 25° 6' of latitude observed and in 56° 2' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 15° 0' NW. At 5 we spoke the Naturaliste; she told us that at 9.45 she had signalled us the height of her masts, 106 feet 8 inches from the truck to the gun deck.

1801-04-30.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from east; the sky cloudy. At 1 bore away to close the commander. By three we were near enough to him. The commander having worn ship, we went onto the starboard tack. At 5 p.m. the mist having kept us from seeing the commander, we shortened sail to wait for him; and at 7.30 we went about, supposing he had gone onto the port tack.
1801-04-30.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, a very thick fog, with rain. The wind light and then a strong breeze from SE to E. Lay to from 8.45 until half past noon on account of the fog. Fired several guns, as did our consort. At noon in 25° 50' of latitude by account and in 55° 27' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-01.journal_anonyme: The wind very variable and in gusts. At noon a thick mist came up and we lost sight of the commander. We fired two guns to which he did not answer. At 1.30 we sighted him and fired a third gun, and he at once answered our signals. We at once trimmed close-hauled on the port tack.
1801-05-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to NE. At noon in 27° 29' 18" of latitude observed and in 55° 53' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 18° 1' NW.

1801-05-02.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from south. The sea smooth, the sky rather dark. At half past five the commander signalled the course ESE.
1801-05-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NW. At 6 the course was signalled and given S 67° 30' E. At noon in 28° 35' of latitude observed and in 57° 51' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 17° 0' NW.

1801-05-03.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from NNE to NNW and north. The commander very close in the SE 5° E.
1801-05-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to WNW. The hand mill was rigged and we ground wheat. At noon in 28° 53' 42" of latitude observed and in 60° 31' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 16° 30' NW.

1801-05-04.journal_anonyme: Winds from N to NNW. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 8.45 the captain signalled the commander the longitude by lunar distances.
1801-05-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to south. At noon in 29° 11' 20" of latitude observed and in 62° 12' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 15° 19' NW.

1801-05-05.journal_anonyme: Winds NNW, very light, the weather very unsettled, a swell running from SW to SSW. Saw many birds.
1801-05-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to SE. At noon in 28° 57' 20" of latitude observed and in 64° 24' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 14° 48' NW.

1801-05-06.journal_anonyme: Winds SE, variable to ESE. The weather fine, a swell running. At 9.30 a.m. went onto the port tack.
1801-05-06.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 28° 35' 36" of latitude observed and in 65° 17' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-07.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky overcast, the sea high and with a little swell. Wind ESE in gusts.
1801-05-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. Saw albatrosses and pintado petrels. At noon in 30° 29' 10" of latitude observed and in 65° 8' of longitude by No. 35.

1801-05-08.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east to ENE, the sky cloudy, a high sea.
1801-05-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NE. At noon in 31° 39' 30" of latitude observed and in 65° 15' of longitude by No. 35. Variation 16° 27' NW.

1801-05-09.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from NE by E. The sea smooth, the weather fine and the sky very clear. Sailing a short distance from the commander. At two in the morning the sea was covered with luminous molluscs.
1801-05-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, with mist and squalls. The wind a strong breeze and blowing hard from NE to N. At noon in 32° 10' of latitude by account and in 67° 19' of longitude by account.

1801-05-10.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from NE by N in gusts, attended with rain.
1801-05-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from NNE. At noon in 32° 46' 30" of latitude by account and in 70° 2' of longitude by account. We signalled the Naturaliste to keep a light all night; she did so, as did we. The 21st [Floréal, 11 May 1801]. Overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts from NNE to NW and SW. At noon in 33° 32' 20" of latitude by account and in 73° 37' of longitude by account. At 6 p.m. we lost sight of the Naturaliste.

1801-05-11.journal_anonyme: The same winds and squally. Continual rain; by the commander's order we kept a light burning all night. But no longer seeing the commander, we sent up a rocket; at 6 he was sighted in the SE by E. The ship labouring a great deal from the violence of her pitching and rolling. The wind NNE, a strong breeze.

1801-05-12.journal_anonyme: A heavy wind from SSW and SW, blowing hard. We struck our topgallant masts and the jib boom and lowered the mizzen gaff. On the morning of the 22nd, the weather having cleared, we swayed up our topgallant masts, ran out the jib boom and hoisted the gaff.
1801-05-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to WSW. At daybreak the Naturaliste was sighted in our wake at a great distance; at 11.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack to wait for her. At 1 she had closed; we signalled her the course S 78° 45' E and shaped it. At noon in 33° 39' 40" of latitude observed and in 77° 12' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 13° 36' NW. The 23rd [Floréal, 13 May 1801]. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze and light from SW to WNW. At noon in 33° 34' 0" of latitude observed and in 79° 50' of longitude by No. 27. At 3.45, being almost becalmed with a heavy swell from the SW, our masts were labouring greatly from the rolling; we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and signalled the Naturaliste to follow our movement. At 5 we spoke her; the commander informed Captain Hamelin that if it freshened we should shape the course S 78° 45' E.

1801-05-13.journal_anonyme: Wind SSW to SW. The wind a strong breeze, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, a very high sea and the ship rolling extremely. The course was signalled E by S.

1801-05-14.journal_anonyme: Winds light from SW to north. A heavy swell running. The course signalled south.
1801-05-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to NNW. At midnight we shaped our course. Saw several albatrosses and many pintado petrels. One of the latter was taken with a line. At noon in 33° 35' of latitude observed and in 81° 7' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-15.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from NW, variable to SSW.
1801-05-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to south. At noon in 33° 22' 50" of latitude observed and in 85° 14' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 13° 36' NW.

1801-05-16.journal_anonyme: The winds south, variable to SSE and ESE. At 7 a.m. on the 26th we sent a boat aboard the commander with an officer to set the marine timekeeper, which had not been wound the day before.
1801-05-16.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the breeze light from SE to NE. At 7.15 the Naturaliste asked to send a boat aboard; we at once hove to. At 8 Citizen Saint-Cricq brought one of the Naturaliste's marine watches; they had stopped, Citizen Faure, who had charge of them, having forgotten to wind them. At 9, the boat having left, we filled and stood on. At noon in 32° 51' of latitude observed and in 86° 44' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-17.journal_anonyme: Winds NE to NNE in gusts. A swell running. At 7 a.m. the course signalled ESE.
1801-05-17.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to NNE. At 7.15 signalled the course S 67° 30' E, which had been given since 4 o'clock. Saw albatrosses, petrels and many pintado petrels; several were taken. At noon in 33° 20' 10" of latitude by account and in 87° 43' of longitude by account.

1801-05-18.journal_anonyme: The same winds in gusts. Laid the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for the commander, who was astern.
1801-05-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh and then a strong breeze from NNE to NNW. At noon in 33° 55' 50" of latitude by account and in 91° 28' of longitude by No. 27.

1801-05-19.journal_anonyme: The same winds in gusts, the commander far ahead of us. We sent up a rocket, and at 3 he answered with a light at the masthead. We took his bearing SE. Saw whales.
1801-05-19.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 34° 30' 40" of latitude observed and in 94° 31' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 10° 11' NW.

1801-05-20.journal_anonyme: The sky cloudy, the sea rather high, the wind a strong breeze from ESE. Saw many albatrosses.
1801-05-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from N to NNW. At 8 the course was signalled and given S 78° 45' E. At noon in 35° 10' 20" of latitude by account and in 98° 42' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 10° 31' NW. At 4 the course was signalled and given east. During the night sent up rockets.

1801-05-21.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, fresh enough. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 8 shortened sail to wait for the commander, who had fallen to leeward. At 8.30 p.m. went about and signalled our tack to the commander.
1801-05-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW, SW, SE, E and NE. At noon in 34° 47' 0" of latitude observed and in 101° 20' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 8° 53' NW.

1801-05-22.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind a light breeze from NNW. Saw many birds and fish of various kinds.
1801-05-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NW. At noon in 34° 38' 20" of latitude observed and in 103° 12' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 9° 20' NW.

1801-05-23.journal_anonyme: The wind NNW, a light breeze, heading east. At 7 the commander made us the signal to bend our cables. At 7.30 p.m. we sounded without finding bottom.
1801-05-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to NW, SW, SE and south. We signalled the Naturaliste to bend her cables, and bent ours. At noon in 34° 13' 30" of latitude observed and in 105° 45' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 8° 31' NW. In the evening the Naturaliste signalled 105° 57' of longitude and asked leave to shorten sail.

1801-05-24.journal_anonyme: The winds WNW, variable to south and SW. We hove to to wait for our boat, which was aboard the commander. At 4.30 we filled and stood on under all sail, the weather misty and rainy.
1801-05-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At noon in 33° 42' 40" of latitude observed and in 107° 51' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 4' NW. At 12.15 the course was signalled S 78° 45' E. At 4.30 made the signal to close. Shortly afterwards we spoke the Naturaliste; the commander ordered Captain Hamelin to keep in our wake at half a league and to sound every two hours, and to warn us by two vertical lights should he find bottom, adding that we should warn him in the same way if we found bottom. At 8 hove to and sounded without finding bottom at 265 fathoms. At 8.30 filled and stood on. At 10.30 lay to on the port tack under the mizzen topsail, the mizzen and its staysail, the main staysail and the fore staysail.

1801-05-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, wind SSE. At 3 the course signalled E by S. At 4 we shortened sail to wait for him; being within hail he ordered us to keep in his wake at half a league's distance and to sound every half hour. Hove to at 7, 8 and 10 and ran out 120 fathoms of line without finding bottom. The commander having gone onto the port tack, we did the same. At midnight, two and four o'clock ran out 120 fathoms of line without bottom.
1801-05-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to NE. At 5 filled and stood on. At noon in 33° 51' 40" of latitude observed and in 108° 29' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 8' NW.

1801-05-26.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, the wind variable from NE to NNE. At 1 p.m. wore onto the starboard tack, and at 10 p.m. went about. At 1 a.m. ran out 120 fathoms of line without bottom.
1801-05-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE. At 7 signalled and shaped the course S 78° 45' E. At noon in 33° 49' 50" of latitude observed and in 109° 44' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 25' NW. The Naturaliste, far astern, was lost sight of at nightfall. Sent up rockets and showed a light at the gaff to give her our position. At midnight we sounded and ran out 200 fathoms without finding bottom.

1801-05-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from NNE. The commander standing in for the land. At 5 it bore from us east 9° S, distant about 5 leagues, the commander out of sight. At 3.30 a.m. we had closed him within hail. At 7 he signalled us land without giving the bearing. At 7.30 we took its bearing in the SSE, with two detached points. At 10 took the bearing of the northernmost land ESE. Noon bearings: the furthest point to leeward that could be seen, east 25° 30' N; the point at which the land seemed no longer to continue, east 33° 10' N; the middle of the land which to windward appeared separate from the first, east 37° 45' N. None of these corrected for 6° 30' of NW variation.
1801-05-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to NNE and light from SSE to E. At 1.30 the Naturaliste was sighted in our wake. At 7.30 the land was sighted; it stretched from S 78° 45' E to N 67° 30' E and appeared to be divided in two parts. We signalled it to the Naturaliste. At noon the land from N 43° E to N 68° E, being in 34° 35' 40" of latitude observed and in 111° 42' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 15' NW. At half past noon the lead gave 104 fathoms, coral and sand. At 7.30 hove to on the starboard tack; the Naturaliste passed under our stern and the commander informed Captain Hamelin that he meant to lie to all night; he gave him leave to send aboard to compare his watches. At 8.30 Citizen Saint-Cricq arrived with the marine watches and left at 9. At 10.30 the boat came back to bring us hay. The dredge was put over and brought up marine specimens; the lead gave from 92 to 100 fathoms, coral, sand and shell. At midnight the land N 15° E.

1801-05-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind varying from SE, SSE and ESE. At half past noon hove to to sound. The lead brought up 93 fathoms, white sand mixed with broken shell. We thought we noticed that the winds set to the south. Bearings taken at sunset: the southern end of a stretch of land we judged to be an island, east 47° N; the furthest part to the north bore N 23° 40' E. At 7.30 passed under the commander's stern and asked his leave to communicate in order to set our marine timekeepers; he granted it and warned us that if the weather stayed fine we should lie to heading north. Soundings: at 9 p.m., 89 fathoms, reddish sand and broken shell; at 10, 11 and 12, 90 fathoms, the same. We lay to on the starboard tack until four o'clock, when we filled and stood on. At daybreak took the bearing of the land east 27° N. At 10, east 38° 10' N.
1801-05-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ENE. Shortly after midnight the land was lost sight of. At 7 we filled and stood on, and the land was seen from aloft. From midnight to noon the lead gave from 100 to 105 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon the land bore from us N 33° E to N 38° E, being in 34° 45' 0" of latitude observed and in 111° 46' of longitude by No. 27. The variation 6° 90' NW [sic]. By the reckoning we had made way to the north and west, and by the observation we had made it to the south and east, which can only be put down to the violence of the currents, which set south and SSE. At 5 took the bearing of the north point in sight N 11° E, the south point in sight N 67° 30' E, and an islet lying near the latter N 78° 45' E. From 5 until midnight the lead gave from 45 to 33 fathoms, sand and coral. During the night we lay to, in sight of land.

1801-05-29.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from east to ESE. The weather fine, the sea smooth. At 4 took the bearing of the easternmost part of the land in sight N 23° 20' E, the westernmost part N 45° E, estimated distance 16 miles. Passed under the commander's stern; he ordered us to heave to. At 8.25 sounded and found 25 fathoms, sand and broken shell. At five in the morning the commander having filled, we did the same. At noon sounded and found 28 fathoms, rock and coral. At the same hour took the bearing of the southernmost point of the land east 38° 30' S and the northernmost N 21° 30' E.
1801-05-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SE. At 5 we filled and stood on, running along the coast at about 6 miles. It seemed to me to offer no safe anchorage: it is fringed with reefs on which the sea broke with force; the dunes are covered with heath and a few bushes are to be seen here and there. The lead giving from 30 to 40 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon, being in 34° 11' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 44' 50" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 4' NW. The northernmost point in sight bore from us N 20° E, the southernmost S 45° E, and a white cape (taken for Cape Leeuwin) S 78° 45' E. At 5 we saw a fire on the shore, which convinced us that the coast is inhabited. At 7.30 we hove to. The Naturaliste passed under our stern and spoke us. The trend of the coast is roughly north and south. Note: Cape Leeuwin lies further south than this white cape.

1801-05-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea; we ran along the coast to the north. At 4 p.m. took the bearing of Cape Leeuwin south 15° 30' E, distant about six leagues. Running along the coast we saw a fire ashore and then several more. We hoisted a lantern at the gaff to make ourselves known to the inhabitants. Soundings: at 8 and 9, 30 fathoms, rock and coral; at 10, 38 fathoms, fine sand; at 11 and 12 the same, mixed with broken shell. At 1 the commander having altered course we did the same. At 2 filled and made all sail. At 6.25 a.m. went about to close the commander, who was far to leeward. At 6.40 sounded in 28 fathoms, sand and coral. At noon we saw that the land stretched away all along to starboard and formed a bight, of which several points could be seen at noon from the quarterdeck.
