Noon bearings: Point P ahead of us S 2° E; Point N furthest astern S 3° 30' E; Point O which we had doubled S 27° W. These points are so named after the surveying engineer's work.
1801-05-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE and ESE. At midnight we were losing the land appreciably and the lead gave no bottom at 60 fathoms; we filled and stood on, close-hauled on the starboard tack under topsails. At 8 crowded sail to close the land, which bore from us S 5° E to N 72° E; Cape Leeuwin S 9° E. At 10.30 saw a thick smoke in the S 27° E. We ran along the coast until noon at 3 miles, when it appeared to take an ESE trend and form a gulf. At noon, being in 33° 22' 20" of latitude observed and in 112° 3' 40" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 25' NW. We took the bearing of the southernmost land in sight S 38° W, and of the cape forming the SW entrance of the gulf S 85° E; the lead having given since 2 o'clock from 54 fathoms to 30, sand, rock and coral. We lay close-hauled on the starboard tack; at 1 went onto the port tack and stood in for the land; the Naturaliste signalled us a danger in the N 22° 30' W. At 5 anchored in 23 fathoms, muddy sand, Cape Géographe bearing N 78° 45' W and a point S 14° E. At 7 the Naturaliste anchored near us. At 11 we dragged two thirds of a cable's length; the mizzen topsail, which had been kept on the mast, was furled and we brought up. The gulf in which we anchored was named Geographe Bay, and the SW point of the gulf, Cape Géographe.

1801-05-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. At a quarter to one we took the bearing of a reef NW by W by compass, distant 2 leagues and a half. At the same moment Cape B S 25° W. At 7.30 we went about and stood to windward of Point O. At 4.30 sounded in 25 fathoms, sand and coral. At 4.30 went onto the starboard tack. At 5.15 the commander let us know by three lights that he was at anchor; he then bore from us S 14° E. We went about and stood on on the port tack. At six we went about again; at a quarter to seven, the commander bearing from us SW by W, we went onto the port tack and, steering for the Géographe, passed under her stern; he ordered us to anchor. At 7 [a figure struck out, illegible] we were anchored in 20 fathoms, muddy sand mixed with blackish gravel, and veered 100 fathoms of cable. Saw several fires on the coast. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 3° S; Point O WSW 2° 30' S; Point P south 7° 30' [one word illegible]. From 4 to 8 we struck the main topgallant mast and stopped the topsails with rope yarns. At 8 a.m. the Géographe had sent her boat ashore, and as ours was about to shove off the commander hailed us to send it only when his was back.
1801-05-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E. At 5 a.m. Citizen Freycinet left in the small boat to survey the country abreast of the anchorage; the gardener and the mineralogist went with him. The longboat and the large boat were put in the water. The first was sent off under the orders of Citizen Piquet to survey the coast and determine the position of Cape Géographe; the astronomer and the surveyor went in her. At noon Cape Géographe bore from us N 86° 15' W. The latitude observed 33° 28' 30" and the longitude by No. 27, 112° 1' 30". At 12.15 Citizen Freycinet was back; he had had great difficulty in landing and had not found a drop of drinkable water. In the evening the boats were hoisted in, and a light was kept at the masthead during the night to mark our position for the longboat.

1801-06-01.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea choppy and the wind in gusts. We sent a boat ashore which did not return until 5. At 7 p.m. the captain was back from his visit to the end of Point P, lying S 37° E. At 7 a.m. we received the order to get under way; at 9.30 we filled with the winds ESE, a fresh breeze. Bearings: Point N S 43° W; Point O S 2° W; Point P S 2° E; and the easternmost land east 2° S.
1801-06-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E, very variable. At 6.30 a.m. hoisted the topsails and hove short; hailed the Naturaliste to get under way at once. At 7.30 Citizen Piquet arrived; he had not been able to land at Cape Géographe nor anywhere near it; the currents had carried him offshore and he had beaten to windward all night without gaining. At 8 we got under way and lay to until 9, when we shaped our course N and N 22° E, close-hauled on the starboard tack. At noon in 33° 19' of latitude observed and in 112° 1' 30" of longitude by No. 27; Cape Géographe then bore from us S 45° W. At half past noon went close-hauled on the port tack, steering S 11° E. At 6 anchored in 23 fathoms, grey sand; saw a very large fire in the S 56° W which lasted 2 hours. The dredge brought up many objects of natural history. Est. lat. 33° 30' and est. long. 112° 13' at the anchorage.

1801-06-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds ESE, a fresh breeze. At 1.10 we went about, as did the commander, and we sounded in 25 fathoms, gravelly sand; at 4, 23 fathoms, the same bottom. Bearings taken at sunset: Point N W 21° 30' S; Point O W 44° 30' S; Point P south 5° 30' W; the end of the land to windward of us east 1° 30' N. At 6.30 saw a fire ashore which we took bearing SW by W. At 6.45 we were at anchor. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 18° 15' N; Point O W 28° 15' N; Point P W 61° 15' N; the easternmost end of the land E 18° 15' N. At 8.30 a.m. filled under all sail. At 10 a.m. went about and sounded in 18 fathoms, sand and shell; at 11, 20 fathoms; at 11.30 went onto the port tack, the same bottom and the same depth as at 11.
1801-06-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light from ENE to south. At 6.45 a.m. Citizen Bonnefoi left in the longboat to survey part of the gulf. At 8 got under way and shaped our course SSW and SSE, close-hauled on the port tack. At 10 saw a very thick smoke in a wood near the shore. Our longboat made us signals of good anchorage near the land. At noon, being in 33° 33' 40" of latitude observed and in 111° 55' of longitude by No. 27. Cape Géographe bore from us N 66° W and another point N 57° E. At noon went onto the starboard tack, heading north. At 2.30 went onto the port tack, heading S 22° 30' E. At 3.30 went onto the starboard tack, heading east. At 4 Citizen Bonnefoi arrived with the longboat. At 5, Cape Géographe N 82° W. At 8 anchored in 18 fathoms, coarse sand, in 33° 27' 40" of latitude by account and 112° 24' of longitude by account. The day's soundings were from 22 to 15 fathoms, grey muddy sand and red sand.

1801-06-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds ESE, a fresh breeze. We sounded every half hour in 18, 16, 16, 18, 19, 19 and 20 fathoms, sand mixed with gravel and broken shell. At 8.10 p.m. we let go the port anchor in 20 fathoms and veered 65 fathoms of cable; the lead brought up, alongside and all about, 20 fathoms of reddish sand mixed with gravel. Bearings of the anchorage: Point N W 4° 45' S, estimated distance 5 leagues; the end of the opposite land, which we shall call J, E 43° 30' N, estimated distance 10 leagues. At 9.15 we got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack.
1801-06-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E to NE. At 8.15 a.m. got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, heading N 11° E. At noon in 33° 15' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 56' 20" of longitude by No. 27, Cape Géographe bearing S 56° W and another point N 56° E (a). At 1 went onto the port tack, heading S 45° E. At 5.30 anchored in 12 fathoms, fine sand, Cape Géographe bearing S 79° W and point (a) N 45° E. Latitude observed 33° 27' 30", longitude by No. 27, 112° 7' 30" at the anchorage. The day's soundings were from 25 to 18 fathoms, coarse red sand. During the night several fires were seen in the bay.

1801-06-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from ESE. At 1.45 sounded in 23 fathoms, reddish sand mixed with glittering gravel; at 4, the same bottom and the same depth. Bearings taken at 4 on the 14th Prairial: Point N, forming the starboard end of the gulf, south 73° W; the port end of the same bight N 65° E, at 10 miles' distance; the end of the land stretching north, called the Paps, N 48° E. At 4.45 the lead brought up 16 fathoms, fine sand. At 6, 14 fathoms, and it kept shoaling from 13 to 14, the same bottom. At the same hour went onto the starboard tack, and shortly afterwards onto the port tack, standing in for the anchorage. At 6.30 we let go the anchor in 13 fathoms, fine sand mixed with broken shell; the soundings were the same all round the corvette from 6 until midnight. The currents setting us onto our cable, we laid the mizzen topsail aback. At midnight we saw a fire on the hill bearing from us S 6° W. Fine weather, smooth sea, and a light breeze.
1801-06-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from E. At 4 a.m. Citizen Bougainville left in the longboat to sound along the coast, and I in the small boat to have grass cut for our livestock; the zoologist and the botanist came with me. At 8.30 the commander and all the scientists went ashore in the large boat. At 4 p.m. I came aboard, Citizen Bougainville at 5.30 and the commander at 6. The latter had seen Aboriginal people, who would not communicate; I had seen no inhabitants but had seen their tracks, and those of a dog's paws. No one had found drinkable water.

1801-06-05.journal_anonyme: At 6 a.m. we sent off two boats to go ashore, one under the orders of Citizen Heirisson and the other under those of Citizen Freycinet. They found bare footprints, which makes us believe there are Aboriginal people here; they also found kangaroo tracks and celery like that of France. The weather fine, the sea smooth and the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. On the 16th at 4 a.m. our two boats were sent off in company with the longboat, which by the commander's order took four days' provisions.
1801-06-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE. At 3 a.m. the longboat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Le Bas; with several of the scientists he was to survey the country and try to communicate with the Aboriginal people. Struck the topgallant masts. During the night kept a light at the gaff to mark our position for the longboat.

1801-06-06.journal_anonyme: The winds having fallen light, we put the dinghy in the water to send the commander a letter the captain had left on board. In the afternoon the wind blew lightly from the east, the sea still with a heavy swell. At 7 p.m. the large boat was back; Citizen Saint-Cricq had seen many Aboriginal people who took flight at his approach. The day before, the commander had seen six Aboriginal men, five of whom fled at his approach; the sixth, an older man, came towards the commander with threatening gestures, pointing to his ship and giving him to understand that he was not looking for him and that he should withdraw from this land, which belonged to him. The commander, seeing that he could learn nothing from this man, took the opposite direction and went off into the woods with all those accompanying him.
1801-06-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE, a high sea. At 9 a.m. struck the topgallant masts. At 2 p.m. the wind fell. At 3 fired a gun and made the signal to recall the longboat. At 4.30 and at 6 fired a gun and showed a light at the gaff. At 7.45 Captain Hamelin came to tell the commander that our longboat had been cast on the shore, but that no one was lost. He himself, in his boat, had been obliged to pass the previous night at anchor offshore and had only reached his ship at nightfall.

1801-06-07.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from the east. At 7 p.m. the captain's boat was back and brought us the unhappy news that the Géographe's longboat was cast away on the coast. The captain wrote at once to the commander, who was in mortal anxiety; a boat was sent off with the letter. The commander, judging that the captain had not given him enough detail, decided to send for him aboard; the captain embarked at once in his boat and returned shortly afterwards.
1801-06-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NE. At 4.15 the large boat was sent aboard the Naturaliste. At 7.30 took the second reef in the topsails, which were stopped with rope yarns, and signalled the Naturaliste to carry out the order received; she asked leave to slip her cable. We hailed her to send our boat back; an officer came to explain to the commander what prevented him from getting under way: in heaving round, his stoppers had parted several times and he had a man hurt. At 8.30 got under way; at 9 shaped our course and steered successively S 78° 45' E, S 67° 30' E, S 45° E, S 22° 30' E and south, the lead giving 11, 10, 9, 8, 7 and 8 fathoms, fine sand. At 11 several people were seen on the shore. At 11.30 we anchored in 8 fathoms, fine sand, Cape Géographe bearing N 85° W and another point N 34° E. Latitude observed 33° 33' 0", longitude by No. 27, 112° 13' 50" at the anchorage. At noon the wind and sea fell; the large boat was sent off with a hawser, provisions and stores for the longboat's crew. Fired two guns. At 3.30 the Naturaliste got under way and came and anchored near us. Captain Hamelin came aboard and informed the commander that after much effort to weigh his anchor it had come up with a fluke broken. At nightfall showed a light at the gaff and burnt a flare every half hour. At 8 the large boat came back and brought Citizen Péron, one of the shipwrecked naturalists. During the night the longboat's crew made a fire on the shore.

1801-06-08.journal_anonyme: Blowing hard from NE, a very high sea. The Géographe's boat came aboard at 4 a.m. with orders to man our large boat and put into it all the gear needed to repair the stranded longboat; the bad weather prevented the two boats from shoving off. At 7 o'clock the commander gave written orders to get under way and anchor within the bay. We at once hove round at the capstan, but the heavy sea tried us greatly and the cable came in only with difficulty; at half past eight all the stoppers parted and the little cable we had got in ran out again, wounding one of our quartermasters severely. At 9 the Géographe was under sail and recalled her boat; one of our officers went aboard her for orders. At 2 p.m. we rigged a voyol to heave with more power at the capstan. At 3 we found the flukes had parted from the shank; we finished getting in the rest of the cable and catted the stump of the anchor. At 3.30 we shaped our course NW by N and anchored at 5 in 5 fathoms of water, fine sand, and veered 50 fathoms of cable, the commander bearing from us SSE. The captain went aboard the Géographe. At 5.30 saw two fires in the SW. A fresh breeze from ENE. On the 19th at 4 a.m. our large boat left with the commander's boat to carry help to the stranded longboat.
1801-06-08.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE to ESE. At 4 a.m. our large boat and the Naturaliste's were sent off with express orders to bring back all the men who were ashore and to abandon the longboat and the gear that had been sent to get her off. The barometer falling fast made us fear bad weather. In the afternoon the two large boats brought back all our people. The longboat was abandoned with a kedge anchor, hawser, tackles, arms and stores. At 8 a boat from the Naturaliste came aboard. Citizen Milius, who commanded her, told us that he came from the shore and had lost one of his boat's crew named Vasse: the sea being very high and breaking with force on the shore, the boat had been obliged to keep at some distance so as not to be swamped; each man had taken to the water to embark, hauling himself along by the boat's grapnel line; all succeeded except Vasse, who, being drunk, was carried away by a sea. At 9 got under way, as did the Naturaliste. The wind at noon; at 11 almost calm, with rain. The barometer still falling.

1801-06-09.journal_anonyme: The wind NE freshening a great deal; our large boat went aboard the Géographe carrying part of the people who had been ashore, and was sent off again to fetch the rest. Seeing that we could not get the longboat off, we abandoned her with all the gear we had landed, and sent up several rockets to mark our position for our two boats, being in great anxiety on their account. At 8 our small boat was back, telling us that the large one was following. At the same moment the ship dragged in a squall and we veered cable; but still driving fast towards the land, the captain decided to get under way. We hove round at once at the capstan, but the ship still casting towards the land, and the capstan meeting little resistance from the cable, we supposed the latter had parted or the anchor been damaged — which we verified at 10.30 p.m., for having then finished hauling the warp aboard we saw that the anchor had only one fluke left. As soon as it was catted we made sail with the winds SSE, variable and very light. Citizen Milius, first lieutenant, took charge of the working of the ship. At 7.30 a.m. a strong breeze, a high sea and the sky overcast.
1801-06-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, almost calm. At midnight it began to freshen, and the wind blew hard in gusts, with a high sea and rain. At 3.30 lay to; at 5 filled and stood on. At noon, in a clear interval, took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 85° W, about 18 miles off. The Naturaliste to leeward, beating like ourselves to get out of the gulf; the wind from NE to north. At noon in 33° 25' 20" of latitude by account and in 112° 5' 50" of longitude. At 4, Cape Géographe S 82° W, about 12 miles off. At 7.30 the Naturaliste was in sight to leeward; at midnight she bore from us SSW at a short distance.

1801-06-10.journal_anonyme: At 1.30 p.m. we wore ship. At 2.30 we sighted the Géographe ahead and to windward of us standing on the opposite tack; at 3.30 wore ship. At 4.30 the commander bearing from us north. At 5.30, at 8 and at midnight wore ship. Bearings taken at 2.30 p.m.: the starboard point of the gulf on entering N 78° W, distant 10 miles. At 3.30 the same point N 86° W, distant 8 miles. Thick weather, the wind blowing hard in gusts.
1801-06-10.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard and variable from NE to NW in gusts, a high sea, with rain. At 1 we lost sight of the Naturaliste. At 3 the southern shores of the gulf bore from us S 45° W, and at 4, S 22° 30' W. At 10, being clear of the gulf, lay to under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the storm staysail and the mizzen staysail. At noon in 33° 46' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 40' of longitude by account. At 1 took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 50° E and the point of the islet (seen on the 8th) S 41° E. At 9 filled and stood on under courses. From midnight to 8 a.m. the lead gave from 20 to 33 fathoms, grey sand; from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. no bottom at 80 fathoms; from 6 p.m. to midnight from 50 to 28 fathoms, rocky bottom.

1801-06-11.journal_anonyme: During the night the kedge anchor was carried away by a sea which parted both lashings. A very high sea, the wind still blowing hard. Given the weakness of our crew, both watches were kept on deck. At 8 a.m. Point N bore from us west. But the winds having headed us 2 points in a squall, we wore ship.
1801-06-11.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from NNW to W; a high sea and rain. At midnight lay to again under the same canvas. At 8 the land stretched from N 22° 30' E to S 45° E. At noon in 34° 5' 20" of latitude by account and in 111° 44' 10" of longitude by account, Cape Géographe bearing from us N 15° E and Cape Leeuwin east, about 9 miles off. At 4, Cape Géographe N 11° E, Cape Leeuwin N 25° E and the point of the islet S 68° E. We have had no sight of the Naturaliste since the 21st at 1 a.m.

1801-06-12.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from WNW to WSW. A high sea, with light rain at intervals. At 8 took the bearing of the northernmost point in sight, north; Cape Leeuwin N 11° E; the point of the islet N 79° E; and the islet S 79° E. At noon the land could no longer be seen. We were in 34° 37' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 53' of longitude by account. At nightfall the wind fell away a great deal.

1801-06-13.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze, variable from W to SW. At daybreak the land was sighted; at 7 filled and stood on, lying close-hauled on the port tack. At 8 the point of the islet N 15° E and another point N 22° 30' W. At noon in 34° 26' of latitude by account and in 111° 55' of longitude by account, the northernmost point in sight bearing N 3° W, Cape Leeuwin N 7° E, the point of the islet N 56° E and the islet N 68° E. At 4.45 took the bearing of Cape Géographe N 28° E, 23 miles off; the White Mountain, which had at first been taken for Cape Leeuwin, east, 10 miles off; Cape Leeuwin S 50° E, 22 miles off. During the night carried little sail so as not to run past Cape Géographe. The topgallant masts were swayed up.

1801-06-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to NW. At 7, having doubled Cape Géographe, we bore away east into the gulf to see whether the Naturaliste might be there. At noon in 33° 31' of latitude observed and in 111° 27' 10" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 50' NW. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Géographe S 73° W and a NE point of the gulf N 55° E. At 5, having seen nothing in the gulf, we hauled to the wind on the port tack; at 6.30 went onto the starboard tack. During the night overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts, with squalls.

1801-06-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to W in gusts. At midnight went onto the port tack. At 8 we were about 18 miles from the land; it appeared to stretch away in the N 22° 30' E and to form a bight. At 11 a very conspicuous point bore from us east, about 12 miles off. At noon in 32° 36' 50" of latitude observed and in 111° 45' 20" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 7° 25' NW. At 6 the land stretched from N 11° E to S 67° 30' E. Went onto the starboard tack. Squally weather, with rain.

1801-06-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze and light from WSW to SW. At midnight went onto the port tack; at 4 onto the starboard. At 8 the land stretched from N 56° E to S 34° E. At 10.45 went onto the port tack, being about 4 miles from the coast, which appears to trend NNE and SSW. It is very low near the shore; inland, fairly high and well wooded mountains could be seen. At noon the northernmost land in sight bore N 34° E, 10 miles off, and the southernmost S 22° E, 21 miles off. At noon in 32° 43' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 56' 30" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 6° 22' NW. The dredge was put over several times and brought up many objects of natural history. At 10, the breeze being from the north, went onto the starboard tack.

1801-06-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather until 10.30, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NE; afterwards overcast and rainy weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard in gusts from N to W. At 3 a.m. went onto the port tack. At 6 bore away east for the land. At 8 took the bearing of a very high mountain inland, S 35° E; we then bore away south and S 11° W and ran along the coast at 2 miles' distance. It runs roughly north and south and is very low; it is not so well wooded as in the gulf. I thought I could see that it was fringed with coral. The sea broke there violently. The lead gave from 8 to 13 fathoms, coral bottom. At 10.15 breakers were seen ahead in the S 10° E at a short distance; we at once hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. The wind freshened by degrees. At noon the land stretched from N 68° E to S 40° E. At noon in 32° 43' 57" of latitude observed and in 111° 53' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 5° 26' NW. At 1 lay to under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail; at 6 lay to with the port side to the wind.

1801-06-18.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, with thunder, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from W to south. At noon in 32° 16' 30" of latitude observed and in 111° 39' 30" of longitude by No. 27. The land bore from us N 79° E at a great distance. At 2 filled and stood on, starboard tack, under the foresail, close-reefed topsails, the storm staysail, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. (The Naturaliste, at anchor off Rottnest Island, sighted us at 2 in the S 22° 30' W, 24 miles off.) At 5 the north point in sight N 45° E and the south point N 79° E. At 9.30, having found ourselves on a shoal of reddish sand, we went onto the port tack and gave the course N 45° W, and at 10, N 67° 30' W. At 9.30 the lead had given 12 fathoms, and a quarter of an hour before, 25 to 21 fathoms, grey sand.

1801-06-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to SW. At 8 the land was seen at the limit of sight. The course was given N 33° 45' W. At noon in 31° 59' 10" of latitude observed and in 111° 6' 30" of longitude by account. The variation in Geographe Bay was 5° 25', the mean of a great number of observations I made there, all of which agreed within 5 minutes. The Naturaliste, which during the gale in the gulf had doubled the north point, had shaped her course for Rottnest Island, the first place of rendezvous, and had anchored there on the morning of the 25th.

1801-06-20.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSW. At 8 the course was given N 11° 15' W. At noon in 29° 15' 40" of latitude observed and in 109° 52' 6" of longitude by No. 27. At 10 and at midnight sounded without finding bottom at 110 fathoms. Water was put on an allowance of 1 bottle a day.

1801-06-21.journal_breton_geographe: Misty weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW, SSW, S, SE, ESE and E, with light rain. At 8 the course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 29° 15' 40" of latitude by account and corrected, and in 109° 30' of longitude by account. Variation 5° 1' NW. At 10 sounded without finding bottom at 70 fathoms.

1801-06-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to south. At 7 the land was sighted; it stretched from N 45° E to east. The course was given N 33° 45' E. The sea was covered with weed. At noon in 27° 23' 50" of latitude observed and in 109° 48' 54" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 4° 27' 20" NW. The land from N 19° E to S 80° E. At 4 it stretched from N 11° E to S 34° E. We bore up N 45° W to run along the coast, which lies roughly NNW and SSE. It does not offer the same appearance as the Leeuwin land: it is very high and sheer. Not a tree is to be made out. At 9.30 shaped the course N 67° 30' W and carried little sail. At 9 the lead gave 55 fathoms and at 11, 52 fathoms, sandy bottom.

1801-06-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to south. At 1 shaped the course N 56° 15' W; at 5 shaped the course N 33° 45' W and crowded sail. At 7 the commander gave orders directly to the helmsman to steer N 22° 30' E, and had the yards trimmed, taking no notice of Citizen Piquet, the officer of the watch, who observed to him that he was useless on deck and that he would leave the watch if the commander wished; and on his orders he left it. At 9 the land was sighted; at noon it bore from us N 11° E to S 56° E. At noon in 26° 1' 35" of latitude observed and in 109° 2' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 4° 20' NW. Bore up north and ran along the west coast of Dirk Hartog Island. We passed through tide rips whose direction was north and south and whose strength may have been 3 to 4 knots, for despite our apparent speed of 6 to 7 knots we doubled the land only very slowly. At 4 bore up N 22° 30' E, at 5 N 33° 45' E. At 5.15 took the bearing of the west point of Dirk Hartog S 22° 30' W and the north point S 78° E; the southernmost of the Dorre islands from N 30° E to N 40° E. At 6 set topsails, heading N 11° 15' E. At 7, Dorre Island from N 50° E to N 8° [E]. Bore up north and N 22° 30' W to draw off from it.

1801-06-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from south to NE. At 2 a.m. lay close-hauled on the port tack. At 4 went onto the starboard tack and crowded sail to close the land. At 8 the northernmost Dorre island S 50° E. At noon in 24° 18' of latitude observed and in 109° 3' 26" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 23' NW. At noon went onto the port tack; at 5 the land from N 68° E to N 85° E; at 8 went onto the starboard tack. Saw very large sharks.

1801-06-25.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to NE. At 2 a.m., having sighted the land in the N 68° E, headed north under topsails. At daybreak it stretched from S 45° E to S 79° E. We lay close-hauled on the starboard tack under all sail. At 9 went onto the port tack; the wind freshened. At 10, the wind a strong breeze, lay to on the starboard tack under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. At noon the land S 67° 30' E, being in 23° 56' 40" of latitude by account and in 109° 15' 32" of longitude by account. At 1 lay to on the port tack. At 4.30 the land in sight from S 45° E to S 68° E, about 24 miles off. A very thick column of smoke in the S 72° E. At 5.30 filled and stood on on the starboard tack under the foresail, close-reefed topsails, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail.

1801-06-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NE to SE. At daybreak the land was sighted from the topgallant crosstrees; crowded sail to close it. At 9 went onto the port tack. At noon in 23° 47' 40" of latitude observed and in 109° 30' 30" of longitude by account, the northernmost point in sight bearing N 80° E and the southernmost S 12° E. We ran along the land to the north of the bay. At 5 took the bearing of the northernmost point in sight N 40° E; a large cape, the nearest, forming the entrance to Shark Bay, S 57° E; the land in sight as far as south. At 7.45 anchored abreast of a cove in 34 fathoms, sandy bottom, the large cape bearing N 33° 45' E and the entrance of the cove from N 55° E to S 45° E. At 10 got under way, because we were dragging and the current was setting us onto the coast; our anchor had fouled its stock. Shaped our course N 11° 15' W, running along the coast at a short distance.

1801-06-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from E to SSE. At midnight steered north, running along the coast. At 4 a.m. lay close-hauled on the port tack; the large cape then bore from us N 45° E, 9 miles off. At 8 bore away south, S 11° 15' W and S 22° 30' W to enter Shark Bay. At 7 the large cape bore from us N 65° E. At 10 the northern Dorre island was sighted to the south. At noon in 24° 38' of latitude observed and in 109° 23' of longitude by No. 27. At noon took the bearing of the north point of the northern Dorre island S 51° W, and the mainland from N 25° E to S 7° E. At 2.30 anchored in Shark Bay in 16 fathoms, muddy sand, the northern Dorre island bearing from N 74° W to S 47° W and the northernmost mainland N 56° E. The large boat, under the orders of Bonnefoi, was sent off to Dorre Island. At 4 the current ran 1 knot, the ebb making, its direction NW. At 8 a fire was seen on Dorre Island, lit by our boat's crew. At 8.15 the tide turned, the flood beginning. During the night a light was kept at the gaff.

1801-06-28.journal_anonyme: We made ready to get under way. On the 9th at 7 a.m. we got under way with the winds NE, a fresh breeze. At noon we sounded in 26 fathoms, sand mixed with gravel and broken shell. The weather fine, the sea smooth, the sky without cloud.
1801-06-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to SSE. At midnight Bonnefoi came back with the large boat. At 7.30 a.m. the commander and all the naturalists went to Dorre Island in the two boats. Saw a great number of whales; fish were taken in abundance and some were salted. At nightfall our people lit a fire ashore; we showed a light at each masthead and burnt flares every half hour. At 9.30 the commander and the naturalists arrived in the large boat. The small one had stayed ashore under the orders of Citizen Piquet, to wait for the zoologist Péron, who had not appeared at the hour fixed for departure.

1801-06-29.journal_anonyme: The weather hazy and squally, with lightning in the west. At 2 p.m. the lead brought up 27 fathoms, grey sand, coral and gravel. The wind ESE, variable to SE. At 11.30 a current was observed setting from NNW to SSE.
1801-06-29.journal_breton_geographe: Latitude observed at the anchorage 24° 46' 20"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 109° 20' 40". Variation, the mean of 7 observations at the anchorage, 6° 1' 7" NW. The tides set NW and SE, and the sea rises 7½ feet. At half past noon the small boat arrived, bringing back Citizen Péron, who, having gone too far into the island, had lost himself there and passed the night in the scrub; at daybreak he had found our people. Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S and SSE.

1801-06-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze from the SSE, variable to ENE and N. At eight in the evening the lead brought up 24 fathoms, sand and rock [several words illegible] every half hour. At midnight we hove to with the port side to the wind. At 7.45 went about onto the starboard tack. Bearings taken at noon: the northernmost peak NE by N; the one to the NE, NE 1° N; the southernmost NE 1° E.
1801-06-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SW. At 7.30 got under way and shaped our course N 45° E, N 67° 30' E, east and S 67° 30' E, the small boat sounding ahead. Saw a turtle. At noon in 24° 44' 4" of latitude observed and in 109° 26' 8" of longitude by No. 27. At 1 anchored in 9 fathoms, fine sand, the north point of the northern Dorre island bearing N 79° W, the mainland S 67° 30' E about 12 miles off. At 2.15 the small boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Bougainville to survey the mainland. During the night a light was kept and a flare burnt every half hour to mark our position for the boat. Variation 5° 22' at the anchorage. At midnight she was back; it had been impossible for Citizen Bougainville to land because of the bar, which broke with force all along the coast and two cables from the shore.

1801-07-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds varying from N to NNW and W. At noon and at four o'clock went about. At 5 p.m. sounded every half hour in 27, 24, 23, 23, 24 and 25 fathoms, rock and coral bottom. We had a great deal of rain during the night. At 4 a.m. wore onto the port tack. Noon bearings: the end of the great southern cliff E 25° 15' S; the north end of the next great cliff E 7° 15' S, estimated distance 11 miles.
1801-07-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from NE to SE. At 6 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course S 11° 15' E, south, S 11° 15' W and S 67° 30' W, the lead giving from 10 to 13 fathoms, grey sand. At noon in 25° 0' of latitude observed and in 109° 30' 35" of longitude by No. 27. The mainland in sight N 70° E. At 4.15 we anchored in 13 fathoms, grey sand, the southern Dorre island bearing from S 45° W to N 85° W. The mean variation of three observations was 4° 13' 42" NW at the anchorage.

1801-07-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds a light breeze at WNW. At 1 the lookout reported breakers inshore and offshore; 20 minutes later they seemed to stretch a long way out to sea, and at the same moment we hauled close to the wind on the starboard tack. From noon to 4 the soundings varied from 21 to 27 fathoms, coral and white gravel mixed with broken shell. From 4.30 to 8 sounded every half hour in 28 fathoms, coral and gravel; 26, 26, 26, 25, rock and gravel bottom. At 4.30 a.m. went about and stood in on the shore tack; at 6 went about again.
1801-07-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to E. At 6 we got under way and shaped our course south, the lead giving from 12 to 11 fathoms. At noon in 25° 19' 26" of latitude observed and in 109° 23' 5" of longitude by No. 27, the east point of the middle peninsula bearing S 71° E and the westernmost point in sight S 13° E. The small boat sounding ahead of us. At 1.30, being in a flat calm, we anchored in 11 fathoms, white sand, the east point of the peninsula bearing S 50° E and the westernmost point in sight S 5° E. At 7 and at 7.15 fired a gun to warn the Naturaliste should she be in the bay; showed a light at the gaff, burnt flares every quarter of an hour and sent up a rocket every half hour to give our position to the small boat, which arrived at 9. The mean variation of three observations was 3° 59' 20" NW at the anchorage.

1801-07-03.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, the sea rather high, the winds varying from NW to N in strong gusts. At 6 p.m. went about onto the port tack. The wind still very violent, with lightning from every point of the horizon. At 10.30 wore onto the starboard tack. About six in the morning we lay to. Continual rain.
1801-07-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to N. At 7.30 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course south under topsails, the small boat sounding ahead. At 9.30 we anchored in 9 fathoms, sand and shell, the east point of the peninsula bearing S 83° E, a fairly conspicuous hill S 25° E, the westernmost point in sight S 3° W. The topgallant masts were struck. Citizen Bonnefoi, who was sounding in the small boat, found off the east point of the peninsula a sandbank with only 2 fathoms on it; at the edge of the bank he found 6 fathoms, and the Géographe then bore from him S 22° 30' E, 9 miles off; the east point of the peninsula S 33° 45' E and the westernmost point in sight S 33° 45' W. The small boat was sent off under Bonnefoi's orders to survey the coast and look for a place fit to set up our observatory. Latitude observed at the anchorage 25° 30' 27"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 109° 25' 37". The wind freshening, at 1 o'clock Citizen Bonnefoi came back; he had not been able to land on the peninsula because the sea broke there with force. At 2 we got under way, casting to starboard towards the land although we had meant to cast to port. We at once bore away and went onto the starboard tack. This manoeuvre had brought us very close to the east point. At 2.30 went about onto the port tack. The wind a strong breeze from NNW to W; overcast and squally weather, the sea rather high. At 3, being very near the east point and the bank, we put the helm down and missed stays; we had only time to gather way and put about again, and fortunately we came round onto the starboard tack. Several people maintained that we had touched at the moment when the ship, being in stays, had gathered sternway. At 4 went onto the port tack; at 5.30 onto the starboard; at 6.30 onto the port; at 11.30 onto the starboard. During the night the wind blowing hard, the sea not very high, with rain. The soundings since getting under way have been from 6 to 11 fathoms.

1801-07-04.journal_anonyme: The wind showing no sign of changing, we kept under the same canvas throughout; squally weather, a high sea and continual rain, the wind WNW in strong gusts.
1801-07-04.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from W to SW. At 2 a.m. lay to with the port side to the wind under the foresail, the main topsail close-reefed, the fore staysail and the mizzen staysail. At daybreak the wind fell. During the day the weather was fine and the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. At 6.45 filled and stood on, the course N 33° 45' E. At 7.15 the northern Dorre island was sighted to the west. At 8 shaped the course N 11° 15' E. At 9.30 the mainland was sighted to the east. At 10 lay close-hauled on the port tack. At 10.30 little Koks Island was sighted in the S 67° 30' W. At noon in 24° 44' 43" of latitude observed and in 109° 25' 32" of longitude by No. 27. The north point of Koks Island S 67° 0' W and the mainland north (the northernmost point in sight). At 1, the bottom having shoaled from 15 fathoms to 6, we bore away N 11° 15' W; the depth increased gradually, and at 2.30 we lay close-hauled again on the port tack. At 6 went onto the starboard tack. At 11, the sea being thought to break on the lee bow, we went onto the port tack.

1801-07-05.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, blowing hard from the west. From 8 to midnight and from midnight to 4 a.m. we sounded every hour without being able to find bottom, running out 87 and 100 fathoms of line. The wind having drawn round to NNW and then to NNW, we trimmed the sails and bore away NE. The weather fine, a swell running.
1801-07-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to E. At 3.30, the soundings having shoaled appreciably, we went onto the starboard tack; at 5.30 onto the port tack. The northern Dorre island was sighted in the S 67° 30' W. At 7 shaped our course S 45° W to stand in for the anchorage. At 8 anchored in 13 fathoms, grey sand. At 9.30 the commander and all the naturalists landed on the northern Dorre island to camp there. The tents, the astronomical instruments and provisions were sent ashore. At 10.30 we moored NE and SW with a bower anchor, having 60 fathoms to starboard to the NE and 50 fathoms to port to the SW, Koks Island bearing N 30° W, the north point of the northern Dorre island N 50° W 10 miles off, the tents N 60° W 8 miles off, a large headland of Dorre Island S 22° 30' W. The topgallant masts were struck, the sheet anchor got ready to let go and a cable bent to it. The two boats came back from the shore and were sent off again to the camp with effects for the commander; they came aboard during the night.

1801-07-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NW. The amplitude at setting gave us 7° 15' of NW variation. At 8.30 p.m. went onto the port tack. Ran out 100 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 1 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 3 hove to on the other tack. Noon bearings: the white cliff E 4° 30' N, estimated distance 23 miles; the nearest peak E 5° 30' S, estimated distance 25 miles; the furthest E 10° 30' S, distance 28 miles.
1801-07-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SE to SSW. At 5 a.m. the boats were sent off to the tents with bread and water. We worked on the rigging and the sails. At nightfall the boats came back loaded with firewood.

1801-07-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather with rain, the winds varying from NW by N to NW and WNW. At 2.45 went about. At 9 a.m. a very violent squall passed over with rain; sounded every half hour and ran out 60 fathoms of line without finding bottom.
1801-07-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE and calm. At 5 a.m. the small boat was sent off to the camp with water and provisions, and the large boat under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to the southern Dorre island. At nightfall the small boat arrived loaded with wood.

1801-07-08.journal_anonyme: Dark weather, the sky overcast, a swell running. A light breeze from WSW to SW by W. The land in sight at a great distance. At midnight hove to and sounded several times without finding bottom. At 6 a.m. filled and stood on.
1801-07-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSW. At 4 a.m. the small boat was sent off to the camp; she came back at 11 loaded with wood and left again at noon for the camp. At 4 the weather turned overcast, the breeze freshened and drew round to SSE, blowing strong, with a high sea. During the night kept a light at the gaff and burnt a flare every half hour.

1801-07-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds a fresh breeze from the SSW and SW. At 1 we sighted the Abrolhos at a middling distance. At 4.45 hove to; at the same hour the lead brought up 34 fathoms, fine sand; the depth and the bottom did not vary until 8. We filled for 10 minutes and then hove to again. At 4 the winds having drawn round to ESE we hove to on the starboard tack. At 6 filled and stood on.
1801-07-09.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE. At 10.30 Citizen Freycinet arrived in the large boat from the southern Dorre island, which he had left the day before at 4 o'clock at the beginning of the bad weather; he had spent the whole night lying to and at daybreak had shaped his course for the ship. At noon the small boat was seen anchored astern of us with a red flag at her mast; the large boat was at once sent off to carry her a line from the ship. At 2, suspecting that the large boat had let go the line, one of the yawls was sent to carry her the end; at 5 all three boats were aboard. The small boat had left the camp the day before loaded with wood; she had spent the night beating without being able to fetch the ship, and had been obliged to throw her wood overboard. At daybreak she had gained a little at the oars, but had been forced to anchor, her crew, who had neither drunk nor eaten, having no strength left.

1801-07-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds light from SE to ESE. From 4 to 8 p.m. the lead brought up 29 to 30 fathoms, blackish sand. At 8 hove to with the port side to the wind, heading SW. At 2 we hove to on the other tack, and at 5.30 a.m. we filled and stood on.
1801-07-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE. At 5 a.m. the two boats were sent off to the camp with provisions and water. Our fishermen, who had taken nothing since we anchored, made a very good haul today. In the evening the two boats came back from the camp. Twelve lashes with a rope's end were given to the seaman Gimes for having threatened to throw Citizen Bougainville, midshipman in charge of the party in the large boat, into the sea.

1801-07-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from E to SSE and SE. At 8 p.m. hove to with the port side to the wind. From 4 to 8 the lead brought up 30 fathoms, grey sand and broken shell; 28, 28, 32 and 33, grey sand and gravel. At 2 a.m. filled and hove to again at 4. At 5 a.m. filled and stood on; at 7 a.m. and at 11 went about.
1801-07-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW. At daybreak the two boats were sent off to the camp. At 10 they came back loaded with effects and left again at once. At 2 the small boat arrived loaded with effects from the camp and went back at once. The topgallant masts were swayed up, the rigging set up and the repair of the sails continued. At 5 the commander and all the naturalists came back aboard in the two boats, which brought the tents, the astronomical instruments and the rest of the effects that were at the camp. The boats were hoisted in. On board 24° 50' 30" was observed at the anchorage, and 109° 12' 46" of longitude by No. 27. The variation 4° 33' NW, the mean of 5 observations. The tides set NNW and SSE and run at one knot and a half. At the camp 24° 47' 30" of latitude and 109° 2' 9" of longitude were observed. At the north point of the northern Dorre island 24° 45' 30" of latitude and 108° 59' 12" of longitude were observed.

1801-07-12.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, the sea smooth, a light breeze variable from N by NW to N and NNE. At 1 the lead brought up 27 fathoms, reddish sand and fine gravel. At 8.30 p.m., being 2 leagues and a half from the coast and standing in for it, we changed tacks.
1801-07-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to N. At 6 a.m. the sheet anchor's cable was unbent and the anchor stowed. At 9 we unmoored; at 11.30 got under way and lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon took the bearing of the north point of the northern Dorre island N 40° W, the south point of the same island S 50° W, the large headland of Dorre Island S 33° W. At noon overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze. Beating to get out of Shark Bay. At 4.45 the north point of the northern Dorre island N 40° W. Continual rain during the night.

1801-07-13.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze from N to NNE and NNW, squally weather, the sea rather high. At 4 wore onto the port tack. At 1.30 a.m. the lead brought up 50 fathoms, reddish sand. Calm about four o'clock, the sky dark with a great deal of rain falling; about 9 it freshened from the NNE.
1801-07-13.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast and rainy weather, a flat calm, a light breeze from NNE, and from S to SSW at 7 a.m. At noon in 24° 31' 32" of latitude by account and in 108° 59' 46" of longitude by account. At 8 squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNE. At 10.30 lay to under the foresail, the main topsail and the mizzen staysail. At 11.45 the wind shifted to W and hauled to NW and NNW.

1801-07-14.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, continual rain, the sky overcast, the horizon loaded, a light breeze variable from NNE, NNW to south. At 7.30 p.m. the lead brought up 37 fathoms, reddish sand. At the same hour the wind shifted to SSW. At 4 a.m. we hoisted a flag at the gaff in honour of the 14th of July. At 11 we sighted the land at a distance of 30 miles.
1801-07-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to WSW. At 6.30 filled and stood on, and at 6.45 shaped the course S 45° E, and at 8 east. At 9.30 the land was sighted in the N 79° E and we steered for it. At 10.30, being abreast of the large cape at the entrance to Shark Bay, we hove to with the port side to the wind. At noon in 24° 17' 16" of latitude observed and in 109° 9' 3" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 3° 35'. The large cape bore from us N 73° E, and the land in sight as far as N 44° E. At noon filled and stood on, the course north. At 4 took the bearing of the large cape S 78° E, the southernmost land S 35° E. At 5.30 the course was given N 11° 15' W. The large cape then bore from us S 43° E, and the land in sight from S 32° E to S 64° E. At 10 p.m. we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn for the fourth time, in 109° 10' of longitude.

1801-07-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, continual rain, a light breeze from NNW to SW. At 4 p.m. fired 21 guns in memory of the 14th of July, whose anniversary was celebrated. At 6.45 a squall got up in the SW with lightning and a little thunder; we steered NNW. At daybreak we sighted the land and made all sail to close it. At noon the lead brought up 47 fathoms, rocky bottom.
1801-07-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SE. At 6.30 the course was given N 11° 15' E. At noon in 22° 17' 3" of latitude observed and in 109° 6' 18" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 42' NW. The course was given N 45° E. At 4 the land was sighted from N 79° E to S 67° 30' E, as far as the eye could reach. At 8 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at midnight hove to on the port tack.

1801-07-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy. A light breeze from SW to SW by W. At 8 p.m. the lead brought up 58 fathoms, fine sand. From 9 to 10 and 11 ran out 70 fathoms without finding bottom. At daybreak sighted the land, which I take to be the entrance to Shark Bay.
1801-07-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE. At 4 filled and stood on, the course N 45° E; at 6.30 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack and crowded sail. At noon in 21° 6' 30" of latitude observed and in 110° 18' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 33' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 13' 0" of longitude. At noon went onto the port tack; at 6 a flat calm. At 8, a light breeze from WSW, shaped the course S 25° E.

1801-07-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to SSW. We ran along Dirk Hartog Island and sounded in 45 fathoms, reddish sand. At 7.45 a.m. we let go the port anchor in 18 fathoms, fine muddy sand, and veered 60 fathoms of cable. At 8 a.m. we sent the small boat away to sound. At 9 it was back and we fired two guns. From 10 until midnight a current setting ESE held the ship almost broadside on.
1801-07-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from E to SW. At daybreak shaped the course east and crowded sail. At noon in 21° 4' 58" of latitude observed and in 110° 54' 50" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 46' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 47' 6" of longitude.

1801-07-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind very light from the south. On the 29th the weather was unsettled and calm; a breath from N by NE gave us hopes of getting under way, but the calm returned. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq to go to Dorre Island, and the dinghy to Dirk Hartog.
1801-07-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WNW to WSW, from SE to NE and from WSW to SW. At daybreak the land was sighted in the S 45° E. At 9 took the bearing of an islet N 78° E, 12 miles off. At noon it bore from us N 66° E, another from S 37° E to S 19° E, and another S 40° W. At noon in 21° 19' 16" of latitude observed and in 111° 1' 32" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 53' NW. The lunar distances gave 112° 26' 57" of longitude. At 3 the last islet bore from us S 67° 30' W.

1801-07-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from N to NNW, running under the fore topsail, mizzen topsail and jibs. At 1.30 let go the anchor in 13 fathoms, sand and fine gravel, and veered 35 fathoms of cable. Bearings of the anchorage: the NW point of Dirk Hartog Island W 13° N; the southernmost visible end of the same island S 9° E; the middle of Dorre Island N 17° W. While running in we sounded and found 15 and 13 fathoms, sand and gravel. At 9.30 p.m. the large boat was back. The dinghy returned at 10.30 a.m.
1801-07-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather in the forenoon and overcast in the afternoon. The wind from WSW, SW, ESE, E, ENE, N, NE, NNE and WSW. At noon in 21° 32' 10" of latitude observed and in 110° 30' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 9' NW. An island S 65° E, another S 62° E, another from S 47° W to S 53° W; it is this last that the commander took for the entrance to the Willem River, and off which he hove to on the 3rd Thermidor [22 July 1801] in the afternoon. The wind a strong breeze, with rain, squalls and gusts.

1801-07-20.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from SW to W. The sky cloudy with light rain at intervals. At 7 p.m. the corvette dragging, we veered to 80 fathoms of cable; the tide set NW, as observed at 8.30 and at 9. At noon the currents had the same set.
1801-07-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SE. At noon in 21° 26' 22" of latitude by account and in 109° 55' of longitude by account. Variation 2° 53' NW. An island south, another from S 34° E to S 50° E. The mainland S 50° W, about 15 miles off. At 4 the land could be seen from aloft to the south.

1801-07-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze from south to SSW. We observed a current setting strongly ESE. At 7 a.m. we weighed the starboard anchor, and when it was up we found the shank broken 2½ feet above the flukes. Let go the starboard anchor. At 9 a.m. sent off a boat under the orders of the chief quartermaster to go to Dirk Hartog and observe the tides.
1801-07-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At daybreak the mainland was sighted from S 11° 15' W to S 33° 45' E; at 8 it could be seen from S 10° E to S 65° E. At noon in 21° 28' 10" of latitude observed and in 110° 20' 48" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 47' NW. The land from S 5° E to S 15° W.

1801-07-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NE to ESE. On the morning of the 3rd we laid out the port anchor, the currents setting ESE.
1801-07-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE. At 5.45 the high land of the mainland from S 5° W to S 34° W; the island taken for the entrance to the Willem River from S 27° E to S 57° E and from S 62° E to S 78° E. At 10 hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At noon in 21° 33' 5" of latitude observed and in 110° 35' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 16' NW. The high land of the mainland S 48° W. Willem Island from S 18° W to S 1° W and from S 2° E to S 33° E. The east point, which bore from us S 33° E at 6 miles, is surrounded by reefs stretching as far as S 35° E. At noon filled and stood on, the course N 45° E. At 8 Citizen Le Bas was to take the watch, but the commander, who had had some difficulty with him that morning, forbade Bonnefoi to have him woken and took his watch himself. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind. The commander hove to at noon under the lee of an island which he took for the entrance to the Willem River. From the deck two islands could be seen, one from S 33° E to S 2° E and the other from S 1° W to S 18° W; and the space between these two islands, from S 2° E to S 1° W, is what he took for the river's mouth. But from the topgallant crosstrees I saw, as did several other people, the two islands joined by a chain of reefs awash, on which the sea broke. I saw land as far as the eye could reach to the south, an islet in the S 35° E and another in the S 75° E.

1801-07-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from ESE. In the afternoon weighed the starboard anchor and let go the port one, veering a range of 80 fathoms. At 11.15 p.m. the current turned back towards the ESE.
1801-07-23.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At daybreak the land was sighted in the S 45° E as far as the eye could reach. At 6.30 filled and stood on under all sail, the course N 45° E. At noon in 20° 6' 8" of latitude observed and in 119° 29' 4" of longitude by No. 27. At 5 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. Variation 2° 21' NW.

1801-07-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear and bright. A light breeze from WSW to N and NE. At 4.30 p.m. slack water; at 5 it set east.
1801-07-24.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. Saw tropic birds. At noon in 19° 8' 35" of latitude observed and in 112° 21' 12" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 59' NW.

1801-07-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from WSW to SE by way of south. The chief quartermaster, coming to report to the captain on his observations of the tides, brought back a pewter plate found on Dirk Hartog Island bearing a Dutch inscription; the captain had another placed beside it and planted a national flag. Shortly afterwards he embarked in his boat.
1801-07-25.journal_breton_geographe: Fine, warm weather, the wind a light breeze from E to south. At noon in 19° 14' 10" of latitude observed and in 112° 49' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 31' NW.

1801-07-26.journal_anonyme: A hazy sky, a choppy sea, a fresh breeze from SW to W. Burnt priming to show our position to the small boat. At 2 a.m. it was back.
1801-07-26.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind light and a fresh breeze from south to W. From 10 until noon we crossed several tide rips whose direction seemed to be NNE and SSW. At noon in 19° 30' 0" of latitude observed and in 113° 51' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 54' NW.

1801-07-27.journal_anonyme: Squally weather with rain, a light air from NNE to north.
1801-07-27.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW to WSW. At 4.45 a.m., having sighted land to the south, we bore up for it and made it out to be an island. At 8 its east point bore from us south and the west point S 10° W, 15 miles off; the mainland could be seen as far as S 45° E. At 8.45 we anchored in 10 fathoms, red sand, the west point of the island bearing S 11° 30' W and the east point S 7° 30'. The mainland being very low, only its highest points could be seen from the deck, and they looked like so many islands. The nearest to the east point of the island bore from us S 6° E, the second S 16° E, the third S 24° E and the fourth S 29° E. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Ronsard to survey the island; the small boat, although deep with water, left at 9.30 to sound 3 miles to the east. The current was then running 1.3 knots. At noon 20° 19' 59" of latitude and 114° 5' 53" of longitude by No. 27 were observed. The small boat was seen anchored 6 miles to the east with a signal at her mast, which made us think she needed help; and having no boat to send her, we went to her with the ship. We got under way at 1 and bore up for the boat; at 2 we anchored very near her and she came aboard (variation 1° 21' NW at the anchorage). Citizen Baudin, midshipman, who was in charge of her, told us that after sounding 3 miles to the east of the ship (as ordered) he had tried to come back aboard, but that the current had carried him away and he had been obliged to anchor and set all his crew to baling out the boat, which they could never get free of water. We lay anchored in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, the west point of the island bearing S 21° W and the east point S 17° W; a rise of the mainland south, another S 9° E, another S 20° E. In the N 51° E the sea formed an eddy that seemed caused by a shoal. During the night a rocket was sent up every hour.

1801-07-28.journal_anonyme: Misty and squally weather, light rain at intervals. A fresh breeze from SW. At noon the tide began to turn to the westward.
1801-07-28.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSW to WNW. At 10.30 Citizen Ronsard arrived in the large boat; he had walked over the island and found very good water there. It is well wooded and landing is easy; he brought back many shells, among them two of the kind called the admiral, which led the commander to name this island, and another small sandy one 2 miles from it which we cannot see from the ship because it is awash, the Admiral Islands. At 10.30 got under way and lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon in 20° 20' 13" of latitude observed and in 114° 10' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 50' NW. At 1 bore away S 67° 30' E towards a very thick column of smoke. At 4 took the bearing of the Admiral Islands from S 33° W to S 67° 30' W, the mainland stretching from S 15° W to S 67° 30' E. Several columns of smoke could be seen at different points of the mainland, the most conspicuous being the one we were steering for. At 4.45, the water having shoaled, we bore up gradually as far as N 56° 15' E. At 5 an eddy formed by a shoal was seen abeam at two cables. At 5.30 took the bearing of the Admiral Island S 34° W, the sandy Admiral island S 5° W, the mainland in sight from south to S 50° E. At 7.30 we anchored in 10 fathoms, grey sand, the mainland bearing from S 24° W to S 57° E (this bearing was taken the next day at daybreak). At the anchorage the currents set east and west and run 1.5 [knots].

1801-07-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from SE to SSE falling away a great deal. Two men were sent to Dirk Hartog with 15 days' provisions to make signals to the Géographe should she appear on the coast. About 8 in the evening the captain held a council on what course to take in the separation we found ourselves in; it was decided that we should wait as long as the quantity of water we had on board would allow, which was down to 70 casks.
1801-07-29.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ENE to SSE. At 6.30 we got under way and lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 11.30 took the bearing of a column of smoke S 5° E, no land being in sight. At noon in 20° 0' 30" of latitude observed and in 114° 46' 0" of longitude by No. 27.

1801-07-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene. Winds from ENE to NW, almost calm. Saw several meteors in the NE.
1801-07-30.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to N. At noon in 19° 43' 30" of latitude observed and in 115° 10' 27" of longitude by No. 27. The variation 1° 39' NW. At noon a very low land was sighted in the S 75° E, having the look of a sandy island. The sea broke on it with force, especially at its southern part, where a chain of breakers began and stretched away to the south. This islet cannot be far from the mainland, for from the topgallant crosstrees I saw a smoke in the distance. At 5 the sandy islet (seen from the crosstrees) bore S 56° E. At 8 calm; at 9 a fresh breeze from WNW, the course was given N 22° 30' E and at 10, N 33° 45' E.

1801-07-31.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to SW in strong gusts. At 4.30 the tide began to turn.
1801-07-31.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to south. At midnight the course was given N 45° E, and at 4, N 56° 15' E. At 6 took the bearing of the sandy islet S 5° W. The course was given east. At noon in 19° 17' 51" of latitude observed and in 116° 8' 14" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 56' NW. At half past noon lay close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 3.30 a column of smoke was seen in the S 45° E, no land being in sight. At 5.30 it was seen stretching from S 35° E to S 33° W, and a large column of smoke S 57° W. At 6, having only 9 fathoms, went onto the port tack. At midnight hove to with the port side to the wind; a strong breeze.

1801-08-01.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a fresh breeze from S by E, SSE and ESE. At noon we got under way under topsails. We sounded and found from 6 to 9 fathoms, sand, coral and broken shell. At 3 let go the starboard anchor in 9 fathoms. Bearings of the anchorage: the visible NW end of Dirk Hartog W 6° S; the SE end of the same island W 39° S; the middle of the island within the bay E 12° S.
1801-08-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 6 filled and stood on, the course given east. At noon in 19° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 116° 22' 9" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 15' NW.

1801-08-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a clear sky. A light breeze S, SE, SSE and ESE. At 10 the tide turned to the SE.
1801-08-02.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to south. At noon in 18° 44' 17" of latitude observed and in 117° 8' 40" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 42' NW. The lunar distances gave 118° 35' of longitude. At 9 hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, winds SSE to SE, almost calm. At 2 p.m. the large boat took 15 days' provisions to go and survey Shark Bay.
1801-08-03.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SE. At 6 filled and stood on, the course east. At noon in 18° 6' 30" of latitude observed and in 118° 3' 0" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 2° 2' NW. At 8.30, having sighted a fire ahead, we went onto the port tack. At 9 the fire bore from us N 50° E; it could no longer be seen at 10.30. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky a little cloudy. A light breeze from ESE to SSE and south. At 2.15 p.m. the corvette made sail until 6 p.m., when we anchored in 8 fathoms, sandy bottom. On the 16th at 11 a.m. a thick smoke was seen on the mainland which had risen all at once. The captain, wondering what could have caused this kind of eruption, sent off the small boat under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq.
1801-08-04.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 1.30 the previous day's fire was sighted in the N 33° E. It disappeared at 4. At 6 filled and stood on, close-hauled on the starboard tack. At 7.15 the land was sighted from the crosstrees from east to N 68° E. At 10 it could be seen from the deck; it appeared fairly high, in the S 56° E. At noon in 17° 28' 16" of latitude observed and in 118° 26' 10" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 14' NW. The land from S 64° E to N 68° E, with several columns of smoke at different points of the coast. At 1 bore away N 45° E and ran along the coast, on which we saw a countless number of fires and smokes. At 4 bore away N 22° 30' E. The northernmost land in sight N 54° E; low, wooded land which appeared to form a bight S 85° E; a great white cliff S 53° E; a white headland S 22° E. At 6 anchored in 9 fathoms, coarse sand and broken shell, the land bearing from S 5° E to N 57° E. An immense fire burned all night in the N 68° E.

1801-08-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from SW to W and N. At 2 p.m. got under way under topsails and staysails. At 5 anchored in 5 fathoms, fine sand. At 9 p.m. the small boat was back and reported that the smoke we had seen came from the fires of the Aboriginal people, gathered to the number of 9, men and women together.
1801-08-05.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to NE. At 6 we got under way and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 7.30 Citizen Piquet, officer of the watch, having the glass set and asking the chief quartermaster whether note had been taken of the time elapsed since getting under way, the commander, who was in bed, called out to him from his cabin that he was tiresome, that it was a question of the lead and not of the glass, and that if the watch wearied him he might leave it, and that he would take it himself; and he did take it. At noon in 16° 53' 20" of latitude observed and in 118° 36' 0" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 42' NW. Took the bearing of a sandy islet S 89° E and the north point of the land in sight N 74° E; at a short distance from that point a bank could be seen stretching far away to the N 22° 30' W, on which the sea broke. Since 8 a.m. the bottom has been very uneven. We were no doubt on the edge of a bank whose direction is at first N by NW, then runs NW, and then takes a northerly direction again. We tried to keep near the course N 45° E but were always obliged to bear away. At 1 we lost sight of the land; at 7 calm. From 8 to 11 the course made good was N by NW; from 11 to noon NW; from noon to 3.30 NW by N; and from 3.30 to midnight N and NE by N. Commander Baudin gave me orders to take the watch in Citizen Piquet's place, and I kept it until Timor.

1801-08-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from N to SSW and south.
1801-08-06.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSW to E. At 2 a.m. the course was given N 45° E and at 5.30 N 67° 30' E. At noon in 16° 0' 14" of latitude observed and in 118° 59' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 29' NW. At 7 calm; the dredge was put over and brought up many objects of natural history.

1801-08-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from south to SSE. At 4 a.m. the longboat was put in the water together with the small boat and the dinghy, and most of the gear was embarked in them for the camp set up ashore to repair the longboat.
1801-08-07.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. At midnight the course was given east. At noon in 15° 40' 41" of latitude observed and in 119° 46' of longitude by No. 27. Variation 1° 36' NW. Land was sighted to the north; at 3 went onto the port tack. At 4 it bore from us from north to N 45° E, and at 5.30 from N 22° W to N 52° E. Calm at 5, the current setting us in the N 45° W; at 9.30 a light breeze. We could not anchor at nightfall, the bottom being coral.

1801-08-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds almost calm, the horizon loaded.
1801-08-08.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SSW. At 4 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 6 filled and stood on, the course N 67° 30' E, crowding sail. At 7 the same land as the day before was sighted from aloft, from S 64° E to S 74° E. At 8.30, having sighted ahead at a short distance a sandbank awash, we bore up north. Having cleared it we resumed our course, and then saw in the S 45° E low land on which the sea broke furiously; at 10 we lost sight of it. At 10.30 a sandbank was seen abeam to windward (S 22° 30' E) 2 miles off. At noon in 15° 17' 40" of latitude observed and in 119° 56' 35" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 34' NW. At 1 the course was given N 78° 45' E. We passed close to a shoal of fish over which there was a very great number of birds; from a distance it might have been taken for a sandbank with the sea breaking on it. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind.

1801-08-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon misty, a light breeze from SSE, SSW and SE. At 1 a.m. the tide turned to the NW.
1801-08-09.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, calm and a light breeze from W to SSW. At 5.45 filled and stood on N 78° 45' E under all sail. At 7 the course was given east; at 8 the mainland was sighted from S 40° to S 68° E. At 10 a flat calm; until noon the current set us S 67° 30' E. At noon in 15° 8' 10" of latitude observed and in 120° 44' 3" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 44' NW, the mainland bearing from S 22° E to S 75° E and an island S 50° E. From noon to 3 the current set us N 45° W. At 3, a light breeze, shaped the course east. At 5.45 took the bearing of the northernmost part of the mainland in sight N 87° E; a sandy islet A S 85° E; the nearest land (of the mainland) S 63° E; an islet S 30° E; the southernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 3° E. At 7.30 a dull roar was heard, caused by a tide rip which we crossed. At 8 hauled to the wind on the port tack.

1801-08-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, the sky cloudy and the horizon misty, a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE.
1801-08-10.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, calm, and a light and very variable breeze. At midnight a fire was sighted in the S 57° E. At 2 hove to with the port side to the wind; at 5.30 filled and stood on, the course N 67° 30' E. Islet A then bore from us S 5° E; at 8 it bore south, and off its west point there were breakers stretching as far as S 12° W; the southernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 34° W; a fairly conspicuous point of the mainland S 11° E; the northernmost land (of the mainland) in sight S 50° E; an islet S 85° E; another east. From 8 until noon a flat calm, the currents setting us S 67° 30' E about 4 miles. At noon in 14° 59' 50" of latitude observed and in 121° 5' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 20' NE. Islet A bore from us S 35° W, a second S 40° E, a third S 44° E, a fourth S 46° E, a fifth S 80° E and a sixth S 88° E. At 8 hauled to the wind on the port tack (heading NE by N). At 8.30 went onto the starboard tack (heading SW by W). At 10.30 onto the port tack (heading NW). At midnight, being in a flat calm, we let go a kedge anchor in 24 fathoms, soft mud. Bearings taken at the anchorage (on the 23rd at sunrise): we were near a chain of islands stretching from S 36° W to S 71° E; island B, the nearest, bore from us S 51° E, 4 miles off. Latitude observed at the anchorage 14° 47' 40"; longitude by No. 27 at the anchorage 121° 25' 0"; the variation NE at the anchorage 0° 7' 20".

1801-08-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a fresh breeze in gusts from S, SSE and SE.
1801-08-11.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to WNW. At 2 a.m. the current set N by NE and ran 1.5 knots. At 7.15 the tide turned. At 7.30 the large boat was sent off under Bonnefoi's orders to survey island B, the nearest. At 9.30 he came back without having been able to land, the sea breaking on every part of the island. At noon we got under way, the course N 33° 45' E. At 4 the course was given N 22° 30' E. At 4.30, having sighted in the N 56° E and N 68° E a breaker lying roughly NW and SE and 5 miles off, we steered north; but the water deepening, we resumed N 22° 30' E. At 5 took the bearing of an islet S 87° E, a second S 88° E, an island N 85° E to east, a third islet N 83° E, a fourth N 80° E, a fifth N 78° E, a sixth N 77° E, a large island from N 74° E to N 69° E. At 8 saw a fire in the S 22° 30' E. At 10, being becalmed, we let go a kedge anchor in 38 fathoms, muddy sand. At 10.30 the current ran 5.5 knots setting S 22° 30' E [sic]. At midnight it ran 0.5 in the same direction.

1801-08-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE.
1801-08-12.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SW to NW. At half past midnight the tide turned and set NNE, its speed increasing to 1.5 knots. At 5 it was 0.9, to the north. At 7 it was slack water; we got under way and shaped our course N 45° E, and at 8 N 67° 30' E. At noon in 14° 15' 12" of latitude observed and in 121° 50' 32" of longitude by No. 27. At noon a reef was sighted between the land and us, stretching NW and SE. At 3.30, having sighted from aloft breakers ahead (N 67° 30' E), the course was given N 45° E. At 4.15, having sighted breakers from N 67° 30' E to N 85° E, we steered N 33° 45' E. At 5.30 resumed the course N 45° E. At 5.45 took the bearing of the land [illegible] of the mainland east; an islet S 19° E; the offshore breaker of that islet S 22° 30' E; the west end of a second islet S 11° E and the west end of a third S 5° W. At 8 we let go a kedge anchor in 35 fathoms, muddy bottom. Bearings at the anchorage: the breakers from N 87° E to S 75° E; the land [illegible] of the mainland S 79° E; the three islets taken at 5.45 appeared to form only one, whose ends bore from us, one S 9° E and the other S 11° W. Calm during the night. From 8 to 9 the current set S 22° 30' W and ran 1 knot; from 9 until midnight it set south.

1801-08-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear and serene, a fresh breeze from ESE to south.
1801-08-13.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SE to NW. At 7.45 we got under way and shaped our course N 56° 15' E; a breaker was sighted between the land and us. At noon took the bearing of the east point of a land supposed to be the mainland S 73° E; the middle of an island S 68° E; the breaker seen in the morning S 34° E; an islet S 6° W; an island from S 15° W to S 8° E; a second islet S 26° W. In the distance two hummocks could be seen, one S 45° E and the other S 48°, supposed to belong to the mainland. At noon in 14° 2' 6" of latitude observed and in 122° 12' 4" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 14' NE. Shaped the course N 73° E at 4. At 8 we let go a kedge anchor in 35 fathoms, muddy sand. Calm during the night. From 8 to 11 the current set SSW and ran 1.3 knots; from 11 until midnight it ran only 0.9 knots.

1801-08-14.journal_anonyme: A smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon the currents set to the SE.
1801-08-14.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, a light breeze and calm, from S to SW. At midnight it was slack water; from midnight to 2 the current ran 0.5 knots and from 2 to 4, 1.5 knots to the NNE. At 6.30 we got under way and shaped our course S 78° 45' E.
