At 8 took the bearing of an islet D south; several hummocks supposed to belong to the mainland from S 7° E to S 24° E; an island C, off whose east point there is a reef, from S 29° E to S 40° E. At 8.30, having sighted a shoal ahead, we steered N 56° 15' E. At 10 the course was given east. At 11 a chain of breakers was sighted stretching from south to east; we bore up N 67° 30' E and then N 56° 15' E. At noon took the bearing of island C from S 47° W to S 38° W; islet D S 31° W; the hummocks of the mainland from S 23° W to S 3° W; the mainland in sight from S 57° E to S 68° E; the chain of breakers stretched from S 8° E to N 58° E, with a sandy islet in the middle of the breakers N 85° E. At noon in 13° 52' 16" of latitude observed and in 122° 36' 52" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 5' NE. The lunar distances gave 123° 19' of longitude. Shortly after noon the chain of breakers was seen to stretch as far as ahead of us (N 56° 15' E); we steered N 22° 30' E and then N 22° 30' W. At 2.30, being in a flat calm with the tide setting us onto the breakers, we let go a kedge anchor in 32 fathoms, muddy bottom, island C bearing from S 25° W to S 22° W and the sandy islet of the breakers S 62° E. At 6 the current ran 1.1 knots to the NNE. At 7.30 it was slack water; it turned shortly afterwards and set SSW. At 10 the current ran 1 knot, and at midnight 0.3 knots.

1801-08-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At 2 p.m. the large boat was back from her mission.
1801-08-15.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from S to SSE. At 1.15 the tide turned, the currents then setting NNE and running more than 1.2 knots. At 6.30 we got under way and steered N 56° 15' E and N 45° E. At 8.30 the colour of the sea showed a shoal; we had 29 fathoms, and a moment later only 20. We bore away and the bottom shoaled to 15 fathoms and then, at 11, to 11; we then hauled to the wind on the port tack. The water deepened and we came round to the north. At 9.30 two white patches like two small banks were sighted ahead (to the north). We steered N 11° 15' E to pass between them and the great bank. At 10.30 breakers were sighted stretching from N 33° 45' E to N 78° 45' E; we steered N 56° 15' W to weather them. At noon a point of the great bank bore from us N 50° E, 6 miles off, being in 13° 34' 18" of latitude observed and in 122° 35' 18" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 26' NE. The course was given N 33° 45' W. At half past noon the point of the bank supposed to be the northernmost bore from us N 22° 30' E. At 7 we let go a kedge anchor in 32 fathoms, muddy bottom; the sea appeared slack. At 8.30 we swung to the flood, which set SW and ran 1.4 knots.

1801-08-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SE.
1801-08-16.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the breeze light from SSE to NE. At 1 we swung to the ebb, setting NE and running 0.7; at 4 it ran 1.3 knots. At 8 it was slack water; at 9.30 we got under way and shaped our course N 56° E. At noon in 13° 24' 49" of latitude observed and in 122° 39' 28" of longitude by No. 27. Variation 0° 36' NE. At 1 a flat calm; at 5.30 the breeze freshened from NE and we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack, the lead giving no bottom at 50 fathoms. At 8, having found 29 fathoms, we bore away N 67° 30' W and N 78° 45' W. The water shoaling further, we hauled to the wind on the port tack, and at 9.30 we anchored in 24 fathoms, sandy bottom; the sea appeared slack. At 10 the current set SW and ran 0.7 knots. At 2 slack water; the current then set NE and ran 1.3 knots.

1801-08-17.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to E. At 6 a.m., the wind having freshened a great deal, we began to heave round, the ship dragging. At 6.45 we got under way and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack; we lost our buoy and buoy rope. At noon in 13° 0' 54" of latitude observed and in 122° 47' 40" of longitude by account. At 8 went onto the port tack. At noon no bottom at 40 fathoms. From noon until midnight we had from 45 to 55 fathoms.

1801-08-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a cloudless sky. Wind SE, a light breeze. At 3.45 p.m. sent off [the boat] under the orders of Citizen Ransonnet with 2 days' provisions to fetch the 2 men who had been stationed on Dirk Hartog.
1801-08-18.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to E. At 3 went onto the starboard tack under the foresail, both topsails double-reefed, the fore staysail, the mizzen and its staysail. At noon in 12° 19' 50" of latitude observed and in 123° 2' 46" of longitude by account. The lead gave from 40 to 43 fathoms.

1801-08-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky serene, the sea smooth, the winds a light breeze from ESE to north. The large boat was back on the 30th. She was sent off again to fetch the rest of the gear.
1801-08-19.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to ESE. At 10 a.m. the commander decided to shape our course for Timor; we headed north, making sail. At noon in 10° 59' 57" of latitude observed and in 123° 37' 52" of longitude by account. During the night overcast weather; we sounded several times without finding bottom at 120 fathoms. At noon the course was given N 45° W and at 9, N 67° 30' W.

1801-08-20.journal_anonyme: Throughout the 24 hours fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from NW, W and SW. Calm at the close of the day.
1801-08-20.journal_breton_geographe: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. At 2 a.m. hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 4 hove to on the port tack; at 5 filled and stood on, the course S 78° 45' W; at 10 it was given west. At noon in 10° 21' 42" of latitude observed and in 121° 34' 31" of longitude by No. 27. At 3.45, in a clear interval, the high land of Timor was sighted from N 11° E to N 68° W. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the port tack, the land stretching from N 36° E to N 80° W, 6 miles off. At 11 went onto the starboard tack.

1801-08-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from NE, SW, south and SE. Calm from 8 until noon.
1801-08-21.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to ESE. At 2 a.m. went onto the port tack. At 6 we bore away west and ran along the southern side of Timor at a short distance. At 10 Roti Island was sighted in the S 56° W. At 11.30, being off the mouth of Semau Strait, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack and ran in; Roti then bore from us south. At noon took the bearing of the south point of Semau S 70° W, the northern part of Roti S 2° E, the south point of Timor with its reefs S 24° E. At 12.45, the breeze having fallen and the tide setting us out (to the south), we anchored in 28 fathoms, muddy sand, the south point of Timor bearing S 15° W, the end of the reefs off that point S 25° W, the south point of Semau S 49° W, a small island off Semau from N 45° W to N 29° W. At 1 the large boat was sent off to Kupang, the Dutch settlement on Timor; we did not know whether the settlement might be in English hands, and the boat carried an Anglo-French flag of truce. Citizen Freycinet, who commanded her, was to inform the governor of our arrival in the strait and of the stay we meant to make at Kupang.

1801-08-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon misty. A light breeze variable from SE to south, SSE and SSW. A fresh breeze. At 7 p.m. Citizen Ransonnet, acting ensign, went to take charge of the camp; and the next morning at 5 Citizen Faure, the surveyor, and I embarked in the large boat to go and survey the north of the bay. Our starboard anchor being foul, we weighed it, after which we let it go in 6 fathoms, sand and weed. Bearings of the anchorage: the north point E 19° N; the south point S 10° E; the camp S 23° 30' S.
1801-08-22.journal_breton_geographe: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SW. At 8 the surveyor landed on Timor with his instruments, abreast of the anchorage; he came back at half past noon. He had been very well received by fishermen living on the strait, who told him that Kupang was in Dutch hands. At 1 Citizen Freycinet arrived from Kupang; he had been very well received by the governor, who was sending us a pilot, a Frenchman in the Company's service, to take us to Kupang. We got under way at once; the cable was found chafed. At 6, after doubling the last point of the strait, the wind shifted to the east; we missed stays, boxed her round to the south and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. We fired a gun, to which Fort Concordia answered with one. We made several boards to gain the anchorage, where at 9.30 we let go the anchor in 24 fathoms, muddy bottom; the topgallant masts were struck at once. Bearings at the anchorage, being moored: Turtle Island from N 11° W to N 17° W; the north end of Semau N 71° W; the west point of Timor S 62° W; Fort Concordia S 9° W; the northernmost point of Timor in sight N 2° E.

1801-08-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from S, NE, SW and SSW.
1801-08-23.journal_breton_geographe: At 9.30 a.m. the commander landed, accompanied by Citizen Bonnefoi. His boat came back with lemons, limes and oranges sent by the governor; we were given leave to communicate with the shore. Several canoes brought poultry and fruit to sell. In the afternoon we moored east and west with a bower anchor; a prau brought us a buffalo, two sheep and firewood, of which we were short. In the evening the commander came back aboard.

1801-08-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the air thick. A fresh breeze variable from SSW, SSE and south. At 5.15 a.m. the camp's dinghy came to fetch the caulkers to work on the longboat.
1801-08-24.journal_breton_geographe: In the morning he landed with all the naturalists, to live ashore. The sails were unbent, the topgallant masts got down and the running rigging unrove. A hospital was set up in the town, where the surgeon-major and all the sick went. All our empty casks were sent ashore.

1801-08-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the horizon loaded, a fresh breeze variable from SSE, south and SSW.
1801-08-25.journal_breton_geographe: The topmasts were struck and the lower yards lowered; the sheet anchor was got ready to let go and a cable bent to it. The crew had fresh meat and fish.

1801-08-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high and the sky cloudless. A fresh breeze from SW and SSW.
1801-08-26.journal_breton_geographe: Work was interrupted, the crew being unwell, which was put down to the water. The carpenters were sent ashore with their tools and planking to build us a longboat there under Citizen Ronsard's direction. A canoe brought us firewood. Some of the local people reported that a three-masted ship had anchored at the entrance to Semau Strait, from which she had got under way, and that they had heard gunfire to the west of Semau.

1801-08-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy. A fresh breeze from SSW.
1801-08-27.journal_breton_geographe: At 4 a.m. Citizen Bonnefoi left in the large boat to try to discover whether this ship might be the Naturaliste. At 9 the commander came aboard; the detachment took up arms (loaded and with bayonets fixed) and he gave orders to take Citizen Piquet, ensign, to Fort Concordia with his effects, and to send him his provisions. Citizen Freycinet obtained leave to take him there alone. He was received ashore by the Dutch guard and taken to the fort, where the sergeant commanding the fort asked him for his sword. After this business the commander went back ashore. At 2.30 Citizen Bonnefoi came back in the large boat; he had coasted the western side of Semau without discovering anything.

1801-08-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the horizon misty, a fresh breeze from SSW. At 5.30 a.m. a Malay named Sodomson, shipped at Mauritius, died of putrid fever.
1801-08-28.journal_breton_geographe: Work was suspended; a large part of the crew went ashore to walk about.

1801-08-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze variable from SSW to SW. At 3 the longboat came loaded with wood and went back ashore at once.
1801-08-29.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order. A working party was set up ashore to fill our casks; at low water we watered in the Kupang river.

1801-08-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SSE.

1801-08-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky overcast, the horizon loaded, a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE.

1801-09-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze variable from SSE, south and east. The large boat came in from her mission to the north of the bay. She brought eight enormous turtles, which gave us great pleasure.
1801-09-01.journal_breton_geographe: Fish were taken with the seine and distributed to the crew; the watering continues.

1801-09-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW. During the night the winds drew round from south to WSW, almost calm.
1801-09-02.journal_breton_geographe: Part of the crew went ashore to walk about. Fish and a small turtle were taken with the seine.

1801-09-03.journal_anonyme: A smooth sea, the sky overcast, the winds very light and variable from WSW, SW and W. We set up our shrouds, stowed our anchors and hoisted in the longboat and the other boats.
1801-09-03.journal_breton_geographe: The coopers went to repair our casks and put on hoops that had been stolen. Fish and a small turtle were taken.

1801-09-04.journal_anonyme: A high sea, misty and squally weather and a cloudy sky. A fresh breeze from W to SW in strong gusts. At 10.20 a.m. we got under way and shaped our course W by N.
1801-09-04.journal_breton_geographe: A prau brought us 2 cords of wood.

1801-09-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze variable from SSW to south. Soundings from midnight to 4: from 1 to 2, 65 and 66 fathoms, fine reddish sand; at 3 and at 4, 80 and 85 fathoms. At noon on the 18th we crossed the Tropic of Capricorn.
1801-09-05.journal_breton_geographe: In the evening Citizen Le Bas, who until now had borne the whole duty alone, entered in the ship's log that, all the midshipmen except one (Bonnefoi) reporting themselves sick, Citizens Freycinet, Bonnefoi and myself were left with the duty.

1801-09-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a high sea and the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SE. From 10 until midnight ran out 85 fathoms of line without finding bottom; from 2 to 4 the same.
1801-09-06.journal_breton_geographe: I went to the hospital ashore for the itch. At 9 p.m. a canoe brought a letter from the commander to Citizen Le Bas, telling him that there were two English frigates and three small vessels anchored in Semau Strait, which was causing much alarm ashore; he ordered him to send Citizen Freycinet at daybreak to reconnoitre them.

1801-09-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea with a little swell, a fresh breeze from ESE to SE. From 10 until midnight sounded without finding bottom. At 10 set the studdingsails and staysails.
1801-09-07.journal_breton_geographe: At 4 a.m. Citizen Freycinet, carrying our passports and a letter from the commander to the English commodore, left for Semau Strait; he was back at 2 and had seen no ship at all. Work was suspended, but no one went ashore; we rested on board. Canoes brought us water.

1801-09-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE. At 3.30 a.m. ran out 87 fathoms of line without finding bottom. At 4 a.m. the breeze got up from the SE.
1801-09-08.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order. 95 sacks of wheat were sent to the hospital to be dried and winnowed by the convalescents.

1801-09-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE to south; we sounded without finding bottom. At sunrise we set the studdingsails.
1801-09-09.journal_breton_geographe: Having tasted the water the canoes were bringing us, we found it brackish and sent it back.

1801-09-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds very light and variable from SSE to SE. From 10 until midnight ran out 85 fathoms of line without finding bottom.
1801-09-10.journal_breton_geographe: The two topmasts were swayed up and the lower yards hoisted. Our boats and some canoes continue to water for us.

1801-09-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze variable from SSE to SE. Ran out 90 fathoms of line without finding bottom.

1801-09-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE, south and ESE. Sounded all night without finding bottom.
1801-09-12.journal_breton_geographe: The mizzen topgallant mast was swayed up.

1801-09-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. The sky cloudy and dark. A strong breeze variable from ESE to SE. Caught a tern.

1801-09-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, the sky cloudy, a fresh breeze from SSE, ESE and east. Sounded without finding bottom.
1801-09-14.journal_breton_geographe: The topgallant masts were got up.

1801-09-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear, the horizon misty, a fresh breeze variable from ESE to SE. Caught two boobies. At 9.15 a.m. sighted land N 5° E. Noon bearings: the westernmost visible end N 18° E; a remarkable peak N 22° E, distance 8 miles; the northernmost visible end N 32° E.

1801-09-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from east to SE and ESE. At 3.10 lost sight of the land. At 9 a.m. bore away for Savu Island; running along the southern side of this island, we saw on the shore several local people and a few huts. Noon bearings: the south point of Savu S 5° W; the visible end of this island N 70° E; the middle of this part of the island S 36° W.

1801-09-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to ENE, south and SE. Sounded all night without finding bottom. From the 30th [Fructidor] to the 1st complementary day [Year 9, 17-18 September 1801]. Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds light and variable from S by W, S by E, SE and E by S. Saw several fires on the coast.
1801-09-17.journal_breton_geographe: Work was suspended; part of the crew went ashore to walk about.

1801-09-18.journal_breton_geographe: The cables were inspected and found in good order.

1801-09-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a cloudless sky, a light breeze variable from E to NW, south and SE. At 3 went about onto the port tack.

1801-09-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At 3.15 p.m. the breeze got up from the SSE. At 8 it drew round to SE by E, making us run 7 knots. At 2 took a reef in the mizzen topsail. Bearings at 10: the visible south point of the land east 30° S, about 30 miles off; the north point east, estimated distance from the furthest land [sentence incomplete].

1801-09-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind variable from WNW, SE, SW, NW. During the night we sounded without finding bottom. Lay to from 4 until 5.15, when we filled and stood on. At 6.15 hove to to put the large boat in the water. She left under the orders of Citizen Freycinet, carrying the national flag and pendant; we hoisted our colours and put a signal flag at the foremast head. Shortly afterwards we sighted a boat ahead of us which seemed to have come from the ship in sight, which we recognised to our satisfaction as the Géographe.
1801-09-21.journal_breton_geographe: At daybreak a three-masted ship was sighted beating in towards Kupang; bets were at once laid that it was the Naturaliste. The commander sent orders to make the private signal, and shortly afterwards we recognised the Naturaliste, which also made the private signal. Our boat was sent off to her with some refreshments. At 1 she anchored near us to the NW, two cables off. She saluted us with 5 guns, which we returned, and at once dressed ship. We sent her fresh water and our boat to help her moor.

1801-09-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze variable from SSW to SE and to east and south. At 1 we anchored in 28 fathoms forward and 26 fathoms aft. In the afternoon the two skiffs and the longboat were put in the water to moor us. At 9 a.m. on the 5th we were moored, the western anchor with a range of 50 fathoms to port, the eastern anchor with a range of 100 fathoms to starboard. Bearings of the anchorage: the middle of the fort of Kupang south, distance 1 mile; the south point of Timor S 65° W, 5 miles; the north point N 7° E, 21 miles; the middle of Sandy Island N 11° W, 5 miles.
1801-09-22.journal_breton_geographe: The ship's outside, the masts and the yards were painted. A little fish was taken with the seine.

1801-11-12.journal_anonyme: Hardly had we arrived at Kupang than we set about overhauling the rigging; the orlop deck was taken up, we watered and fresh provisions were embarked. The town of Kupang is defended by a poor fort, and more surely by the courage of the Malays. The English took Kupang during this war, but the men left to garrison the fort were massacred by the Malays and Timor returned into Dutch hands. During our stay the nights and mornings were calm; about 11 the breeze often got up very strong, the winds being then NW and NNW. They fell away at the close of the day and drew round to east and SE. On the 1st Brumaire [Year 10, 23 October 1801] we sighted a frigate standing in for Kupang Bay. Commander Baudin sent a boat aboard her under the orders of a midshipman carrying our passports; on our boat's return we learnt that the frigate sighted was the Virginie, which had come to attack us. As soon as the English frigate's captain had seen our passports, he filled and beat out of the bay. During our stay we lost two men from dysentery. The Géographe lost 5, among them Citizen Riedlé, the gardener-botanist, a man full of zeal for his calling; he was given the same funeral honours as would have been paid to the head of the expedition. He was buried beside Mr Nelson, Captain Bligh's gardener-botanist, who also died at Timor. We lost 9 men by desertion.
1801-11-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: In the evening we unmoored; the cable was found chafed about 20 fathoms from the bend. The second anchor was weighed and let go again at once. The small boat and the yawl were hoisted in.

1801-11-13.journal_anonyme: At five in the morning we got under way with a light breeze from SE. At noon we took the compass bearing of the NW point of Semau W 29° S, 5 miles off, and the NW end of Sandy Island E 11° N, distance 8 [miles].
1801-11-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE, SE, E, NE, NNW, WNW, W, WSW and SW. At 4 a.m. the topgallant masts were rigged and the topsails hoisted, stopped with rope yarns. At 5 got under way with the Géographe and shaped our course N 33° 45' W, N 56° 15' W and N 67° 30' W to leave the bay. At 11, the wind having hauled to the NW, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At noon, the commander having gone onto the port tack, we followed his movement. The NW point of Semau then bore from us S 61° W, 5 miles off, and the NW point of Turtle Island N 79° E, 8 miles off. At 4, Roti Island from S 84° W to S 88° W, and Batu Island N 45° E. The captain cancelled the distribution of hens made on the 20th; he gave 100 to the officers, 50 to the chief petty officers, 30 to the second petty officers, 20 to the petty officers, and the rest to the sick.

1801-11-14.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from WNW to SW, the weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, the course NNW. At 4 a.m. we steered S by E, with a great deal of thunder and lightning. At noon took the bearing of the island of Roti S 46° 30' W.
1801-11-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8 took the bearing of the SW end of Semau S 78° E, the part of Timor in sight N 69° E. At 9 we passed under the commander's stern; he gave us the course south. Variation 0° 58' NW. At noon, being in 10° 3' 30" of latitude, we took the bearing of Dorr Island S 46° E, 18 miles off by the observed latitude and the bearing. The longitude was 120° 45'. It is from there that I took my point of departure. Savary, boatswain's mate, died of dysentery. It was signalled to the commander.

1801-11-15.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from WSW to SW, the weather fine, the sky clear and the sea smooth. At noon a man named Savary died, which was announced to the commander by the agreed signal.
1801-11-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to ESE. At noon in 9° 38' 32" of latitude observed and in 120° 15' 46" of longitude by the watches. The variation 1° 5' 40" NW. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' W.

1801-11-16.journal_anonyme: The winds from south to SSE and ESE, the course SW and SSW, fine weather, smooth sea, the air rather thick and the winds light. At noon we sighted the land of Savu; we took the bearing of a very conspicuous headland SSE.
1801-11-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from ESE to SE. The commander signalled the death of a man (Sautier, gardener). At noon sighted Savu Island in the S 22° 30' E, being in 10° 4' 13" of latitude observed and in 119° 53' 3" of longitude by the watches. At 8.30 observed 1° 5' 30" of NW variation. At 1 the course was signalled S 11° 15' W. At 6 took the bearing of Savu from S 17° E to S 67° E and Benjuar Island from south to S 9° W. At midnight Benjuar Island bore from us S 22° 30' E. There was a fire on it.

1801-11-17.journal_anonyme: The wind varying from SE by E to south, a light breeze. At 1 the commander signalled the course S by W. At 4 took the bearing of the NW end of Savu S 10° E; the SE end E 41° S; Benjuar Island S 7° W.
1801-11-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 4, Benjuar Island from S 68° E to S 85° E, 5 miles off. At 6.30 New Savu was sighted in the S 30° W. At noon it bore from us N 30° E, 15 miles off, being in 11° 2' 10" of latitude observed and in 119° 18' 39" of longitude by account.

1801-11-18.journal_anonyme: Winds variable from SE, south and SSW. Fine weather, the sea smooth, a light air. The commander signalled us the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to SSW. At 1 hove to to wait for the Géographe. At 1.45 she had closed; we filled and stood on. At 8, 0° 49' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 36' 20" of latitude observed and in 118° 29' 3" of longitude by account. The cables were unbent and the anchors secured in their stowage.

1801-11-19.journal_anonyme: Winds variable from S, SSE to SW, almost calm, the weather fine, the sea smooth. The commander signalled the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SW. The commander signalled us the death of a man (Corroyer). At 7.45, 1° 8' 40" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 33' 12" of latitude observed and in 117° 29' 15" of longitude by account.

1801-11-20.journal_anonyme: Winds from S, SW and WSW. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky serene, a fresh breeze.
1801-11-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to WSW. At noon in 11° 37' 10" of latitude observed and in 116° 47' 51" of longitude by account.

1801-11-21.journal_anonyme: The winds variable from W to SW, the sea and the weather fine, the breeze pleasant.
1801-11-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant wind from SSW to W. At noon in 12° 20' 50" of latitude observed and in 117° 22' 45" of longitude by account. At 4, 1° 8' 40" of NW variation.

1801-11-22.journal_anonyme: The winds varying from W to WSW and WNW, the weather fine, a swell running from the SW and a fresh breeze.
1801-11-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to W. At 8, 1° 46' 20" of NW variation. Saw a tropic bird. At noon in 13° 5' 10" of latitude observed and in 117° 42' 51" of longitude by account. We shifted our suit of sails.

1801-11-23.journal_anonyme: The winds from W to WSW, a fresh breeze. The commander signalled the course SW by S; he also signalled the death of a man of his crew.
1801-11-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. We spoke the commander, who gave us the course S 33° 45' should the wind draw aft. He signalled us the death of a man (Mantel). At noon in 14° 2' 0" of latitude observed and in 117° 55' 33" of longitude by account, and in 117° 35' 0" of longitude by the watches. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds. At 5.45, 2° 3' 20" of NW variation.

1801-11-24.journal_anonyme: The winds varied from NW, W and WSW. At 9 we began to lie our course. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds.
1801-11-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to SSW. At noon in 14° 55' 35" of latitude observed and in 117° 46' 0" of longitude by the watches. At 5, 1° 48' 0" of NW variation. Saw a shark. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 45° W.

1801-11-25.journal_anonyme: Winds SW, WSW and SSW, a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea smooth, the sky serene throughout the twenty-four hours. At 8 a.m. a topman named Fanfan died of dysentery.
1801-11-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to SSW. At 7.30, 0° 57' 26" of NW variation. Hubert, known as Fanfan, died of a disease of the liver. At noon in 15° 38' 0" of latitude observed and in 117° 58' of longitude by the watches.

1801-11-26.journal_anonyme: Winds W to SW and SSW, a light breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. The winds varied from W to WNW and WSW. At 8 a.m. a man named Ivan died of dysentery.
1801-11-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from WNW to SW. Le Bouru died of dysentery. At 8.30, 0° 32' 20" of NW variation. We spoke the commander, who urged the captain to use every means to keep the ship from making so much leeway, having been told that she was always very slack; he answered that this was not surprising, as she was too much by the head. At noon in 16° 14' 24" of latitude observed and in 118° 6' 0" of longitude by the watches, and in 118° 11' 0" of longitude by lunar distances.

1801-11-27.journal_anonyme: Winds WSW to SW, very light throughout the 24 hours.
1801-11-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8.30, 1° 47' 10" of NW variation. At noon in 15° 59' 51" of latitude observed and in 117° 49' 30" of longitude by account. At 4.45, 1° 54' 50" of NW variation.

1801-11-28.journal_anonyme: Winds SW and S by W; at 9 they drew round to NW and held there all night. Fine weather. A light breeze.
1801-11-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At noon in 15° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 116° 55' 42" of longitude by account.

1801-11-29.journal_anonyme: The winds S by W to south; during the night they were SSW, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-11-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At 7.45, 1° 42' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 14° 46' 24" of latitude observed and in 115° 54' 24" of longitude by account.

1801-11-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WSW to SSW. At 8.15, 2° 40' 40" of NW variation. Saw tropic birds and flying fish. At noon in 14° 53' 38" of latitude observed and in 115° 17' 42" of longitude by account.

1801-12-01.journal_anonyme: Winds SSW, a fresh breeze; at 11 they drew round to SE and we lay our course SW. Fine weather, smooth sea.
1801-12-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 8, 1° 22' 30" of NW variation. At 6 we asked the commander leave to communicate; he having granted it, we lay under topsails to wait for the Géographe, which was to windward at a great distance and was bearing down on us. At 7 hove to; our boat carried half a bullock, which Citizens Milius and Saint-Cricq were sending to the commander and the officers of the Géographe. At 8.30 we filled and stood on. At noon in 15° 0' 24" of latitude observed and in 114° 16' 12" of longitude by account. Saw tropic birds. At 4, 2° 8' 50" of NW variation. On the evening of the 10th I received orders to take Citizen Milius's watch, he having been ill for several days.

1801-12-02.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from SSE and south; during the day they drew round to S, SSW and SW. Fine weather, a swell running.
1801-12-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At 7.30, 1° 9' 0" of NW variation. At noon in 11° 8' 49" of latitude observed and in 113° 16' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-03.journal_anonyme: Winds SSE to south, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. The currents appeared to set strongly to the north.
1801-12-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 15° 1' 46" of latitude observed and in 112° 9' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-04.journal_anonyme: Throughout the twenty-four hours the winds varied from south to SSE. A strong breeze, a high sea, the weather clear enough.
1801-12-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SSE. At noon in 15° 15' 16" of latitude observed and in 111° 4' 0" of longitude by account. During the night the wind a strong breeze in gusts.

1801-12-05.journal_anonyme: Winds S by E to south, a strong breeze, the sky cloudy, a heavy swell running. Saw tropic birds and frigate birds.
1801-12-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 15° 41' 21" of latitude observed and in 109° 51' 54" of longitude by account.

1801-12-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At 8.30, 3° 19' 0" of NW variation. At noon in 16° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 33' 30" of longitude by account.

1801-12-07.journal_anonyme: Winds south to SSE, a fresh breeze in gusts, fine weather, a swell running. Saw tropic birds.
1801-12-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to SE. At noon in 16° 28' 43" of latitude observed and in 106° 59' 30" of longitude by account. At 3.30 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' W.

1801-12-08.journal_anonyme: Winds south to SSE, SE and SE by S, a strong breeze, a high sea, the sky cloudy. The commander signalled the course SSW.
1801-12-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 17° 27' 0" of latitude observed and in 105° 47' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-09.journal_anonyme: The winds SE, a strong breeze, the sky cloudy, a high sea, the ship pitching heavily. Saw several petrels and some flying fish.
1801-12-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSE. At noon in 18° 37' 18" of latitude observed and in 104° 44' 48" of longitude by account.

1801-12-10.journal_anonyme: Winds SE to SE by S, a strong breeze and in gusts, the weather overcast and misty. At 6.30 a.m. the main jib split.
1801-12-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 8, 3° 56' 20" of NW variation. The flying jib boom was rigged in. At noon in 19° 46' 40" of latitude observed and in 103° 37' 30" of longitude by account.

1801-12-11.journal_anonyme: The winds SE to ESE, a strong breeze, the weather fine, a high sea and the sky cloudy.
1801-12-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to ESE. Spoiled coconuts were served out to the crew. At noon in 21° 12' 34" of latitude observed and in 102° 49' 24" of longitude by account, and in 100° 52' 40" of longitude by lunar distances. The commander signalled the course S 11° 15' W.

1801-12-12.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to SE, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea. At noon the commander signalled the course S by W.
1801-12-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to E. At 7.15, 4° 0' 0" of NW variation. Saw a pintado petrel. At noon in 22° 12' 34" of latitude by account and in 100° 26' 46" of longitude by account. At 4.15, 3° 33' 30" of NW variation.

1801-12-13.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to E by S, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky clear, and cloudy during the night.
1801-12-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 8.15, 4° 33' 30" of NW variation. At noon in 24° 3' 37" of latitude observed and in 100° 1' 4" of longitude by account.

1801-12-14.journal_anonyme: The winds SE by E to SSE and SE, a fresh breeze. Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy.
1801-12-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to SSE. At 7.15, 5° 18' 20" of NW variation. Saw a petrel. At noon in 25° 36' 38" of latitude observed and in 99° 5' 10" of longitude by account. At 4.30, 6° 45' 10" of NW variation.

1801-12-15.journal_anonyme: A light breeze SE to SE by S. Overcast weather, the sea smooth, the night damp. At noon the winds varied from SE by S to E by S.
1801-12-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 26° 34' 12" of latitude observed and in 98° 19' 28" of longitude by account. At 2, at the request of the ship's surgeon, the captain asked the commander to send us his surgeon; the commander having consented, we hove to and sent a boat aboard the Géographe. She brought Citizens L'Haridon and Péron, who consulted with our surgeons on the illness of Citizen Levillain, the zoologist. At 4 they returned to their ship, and at 4.15 we filled and stood on.

1801-12-16.journal_anonyme: Winds ESE to SSE, a fresh breeze, misty weather, the sky overcast. At 2 a boat was sent to the Géographe to fetch the surgeon-major.
1801-12-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 27° 38' 16" of latitude observed and in 97° 41' 58" of longitude by account.

1801-12-17.journal_anonyme: Winds SE to SSE and ESE. A light breeze, the sky overcast, the weather misty.
1801-12-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SE to SW. At 8.15, 6° 46' 0" of NW variation; 7° 51' 40" at 5.15 in the evening. At noon in 28° 22' 53" of latitude observed and in 97° 1' 16" of longitude by account. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E. At 1.30 he cancelled the previous signal and signalled the course S 67° 30' E; at 3.15 he made the signal to steer a point to windward of the course signalled.

1801-12-18.journal_anonyme: Winds south, a fresh breeze. At half past noon went about and headed ESE. In the afternoon the winds varied from SSW to SW and we steered SE by E. In the forenoon the winds freshened and the topgallant masts were struck.
1801-12-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to south. At noon in 29° 10' 35" of latitude by account and in 99° 20' 46" of longitude by account.

1801-12-19.journal_anonyme: Winds SSW, blowing hard. Dark weather, the sky cloudy. In the forenoon the winds varied from S by W to SSE, a light breeze.
1801-12-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SSE. The topmast backstays were set up. At noon in 29° 20' 41" of latitude observed and in 101° 3' 52" of longitude by account.

1801-12-20.journal_anonyme: Winds SSE, a light breeze. The weather fine, the sea smooth. During the night the winds varied from SSW to SW by S. The course SE by E.
1801-12-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SW. At noon in 29° 34' 29" of latitude by account and in 102° 12' 16" of longitude by account. All night the Géographe was astern at a great distance. At 5.45, 8° 0' 0" of NW variation.

1801-12-21.journal_anonyme: The winds SW to WSW, a fresh breeze, fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, heading SE by E.
1801-12-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south. At 2 a.m., having lost sight of the Géographe, we shortened sail to wait for her. At daybreak she closed and we crowded sail. At noon in 30° 18' 37" of latitude observed and in 104° 9' 52" of longitude by account. At noon the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 4.15, 6° 55' 0" of NW variation.

1801-12-22.journal_anonyme: The winds SW by S until midnight, when they drew round to south and SSE, a strong breeze. The commander signalled the course SE.
1801-12-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SSW. At noon in 30° 31' 1" of latitude by account and in 106° 14' 22" of longitude by account. At 8 a main topmast backstay parted and was replaced for the time being by a lee backstay. At 9 Citizen Levillain died.

1801-12-23.journal_anonyme: Squally weather, a strong breeze from south to SSW. At 8 the main topmast backstay parted close to the crosstrees. Citizen Levillain, the zoologist, died of a bloody flux.
1801-12-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSW to SSE. At daybreak the main topmast backstay was set up again. At noon in 30° 1' 38" of latitude observed and in 107° 58' 16" of longitude by account.

1801-12-24.journal_anonyme: A high sea, the weather overcast, the wind a strong breeze from south to SE and SSE. At 8 a.m. wore ship.
1801-12-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SE. At noon in 30° 9' 28" of latitude observed and in 109° 0' 28" of longitude by account. At 4.45, 6° 57' 0" of NW variation. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E.

1801-12-25.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, a swell running, a strong breeze from SE. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E.
1801-12-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At noon in 31° 25' 50" of latitude observed and in 108° 4' 4" of longitude by account.

1801-12-26.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 5 went about. At 9.30 a.m. the course was signalled S 45° E.
1801-12-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSW. At 9.30 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 11 we had a squall in which the middle staysail was split; in hauling it down it was shifted. At noon in 31° 55' 2" of latitude by account and in 107° 42' 10" of longitude by account. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E.

1801-12-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SSE. At 5.30 p.m. the commander signalled the course S 22° 30' E in case the winds should draw aft.
1801-12-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 31° 39' 10" of latitude observed and in 109° 13' 4" of longitude by account. Saw albatrosses and petrels.

1801-12-28.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a fresh breeze from south to SSE. At 8.15 the commander, after closing us, went about, and we did the same.
1801-12-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SSE. At noon in 31° 49' 38" of latitude observed and in 108° 57' 40" of longitude by account.

1801-12-29.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south to SE. At 9 squally weather with fairly violent gusts; the dinghy was put on the gratings to be repaired. At 7.30 a.m. went onto the port tack.
1801-12-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. Saw albatrosses. At noon in 31° 59' 56" of latitude observed and in 108° 23' 58" of longitude by account. At 3.30 the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SW.

1801-12-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, calm until 3, when the breeze got up from the south, variable to SW and SSE by way of south. Obs. lat. 32° 12' 22".
1801-12-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to SE. At noon in 32° 12' 23" of latitude observed and in 109° 20' 46" of longitude by account. At 6, 6° 47' 10" of NW variation.

1801-12-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to east. At half past noon went onto the port tack and made all sail.
1801-12-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At noon in 33° 15' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 33' 22" of longitude by account.

1802-01-01.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a light breeze. The effects of the late Le Bourgeois and Savary were sold.
1802-01-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from SE to SW. The effects of the late Bourgeois and Savary were sold. At noon in 34° 0' 0" of latitude observed and in 107° 50' 22" of longitude by account.

1802-01-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south. At 1.30 changed tacks. The effects of Citizen Levillain were sold.
1802-01-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from SSE to SSW. The mizzen topgallant mast was wedged and its shrouds and backstays set up. The effects of the late Levillain were sold. At noon in 34° 4' 0" of latitude observed and in 108° 51' 10" of longitude by account. At 1 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 5.30 he was to leeward at a great distance. We supposed he was steering S 67° 30' E and that we had mistaken the colour of the flags giving the course; so we bore away S 67° 30' E, and east, and closed him.

1802-01-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A light breeze from south to SSW and W. At 1.45 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. At 5.30, being far to leeward, we supposed he was steering S 67° 30' E and that we had mistaken the colour of the flag that gave the course; we at once bore away S 67° 30' E.
1802-01-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from S to SSW. At 6 a flat calm; at 8 the breeze got up from WNW and blew from WNW to W, a fresh breeze. At noon in 34° 10' 0" of latitude observed and in 109° 54' 46" of longitude by account. At 6 the commander signalled the course S 33° 45' E for 8 o'clock. At 11 we had a slight squall with rain; the fore studdingsail boom broke as the studdingsails were taken in.

1802-01-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from W to WNW; set the studdingsails and royals. The commander signalled the course for 8 o'clock as S 33° 45' E. At 4 a.m. overcast weather, a strong breeze and a high sea.
1802-01-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to WSW. A high sea. Two large pieces of wood passed alongside. At noon in 35° 12' 34" of latitude observed and in 112° 44' 16" of longitude by account. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. Saw a whale. During the night the wind in gusts, with rain and frequent squalls.

1802-01-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from W to WSW. At 5 the commander signalled the course S 45° E. In the forenoon the weather cleared.
1802-01-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea. The wind a strong breeze from W to SW, with rain. At noon in 36° 28' 23" of latitude observed and in 115° 56' 58" of longitude by account.

1802-01-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze and in gusts. At 1 lowered and clewed up the main topsail to repair it. As soon as it was repaired we took the 2 reefs and sheeted home. At daybreak the weather turned fine; we rigged out the studdingsails and made all sail.
1802-01-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to NW. Saw albatrosses, petrels, bonito and weed. At noon in 37° 40' 15" of latitude observed and in 118° 41' 40" of longitude by account. At 4 the Géographe was far astern and was not crowding sail; we shortened ours. At 7.15 hove to on the port tack, and at 8 filled and stood on.

1802-01-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a fresh breeze from NW to W. At 7.15 hove to to wait. At 8, having closed, we filled and stood on.
1802-01-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to W. At 2.30 the main topsail tie and lift parted; all was repaired by 3.30. At noon in 39° 18' 41" of latitude observed and in 121° 34' 34" of longitude by account. At 5.30, 5° 40' 40" of NW variation. Rain during the night.

1802-01-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sky cloudy, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from NW; all sail set, studdingsails and royals.
1802-01-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from NW to WSW, with rain. At 2.30, in a squall, the main topsail sheet parted; by 3.30 the damage was repaired. At noon in 41° 8' 14" of latitude observed and in 124° 16' 40" of longitude by account. The commander signalled the course S 67° 30' E.

1802-01-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from W to WSW. At noon the course was signalled S 67° 30' E.
1802-01-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to WNW. Saw a great deal of seaweed. At noon in 42° 7' 2" of latitude by account and in 128° 5' 28" of longitude by account. During the night the wind blowing hard in gusts, with rain; kept the topsails reefed. In the night of the 9th [Nivôse, 30 December 1801] I had a high fever which forced me to keep my bed all through the 10th [Nivôse, 31 December 1801]; on the 11th [Nivôse, 1 January 1802] I was a little better, and a purge and an emetic set me up. It was not until the 14th [Nivôse, 4 January 1802] that the surgeon-major allowed me to resume my watch. I was still weak, but within 4 days I was in as good health as before my illness.

1802-01-10.journal_anonyme: Overcast and fresh weather, a high sea and the wind a strong breeze from W to WNW and SW. Saw a whale and some seaweed.
1802-01-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to WNW. Saw a whale and a great deal of seaweed. At noon in 40° 57' 53" of latitude observed and in 132° 8' 16" of longitude by account. At 2 the commander signalled the course S 78° 45' E. In the course of the day the five courses and topsails were shifted. Variation 2° 38' NE.

1802-01-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from NW. We shifted the foresail and the main topsail. The commander signalled the course S 78° 45' E.
1802-01-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from W to NNW, with rain. The sails unbent were examined and condemned, except the foresail. At noon in 43° 38' 29" of latitude by account and in 136° 36' 16" of longitude by account.

1802-01-12.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, rain at intervals, a high sea and a strong breeze from NW to W. At 6.30 the commander made the signal to bend our cables.
1802-01-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to W, with rain. At 6.30 the commander signalled us to bend our cables, which we did, and got the anchors ready to let go. In a squall the fore studdingsail boom broke; it was at once replaced by one from the main yard. At noon in 43° 31' 30" of latitude observed and in 141° 2' 40" of longitude by account. At 5, 6° 22' 30" of NE variation. At 10 the commander having hove to on the starboard tack, we did the same, after lowering the topsails on the caps.

1802-01-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NW to W and SW. During the night the commander having hove to, we did the same. At 3.45 we sighted the land in the N 45° E. We signalled it to the commander. We closed the coast and ran along it. At 8 took the bearing of the SW cape N 22° 30', distance 9.5 miles; the Mewstone S 85° E, distance 5 miles; the westernmost of the Maatsuyker Islands from N 49° E to N 46° E, distance 4 miles.
1802-01-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. At 3.45 the land was sighted in the N 45° E. We signalled it to the commander at once. At 4 we signalled it again. At 4.30 filled and stood on and closed the land, which we made out to be the SW cape of Van Diemen's Land. At 8 took the bearing of the SW cape N 22° 30' W, 10 miles off; the westernmost of the Maatsuyker Islands from N 49° E to N 56° E, 4 miles off; and the Mewstone S 85° E, 5 miles off. At noon took the bearing of the South Cape N 48° E, 4 miles off, and the Mewstone S 67° 30' W. Latitude by account 43° 33' 6", the same by the bearing 43° 44' 0"; longitude by account 143° 50' 22", the same by the bearing 144° 30' 0". Running very close along Van Diemen's Land and shaping our course to enter D'Entrecasteaux Channel. At half past noon we spoke the commander, who ordered us to keep ahead of him. Several fires could be seen at the head of Recherche Bay. At 1.30 breakers were sighted ahead at a short distance (these breakers are marked on D'Entrecasteaux's chart and lie between the south point of Anse des Ormiers and the Sterile Islands). The captain, who took them for canoes of the Aboriginal people coming aboard, said "let her come to port"; and I, who had the watch, repeated his order and had it carried out by the helmsman, who kept hauling his tiller to port. But a few minutes later, being already almost in the wash of the breakers, everyone having cried out that we were on the breakers, we hauled smartly to the wind on the starboard tack and weathered the Sterile Islands handsomely. The commander, who was keeping astern at some distance, followed our movement. At 3.15, being a little offshore, we bore away for Cape Bruny. The commander, who at that moment was taking in reefs, held his wind a while longer and at last shaped his course as we had. Having reached the mouth of the channel, we ran in; and after doubling Pointe Labillardière and the NE point of Partridge Island, we hauled to the wind to gain the anchorage of the Grande Anse in Bruny Island. At 4.15 we let go the anchor in 28 fathoms, black mud, under Partridge Island, Huon Island bearing S 88° E, Lahaye Island N 51° W, and the north point of Partridge Island N 82° W. At 4.45 the commander anchored S 30° E of us, two cables off. We asked his leave to put the boats in the water and to send one aboard him, which he granted. The boats were put in the water and we sent for the Géographe's doctors to see Citizen Milius, who was still ill. I went with the captain aboard the Géographe and had the pleasure of embracing my friends. The dinghy went fishing under Partridge Island and came back without having taken anything.

1802-01-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, standing in to enter D'Entrecasteaux Channel and running very close along the land. At noon spoke the commander, who ordered us to keep ahead of him. We crowded sail; several fires could be seen at the head of Recherche Bay. At 1.30 we sighted several lines of breakers ahead. We at once hauled close to the wind on the starboard tack to weather the Sterile Islands; the Géographe followed our movement. At 3.45 we bore away for Cape Bruny; having reached the mouth of the channel we ran in and made for the anchorage of Grande Anse. At 4.15 we let go the starboard anchor in 28 fathoms, black mud. Bearings of the anchorage: the point of Partridge Island S 82° W; Lahaye Island N 54° W; Huon Island S 88° E. At 5 a.m. the longboat was sent off to look for a watering place.
1802-01-14.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from S to WSW, with squalls and rain. At 5 a.m. I left in the longboat to water in Port Espérance or in the Huon River; Citizens Freycinet, lieutenant, Faure, surveyor, and Bailly, mineralogist, took the opportunity to come along. At 8 the captain and some of the officers and naturalists landed on Bruny Island and communicated with the Aboriginal people. The dinghy went fishing and took nothing. In the evening all the boats (except the longboat) came back aboard. An inclination of 68° 36' 0" was observed in the Grande Anse.

At 5 a.m. I left in the longboat, manned with 7 men and provisioned for 2 days, to water in Port Espérance; and should I be unable to water there, I was to go to the Huon River. Citizens Freycinet, Faure and Bailly came with me. The weather was overcast and squally with rain; a good breeze from the south carried me to Port Espérance in very little time. I closed the south point and ran along the coast within a boathook's length. I went into the cove where D'Entrecasteaux marks a stream; the longboat touched, and having got off without difficulty, I landed on the starboard point with Citizens Freycinet, Faure and Bailly. We made for the stream; it was dry, with only brackish water in a few holes. Having re-embarked, I crossed the harbour to look for another stream marked on the chart abreast of the first. I tried to land thereabouts, but it was impossible (the shore being foul, and the longboat touching on a muddy sand bottom at some distance from the beach). I ran along the shore and saw a trickle of water running over the sand; seeing no convenience for watering there, I decided to go to the Huon River. The wind was a strong breeze in puffs and very variable; I beat for 3 hours between Lahaye Island and the north point. At last I put the men to the oars, and having doubled the north point with great difficulty, I made sail and shaped my course for the Huon River. I closed and ran along the right bank. At sunset, finding myself abreast of Port des Cygnes, I went in after doubling the second point to starboard. I sighted the Géographe's longboat in a cove; I bore up for her and landed beside her. I learnt that when the longboat had come alongside the shore, several Aboriginal people had run up with cries of joy, that the eldest (probably the head of the family) had thrown his arms round the neck of Citizen Freycinet the elder, commanding the longboat, and that they had taken him to their huts.

After searching the cove without finding water, I came back to the boats, where I found Freycinet the elder and 6 Aboriginal people: 2 men, a young woman and 3 little boys. The elder of the men had a short, curly beard; their hair was woolly and smeared with a kind of red grease. The two men and the woman, who must have had hair on their private parts, had shaved it. The woman had her face smeared with black; and to show us how she blackened it she rubbed both hands on a burnt tree, puffed out her cheeks and drew her hands over them from her ears to her nose and eyes. She then wanted to do as much to each of us. They each had a kangaroo skin which covered their shoulders only. The men did not appear to us jealous; they let us caress the young woman, who seemed to take some pleasure in it. We loaded them with presents; they took everything eagerly and, without examining it, handed it to the woman, who stowed it in her kangaroo skin. Several times I tried to make them look in a mirror and held it before their eyes, but they at once turned away sharply. I also tried to show them the use of knives by cutting wood in front of them; they paid no attention and threw themselves on the knife to get it, and as soon as they had it they gave it to the woman. The only thing that held their attention was a tricolour plume I had on my hat; I gave it to the younger of the men, who at once put it in his hair, and the elder seemed vexed that I had not given it to him. Before we arrived they had stolen a bottle of brandy from the Géographe's longboat and hidden it in a hollow tree, where the boat's crew, who had seen them do it, recovered it. When we re-embarked, all of them (except the eldest) got into my longboat; but we had scarcely shoved off when the eldest called them, and they took to the water. They made signs to us as long as we could see them.

I passed the night, with the Géographe's longboat, in a very fine cove next to the last. At daybreak the Freycinets and I went round it on foot, hoping to find fresh water there. We found several streams, which we went up; the water was drinkable only too far from their mouths for the ships to water there, though we filled a few breakers. After our round we re-embarked. Freycinet the elder sounded the cove, and I shaped my course for the head of the harbour, running along the land within a boathook's length. Having reached it, I ran along the shore to port, and seeing no stream I resolved to return aboard, having only two meals' provisions left. I gave the order to steer out of the harbour. A short distance from where we had passed the night I met the Géographe's longboat standing for the head of the harbour. Freycinet the elder hailed me and asked what I was about; I answered that I was going back aboard. He told me he was going to dine at the head of the harbour on a swan he had just shot. Whereupon Freycinet the younger, without warning me, gave the coxswain orders to steer for the head of the harbour; we set our sails and chased swans. Right at the head of the harbour the water shoaled suddenly and we grounded on soft mud. We rowed, poled, got off, and grounded again. Citizen Freycinet had taken the tiller and I had taken an oar. We had been rowing some minutes when I gave the order to pole; Citizen Freycinet appeared displeased and spoke harshly to me. The boat's crew did not know which of the two to obey. I observed to Citizen Freycinet that the captain, having entrusted the longboat to me, had thought me capable of handling her and that I answered for her. He said no more; I repeated the order I had given, and shortly afterwards the longboat was afloat. I had her anchored to give the crew a moment's rest and let them dine. I then had it out with Citizen Freycinet, and the longboat being out of all danger, I offered to hand over the command of her to him. He took it. We landed near the Géographe's people and dined there. In the evening we left in company with the Géographe's boat, and on the 26th [Nivôse, 16 January 1802] at 5 a.m. we arrived aboard. I reported to the captain what had passed. He blamed Citizen Freycinet's conduct and told me I had been wrong to give up the command of the longboat to him.

1802-01-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather and a strong breeze from S to SSW. All the boats were back except the longboat.
1802-01-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to W. The captain and the officers landed on Bruny Island and came back aboard at noon.

1802-01-16.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the wind fell away a great deal. In the afternoon the breeze varied from SSW to W, N and NNE. At 6.30 a.m. the longboat was back, not having been able to find a convenient place to water.
1802-01-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW. At 5 a.m. I came back aboard with the longboat without having been able to water, either in Port Espérance or in Port des Cygnes. In the latter I had a dispute with Citizen Freycinet and handed over the command of the longboat to him (see my report to the captain). At 8 Citizen Faure, the surveyor, was sent off in the large boat to sound the inner part of the Grande Anse. Our longboat, in company with the Géographe's, went for firewood on Partridge Island; the sick were sent there to walk about a little. I took the opportunity to go shooting on the island. At 4 p.m. the weather turned overcast and stormy and the wind freshened from the WNW. Our longboat being loaded, we made haste to leave so as to reach the ship before the storm broke; but we were scarcely halfway when the wind came on to blow hard, with a high sea, thunder, lightning and pouring rain. We did not take in an inch of sail; two cables from the ship the foremast broke off level with the collar, and before the grapnel and its rope could be got ready we drove and anchored in the ship's wake. At 6, the breeze having fallen a great deal, we came aboard. Citizen Faure came back in the large boat at nightfall. The draught was taken: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 10 feet 10 inches, difference 1 foot 1 inch. Citizen Maurouard, midshipman of the Géographe, in charge of a party in a boat, received a spear wound in the shoulder on Bruny Island.

1802-01-17.journal_anonyme: The weather, fine enough at first, turned overcast; the wind freshened from the WNW and the storm broke at 4.30 with a great deal of rain. At 5 a.m. the commander made the signal to get under way; at 8.30 we were under sail, and at 10 and at noon we were abreast of Pointe Riche, forming the southern entrance to Isthmus Bay.
1802-01-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to N. At 5 the commander made the signal to get under way. At 9.30 got under way and shaped our course up the channel. We had great difficulty weighing our anchor; we broke a messenger and then rigged a voyol. At noon, being abreast of Isthmus Bay, the wind headed us; we beat until 2.30 without being able to weather Green Island. The commander then having anchored east of Green Island, we anchored in 7½ fathoms, muddy sand, Pointe Legrand bearing N 3° W, the Géographe and the middle of Green Island N 22° E, Pointe Riche S 33° E, and Satellite Island from S 15° W to S 22° W. Citizen Faure went to sound the channel; he saw a seal on Green Island. Several officers and naturalists landed on Van Diemen's Land abreast of the anchorage.

1802-01-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze with strong gusts at intervals from W to NW. Being near Green Island, we anchored on the opposite side of the channel in 7½ fathoms, muddy sand. Satellite Island bore from us S 15° W to S 22° W; Pointe Riche S 33° E; the middle of Green Island N 22° E; Pointe Legrand N 3° W. Pointe Legrand bore from us N 22° E, past Green Island.
1802-01-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW to NW in gusts, with rain. Despite the bad weather we ran out a warp towards Pointe Legrand and hauled in on it, being obliged to let go the bower anchor in heavy gusts. At 5 the wind hauled to the W and drew round to WSW. At 6 we got under way and shaped our course for the North West Port; at 7 doubled Pointe Legrand and at 7.45 Pointe Gicquel. At 8 we anchored at the entrance of the North West Port, Pointe Legrand bearing S 12° W, Pointe Gicquel S 25° W, Pointe Pierson N 36° E and Pointe de la Sortie N 54° E.

1802-01-19.journal_anonyme: In the roads of the North West Port, Van Diemen's Land. We warped in towards the anchorage; at 3.30 the breeze got up and we hoisted our topsails, but having dragged our kedge anchor we let go a bower. At 6 p.m. we got under way and anchored at the entrance to the North West Port. Bearings: Pointe Legrand S 12° W; Pointe Gicquel S 25° W; Pointe Pierson N 36° E; Pointe de la Sortie N 54° E.
1802-01-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from W to NW. A dog was heard barking ashore. The Aboriginal people lit many fires at different points of the coast. Officers and naturalists landed on Bruny Island to try to communicate with them, but they fled at their approach. The longboat, with a working party, went for firewood to Pointe Gicquel. Two catamarans were seen crossing the channel from Pointe Pierson to Pointe de la Sortie, in one of them four Aboriginal people and in the other six. The captain dredged all the afternoon and took a considerable quantity of scallops. The longboat came back at nightfall loaded with wood. At 6 the Géographe anchored near us.

1802-01-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, winds from N to NNW, a light breeze. The longboat went for wood. The large boat was sent off to the North River.
1802-01-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW, with heavy gusts and rain. At 5 the longboat, with a working party, went for wood. At 6 I was sent off in the large boat to go up the North River to look for a watering place for the ships; I was armed with two blunderbusses and four muskets and had 4 days' provisions. At 2 p.m. the ship dragged, veered cable and then let go a second anchor. The yards were sent down and the topgallant masts struck. The longboat came back loaded with wood.

1802-01-21.journal_anonyme: Squally weather. A fresh breeze from WNW with strong gusts and rain. At 2 we dragged and veered 12 fathoms of cable; shortly afterwards let go the port anchor.
1802-01-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from WNW in gusts, with light rain at intervals. At daybreak the captain left in the longboat to look for a watering place. The two anchors were weighed and one let go in 30 fathoms, mud and shell, Pointe Legrand bearing S 13° W, Pointe Gicquel S 61° W, and Pointe de la Sortie N 45° E. At 9 p.m. the captain came back with the longboat; he had not found a watering place, but he brought back a great quantity of oysters, which were distributed to the crew.

1802-01-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WNW to W in strong gusts. The wind having fallen, the commander gave us orders to warp in. At 10 the large boat came back from her mission to the North River; she found there a very convenient watering place.
1802-01-22.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NNE. By the commander's order we warped into the head of the port. At 5.30 p.m. we got under way with a light breeze from NE and stood into the port. At 6.15 we anchored in 16 fathoms, muddy bottom [corner torn], Pointe Gicquel bearing S 22° E and Pointe de la Sortie N 84° E.

At 10 a.m. I came in from my errand; before coming alongside, the captain ordered me to go and report my mission to the commander. I informed him that I had found a very convenient watering place; he told me that for the present it was of no use to us, because Citizen Ronsard had found a river at the head of the port where we should water. I came back aboard and gave him the following report:

By your orders I left the ship on the 30th Nivôse [20 January 1802] at 6 a.m. in the large boat, armed and provisioned for four days. I was to go up the North River to see what facility there might be for watering the corvettes, and to be back aboard on the morning of the 2nd Pluviôse [22 January 1802]. The weather was fine enough and the wind a fresh breeze from the north; I was obliged to beat at the river's mouth. The weather turned squally and the wind blew hard in gusts from the north with rain. I was reduced to carrying only the foresail and mainsail, both reefed; yet by taking advantage of the wind's small shifts (and probably helped by the tide) I reached by nightfall the cove where D'Entrecasteaux marks a stream (on the left bank at the foot of the plateau). I made the boat fast in a little creek to starboard and went with three armed men towards the stream, where I found very good water. The tide was then low; I came back to the boat, and having embarked, I went in with the first of the flood to the head of the cove, hugging the land to starboard close enough to touch the oars on shore, finding 3 fathoms, 2½, 2, 1½ and 1 fathom, where I landed 200 paces from the watering place, afloat; and there I had my breakers filled, and a tierce I had with me. I sounded the cove: I had 5 fathoms in the middle and on the starboard side; the port side is low and muddy. This watering place is very convenient; there is anchorage for the corvettes abreast of the cove in 10 and 15 fathoms, and even in the cove in 5 fathoms. The longboats can come alongside the bank at low water and load there. The only labour would be to roll the casks from the watering place to the boats, over 200 paces of dry, level ground.

I passed the night in this cove, and on the 1st Pluviôse [21 January 1802] at daybreak I left it to go up the river. I had to beat the whole way with a fresh breeze. Having got about 3 miles beyond the place where D'Entrecasteaux's boats had been, and having found from that point 5 fathoms down to 2½, I met a very violent current at a point which hid the river's course from me. Yet the tide was low, for several branches partly sunk in the mud, with shells on them, showed how far the tide rose. I rowed in the middle of the river, along the right bank, along the left bank, without being able to stem the current. I landed on the left bank near the point I had not been able to double, and after walking some time along the river I saw that beyond the point it ran NW and then appeared to divide into two arms, one running N and the other WSW. However much I wished to find the river's source, I thought I ought to stop my survey there: you had fixed the 2nd for my return, and besides my mission was fulfilled, since I had found a watering place. I went down the river and passed the night at the same place as the night before (the Watering Cove). I shot several swans there, and sounded the cove more carefully. At daybreak I left it and reached the ship at 10 a.m. Going down the river I sounded it and found from 10 to 20 fathoms.

On the strength of the report I had made to him, the commander sent off his large boat under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to go up the river. He was favoured by the wind, which he had aft the whole way; the first evening he slept 3 miles above the place where I had been stopped, and met no violent current. He examined the arms I had seen: the WSW one was the river's course, the other only a very large inlet. He went up the river as far as it was navigable by boat and on foot, about 9 miles, without seeing its source.

During our stay in the North West Port the sick were put ashore every fine day; they were given 2 armed men to guard them, and these two men cut firewood for us.

1802-01-23.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from N to NW and NE. At 5.30, being at the end of the warp and the breeze freshening, we got under way under fore-and-aft sails and let go the anchor in 16 fathoms, muddy bottom. Bearings of the anchorage: Pointe Gicquel S 22° E; Cape de la Sortie E 6° N. We moored east and west.
1802-01-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: The weather was fine and the wind a light breeze from N to NW. At 6 a.m. the large boat, with 15 days' provisions, was sent off under the orders of Citizen Faure, surveyor, to survey the North Bay and the passage marked on D'Entrecasteaux's chart between Van Diemen's Land and Tasman Island. At 7 our longboat, in company with the Géographe's, went to water at the head of the port. We moored east and west with a kedge anchor. Draught: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 11 feet 2 inches, difference 0 feet 9 inches. The observatory was set up on a small islet at the head of the port, at the mouth of the river.

1802-01-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the winds east, variable to SE, almost calm. During the night a very thick fog kept us from making out the coast; during the night the winds went right round the compass and varied from [one word illegible] WNW, W and WSW, a strong breeze. Citizen Saint-Cricq embarked in the dinghy with his instruments to go to the observatory set up at the head of the North West Port.
1802-01-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from WNW to SW in gusts; it fell away at nightfall.

1802-01-25.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze in gusts from WSW, south, SW and W. At 7.30 a working party of 6 men was sent ashore to stay there and fill the casks.
1802-01-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from W to NW. At 6 a.m. the longboat came in loaded with water. She left again at 7.15 with a working party of 7 men commanded by a midshipman, who are to stay at the watering place to fill the casks, roll them down and raft them, so that the longboat may find them ready and have only to take them in.

1802-01-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, wind east, a fresh breeze. Calm all the afternoon. From 4 to 10 the breeze got up from NE to ENE, freshening a great deal; at noon it was blowing hard from that quarter.
1802-01-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NNE to ENE. At 9 p.m. a musket shot was thought to have been heard ashore to the NE; the yawl was at once sent away armed, and found no one.

1802-01-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. A strong breeze from ENE to NNE. The longboat went watering.
1802-01-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 4.15 a.m. the longboat came in. She weighed the kedge anchor and carried it SW of the bower, so that we are now moored NE and SW. Overcast weather; the breeze freshened and blew strong in gusts from NW to W. At 6.30 (on the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1802]) the mooring hawser parted; we veered cable to 150 fathoms. The longboat weighed the kedge anchor; not being able to get the end of the hawser, which was foul of the flukes of the bower anchor, we unbent it and put a buoy on the end. The longboat left for the watering place. At 9 a second anchor was let go.

1802-01-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze from WNW to NW in heavy gusts. It fell away about four o'clock. The longboat came aboard with her load of water. She left again at once for the watering place.
1802-01-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to NW. At 3.30 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place and left again at once. A little rain.

1802-01-29.journal_anonyme: Rainy weather, the sea smooth, a strong breeze in [one word illegible] puffs from NW, WSW, WNW and W. The longboat came in with her load of water. She was sent off again at once.
1802-01-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from NW to WSW. At 4 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place and left again at 6. The carpenters went to cut wood and brought back several pieces.

1802-01-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, blowing hard in heavy gusts from W to WSW and WNW. In the forenoon they drew round to SE and SSE, almost calm. We were busy stowing the sheet anchor.
1802-01-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a pleasant wind from WSW to SE. The carpenters went back to cut wood. The commander and the captain communicated with the Aboriginal people on Bruny Island and handed out trinkets to them; at the moment they were embarking they received a volley of stones, which wounded no one. The commander alone had the misfortune to take one on the back, which did him no harm. It was the same group that had wounded Citizen Maurouard with a spear.

1802-01-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, a light breeze variable from SE to east and SSE. The captain communicated with the Aboriginal people of Bruny Island. The winds drew round to SW, NW, NNE and ENE, a light breeze. The longboat came in with her load of water.
1802-01-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNE, S and WSW. The carpenters went to cut wood. At 7 the longboat came in from the watering place and went back there at 11.
