1802-02-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the sky cloudy, the winds very light from ENE, east, NW and SW. At noon squally weather and the winds a strong breeze from SW to NW. The longboat came in with her load of water.
1802-02-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from SW to W. At 7.15 a.m. the longboat came in from the watering place. She went to fetch firewood cut by the two men guarding the sick; at 1 she brought in her load and left at 3 for the watering place. Draught: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 10 feet 8 inches, difference 1 foot 0 inches.

1802-02-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze variable from WNW to W. The longboat left for the watering place. The forenoon was almost calm; the carpenters worked on the starboard hawse bolsters.
1802-02-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. The carpenters worked at shifting the hawse bolsters. Fish were taken and distributed to the crew. Citizen Faure came in at 4.30 in the large boat. He had surveyed the North Bay and had found no passage between Van Diemen's Land and Tasman Island, which is joined to the land by a spit of sand; he had found fresh water in many places. The captain brought back many fish and oysters, which were distributed.

1802-02-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds light and variable from ENE to NE and WNW. At 4 the large boat came back from her duty; she found that Marion Bay does not communicate with Frederick Hendrik Bay, only a narrow spit of sand separating them, so that Abel Tasman Island is no more than a peninsula; and she was unable to communicate with the Aboriginal people.
1802-02-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. At daybreak swayed up the topgallant masts. The longboat came in from the watering place and left again at once, empty, to fetch the remaining casks and bring back the party stationed at the watering place. We sent to fetch from the shore the pieces of timber the carpenters had cut. The astronomical instruments came back aboard.

1802-02-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds light and variable from ENE, NE, NNE, N and NW. The observatory was struck, as was the camp set up ashore for watering.
1802-02-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. The starboard anchor was weighed and 100 fathoms of the port cable hauled in. At noon the longboat came in from the watering place with the rest of the casks full, the working party and the effects from the camp. She was hoisted in, as was the large boat.

1802-02-05.journal_anonyme: Misty weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from east to south and SSE. At half past noon the longboat was back. On the 16th at 4 a.m. hove short, sheeted home and hoisted the topsails; the misty and almost calm weather prevented us from getting under way, and we lowered and furled the topsails and veered 6 fathoms of cable.
1802-02-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, calm. At 4.15 a.m., having a light air from the south, we hove short, hoisted and sheeted home the topsails; but a flat calm coming on, we furled the topsails and lay at long stay. We had caught the end of the hawser that parted on the 7th [Pluviôse, 27 January 1802] and kept it aboard.

1802-02-06.journal_anonyme: Misty weather, the sea smooth, a flat calm. The breeze got up from the NNE and drew round, freshening, to NW, W and SW. The corvette dragging fast towards the land, we struck our topgallant masts. The Aboriginal people lit fires round the shores of the port.
1802-02-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm; the heat was stifling. At 2.30 a.m. a light breeze got up from NNE, drew round to NW and W, freshening, and at last to SW, a strong breeze with violent gusts. At 5 we had dragged and veered cable, and slipped the hawser with a buoy whose lashing gave way. At 6 the topgallant masts were got down. At 7.30 we dragged and let go a second anchor, the wind blowing hard from WSW to SSW. The Aboriginal people lit many fires round the shores of the port; we saw five of them on the nearest shore, each with a brand in his hand, setting fire everywhere. At nightfall the wind fell away, and it was calm during the night.

1802-02-07.journal_anonyme: A strong breeze in gusts from SW, SSE and south; it fell away in the afternoon. We made attempts to get under way, but a calm coming on we let go a bower anchor.
1802-02-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather. At 4.15 a.m., a breeze from NNW, we weighed both anchors in turn and got under way under topsails. We hauled in 50 fathoms of the hawser, which had stayed foul of the anchor's flukes, and took the draught: aft 11 feet 11 inches, forward 11 feet 7 inches, difference 4 inches. At 7.30 a flat calm; anchored and lay at long stay with the topsails hoisted. The breeze got up from the south and veered as far as east. At nightfall the commander signalled us to follow his movements; accordingly we lowered the topsails and veered cable.

1802-02-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather; throughout the twenty-four hours a very light breeze variable from south to ESE and SE. In the forenoon the commander having squared his yards, we did the same.
1802-02-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from E to NE. Fish were taken and distributed.

1802-02-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a little misty; shipped the winter spar. A fresh breeze from E by S to NE. The dinghy brought back fish and went straight back to the fishing.
1802-02-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. At 4 p.m. the large boat was put in the water and sent off to Bruny Island with Citizen Leschenault, the botanist. She was back at 8.15 and was hoisted in, together with a catamaran she had found adrift in the channel.

1802-02-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm. At 4 the large boat was put in the water and sent off to Bruny Island with Citizen Leschenault, the botanist. At 8 p.m. she was back; she was hoisted in, together with a catamaran belonging to the Aboriginal people which they had found adrift in the middle of the channel. From the 21st to the 22nd [Pluviôse, Year 10, 10-11 February 1802]. Overcast, misty weather, fine rain throughout the twenty-four hours, a flat calm.
1802-02-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a flat calm. Fish were distributed to the crew. Rain during the night.

1802-02-13.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather. A light breeze from south and SE, with fine rain until four in the morning. The dinghy left for the fishing.
1802-02-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from E to ESE. Latitude of the observatory, North West Port: 43° 1' 1"; longitude 145° 5' 0"; variation NE 10° 25' 0".

1802-02-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from east to ESE. At 4.30, the breeze being from the NW, we hove round on the cables, and at 5 hoisted the topsails; at 5.30 got under way and made all sail, ranging along Van Diemen's Land. After doubling the east point of the North West Port the winds headed us; we beat between Pointe Pierson and Pointe de la Sortie without being able to weather the latter, and on the 10th board we anchored in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom. Bearings of the anchorage: Pointe Gicquel S 44° E; Pointe Pierson N 15° E; Pointe de la Sortie N 75° E.
1802-02-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a breeze from NNW. At 5.30 we got under way and shaped our course to leave the port, hugging the eastern shore of the port, after doubling its east point. The wind headed us, drawing round to NE and ENE; we beat between Pointe Pierson and Pointe de la Sortie without being able to weather the latter. At 9, on the tenth board, we anchored in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom, Pointe Gicquel bearing S 44° W, Pointe Pierson N 15° E, and Pointe de la Sortie N 75° E. The breeze varied from east to west by way of north.

1802-02-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to east. During the night the wind drew round to W, a fresh breeze; stopped the topsails with rope yarns. The winds hauled to the SW and drew round to south; the topsails were lowered.
1802-02-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to NE by way of east; a little rain.

1802-02-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from ENE to NE. At 5 a.m. loosed the topsails and got under way on the starboard tack, the winds a light breeze from NNW to NE. Being under Van Diemen's Land we were taken aback and went onto the port tack; at 6.30 we let go the anchor.
1802-02-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the breeze from NE to NNW. At 5 a.m. we got under way on the starboard tack; being close in with Van Diemen's Land, we were taken aback and went onto the port tack. At 6.30, the commander having anchored, we did the same. The rigging was set up. The wind, a fresh breeze from NNW, hauled to N, NNW, NW, W and SW. At 6 a flat calm. At 6.15 the breeze got up from SE to SSE. The commander signalled us to get under way at once. At 7.15 we were under sail, shaping our course to leave the channel. At 8, after doubling Pointe de la Sortie, we anchored in 14 fathoms, the south end of Willaumez Island bearing east, Pointe de la Sortie S 22° W and Pointe Pierson S 50° W. Calm during the night.

1802-02-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from NNE, N, NNW, NW, W and SW. It fell calm; at 6 the breeze got up from SE to SSE. The commander made the signal to get under way; at 7 we were under sail and shaped our course to leave the channel. After doubling Pointe de la Sortie we let go the anchor; at 10.30, the breeze having settled in the SE, we got under way under our fore-and-aft sails; shortly afterwards we sheeted home the topsails and took in the courses, a fresh breeze from SE. At noon took the bearing of Pointe de la Sortie N 72° W; Pointe de la Direction N 4° 30' E; and Cape Trobriand S 1° E.
1802-02-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to south. At 9.15 a.m. we got under way and beat between Bruny Island and the northern peninsula to weather the Tasman Peninsula and reach Maria Island. At noon Pointe de la Sortie N 72° W, Pointe de la Direction N 5° E, Cape Trobriand S 1° E. At 4, Pointe de la Sortie N 73° W, Pointe de la Direction N 59° W, Cape Trobriand S 9° W, Cape Cannelé S 6° W. At 11.30 a flat calm.

1802-02-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea. During the night sounded every half hour and found from 28 to 40 fathoms. We rigged the topgallant masts after cutting off their poles. A fresh breeze from SE, south and SSW.
1802-02-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N, SW, S, SSE. At midnight the course was given S 45° E. Cape Trobriand then bore from us S 34° W, 3 miles off. At 4 it bore S 68° W; the wind having headed us, we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 8 the course was given S 78° 45' E. Cape Raoul bore from us N 8° E, Cape Pillar N 58° E and Little Tasman Island N 70° E. We bore up by degrees to N 11° 15' W. At 10.15 doubled Tasman Island. At 11.15 doubled the great Hippolyte Rock. At noon, in 43° 8' 30" of latitude observed, it bore from us S 8° W. The topgallant masts were rigged, their poles having been cut off, and the topgallant sails bent. At 3.30 we ran into the channel separating Maria Island from Van Diemen's Land. At 4.15 anchored near the Géographe in 10 fathoms, fine grey sand, an islet in the channel bearing N 19° W, the northernmost point of Van Diemen's Land in sight N 6° W, the northernmost point of Maria Island in sight N 4° E, the SW point of the same island S 29° E, the southernmost cape of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 9° E, Cape Frederick Hendrik S 3° E, Cape des Sarcelles S 45° W. During the night the wind a strong breeze from E to NNE. A little fish was taken.

1802-02-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 3 we ran into the channel that separates Van Diemen's Land from Maria Island; at 4.15 we anchored in 10 fathoms, fine grey sand, and veered 50 fathoms of cable. Bearings of the anchorage: the westernmost visible end of Maria Island N 4° E; Cape Frederick Hendrik S 3° E; the south end of the same island S 29° E; Cape des Sarcelles S 45° W; the southernmost visible cape of the Tasman Peninsula S 9° E.
1802-02-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NNW. At 3.30 the large boat, provisioned for 10 days, was sent off under the orders of Citizen Faure to survey the Schouten Islands. At 6 the captain left for Frederick Hendrik Bay. I landed on Maria Island abreast of the anchorage with our botanist and the second surgeon, and, shooting as we went, reached the head of Oyster Bay. I looked there for the watering place marked on Cox's chart and found none; I saw only a pool of brackish water and the bed of a stream where there might be fresh water in the rainy season. At spring tides the sea rose into the pool, for there was a channel traced in the sand and marine plants round its edges. In the evening, coming back, we found a grave near a hut of the Aboriginal people; we turned over the earth and our surgeon recognised among the ashes and charcoal human bones that were partly burnt. The grave was covered with grass and small pieces of bark held down by two spears whose ends were driven into the ground, the whole covered with large sheets of bark that we had difficulty in moving. We put everything back as we had found it and came back aboard. In our walk we saw no Aboriginal people; we found several huts, in one of which they had slept not long before, for the grass was still fresh and there were crayfish shells recently grilled. We found fresh water in several holes. At 5 p.m. the weather turned overcast and it freshened. The topgallant masts were struck and a light shown at the gaff for the captain's boat. At 11 the wind drew round to SE, a strong breeze.

1802-02-20.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the wind light from NNW. At 5 the weather turned overcast and it freshened from the north; veered 30 fathoms of cable and struck the topgallant masts. The dinghy went fishing; the longboat was sent off with 3 days' provisions under the orders of Citizen Freycinet. From the 1st to the 2nd [Ventôse, Year 10, 20-21 February 1802]. Overcast and misty weather, the wind ESE, a fresh breeze. The dinghy came back from the fishing with a great many fish and crayfish. At 6 a.m. the commander cockbilled his yards and put his pendant and his ensign at half mast on account of the death of the zoologist Maugé; we did the same. At 9 the body of the deceased was carried ashore and buried; all the officers of both ships attended his funeral.
1802-02-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to ESE. At 1 a.m. the captain came in in his boat. At 10 a.m., on the commander's signal, the longboat was put in the water. At 11 she was sent off under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to survey the coast from Cape des Sarcelles to the northernmost point in sight from the anchorage. Many crayfish were taken and a meal of them distributed to the crew. At 2 the carpenters went to Maria Island to cut wood and brought back several pieces.

1802-02-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from NE to SE. The dinghy carried the sick ashore. At 3 squared our yards, following the commander's example. The dinghy came back from the fishing and brought a great quantity of crayfish.
1802-02-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SSW to SE and to N. Many crayfish were taken and given to the crew. At 5 p.m. Citizen Freycinet came in with the longboat; as she was making a great deal of water she was hoisted in at once to be repaired. Light rain during the night.

1802-02-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SE to N. At 5 the longboat came in from her expedition; she had surveyed from Cape des Sarcelles as far as the northernmost point of the Van Diemen's Land anchorage. She was making a great deal of water; she was hoisted in and put on the gratings to be repaired.
1802-02-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, a flat calm and continual rain. The dinghy went to Oyster Bay for oysters and brought back a full load.

1802-02-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm, continual rain. The dinghy came in loaded with oysters. At 7.45, having dragged in a squall, we veered 80 fathoms of cable.
1802-02-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW to NNE. At 5 the dinghy left for Oyster Bay. At 7 the wind a strong breeze from SSE. At 7.45 we dragged and veered cable. At noon the wind blowing hard from SSW, a high sea. At nightfall the wind and sea went down a great deal. A light was kept at the gaff on account of the dinghy.

1802-02-25.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea, the wind blowing hard from WSW. At sunset the wind and sea went down a great deal. Kept a light at the gaff all night to show our position to the dinghy. At 6.30 a.m. the captain embarked in his boat to go and meet her. At 10.30 a.m. the dinghy came in loaded with oysters.
1802-02-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a flat calm. At 10.30 the dinghy came back loaded with oysters. The breeze from N to NNW.

1802-02-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to NNW. At 2 furled all sail. The dinghy went fishing. In the forenoon weighed the port anchor to inspect it; as soon as it was up we let it go again in 13 fathoms, fine sand. Obs. lat. taken ashore while at anchor 42° 42' 10"; long. 145° 54' 0".
1802-02-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNW. The anchor was weighed and another let go in 13 fathoms, fine sand. The sick went ashore. At 11.30 Citizen Faure came in in the large boat. He had examined the supposed Schouten Islands and found only one and several small islets; what was taken for the Schouten Islands is only a very high peninsula joined to the land by a very low neck. The masts were swayed up and the topgallant sails bent. On the commander's signal the large boat was hoisted in. At nightfall the sick came back aboard. During the night the breeze from SW. Latitude of the anchorage 42° 38' 30"; longitude 145° 17' 17"; variation on Maria Island 11° 37' 0" NE.

1802-02-27.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NNW. Swayed up the topgallant masts and squared the yards. On the commander's signal, hoisted in the large boat. At 9 got under way, a light breeze from NNE, standing SSE to weather the rocks off the SW point of Maria Island; at 10.30 went onto the port tack. Bearings taken at noon: the easternmost visible point of Maria Island N 38° E; an islet taken from the anchorage N 20° W; Cape Frederick Hendrik S 6° W; the southernmost visible cape of the Tasman Peninsula S 6° E. Obs. lat. at noon 42° 44' 4" south.
1802-02-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a breeze from SSW which hauled to south and east and settled at NNE. At 9 got under way and shaped our course S 22° 30' E to double the SW point of Maria Island. At 10.30 the air drew round to SSE; we were taken aback and lay close-hauled on the port tack, standing for Cape des Sarcelles. The breeze freshened, drawing aft as far as north. At noon, being in 42° 44' 4" of latitude, we took the bearing of the northernmost point of Maria Island in sight N 38° E, the islet in the channel N 20° W, Cape Frederick Hendrik S 6° W, and the southernmost cape of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 6° E. At 4, Schouten Island N 6° W, Maria Island from N 27° W to N 61° W, Tasman Island S 20° W. At 6, the NE point of Maria Island N 45° W, Tasman Island S 43°, Cape Pillar S 47° W. At 10, not seeing the Géographe, we showed a light at the foremast head; it stayed there until 11.45 without her answering.

1802-02-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NNE to N and NW. Took the bearing of the middle of Schouten Island N 6° W; the visible north part of Maria Island N 27° W; the south point of the same island N 61° W; Little Tasman Island S 20° E. At 9 p.m. sounded without finding bottom at 80 fathoms.
1802-02-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from N to NW. At midnight the Géographe was sighted. At noon in 42° 59' 50" of latitude observed and in 146° 33' 0" of longitude by the watches. Took the bearing of the NE point of Maria Island N 41° W and Tasman Island S 47° W. At 5.15, 10° 58' 40" of NE variation; at 6.30, 11° 19' 10" the same. Fine rain and thick mist during the night.

1802-03-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from north. At 10.30 p.m. we lost sight of the commander; kept a light all night. At 1.45 a.m. we sighted him ahead and at very little distance; crowded sail to close him. At 8 went onto the starboard tack.
1802-03-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Misty and rainy weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW and NNE. At noon in 42° 39' 38" of latitude observed and in 147° 49' 54" of longitude by account. At 5, 10° 11' 0" of NE variation.

1802-03-02.journal_anonyme: Misty and rainy weather, a fresh breeze from north. At 8.15, after missing stays twice, wore onto the port tack. At 6.30 a.m. went onto the starboard tack.
1802-03-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Very misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to NNE. At noon in 42° 17' 41" of latitude observed and in 147° 36' 30" of longitude by account. In the afternoon the bell was rung every quarter of an hour and swivel guns fired. The 12th [Ventôse, 3 March 1802]. Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNW to NNE. At 8.15, 9° 28' 0" of NE variation. At noon in 41° 50' 20" of latitude observed and in 147° 33' 0" of longitude by account. At 2 a flat calm; at 3.15 the breeze got up from the SE. We lay under topsails with the yards square, making short boards to starboard and port to wait for the commander, who had signalled no course. At 7.15, being within hail, he ordered us to lie close-hauled on the starboard tack under topsails until midnight; from midnight to 4 to steer S 22° 30' W; and that then, if the weather allowed, we should bear away west to close the land. Should he lie to, he was to warn us by a swivel gun. From 8 until midnight the commander showed us a light every half hour.

1802-03-03.journal_anonyme: A light breeze from north. A smooth sea, a very thick fog; rang the bell to make ourselves heard by the commander. At 6.30 changed tacks on the commander's signal.

1802-03-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 4 went onto the starboard tack to close the commander; he ordered us to keep close-hauled on the starboard tack until midnight, and from midnight to 4 to steer SSW. Overcast weather during the night and the wind a strong breeze in puffs. At 6.30 we lost sight of the commander.
1802-03-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, a light breeze from ESE to SSE. At midnight went onto the port tack, the course S 22° 30' W. The commander, on the same tack, then bore from us N 11° W; at 12.15 we lost sight of him to the north. We sent up several rockets without his answering. At 4 shaped the course west. At 6.15 the Géographe was sighted in the S 45° E, and at 6.30 further south. We then shaped the course S 22° 30' W; having lost sight of her again, we resumed the course west. The mist very thick; we fired several swivel guns without answer. At noon in 41° 29' 52" of latitude observed and in 147° 11' 0" of longitude by account. At 3, in a clear interval, we saw an eclipse of the sun for about 2 minutes. At 6.15 we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack under topsails. The wind a strong breeze during the night.

1802-03-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, almost calm from the SSW. At 1 the breeze got up from the ESE and freshened steadily. At 6 sighted the land in the west, and at 6.30 sighted the commander in the ENE. We fired three swivel guns to make ourselves seen.
1802-03-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE to E. At 2 went onto the port tack, the course S 67° 30' W. At daybreak crowded sail and shaped the course N 56° 15' W. At 6 land was sighted to the west, and at 6.30 the Géographe in the ENE; we fired swivel guns so that she might see us. At noon in 41° 31' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 43' of longitude by account. The land in sight from S 4° W to N 33° W. At 7 a flat calm; the Géographe, out of sight, did not answer the lights we showed.

1802-03-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from ESE to east and NE. At 4 took the bearing of the southernmost visible end S 8° E; the northernmost visible end N 16° W. At 4 went about onto the starboard tack. At 9 a.m. we came up with the commander, who told us he was going to send a boat to the coast; he ordered us to keep close-hauled. At 10.15 the commander hove to and put his boat in the water. We then lay close-hauled on the port tack.
1802-03-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to N. At 3.30 the commander was sighted in the S by SE. At 5, 7° 10' 42" of NE variation; at 8, 7° 35' 0" the same. At 9.45 we spoke the commander; he told us he was going to send his large boat to the coast and that meanwhile we should stand off and on. At noon in 42° 10' 9" of latitude observed and in 146° 49' 36" of longitude by account. The north end of Maria Island S 20° W, the north end of Schouten Island S 38° W, the Schouten isthmus S 81° W. At 5 p.m., in going about, when the after sails were shifted, the main topgallant brace not having been let go, the yard broke in the middle. At 8 the Géographe showed a light at her masthead; she then bore from us N 56° E on the port bow. At 8.15 she sent up a rocket; we were to windward of her and very close; she still had her light and was lying to. We bore away before the wind and hauled to the wind to leeward of her under all sail. She was ordering us to repeat the signals she would make for her boat, which had not yet returned. As we ran alongside her — fortunately she got off with her spritsail yard and we with our crossjack yard, both of which broke. At 11 our damage was repaired. We sent up rockets and fired a swivel gun to imitate the commander, whom we lost sight of at 10 in the S 56° W.

1802-03-07.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze, the sea smooth, keeping the same tack as the commander. At 8.15 he sent up a rocket; we were ahead of him. He was then lying to; we bore away to pass under his lee. The commander ordered us to repeat what they should do at the same instant; his spritsail yard fouled our main shrouds, and his jib boom caught our crossjack yard and broke it. We set about repairing the damage.
1802-03-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a pleasant breeze from NNW to NNE. At daybreak the commander was sighted. At 8 the Schouten isthmus S 64° W. At noon in 42° 3' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 34' 42" of longitude by account. At 5.30 the commander fired several guns; he then bore from us N 40° W at a great distance. At 5.45 the Schouten isthmus S 57° W and Maria Island S 24°. At 7 a flat calm, the weather overcast in the S 45° E with the look of wind. At 8 it blew hard from the SE; shaped our course north. At 10 lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, the wind blowing hard with a high sea. During the night we fired a swivel gun and sent up a rocket every half hour.

1802-03-08.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from N to W and SW. Changed tacks several times. At 9.15 fired a swivel gun to make ourselves seen by the commander. At 5 the land in the west; at 7 p.m. the commander was not to be seen. Took the bearing of the southern end of Van Diemen's Land S 5° E; Eddystone Rock W; the northern end of Van Diemen's Land N 28° W; the southernmost of the Furneaux Islands N 11° E.
1802-03-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to W by way of S, E and N. At midnight shaped the course north. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze. We had no sight of the Géographe. At 8.45, 7° 46' 30" of NE variation, shaping our course for Banks Strait and running along the coast. At noon in 41° 11' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 29' 6" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands N 11° W, Eddystone Rock west, and Van Diemen's Land from S 5° E to N 28° W. At 3.45 a ship was sighted in the S 68° E which was thought to be the Géographe. We bore away for her and were not long in making her out to be an English schooner lying to. At 6.15 we hove to to windward of her and showed our colours; she at once filled and crowded sail. We did the same and steered for her. Having soon come up with her, we hailed her that we were a ship of discovery and a friend. She then hove to again, and so did we. I went aboard her with Citizen Milius and we came back aboard at 7.30. We filled and stood on and the schooner held her course. She was the Endeavour of Port Jackson, from which she had sailed 18 days before, bound for Maria Island to fish and to hunt seals and kangaroos. She was manned with 14 men and a boy. The wind a strong breeze during the night.

1802-03-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, the wind a fresh breeze from N to W and SW. At noon fired a swivel gun to make ourselves seen by the Géographe, which was thought to be in sight to the south. At 3.45 we sighted a ship in the ESE which we took for the Géographe; we bore away for her and were not long in recognising her for a schooner. We hoisted our colours and Citizen Milius went aboard; she was the Endeavour of Port Jackson, from which she had sailed 18 days before; she was fur sealing.
1802-03-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SW. At noon in 40° 22' 39" of latitude observed and in 146° 43' 54" of longitude by account, the Furneaux Islands bearing from N 68° W to S 68° W. At 4.30 the wind shifted from W to SE and veered to ESE and SSW; the sea driven from the west and breaking against the SE wind made us appear ringed with breakers. At 5.45 we saw a waterspout. At 6 the Furneaux Islands bore from N 33° W to N 66° W, and Van Diemen's Land from S 22° W to S 66° W.

1802-03-10.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW, south and SE. At 4 took the bearing of the northern end of the Furneaux Islands N 40° W, the southern end N 55° W. At 4.30 the winds having shifted to SE we went onto the port tack. At 8 a.m. took the bearing of the southern end of Van Diemen's Land S 15° E; the northern end N 70° [illegible]; the southern end of the Furneaux Islands N 18° W, the northern end N 14° E. At 9 we sighted a ship at anchor between Swan Island and the land of the Furneaux Islands. At 10 hove to and put the large boat in the water to go aboard the ship sighted.
1802-03-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to NE. At 8 took the bearing of Van Diemen's Land from S 15° E to N 76° W, Swan Island N 56° W, and the Furneaux Islands from N 18° W to N 14° E, manoeuvring to run into Banks Strait. A ship was sighted at anchor under Swan Island; shortly afterwards we made her out to be an English brig. The large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Milius to go aboard her. At noon in 40° 44' 58" of latitude observed and in 146° 14' 12" of longitude, the north point of Swan Island bearing N 75° W. At 12.15 a boat we had taken for the brig's came aboard. What was our astonishment! It was the Géographe's large boat, which she had put in the water on the 15th [Ventôse, 6 March 1802] at 10.15 a.m. abreast of the Schouten Peninsula. This boat had tried to come back aboard the Géographe on the evening of the 15th, but seeing us standing out to sea and having lost sight of us at nightfall, she had made for the land and run along it as far as Swan Island, where very fortunately she had found the English brig, who gave them provisions of which they were short. Citizen Maurouard, midshipman commanding the boat, had at once made for Banks Strait, knowing that the ships were to pass that way. At 1.45 we anchored in 19 fathoms, muddy sand, the north point of Swan Island bearing S 61° E, the SW point of the same island (past Hunting Islet) S 35° E, the westernmost end of Van Diemen's Land in sight S 48° W, the west end of the Furneaux Islands (an islet) N 38° W, their east end N 27° W. At 3.30 Citizen Milius came back from the brig, which was the Harrington, Captain Campbell, of Port Jackson, bound on a sealing and fishing voyage. At 7.30 the Harrington passed alongside; Captain Campbell promised ours to come and dine with him the next day.

1802-03-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm, a light air from NE to NNE. At 12.15 the boat we had taken for the brig's boat came aboard; it was the Géographe's large boat, which she had put in the water on the 15th at 10.30 a.m. This boat had tried to close us, but seeing us standing out to sea and having lost sight of us at nightfall, she had made for the land. They had run along it as far as Swan Island, where they found the English brig, who gave them the provisions they lacked. At 10.45 anchored in 19 fathoms, muddy sand, and veered 150 fathoms of cable. Bearings: the northern end of Swan Island S 61° E; its SW end (past a hunting islet) S 35° E; the westernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 48° W; the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 38° W; their eastern end N 27° W. At 3 Mr Milius was back in the large boat; she was the Harrington of Port Jackson, Captain Campbell.
1802-03-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNE to NNW. At daybreak the large boat was sent off to Point Portland under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, who was to make observations there. At 8 the brig Harrington, which lay anchored 2 miles west of us, got under way and shaped her course S 67° 30' W. At 7 p.m. the large boat came in from Point Portland.

1802-03-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from NNW and NNE. Began painting the ship's outside. The large boat came back from Cape Portland. The Géographe's boat was put in the water to go and survey from Eddystone Rock as far as Swan Island.
1802-03-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to WNW. At 8 a.m. the Géographe's boat was sent off with Citizens Maurouard and Boulanger to survey the coast from Eddystone Rock to Swan Island; she had 5 days' provisions. The dinghy went fishing to the Furneaux Islands. The corvette was painted. At 9 Citizen Saint-Cricq went to make observations on Swan Island; I landed there with my gun, as did several officers and naturalists. We sent the boat back, and she carried Citizen Milius to Hunting Islet. At nightfall she came to fetch us from Swan Island and took us to the islet; we killed a seal there, which we left. We loaded the boat with geese, penguins and other birds that we took in burrows under the grass; we came back aboard at 2 a.m. (on the 22nd [Ventôse, 13 March 1802]).

1802-03-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from NW to WNW. At 6 the large boat was back from Swan Island; we went on painting the ship's outside. At 2 everyone came in in the large boat with a very good bag. At 4.45 slack water; at 5.15 the ebb, and at 11.30 the flood.
1802-03-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a flat calm. The dinghy came in from the Furneaux Islands with a little fish and loaded with young seals. I was put ashore on Hunting Islet with three men and two days' provisions to kill seals; I had my gun and was well supplied with powder and shot. It was a pleasure party for me. At 8.30 p.m. the large boat was sent off to Port Kent (in the Furneaux Islands) with Citizen Faure, surveyor, and several naturalists. Latitude observed at the anchorage 40° 38' 50"; longitude 145° 51' 0". NE variation on the 19th [Ventôse, 10 March 1802] at 4.15 p.m., 10° 6' 0"; on the 20th [Ventôse, 11 March 1802] at 8.45 a.m., 9° 12' 0"; the same day at 5.30 p.m., 10° 4' 30"; at 6.30 p.m., 10° 35' 0"; on the 22nd [Ventôse, 13 March 1802] at 8.30 a.m., 9° 23' 20". The flood sets west and the ebb east. The greatest rate of the current is 2.8 knots. Citizen Milius proposed that I should go to Hunting Islet to kill seals. I accepted with pleasure, took 3 men with me and 2 days' provisions, and had myself landed on the west side of the islet. The weather was superb and I promised myself much amusement from the trip.

1802-03-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a flat calm. The dinghy came back from the fishing with few fish. The large boat landed Citizen Breton with three men. At 8.30 she left for Port King in the Furneaux Islands with Mr Faure, the surveyor, and Bailly, the mineralogist.
1802-03-14.journal_breton_naturaliste:
At 1 a.m. the wind blew a strong breeze from ESE. The topgallant masts were struck; the weather overcast at noon. The cable, having to bear the force of the wind and the flood tide, chafed badly; at 3.30 it parted. Another anchor was let go at once and the parted cable hauled in. We dragged until 5, when the cable held. The wind blowing hard in gusts; at 6.15 the cable parted. We at once lay to under the fore staysail, the storm staysail, the mizzen and its staysail, and hauled in the parted cable. At 9 took the bearing of a fire in the S 22° 30' E. During the night squally weather, with thunder, lightning and pouring rain.

At daybreak, each of us having armed himself with a handspike, we went hunting. We killed several enormous seals which we found asleep on the grass. We skinned them for the hides and took only the livers and kidneys, which we ate and which I found excellent. In the forenoon we took birds in their burrows, and this, with the kidneys, gave us a passable dinner. The weather had turned overcast and seemed likely to grow bad; the sea broke terribly on the east side of the islet. In landing I had taken the ship's bearing past a point at noon; I saw her much further west. I supposed she had dragged; shortly afterwards the mist hid her and I saw her no more. The wind blew hard from the east. At the close of day, being at the south part of the islet, I saw a boat doubling the south point of Swan Island and landing on its SW side; I had no doubt it was the Géographe's boat, which had left the ship on the 21st to survey from Eddystone to Swan Island. The night was horrible, with pouring rain and thunder, the sky on fire; and having no shelter we were soaked through. The bad weather, with the anxiety our situation caused me, made me pass a dreadful night.

1802-03-15.journal_anonyme: Cloudy weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from east to ESE, a swell running. The cable chafing extremely, at 3.45 it parted; the starboard cable was at once bent round the mast and at 4 the anchor was let go. We had doubled the turn round the bitts and clapped on breaking stoppers at intervals. The turns came off the bitts and the cable ran out to the end with 4 or 5 fathoms lashed to it; we let go the bend at the foot of the mast and took a turn round the bitts, having first bent a spare brace to serve as a buoy rope on the buoy. We hauled in the port cable, which had parted near the bend; we dragged until 5, when the cable [one word illegible] end on, the wind still blowing hard. At 6.15 the starboard cable parted and we lay to on the starboard tack.
1802-03-15.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard, a high sea. At 6 a.m. the Furneaux Islands were sighted in the N 45° E. A cable and an iron chain were bent to the mooring anchor. At noon in 40° 27' 26" of latitude by account and in 145° 29' 0" of longitude by account. At 2 land was sighted in the N 22° 30' E. At 6 rain, mist and thunder; the wind fell a little and the sea went down a great deal. We sounded exactly every half hour and found from 21 to 39 fathoms, coral bottom.

At daybreak we went hunting again and killed several more seals, which did us good, for we had no provisions left. I had the meat taken and smoked, not knowing to what we might be reduced. The rain was useful to us: every hollow in the rocks was filled with water, which I found drinkable. I had a breaker I had with me filled, and several bottles that had held brandy and vinegar, and urged my three men not to touch them but to go and drink from the hollows as I did. In a clear interval I saw the Furneaux Islands and did not see the ship. I no longer doubted that the bad weather had forced her to get under way. I went at once to the south part of the islet, and having seen the boat in the same place as the day before, I put my handkerchief on the end of an English oar (a) that was on the beach and planted it in the rocks. Shortly afterwards I saw several people run from the boat behind some rocks, almost certain that my signal had been seen. I left it there and went to reassure my men. About 4 o'clock Citizens Maurouard and Boulanger came in the Géographe's boat to fetch us and took us to Swan Island. We shared the little provisions they had left; they had dug a well which gave us very good water; I had my gun, which gave us game. There was a great quantity of geese, which were our chief food while we waited for the Naturaliste.

On the morning of the 26th [Ventôse, 17 March 1802] a boat was seen coming from the Furneaux Islands and standing for Hunting Islet; we made her a signal with a handkerchief and a musket shot, and she came and joined us. It was our large boat, which had left the ship on the evening of the 22nd for Port King, where she had ridden out the bad weather. Captain Hamelin had told midshipman Brèvedent that should he not find the ship at the same anchorage, he was to come and fetch me from Hunting Islet and then make for Waterhouse, where we should wait for him, or he for us. Accordingly we left Swan Island, 25 people in the two boats, and shaped our course for Waterhouse, where we arrived at nightfall and slept.

1802-03-16.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard [illegible] from the ESE [illegible], a high sea. At 2 sighted the land in the N 22° 30' E; at [illegible] the wind fell away. Rain, mist and thunder; the weather having turned [illegible] we set our courses. On the [illegible] tack.
1802-03-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: At 2.30 a.m. we had a heavy squall, after which the wind fell away by degrees. At daybreak fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE; land was sighted to windward and the topgallant masts swayed up. At 9 filled and stood on. At noon the land from S 22° W to S 45° E, being in 40° 40' 22" of latitude observed and in 145° 0' 30" of longitude by account. At 4, Flat Island S 55° E. At 5 the weather turned overcast and it freshened; during the night the wind a strong breeze.

1802-03-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a fresh breeze from east to ESE. [Illegible.] At 2.30 went about; took the bearing then of the westernmost visible end of the land S 35° W; the easternmost visible end S 68° E; Flat Island S 79° E.
1802-03-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ESE to ENE. At 10.30 the Furneaux Islands were sighted N 50° E. At noon in 40° 41' 40" of latitude observed and in 145° 28' 6" of longitude by account, the Furneaux Islands bearing from us N 60° E, Rocky Islet S 10° E, the land from S 7° W to S 65° E.

1802-03-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from east. At 6.30 took the bearing of Waterhouse Island from S 4° E to S 30° E. At 7 we [illegible] the large boat, which was standing towards us; at 7.15 went about and bore down on her; at 7.45 hove to with the lee side to the wind. At 8 the large boat came in with everyone aboard.
1802-03-18.journal_breton_naturaliste:
Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to SE. At 6.30, Waterhouse from S 4° E to S 30° E. At 7.15, standing on the north board, a boat was seen making for the ship; we at once went about and bore up for her. At 7.45 we hove to to wait for her. At 8 I came aboard in our large boat with Citizen Leschenault, midshipman Brèvedent in charge of the party, and 2 of the boat's crew. The Géographe's boat and a large part of our people had stayed at Waterhouse, thinking the ship was going to anchor there. The boat was hoisted in at once and we put the ensign at half mast and fired a swivel gun to call the Géographe's boat. At 8 Waterhouse bore from us S 16° E to S 44° E. At 9 filled and stood on. At 9.30 hove to; the Géographe's boat came in, having again left several people behind — among others Bailly the mineralogist, who wanted to stay at Waterhouse because, he said, the ship was to anchor there. The captain sent the boat off at once to bring back the rest of the people, sending word to the obstinate mineralogist that if he did not come back at once he would leave him ashore. Filled and stood on. At noon in 40° 48' 30" of latitude observed and in 145° 52' 48" of longitude by account. At 2.15 hove to; the boat came back with the rest of the people and was hoisted in at once. At 3 filled and stood on. At 4, Waterhouse from S 2° E to S 14° E. During the night squally weather with light rain, the wind a strong breeze, with lightning.

At daybreak the Naturaliste was seen standing for the island. I proposed going aboard at once, but everyone said she was going to come to the anchorage and that we must wait for her. At 6 she took the north board. I embarked in our boat with 4 men and reached the ship at 8.

1802-03-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to [illegible]. At noon took the bearing of the northern end of Swan Island S 62° E; its southern end S 49° E; the easternmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 46° E; the westernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land S 45° W; the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 20° W.
1802-03-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NW to south. At 10.30, being roughly at the place where the two anchors had been lost, we hove to and filled several times to try to make out their buoys. At noon took the bearing of the west end of the Furneaux Islands (an islet) N 20° W, their east end N 54° E, the north end of Swan Island S 62° E and its south-west end S 49° E. (a) This oar was found by us when we landed on the islet for the first time (on the 21st [Ventôse, 12 March 1802]); it had been picked up to be carried aboard and was fortunately forgotten, for there was not a piece of wood on the islet but what the sea brought. At 2, having been unable to make out our buoys, the captain decided to go and look for the Géographe to the south; we made sail to leave the strait. At 4 Swan Island bore from us N 57° W to N 61° W. There was an eclipse of the moon of nearly 5 digits; it ended about 10.30. During the night overcast weather, with rain.

1802-03-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, lying to on the starboard tack, a fresh breeze from W to south and SE. At 2 we were at the place where we had lost our two anchors; we hoped to make out the buoys, and not seeing them we bore away to go in search of the Géographe. There was an eclipse of the moon of nearly five digits; it ended at 10.30.
1802-03-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSE to W by way of NE. At noon in 41° 29' 33" of latitude observed and in 146° 37' 30" of longitude by account. Van Diemen's Land still in sight. At 10.30 the weather turned overcast. At midnight hove to. During the night we burnt priming and sent up a rocket every half hour.

1802-03-21.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, the wind a light breeze from NE to W and NW. The sea smooth. At 4 the land in sight from N 24° W to S 5° E. We hove to during the night. At 8 a.m. took the bearing of Maria Island from S 54° W to S 41° W; the northernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 25° W; the south end of Schouten Island N 64° W. At noon took the bearing of the south end of Schouten Island N 68° W, 8 miles off.
1802-03-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from N to WNW, a high sea. At 5 lay to. At 8 Maria Island from S 41° W to S 54° W and the south end of Schouten Island N 64° W. At noon in 42° 18' 45" of latitude by account and in 146° 33' 18" of longitude by account.

1802-03-22.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze in gusts from NW to W and SW. A high sea; the middle of Schouten Island bore from us N 84° W. At 10 blowing hard in gusts, a very high sea, the weather overcast.
1802-03-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from W to SW, a high sea and rain. At 8 the land in sight from S 45° W to S 68° W, 30 miles off. At noon in 41° 51' 0" of latitude observed and in 147° 15' 24" of longitude by account.

1802-03-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze W to SW in gusts, light rain at intervals. At 7.15 a.m. went about.
1802-03-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind blowing hard from SSW to WNW in gusts, a high sea and rain. At noon in 42° 1' 3" of latitude observed and in 148° 3' 34" of longitude by account. The weather cleared and the wind and sea went down. At 1.30 we filled and stood on under courses. At 4 fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze.

1802-03-24.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, blowing hard from SW. At 1 the wind and sea went down; our main topsail having split, a new one was bent. About 8 p.m. the winds drew round to NW and freshened.
1802-03-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind freshening and blowing strong in gusts at 3 a.m. from NNW to WSW. At noon in 42° 14' 26" of latitude observed and in 147° 7' 0" of longitude by account. At 1.45 land was sighted to the west; at 6 Maria Island bore from us from S 58° W to S 65° W and the south end of Schouten Island S 88° W.

1802-03-25.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, blowing hard from NW to W and SW in heavy gusts, a high sea. At 1 the land sighted in the west stretched from N 45° W to S 55° W. Saw a fire on Schouten Island. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from S 58° W to S 65° W; the northernmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 45° W.
1802-03-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to SSW. At 4 a.m. Maria Island bore from us S 75° W. At 8, Schouten Island from N 87° W to S 86° W and Maria Island from S 60° W to S 49° W. At noon in 42° 31' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 55' 13" of longitude by account. At 6, Maria Island from S 56° W to S 61° W and the islet south of Schouten Island N 89° W. During the night squally weather, with rain.

1802-03-26.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a strong breeze from SW. A high sea; during the night overcast and squally weather and we reefed the topsails several times. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from S 78° W to W; Schouten Island from N 67° W to N 64° W.
1802-03-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SW to SSE, with light rain at intervals. At 10.30, 9° 50' of NW variation. At noon in 42° 39' 2" of latitude observed and in 147° 9' 25" of longitude by the watches; by account 146° 58' 24" of longitude. At 6, Schouten Island from N 37° W to N 41° W and the NE end of Maria Island N 78° W. At 11 calm, the weather overcast.

1802-03-27.journal_anonyme: Weather fine enough, a swell running, a light breeze from SSW to south, with light rain at intervals. About 3 a.m. the winds hauled to the east and freshened. In the forenoon saw whales. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island from N 73° W to N 80° W; Schouten Island from N 26° W to N 39° W; Tasman Island S 30° W.
1802-03-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to NE. At noon in 42° 45' 34" of latitude observed and in 146° 39' 7" of longitude by account, Schouten Island bearing from us N 26° W to N 39° W, Maria Island from N 73° W to N 80° W and Tasman Island S 30° W. Saw a whale. At 6 took the bearing of the high land (the supposed Schouten Islands) forming Schouten Island and the Schouten Peninsula, from N 18° W to N 38°; Maria Island from N 73° W to S 80° W; and the southernmost end of the Tasman Peninsula in sight S 30° W.

1802-03-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from N and NE, the sea smooth. At 6.30 a.m. the winds drew round to NW. Having been taken aback, we boxed her round. At noon took the bearing of the NE end of Maria Island N 46° W.
1802-03-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from N to SSE by way of west. At 8 Tasman Island bore from us S 30° W and the NE end of Maria Island N 65° W. At noon in 42° 55' 8" of latitude observed and in 146° 38' 25" of longitude by account. The wind having drawn aft, we steered N 33° 45' W and N 11° 15' W. Saw many tuna and porpoises. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Pillar S 18° W, Maria Island from west to N 51° W. At 9.30 hove to abreast of Schouten Island. Light fine rain.

1802-03-29.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the wind a light breeze from SW, south and SSE. Saw a considerable quantity of tuna and porpoises. At 9.30 p.m. hove to under the main topsail. At midnight, being very near Schouten Island, we filled and stood on; at 1 hove to again until 5, when we filled and ran along the coast at a distance of 2 miles. It is clear and well wooded but offers no shelter from the winds off the sea. At noon took the bearing of the middle of a low stretch of land having the look of an island S 19° W; the land from S 10° E to N 19° W.
1802-03-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to SE. At midnight, being too near Schouten Island, we filled to draw off and hove to again at 1. We sent up a rocket every hour. At 5 filled and stood on, running along the coast at 2 miles' distance. It is clear and well wooded. At 8.45, 8° 31' of NE variation. At noon in 41° 44' 41" of latitude observed and in 146° 34' 49" of longitude by account. At 3 we were abreast of a small well-wooded island where the Géographe's boat had found shelter from the winds off the sea, and fresh water; it lies in 41° 21' 50" of latitude. It is the only place on the coast we have run along where a ship can shelter from the winds off the sea. According to Citizen Maurouard there is good anchorage between the land and the island, and it can be entered by either the north or the south passage. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the starboard tack.

1802-03-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to SSE and south. At 3 we took the bearing, to the west of us, of a small and fairly well wooded island where the Géographe's boat had found shelter from the winds off the sea, and fresh water; it lies in 41° 21' 51" of south latitude. It is the only place on the east coast of Van Diemen's Land where a ship can take refuge. It lies a short distance from the land, and one may run in by either the south or the north passage. At noon took the bearing of Van Diemen's Land from S 18° W to S 86° W; the Furneaux Islands from N 54° W to N 18° W.
1802-03-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from S to NW by way of east. At 2 a.m. hove to; at 5 filled and stood in to close the land. At 8.30, 9° 54' 30" of NE variation. At noon in 40° 49' 17" of latitude observed and in 146° 50' 25" of longitude by account, manoeuvring to run into Banks Strait. At 5.30 the air having come from the west, we steered offshore; shortly afterwards it came back to ESE. We hauled to the wind on the starboard tack. At 6 Swan Island S 81° W. At midnight calm; lay to.

1802-03-31.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the winds east, almost calm. At 1 a.m. hove to under the main topsail. At 3 filled and stood on, and at 4 hove to again in the same way. We got a kedge anchor ready to let go. At noon took the bearing of the middle of Swan Island S 75° W; the Furneaux Islands from N 65° W to north.
1802-03-31.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm with very variable light airs. At 5 filled and stood west with a light breeze from SE. At 8 the north point of Swan Island bore from us S 69° W. At 9.30, 10° 6' 40" of NE variation. At noon in 40° 41' 26" of latitude observed and in 146° 41' 31" of longitude by account, Swan Island (its middle) bearing from us S 75° W. At 2.30, the breeze from the west, we made several boards until 6.30, when we fell into a flat calm. At 7.15 we let go a kedge anchor in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom. Bearings of the anchorage taken at daybreak: Swan Island (its middle) S 19° E, and the Furneaux Islands from N 42° E to N 28° W.

1802-04-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from NW to west. A calm coming on, at 7.15 we let go the kedge anchor in 19 fathoms, gravel bottom, and veered 50 fathoms of hawser. At 6.30 a.m. got under way under topsails and made all sail. At noon took the bearing of the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 5° W; the eastern end N 50° E; the north end of Swan Island N 88° E; Waterhouse Island from S 48° W to S 59° W.
1802-04-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSE to ENE. At 6.30 a.m. got under way and shaped our course for Waterhouse. At 8, the Furneaux Islands from N 32° W to N 56° E, Swan Island from S 64° E to S 51° E and Cape Portland S 19° W. At 8.15, 9° 54' of NE variation. At noon in 40° 41' 42" of latitude observed and in 146° 15' 49" of longitude by account. The Furneaux Islands from N 5° W to N 50° E, the north end of Swan Island N 88° E, Waterhouse from S 48° W to S 59° W. At 1 both large boats were sent off under the orders of Citizens Heirisson and Maurouard to go round Waterhouse and look for any orders the commander might have left there. At 5.45 we let go a kedge anchor in 23 fathoms, grey sand and broken shell, the Furneaux Islands bearing from N 16° E to N 56° E, the easternmost end of Van Diemen's Land in sight N 78° E, the north point of Waterhouse S 87° E, its SW point S 23° E, Flat Island S 66° W.

1802-04-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east to ENE. Our large boat and the Géographe's boat were put in the water to go round Waterhouse and look for any instructions the commander might have left there. At 5.45 let go a kedge anchor in 20 fathoms, grey sand mixed with broken shell, and veered 60 fathoms of hawser. Bearings of the anchorage: the western end of the Furneaux Islands N 16° E; the eastern end N 56° E; the easternmost visible end of Van Diemen's Land N 78° E; the westernmost end S 52° W; the north end of Waterhouse S 87° E; the south end S 23° E; Flat Island S 66° E. At 10 a.m. both large boats came back without having found anything to show that the commander had been there.
1802-04-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a light breeze from NNE to SE. At 10 both boats came in from Waterhouse, where they had found nothing to show that the commander had been there. The sick were sent to Waterhouse; the seamen known as shooters were sent there to shoot for the crew. At half past noon the large boat was sent off under the orders of Citizen Freycinet to Port Dalrymple. Draught: aft 11 feet 8 inches, forward 11 feet 5 inches, difference 3 inches. At 11 p.m. the sick and the shooters came back aboard; the shooting was not as good as might have been expected.

1802-04-03.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze varying from NNE to ESE. Our large boat was sent off to Port Dalrymple.
1802-04-03.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and a light breeze from ESE to north. At 10.30 I went with Citizen Milius and several others to shoot on Van Diemen's Land. The dinghy, which had been fishing at Waterhouse, brought back a little fish. At nightfall a light was shown at the gaff and priming burnt every half hour.

1802-04-04.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze variable from east to north. We kept a light at the gaff until the arrival of our boat, which was back at 1 a.m.
1802-04-04.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to WNW. At 1.15 we came in from Van Diemen's Land, where we had spent the 13th [Germinal, 3 April 1802]. We saw many kangaroos there; we were able to fire at only one, which we missed. We found good water and a watering place on the shore where it would be very easy to water in fine weather, because the boat could come alongside the rocks and fill the casks with a hose. Geese and other birds were killed and distributed. Latitude observed at the anchorage 40° 45' 34"; longitude 145° 37' 00". NE variation on the 12th [Germinal, 2 April 1802] at 8.30 a.m., 9° 22' 00"; the same day at 4.30 p.m., 10° 08' 40"; at 5.45 p.m., 10° 12' 30"; on the 14th [Germinal, 4 April 1802] at 4 p.m., 10° 48' 20"; at 5.45 p.m., 10° 13' 30"; on the 15th [Germinal, 5 April 1802] at 6.15 a.m., 9° 30' 40". The tides were scarcely perceptible; the flood sets SW and the ebb NE. The greatest rate of the current was 1.0 knot.

1802-04-05.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from north to WNW. Calm for the rest of the day. At 7.30 the breeze got up from the ENE. We fired a gun to call the dinghy and hoisted our topsails; at 11 the dinghy being back, she was hoisted in.
1802-04-05.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from ENE to south. The boats were hoisted in. At 10.30 hoisted the topsails and fired a swivel gun to call the yawl, which was fishing; at noon she came in and was hoisted in. At 1.30 we got under way and shaped our course S 67° 30' W for Port Dalrymple, where we were to pick up our large boat. At 6 the middle of Waterhouse bore from us N 76° E, 5 miles off, and Flat Island S 66° W, 7 miles off. At 8 a flat calm. During the night overcast weather with continual light rain.

1802-04-06.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from ENE to ESE. At 1.30 got under way and made all sail, studdingsails to port. It fell calm all at once. At 6.30 took the bearing of the middle of Waterhouse Island N 76° E, about 5 miles off; Flat Island S 66° W, 7 miles off. The breeze having freshened, made all sail. At 2, being very close to Flat Island, within a mile, and unable to weather it, we wore ship and made sail to work to windward.
1802-04-06.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a light breeze and calm. At 8 a.m. Flat Island bore from us S 19° W, 4 miles off. At 11.30 the breeze allowed us to shape our course S 45° W. At noon in 40° 49' 34" of latitude by account and in 145° 15' 36" of longitude by account, Flat Island bearing from us S 81° E to S 88° E, 3 miles off. At 6 it bore N 56° E and Rocky Islet S 55° W.

1802-04-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light air from N to south by way of east. At 5 a light breeze got up from the WSW. We lay close-hauled on the port tack. During the night a fresh breeze from south to SSE and SE. At midnight hove to with the main topsail to the mast; at 2 filled and set the courses. At 9.30 a.m., being abreast of Port Dalrymple and seeing our boat, we clewed up our courses and fired a swivel gun. At 10 wore onto the starboard tack, lying to under the main topsail. The large boat came in and was hoisted in at once; at 11 filled and made all sail, studdingsails to starboard.
1802-04-07.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and misty weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to E. At 1, Rocky Islet S 11° E, 1 mile off. At 8 it bore from us S 85° E. At 9, being abreast of Port Dalrymple, we fired a swivel gun to call our boat, which was sighted at 9.30 under the land. At 10 hove to; she came in and was hoisted in. At 11 filled and stood on, the course north. At noon in 40° 56' 16" of latitude by account and in 144° 42' 6" of longitude by account. At 6 hove to with the port side to the wind.

1802-04-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, light rain, a fresh breeze from SE to east and ESE, freshening. At 7 sighted the land in the N 10° E. At noon took the bearing of island (A) S 66° E; a low island (G) N 70° E; another, a sugarloaf, N 58° E; (M) N 50° E; Wilson's Promontory N 35° E; a very conspicuous white rock, pierced in its western part, N 7° E. Wilson's Promontory, by Citizen Saint-Cricq's observations, lies in 39° 10' 54" of south latitude and 147° 37' 31" of east longitude. Islet A lies in 39° 26' 57" of latitude and 144° 52' of east longitude.
1802-04-08.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from ENE to SE. At 5 a.m. we filled and stood on, the course N 11° 15' W. At 7.15 a very high islet (A) was sighted in the N 10° E. At 10.25 it bore from us east (true); a neighbouring islet D N 86° E; another S 85° E (B). At noon in 39° 16' 28" of latitude observed and in 144° 32' 0" of longitude. Took the bearing of a very conspicuous white rock, pierced on its west side, N 7° E; Wilson's Promontory N 35° E; a rock M N 50° E; a very high islet P N 58° E; another, C, low, N 70° E; islet A S 66° E. From this bearing and that of 10.25, islet A lies in 39° 26' 57" of latitude and 144° 52' of longitude. At 12.45 we hove to and put the Géographe's boat in the water; she was provisioned for 15 days and left at 1.30 under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, accompanied by Citizen Boulanger, surveyor, to fix the promontory and survey the coast as far as Western Port. At 1.45 we filled and stood in for the promontory. At 3.15, being very near it, we bore away N 65° 15' W and ran along the islets at its end. At 4.30, 8° 45' 30" of NE variation; at 5.45, 8° 29' 0" the same. At 6 took the bearing of a very conspicuous cape N 45° E and another, A, N 33° W, half a mile off. Between these two capes there is a large bight. Cape A lies in 38° 53' 30" of latitude and 144° 13' 50" of longitude. At 6 we hauled to the wind on the port tack. At 9 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; the wind a strong breeze, the weather overcast, with light rain. At midnight filled on the port tack, the land in sight to the NE.

1802-04-09.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from east to SE and NE. The Géographe's boat was put in the water with fifteen days' provisions under the orders of Citizen Saint-Cricq, lieutenant, and Boulanger, the surveyor, to determine the position of the promontory. At 9 p.m. went onto the starboard tack, lying to under the main topsail; the lead brought up 40 fathoms, rocky bottom. At 6 filled and made sail. At noon took the bearing of cape (B) N 41° E; Western Island N 46° W, about 10 miles off.
1802-04-09.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from N to S by way of east. At 3.30 hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 6 filled and stood on. At 7.30 Cape A bore from us east, 11 miles off. At noon in 38° 46' 0" of latitude observed and in 143° 55' 6" of longitude by account, a cape B bearing N 41° E and Western Island N 46° W, 10 miles off. At noon the large boat and the small boat were put in the water and provisioned for 10 days. At 1.45 they left under the orders of Citizen Milius, accompanied by Citizen Faure, surveyor, to survey Western Port. At 4.15, 9° 16' 0" of NE variation; at 5.15, 9° 14' 30" of variation; at 5.45, 38° 48' 19" of latitude observed. At 4 the promontory S 70° E, cape B N 55° E, Western Island from N 27° W to N 32° W, the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 61° W. At 5.30 the promontory S 75° E, Western Island N 14° W.

1802-04-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from ESE. The large boat and the small boat were put in the water, one under the orders of Citizen Milius, frigate captain, and the other under those of Citizen Brèvedent, midshipman; they left to survey Western Port. Western Island lies in 38° 35' 10" of latitude and 143° 21' 55" of longitude, by Citizen Saint-Cricq's observations. Cape A lies in 38° 53' 30" of latitude and 144° 13' 48" of east longitude.
1802-04-10.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from WNW to S, and calm. At 8.45, 8° 34' 50" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 58' 36" of latitude observed and in 143° 43' 12" of longitude by account. At 4 Western Island N 8° W, 14 miles off. At 4.30, 9° 54' 20" of NE variation. At 6, Western Island from N 6° W to N 15° W, 8 miles off.

1802-04-11.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to south and to the west. At 4 took the bearing of Western Island N 8° W, about 14 miles off. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind. At 4 hove to on the other tack; at 7 a.m. filled and stood on. At noon Western Island N 47° W; Cape Bon N 75° W.
1802-04-11.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from SSW to W. At half past midnight hove to; at 7 filled and stood on. At 7.30, 8° 6' 20" of NE variation. At 8, Western Island N 48° W. At noon in 38° 55' 26" of latitude observed and in 143° 50' 54" of longitude by account. Western Island N 27° W, cape B N 75° E. At 6, the middle of Western Island N 10° W, 9 miles off.

1802-04-12.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from SW to SSW and NW. At 6 took the bearing of the middle of Western Island N 10° W, about 9 miles off. At noon we had it bearing from N 2° E to N 7° W, 3 miles off.
1802-04-12.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, a light breeze from N to SSE by way of west. At 8, Western Island N 4° W, 9 miles off. At 10.30, 7° 24' 0" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 38' 20" of latitude observed and in 143° 35' 30" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 2° E to N 7° W, 3 miles off. At 4, cape B N 83° E, and Western Island from N 16° W to N 25° W. The Géographe's boat was sighted standing towards us; at 4.30 hove to. Citizen Saint-Cricq came in from his errand; the boat was hoisted in and at 5 we filled and stood on. At 6, Western Island from N 30° W to N 38° W and cape B N 86° E. During the night overcast and stormy weather.

1802-04-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At half past noon hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 3 filled with the winds south to SSE and SSW. The Géographe's boat was sighted; we hove to and at 4 she was hoisted in. At 2 a.m. hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 4 hove to on the other tack. At noon Western Island N 35° W, about 8 miles off.
1802-04-13.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SSE to SW. At 2 hove to; at 7.30 filled and stood on. At 8, Western Island from N 38° W to N 47° W and cape B S 88° E; hove to. At 10.15 filled and stood on. At noon in 38° 37' 20" of latitude by account and in 143° 37' 48" of longitude by account. Western Island N 35° W, 8 miles off. At 4 it bore N 45° W, 15 miles off, and at 6.15 N 38° W, 9 miles off.

1802-04-14.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a strong breeze from SSW to south and SW. We beat all night abreast of Western Port. At 4 hove to; at 6 filled and stood on. At noon took the bearing of Western Island from N 21° W to N 30° W, 3 miles off; Cape de la Roche N 89° E.
1802-04-14.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from S to SW. At 4 hove to and at 6 filled and stood on. At 8, 8° 8' 50" of NE variation. Cape B N 38° E and Western Island N 37° W, 12 miles off. At noon in 38° 37' 10" of latitude observed and in 143° 31' 54" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 21° W to N 30° W, 3 miles off, and cape B N 89° E; the breeze light. At 4 a flat calm, Western Island from N 38° W to N 43° W.

1802-04-15.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to SE by way of south. At 11.30 hove to on the port tack, Western Island from N 3° W to N 23° E, half a mile off.
1802-04-15.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the breeze light from SE to ENE. At 8, Western Island N 16° W, 9 miles off. At 9, 6° 19' of NE variation. At 11.30 hove to and at noon filled and stood on. At noon in 38° 34' 34" of latitude by account and in 143° 24' 42" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 3° W to N 23° E, half a mile off. At 4 the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 57° W, Western Island N 31° E, and cape B N 55° E. During the night the wind a strong breeze. Wilson's Promontory lies in 39° 10' 54" of latitude and 144° 37' 31" of longitude. Western Island lies in 38° 35' 10" of latitude and 143° 21' 55" of longitude.

1802-04-16.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SE to east and to NE by way of north. At noon filled and stood on. At noon took the bearing of Western Island N 7° E, 9 miles off; the western end of the mainland N 62° W.
1802-04-16.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from E to NE. At 8, Western Island N 6° E, 9 miles off. At 8.45, 6° 28' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 38° 44' 36" of latitude observed and in 143° 33' 48" of longitude by account. Western Island N 7° E, 9 miles off, and the westernmost end of the mainland in sight N 62° W. At 4, Western Island from N 11° W to N 24° W. At 4.30, 8° 1' 40" of NE variation.

1802-04-17.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth and the wind a strong breeze from east to NE and to NW by way of north. At 3 p.m. bore away for Western Island; at 5 lay close-hauled on the port tack. At noon took the bearing of Western Island from N 53° W to N 56° W. From the bearing of the promontory, which lay a mile north of us, I concluded its latitude to be 39° 10' 26".
1802-04-17.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NE to SW by way of north. At 8.30, 6° 26' of NE variation. At noon in 38° 42' 17" of latitude observed and in 143° 51' 24" of longitude by account. Western Island from N 53° W to N 56° W. At 3.30, having sighted our two boats, we hove to; at 4 the large one, with Citizen Milius, came in and was hoisted in at once. At 4, Western Island N 34° W, 9 miles off. At 5.15 the small boat came in and was hoisted in. At 6, Western Island N 43° W. At 8 we filled and stood on, the course S 45° E. The weather turned overcast with light rain; at midnight we hove to.

1802-04-18.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from WSW to SW. The two boats came in at 5.15 and were hoisted in at once. At midnight hove to with the starboard side to the wind; at 4.30 filled and wore onto the starboard tack, and shaped our course to leave the strait.
1802-04-18.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm, and a light breeze from SW to SSW. At 4 we filled and stood on, the land from N 22° E to S 79° E. At 8, cape A N 28° W, the promontory S 84° E, islet P S 70° E. At noon, cape A N 34° W, the promontory S 77°, 6 miles off, islet P S 68° E. By this bearing we were in 39° 8' 45" of latitude and 144° 30' 18" of longitude. At 6, cape A N 46° W, the white rock N 71° E, the 2 islets C S 86° E, islet P S 81° E, islet A S 57° E. At midnight the promontory N 85° E, 15 miles off.

1802-04-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a flat calm. At 1.30 the breeze got up from the SW. Made all sail. At 7 p.m. clewed up and furled the topgallant sails and struck the main topgallant mast to repair it. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the north, the promontory bearing N 85° E, 5 leagues off; we wore onto the port tack and passed between the islets and rocks of the promontory. At noon took the bearing of two rocks, one N 42° E, the other N 78° W, half a mile off; the promontory N [illegible], 9 miles off; the sugarloaf N 88° W; islet A S 25° E; rock D S 57° E; an island H N 70° E.
1802-04-19.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to NE. At 1.30 we hove to, and at 3 filled and stood on. At 4 the promontory N 68° E. At 5 shaped our course to double the promontory, hauling to the wind on the port tack. At 8, cape A N 46° W, the white rock N 78° E 1 mile off, the 2 islets C S 82°, islet P S 75° E and islet A S 56° E. At 8.55 the white rock bore abeam, true north, 3 cables off. At 9.50 the promontory bore abeam, true north, 1 mile off. We passed among the islets and rocks of the promontory, leaving to port the white rock, the islets C and rock M, and to starboard islet A, islet D, islet P and so on. At noon in 39° 14' 20" of latitude observed and in 144° 58' 0" of longitude by account, the promontory bearing N 63° W, the islets C one N 42° W and the other N 78° W, half a mile off, islet P N 88° W, islet A S 25° E, islet D S 75° E, and an island H N 70° E. At 4 took the bearing of the northernmost end of the mainland in sight N 76° W, the promontory N 76° W, islet P S 85° W and islet D S 16° E. At 4.30, 7° 26' 20" of NE variation. At 5.30 the promontory N 80° W, the middle of island H N 66° E, another island S 68° E. At 8 the wind drew round to the west, freshening; we shaped the course N 56° 15' E. At 10 the wind blowing hard in gusts, a high sea, with rain.

1802-04-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from NE to W, SW and NW. At 10 the wind blowing hard in gusts, the weather overcast and squally, a high sea, a great deal of rain. At 6 a.m. land was sighted to windward; at 8 it stretched from N 23° E to N 45° W. The wind still a strong breeze. At noon the land from N 22° W to N 70° E.
1802-04-20.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW to NW. At 6 the land was sighted; at 8 it stretched from N 22° E to N 45° E, and at noon from N 22° W to N 70° E. At noon in 37° 57' 40" of latitude observed and in 147° 9' 12" of longitude by account. At 4, Cape Howe N 32° E and the southernmost end of the mainland in sight S 76° E. At 5.30, Cape Howe N 20° E; the land in sight during the night.

1802-04-21.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a strong breeze from NW. At 4 took the bearing of Cape Howe N 32° E; the visible end of the land S 76° W. At 4.30 the weather cleared. At noon land in sight from N 45° W to S 61° W. At noon we found the same latitude, the same longitude and the same variation that Cook found. We were also at the same distance from the land and in the same month.
1802-04-21.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather with frequent squalls, the wind a strong breeze from NW to W, a high sea. At noon in 36° 18' 4" of latitude observed and in 148° 48' 42" of longitude by account. At 4, the Pigeon House N 18° W and Mount Dromedary S 54° W. During the night the wind blew hard. At 4.30 p.m., 9° 50' 50" of NE variation.

1802-04-22.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from SW to W and NW. At 4 a.m. Mount Dromedary bore from us S 54° W, the Pigeon House N 18° W. At 5.30 blowing hard from the west, a high sea. At 3.15 a.m. the wind having fallen a little, set the mizzen topsail. At daybreak the land as far as the eye could see in the west (from aloft); at 5 it stretched from W to N 45° W. At 11 went onto the starboard tack.
1802-04-22.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a strong breeze from W to NNW. At daybreak the land was sighted as far as the eye could reach to the west. At 8.15, 10° 6' 20" of NE variation. At noon in 34° 28' 38" of latitude observed and in 149° 44' 0" of longitude by account. At 5.45, Cape St George S 80° W.

1802-04-23.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a strong breeze from NW to NNW. At 5 p.m. Cape St George S 82° W. At 8 wore onto the starboard tack. Furled the main topgallant sail and clewed up the main topsail to repair it. At noon the land in sight from S 15° W to N 45° W.
1802-04-23.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from NNW to W. At noon in 35° 11' 26" of latitude observed and in 148° 41' 42" of longitude by account.
