The land from N 34° W to S 45° W. At 8 a.m., 10° 40' 10" of NE variation. At 3.15 we had a heavy squall from the west. During the night squally weather, the wind a strong breeze. The land has been in sight throughout.

1802-04-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea; went about onto the starboard tack. A strong breeze from SW to W and SSW. At 4.30 the middle of the entrance to Port Jackson S 73° W. At 5 p.m. we heard a salute of 9 guns fired; we supposed it was in honour of St George's day. At 7.30 p.m. the weather turned overcast and the wind blew hard; we stayed under our courses. At 6.30 hove to and put the large boat in the water; Mr Milius was about to embark in her to go up to Port Jackson, but rain came on and the boat was veered astern. At 8 a.m., having seen a boat standing towards us, we hove to; the pilot came aboard and we at once beat to windward. At 11.45, under North Head, having missed stays, we wore ship; in this last movement our large boat, which was in tow, capsized and the painter parted. Our small boat, together with the English boat, was sent to save the boat's crew and to take the swamped boat in tow to carry her ashore.
1802-04-24.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, the wind a fresh breeze from W to SSW. At 11 we showed our colours and the flag of truce. At noon in 33° 47' 23" of latitude observed and in 148° 50' 36" of longitude by account. Signals were seen on the south point of the entrance to Port Jackson, which bore from us S 65° W to S 68° W, and the land from N 26° W to S 56° W. At 4 the entrance to Port Jackson S 73° W, and at 5.30 N 62° W. We heard a salute of 9 guns fired; we thought it was in honour of King George's birthday. At nightfall a fire was lit at the entrance to Port Jackson; at 6 it bore from us S 59° W, at 8 S 54° W, at 10 S 85° W, at midnight N 79° W. During the night the wind blew hard, the weather overcast, with rain and thunder.

1802-04-25.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from WSW to SSE. At 6.15 we hove to and put the large boat in the water. Citizen Milius and I were to embark in her to go to Sydney and inform the English governor of our arrival and the object of our voyage; but the weather appeared so bad to Citizen Milius that the boat was veered astern. At 8, having sighted a boat standing towards us, we hove to to wait for her. At 8.15 she came aboard and brought us an English pilot; he at once made sail to gain the port. At 9 a swivel gun was fired to confirm our colours. At 11.45, under North Head, we missed stays and wore ship. In this last movement the large boat (which was in tow and under sail) capsized and her tow rope parted. The pilot's boat and our small boat at once went to save the boat's crew and to take the boat in tow and beach her. At 3.30 we anchored at the entrance to the port in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, North Head bearing N 67° E, South Head S 52° E, Camp Cove S 16° E, Bradleys Head S 36° W and Middle Head N 65° W. At 4.45 Citizen Milius and I left in the Géographe's boat for Sydney. Squally and very overcast weather, with pouring rain, the wind from WSW to SW.

1802-04-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SW to SSE. At 1.45, the wind having drawn aft, we bore away for the entrance to the port and shortened sail by degrees. At 3.30, having doubled South Head very close, we let go the anchor at the mouth of the channel in 10 fathoms, sandy bottom, and veered 60 fathoms of cable, South Head bearing S 52° E; Camp Cove S 16° E; Bradleys Head S 36° W; Georges Head S 48° W; Middle Head N 65° W; North Head N 67° E by compass. As soon as the sails were furled, the Géographe's large boat was put in the water and left for Sydney Town; the wind a strong breeze, squally weather and rain. At anchor at the entrance to Port Jackson.
1802-04-26.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, the wind a strong breeze from SW. A meal of provisions was sent to the crews of the large and small boats by a fishing boat. The governor sent vegetables. I came back aboard with an English officer to invite the captain to dine with Colonel Paterson, the lieutenant-governor (Governor King was at Parramatta); he excused himself on account of the bad weather, and I went back to Sydney with the officer. The topgallant masts were got down. An orderly brought the captain a letter announcing the governor's arrival at Sydney. At nightfall a small fishing boat brought Citizen Moreau, who had been in the small boat. He had been obliged to have the small boat in which he came carried by hand from the beach where the boats lay to the inside of the harbour. He asked the captain to send provisions to the boats' crews, who were without; and this contemptible man, who counts every mouthful of his crew's food and would feed them on grass if he could, ordered that only one meal be sent them, saying that if more were sent the rogues would not come back aboard and would rather stay ashore idling. Citizen Moreau observed to him that it was impossible for the boats to come back with him in them, that they had tried several times to return aboard and had always been forced to put back on account of the sea and the wind; that the wretched boats' crews, who had had only one meal since the morning before, would have died of hunger had not one of the English boatmen lent him money to buy them a little fish; that they were soaked and had neither shelter nor a change of clothes; that one of them was injured; and that they would therefore be better aboard if they could get there. None of these truths made any impression on this hard and barbarous man: only one meal of provisions was sent to the boats' crews.

1802-04-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the winds a strong breeze from south to SSW. Almost continual rain. At 3 a [boat] came aboard to invite the captain, on Colonel Paterson's behalf, to dine with him; but the bad weather prevented him from accepting the invitation. The topgallant masts were struck and the topmasts got down. An orderly brought packets to the captain to announce the governor's arrival at Sydney Town (he was in the country when we arrived at Port Jackson). A fishing boat brought me back on board.
1802-04-27.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast weather, the wind a fresh breeze from SW to south, with continual rain. The longboat was put in the water. Citizen Milius and I came back aboard. A warp was run out.

1802-04-28.journal_anonyme: A fresh breeze from south to SSW and SW, continual rain. At 3 our boat left for Sydney Town. We ran out a warp and hove round on the cable, but the wind having freshened we left off the work with 45 fathoms of cable out. At 5 a.m. weighed the bower anchor and hove round on the hawser; being at long stay we let go the bower anchor. The captain embarked in his boat with the officers and scientists to go and pay a visit to the governor. At 11.30 our large and small boats came aboard undamaged; only a seaman named Happeday had his shoulder crushed in the wreck of the large boat.
1802-04-28.journal_breton_naturaliste: Overcast and rainy weather, a light breeze from SSW to WSW. The governor sent us vegetables. At 7 the captain, accompanied by the officers and naturalists, went to pay a visit to the governor; they were back at 2. At 11.30 a.m. our two boats came in. Only one man, Happedey, had a dislocated shoulder. From 5 a.m. until 4 p.m. we warped.

1802-04-29.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a light breeze from SSW, SW and WSW, with light rain until 4. At 1 weighed the bower anchor and hove round on the hawser. At 2 the captain and all those with him came back from Sydney Town. At 4 weighed the kedge anchor and let go the bower, which proved to be foul, and hove round on the hawser. When we were at long stay on the hawser we ran out a warp and catted the bower anchor. At 9.15 weighed the kedge anchor, on which we were up and down, and hove round on the warp. A sloop bound for Tahiti sailed from Port Jackson.
1802-04-29.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather, calm. We warped from 4 a.m. until 9.30. The Nautilus, a private vessel fitted out as a letter of marque and bound for Tahiti, left the port. At noon Captain Scott of the sloop Porpoise came to announce the governor's visit. At 1 the sloop Lady Nelson, carrying the governor and his suite, passed under our stern. We saluted her with three cheers of "Long live the Republic". The governor and the civil and military officers of Sydney came aboard, where they stayed until 2. The captain, the officers and the naturalists went to Sydney to the dinner given by the governor. We warped as soon as they had left. At 3.15, being under Bradleys Point, we got under way with a light breeze from NNW. At 5 we anchored in 11 fathoms, muddy bottom, and at once moored NNW and SSE with a kedge anchor, in Neutral Bay, near Rock Island.

1802-04-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm at noon. Captain Scott, commanding the sloop Porpoise, came to announce the governor's visit. At 1 the brig Lady Nelson, carrying the governor and his suite, passed under our stern; he was greeted with three cheers of "Long live the Republic". He came aboard at once with the civil and military officers of Sydney Town. He left at 2 and was followed by the captain and his officers. At 2.30 ran out a warp; the kedge anchor was weighed at once and, the tide carrying us in, towed by the longboat and the large boat, a light air came on and we set our fore-and-aft sails. At 5 we let go the anchor in 11 fathoms, muddy bottom, and veered 40 fathoms of cable. The longboat carried out a kedge anchor and we moored NNW and SSE with 90 fathoms of cable out.
1802-04-30.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. At 2.30 a.m. the captain, the officers and the naturalists came aboard. The mainsail and main topsail, which needed repair, were unbent. The longboat made one trip for water. A large English three-master came in, loaded with whale oil.

1802-05-01.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm; hoisted in our large boat. At 4 a three-master came into the port from the whale fishery. The longboat went watering.
1802-05-01.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. The sick were sent to the hospital at Sydney. The longboat made two trips for water. A notice was read to the crew by which Captain Hamelin warns the inhabitants of the colony that he will not be answerable for debts contracted by his crew. During the night the wind a light breeze from SSW to WSW. The establishment of the port at Sydney Cove is 8 o'clock; the tide rises there 7 feet 6 English inches.

1802-05-02.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, calm. The longboat went for water and wood; the sick were carried to the hospital; the cables were got out of the hold to come at the bar iron. During our stay at Port Jackson we watered, fresh provisions were embarked and we got wood. On the 13th [Floréal, Year 10, 3 May 1802] tents were set up ashore for the observatory. A Frenchman authorised by the governor was shipped aboard and came on board. At 5.30 p.m. on the 19th [Floréal, Year 10, 9 May 1802] the ship Investigator came into the port, having left England 10 months before and coming from the SW coast, where she had met the Géographe in 35° 41' south and 126° 49' east longitude. On the 20th [Floréal, Year 10, 10 May 1802] at 5 an English longboat brought us an anchor. At 7 a.m. on the 21st [Floréal, Year 10, 11 May 1802] an English ship brought the news of the preliminaries of peace. The winds were constantly from WNW to WSW and sometimes from the east. We embarked as provisions [one word illegible], potatoes, [one word illegible] and wheat [two words illegible]. At 7 we made ready to get under way. At 10.15 we were under sail.
1802-05-02.journal_breton_naturaliste: Fine weather and calm. The longboat made one trip for water. An observatory was set up on Green Point.

1802-05-19.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a light breeze from WSW, SSW and south; the wind came on to blow hard. At daybreak a man not belonging to the crew was found; he said he was an English soldier and had come aboard by swimming during the night of the 27th to the 28th [Floréal, Year 10, 17-18 May 1802].

1802-05-20.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a strong breeze from south, SE, W and NW. At noon the land from N 28° W to S 48° W.

1802-05-21.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sky cloudy, a light breeze from W to S and SE. At daybreak sighted the land; at noon it stretched from N 29° W to S 51° W.

1802-05-22.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from SE to S by E. At 12.15 went onto the starboard tack. At 10 a.m. changed tacks.

1802-05-23.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze from SE. The sea smooth. At 6 p.m. went onto the starboard tack; at 6 a.m. onto the port tack.

1802-05-24.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, the sea smooth enough, a fresh breeze from SE to south and SSW. At 8 wore onto the starboard tack. The wind freshened steadily and blew hard, with a high sea. At midnight took all the reefs in the main topsail; the fore topsail split while we were taking in the reefs. During the night the port cathead was carried away by a sea. The fore topsail was repaired and the port cathead was made good.

1802-05-25.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a fresh breeze from south to SSW. A high sea. Continual rain. At 6 wore onto the port tack; at 9.45 wore onto the starboard tack; at 11 set the mizzen topsail.

1802-05-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a swell running, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW. Shook out the reefs of the topsails. At 10 a light breeze got up from N by E; rigged out the studdingsails to starboard.

1802-05-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast and misty weather, a swell running, a light breeze from NW, from south to SW.

1802-05-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea smooth, the wind a fresh breeze from SSW to WSW. The wind having freshened, we took all the reefs in the topsails. At 4 a.m. the weather cleared; at 10 overcast weather, a fresh breeze in gusts.

1802-05-29.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind a strong breeze in gusts from SW. At daybreak the port cathead was found carried away and was repaired at once. At 10 the wind a light breeze, the weather fine, the sea rather high.

1802-05-30.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, the sea rather high, a light breeze from SW to NW by way of west. At 6.30 a.m. wore onto the starboard tack.

1802-05-31.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea [one word erased, illegible], a light breeze from NW to W and SW. At 6 p.m. went onto the port tack.

1802-06-01.journal_anonyme: The weather fine enough, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW to south and SW. At 6 and 9 a.m. changed tacks.

1802-06-02.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SSW, almost calm. At 4 a flat calm. At 9.30 the breeze got up from the ENE; rigged out the studdingsails and made all sail. Shook out all the reefs.

1802-06-03.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a strong breeze from NE to east and ESE. At 8 a.m. took in the studdingsails and lowered the main jib to half mast.

1802-06-04.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a strong breeze, a high sea. At 3.30 shaped our course S 56° 15' W. From SE to SSE.

1802-06-05.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running; the wind, at first a strong breeze, fell away as it hauled from south to SW. At noon the course was set S 78° 45' W.

1802-06-06.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a swell running, a fresh breeze from W to SW. At 12.15 wore onto the starboard tack. At 8 blowing hard in gusts. A very high sea.

1802-06-07.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the wind a light breeze from WSW to W and NW. At 8 went about onto the starboard tack. In the forenoon Mabulot, gunner, received 15 lashes with a rope's end for striking the second gunner's mate. On the evening of the 17th the rations were reduced as is known. For breakfast 6 ounces of boiled wheat were served, and for dinner half a pound of bread, 6 ounces of beef and four ounces of salt pork. This measure did not take effect until the morning of the 18th.

1802-06-08.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea and the wind a fresh breeze from NW to NNW. The wind freshened steadily; by midnight it was blowing hard. The fore staysail halliard parted and the main topsail split.

1802-06-09.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, the wind blowing hard, a high sea, from W to WSW and WNW. In the gusts the [one word illegible] of the mainsail parted, and for all the speed with which it was clewed up, the sail was torn from its bolt-rope; we unbent it at once. At 1 the captain held a council on what remained for us to do in the situation we were in: there were only 37 days' provisions left on board, and could we hope to reach Mauritius in 74 days on half rations? It was decided to put back to Port Jackson. After taking the second reef in the main topsail we wore onto the starboard tack and headed N 67° 30' E.

1802-06-10.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, a swell running, a light breeze from WSW and south. A new mainsail was bent.

1802-06-11.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, light rain, the sea smooth, a light breeze from SW to east and NE. At 8.30 a.m. went onto the starboard tack.

1802-06-12.journal_anonyme: The weather, overcast at first, cleared; the sea smooth. A light breeze from ESE to SE.

1802-06-13.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a light breeze from east. At 5.45 went onto the port tack. At 8.30 a.m. onto the starboard tack.

1802-06-14.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SE. At 8.30 p.m. and at 2 a.m. changed tacks.

1802-06-15.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea smooth, a light breeze from east to SE. In the forenoon it freshened and blew in gusts.

1802-06-16.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea and the wind a strong breeze from SE to SSE. At 6 p.m. and at 6 a.m. changed tacks.

1802-06-17.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SSE to south. At 4 sighted Van Diemen's Land in the east. At 4.45 p.m. and at 4.30 a.m. changed tacks.

1802-06-18.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from SE. At 5 p.m. changed tacks; at 2 a.m. the same.

1802-06-19.journal_anonyme: Overcast and squally weather, a swell running, a light breeze from south, SW and SSE. At 3 Van Diemen's Land was sighted; it stretched from north to N 22° 30' E. At 4.15 p.m. and at 8.30 changed tacks.

1802-06-20.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky cloudy, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SSW, south and SW. At noon the course was set N 67° E. At 6.30 land was sighted in various quarters from N 67° 30' W as far as S 67° 30' W. At 8 it stretched from N 64° W to S 85° W. At noon took the bearing of Maria Island N 86° W.

1802-06-21.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth. A fresh breeze from W to WNW. At noon the course was set N 11° 15' W. At 4 took the bearing of the middle of Maria Island S 65° W and the high land of the Schouten islands and peninsulas from S 80° W to N 77° W. At daybreak the land was sighted a long way off from the crosstrees; it stretched from N 34° W to S 22° W. At noon in sight in the west at a very great distance.

1802-06-22.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from W to WSW and SW. At 8 p.m. it freshened and blew in gusts. At 6 a.m. the land in sight in the NW. At 8 it stretched as far as N 15° 15' E. The course was given north and then N 11° 15' E. At noon the land from N 15° W to S 44° W.

1802-06-23.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from SW. At 4 the land from N 16° W to S 4° W. At 6.30 saw a fire abeam. At 8 a.m. the land from N 20° W to S 21° W. At noon took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 5° W, the Pigeon House S 86°, and the end of the land S 39° W. Almost calm. The corvette was painted.

1802-06-24.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, almost calm. At 3 a light air from the north drew round at once to the east and we wore onto the port tack. At 4 took the bearing of Long Nose Point N 6° W, the middle of Jervis Bay N 18° W, the Pigeon House S 67° W, the southernmost visible end of the land S 27° W. At 2 a.m. wore onto the starboard tack. The wind drew round to the north and freshened. At 9.15 a.m. sighted a ship abeam standing on the opposite tack. The cables were bent. Obs. lat. 34° 59' 27"; est. long. 148° 38' 42".

1802-06-25.journal_anonyme: The weather fine, the sky overcast, the sea smooth, a fresh breeze from north. At 2 p.m. and at 6.15 p.m. changed tacks; at 2 a.m. the same. At 11 very high land was sighted from N 56° W to W. Obs. lat. 34° 20' 22"; est. long. 148° 16' 36". Var. 13° 13' 20" NE.

1802-06-26.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, the sea rather high, a strong breeze from N, NW, SW and south. At 1, at 6 and at 9 changed tacks. At 2 a.m., at 5 and at 9 changed tacks. At 8 the land in sight but very hazy. Est. lat. 34° 1' 28"; est. long. 148° 27' 30".

1802-06-27.journal_anonyme: Overcast weather, a high sea, a strong breeze from south to SSE and SE. At 4 and at 8 p.m. changed tacks; at 1.30 the same. At 7 sighted the land from N 45° W to S 45° W. Got the port anchor ready to let go. At 10.15 hove to with the main topsail to the wind, the land at a short distance. Obs. lat. 34° 23' 33"; est. long. 148° 15' 12".

1802-06-28.journal_anonyme: Fine weather, smooth sea, a fresh breeze from south, SE and ESE. At noon filled and stood in to close the land; after coming very near it we ran along it at a mile's distance. At 5 p.m., being off the mouth of Port Jackson, we lay close-hauled on the starboard tack, the lighthouse light bearing S 85° W. At 9 went onto the port tack. At 4 a.m. hove to; at 8 filled and stood on. At 9.30 a.m. we shaped our course to run into the port, and at 11.30 we anchored between Middle Head and South Head. Lat. 34° 3' 9"; long. 148° 26' 12". The latitude determined at the observatory was 33° 51' 10" and the longitude 149° 5'. Var. 9° 40' 0" NE. We found the commander there, arrived 10 days before; he had three quarters of his crew in hospital. The captain went aboard the commander and from there ashore, which was his place of residence.

1802-11-18.journal_anonyme: On the 26th Brumaire we lay anchored at the mouth of the port, where we had anchored. At 4.30 we hoisted our topsails and got under way, as did the commander. At 6.30, being outside the heads, the pilot left us and we steered out to sea. The winds south to S by W, a strong breeze. At 12.10 the commander made the signal to change tacks, which we did at once. Lat. 34° 1' 24"; long. 149° 19' 30".

1802-11-19.journal_anonyme: The weather overcast, a high sea and a strong breeze from south to SSE and SE. At 3 changed tacks; at 8 hoisted a light at the gaff which we kept all the watch. At 4.25 and 5.30 changed tacks. We were at first standing in to close the commander; at 7.50, he having gone about, we did the same. The land in sight from W to SW. Obs. lat. 34° 20'; long. 149° 54' 30".

1802-11-20.journal_anonyme: Cloudy weather, the sea less swelly, a fresh breeze from east to NE and north. At 3 passed under the Géographe's stern; she ordered us to steer south. At 4 and at 5 laid the mizzen topsail to the mast to wait for the Géographe and the Casuarina. At 6 sighted a sail in the SW; at 7 she was made out to be a schooner. The Géographe hove to and sent a boat aboard her, the distance from the land about six leagues. Obs. lat. 36° 3'; long. 149° 43' 58".
